improve its economic cohesion and development by liberalizing or privatising policies, by deregulating labour which makes employment precarious and by reducing levels of social protection or by tax reforms which reduce the adequacy and progressivity of tax systems. the international economic situation, mr aznar, also calls for imagination and flexibility. we do not think it is appropriate to face it with a rigorous and excessively restrictive conception of the stability pact. the near recession that the world economy is going through is not very questionable today, mr. aznar. the european union needs political impetus and democratization in economic decision-making. we need budgets geared to employment and economic and social cohesion. the stability pact must be made more flexible and at least preserve public investment in the event of excessive deficits, as a necessary element for the future development of the union and, also in the short term, as a factor that stimulates and multiplies economic activity. it is essential to complete the single currency with a process of harmonization in the fiscal, labour and social fields, by building a genuine economic policy - not just monetary - and by making strong progress in the social europe of the community. finally, mr aznar, we are concerned that there is no attempt to promote public services from a social point of view in the european construction. many reforms are in the making, and in our european countries, strategic sectors with public monopolies are often converted into private oligopolies, making public control of them more difficult and without this actually improving their effectiveness. i could give you examples from different countries on the situation of rail transport, on sanitation systems or on electricity supplies. the european council in barcelona, in the context of the european council in madrid, has been a very positive and positive step towards the creation of a european social area. agreement, mr aznar, must be concluded this semester, as the spanish presidency has said and i agree with it. otherwise, enlargement will not be possible in 2004. in this connection, mr aznar, i would like to make the following observation: a union of 27 - with enlargement to 10 states - will increase the area of the european union by 34%, increase the population by more than 28%, but the community income will increase by only 5%. does the political challenge of enlargement be understood? does the commission understand the potential for social problems to be exacerbated by enlargement? in the european union, 16% of the population now live on an income per head 90% below the community average, and in the union of 27 states, for example, this proportion would rise to 34%. we therefore believe that for the first time - unlike the so-called delors packages, where in successive enlargements of the internal market there were firm commitments to decisive increases in economic and social cohesion - we are now in a situation where economic and social cohesion - as expressed in the delors packages - must be absolutely strengthened and increased. we would therefore like an unambiguous signal in this respect. the agricultural negotiations may end with the application of a transitional period to allow the passage of the 2006 budget. the problem will be what to do next. agriculture, like any other economic activity, requires prospects and the negotiations should be accompanied by clear signals on the future of agricultural policy, where we will surely hear some calling for the dismantling of common policies in the name of budgetary savings. we are not going to be able to do that, because we are not going to be able to do it in the future. the question of the structural funds puts the future political design of the european union in the foreground - as i did when i referred to the delors packages. a larger european union will require greater efforts to increase economic and social cohesion between regions. we must build an area of freedom, justice and security for citizens, with full respect for the democratic traditions of our countries and for the fundamental human rights recognized in our charter. there is no place for terrorism in this space. terrorism is our enemy, but there must also be no room for laws and repressive measures which have nothing to do with this fight and which contribute to reducing the legal and judicial guarantees of citizens. the construction of this area of freedom must also be the occasion for achieving a very high level of harmonization of legal guarantees. in the field of foreign, security and defence policy, mr president-in-office of the council, i shall make a few very specific references for the sake of brevity. the spanish presidency has the responsibility to ensure that the european union and the european parliament, in collaboration with the spanish presidency, take a decisive step in the search for a just solution to the middle east. we believe that it must be very clear that the decisions of the united nations and international law must be respected and that the illegal and military occupation of the palestinian state by israel must cease. the intention to continue improving the currently stalled barcelona process is to be welcomed. the countries of the southern mediterranean need to be genuinely integrated into the region. the development of the region cannot be based exclusively on aid or trade concessions from the european union, individually with each of the mediterranean countries. more europe means playing our part in regional stabilisation and promoting economic development in our neighbourhood. the creation of the euro-mediterranean development bank self-determination, as agreed by the united nations. the position taken by the spanish government on this issue, which is faithful to spain's responsibility towards the saharawi people and respectful of international law, is commendable. it is with latin america that the spanish presidency must make greater efforts, precisely at crucial moments, such as the acute crisis in colombia or the collapse of the economy in argentina. the european parliament unanimously voted in favour of a negotiated solution to the long-running conflict in colombia, rejecting the us military approach to the same issue commission. – mr president, i wish to thank the rapporteur, mr zappalà, for the considerable amount of work he had done on this most complicated and important issue, as many members have said this afternoon. in may 2000, the commission adopted two proposed directives designed to simplify and modernise community public procurement rules. those proposals contain significant new developments to adapt the directives to modern procurement requirements. in the interest of simplification, the commission has proposed a recasting of four existing directives merged into two new ones. i note that parliament has taken advantage of this recasting of the four directives to question the community acquis in areas where the commission has not proposed any changes. i refer here in particular to the amendments raising the thresholds, which will significantly reduce the directives' scope, above all – may i say to mrs mccarthy – with respect to small and medium enterprises. if those proposals were to be adopted, the commission would have to give serious thought as to whether the proposal should be retained at all. many of the amendments put forward will help make an important contribution to better procurement and are to be welcomed. the commission supports those amendments which add to the simplification and modernisation process. they are amendments: nos 1, 3, 167, 141, 4, 13, 16, 17, 24, 28, 34, 36, 174, 40, 50, 128, 53, 79, 80, 85, 88, 97, 109 – to the extent that it concerns production processes – and 112. the commission can also accept the substance of a number of amendments, subject to some drafting changes, namely amendments nos 2, 10, 42 in part, 45, 46, 47, 123, 52 in part, 93 and 95 in part, 109, 110 and 154 concerning the extent to which environmental considerations can be taken into account at different stages of an award procedure. similarly, amendments nos 11, 15, 48 in part, 51, 129, 52, 86, 87, 124, 89, 100 in part, 110 and 164 concerning the need to ensure that tenderers comply with employment law, can be included in the directive in an appropriate form. that is also partially the case for amendment no 163 concerning information on sub-contracting. integrity and confidentiality of data supplied by operators. concerning confidentiality of data, part of amendment no 31 can be accepted, though amendment no 77 would then be superfluous and would have to be rejected. various amendments concerning the competitive dialogue, in particular as regards payment of participants, can be taken into account, more specifically amendments nos 9, 56, 57 in part, 58 in part, 137 in part, and 138. various amendments which i would describe as explanatory and which deal with a range of subjects are also acceptable, namely amendments nos 7, 125 in part, 18, 142, 26, 30, 35, 46 in part, 70, 113, 114, 121, 132, 153, 169, 170 and 171. subject to drafting changes, the substance of amendment no 147 concerning the applicability of the treaty below the thresholds is also acceptable, if placed in a recital. on the other hand, the commission has no alternative but to reject amendments which call into question the community acquis, detract from modernisation of the directives or make the regime more complex. accordingly, the commission cannot accept the following amendments: amendments to raise the directives' thresholds – as i said earlier – by 50%, the effect of which would be to remove from the scope of the directives a large number of contracts currently covered, namely amendments nos 32, 33, 67, 130, 101, 105 and 106. the unfortunate consequences of these amendments are not alleviated by amendment no 147, however good its intentions. in fact, the raison d'être of the directives is not in itself sufficient without the detailed procedural rules of the directives to guarantee uniform and legally certain application and to safeguard the rights of economic operators through efficient remedies. amendments introducing new exceptions to the scope of the directives without appropriate justification, the effect of which would be to remove a number of public contracts from community competition, namely amendments nos 37, 38 in part, 122, 136, 150 and 157. amendments which undermine the very objective of public procurement rules, which is to ensure that public purchasers do not allow their decision to be influenced by non-economic considerations, namely amendments nos 12, 14, 98, 134, 140 and 166 concerning award criteria which allow for the possibility of using non-economic – and in particular social and environmental – criteria. amendments which weaken attempts to modernise the directives by reducing the scope for using electronic procurement, namely amendments nos 70 in part, 73, 75, 102, 103, 115, 117 and 131. amendments imposing disproportionate requirements on smes through the regulation of subcontracting and other requirements, namely amendments 42, 48 in part, 49, 76, 100 in part, 116, 133, 152 and 159. amendments which reduce transparency in calls for competition, in particular amendments nos 62, 68 and 78, and which extend the scope to negotiate, namely amendments nos 57, part of 61, 66 and 151. amendments which restrict the use of framework agreements with no apparent justification, namely amendments nos 25, 27, 135, 139, 63, 64 and 158. amendments introducing environmental considerations into award procedures in a manner incompatible with the directives, namely the part of amendment no 45 concerning eco-labels, no 92 concerning the selection stage and no 109 regarding the definition of technical specifications and their compatibility with the environment. amendments which are not compatible with the flexible nature of the competitive dialogue, in particular amendments nos 55, 58 in part, 59, 60 and 160. amendments containing additional cases where persons convicted of certain offences would face mandatory exclusion; in the proposed mechanism, only those cases subject to criminal sanctions in all member states should be included. it is not, therefore, possible to take account of some of these cases, namely amendments nos 81, 82 and 83. on the other hand, some of these cases are already covered by the optional exclusions contained in article 46(2). amendments nos 84 and 90 should also be rejected, since they could lead to a situation where it is not possible to contract with a company which is trying to re-establish itself financially. amendments which are superfluous or likely significantly to change the effect of other provisions in the commission. – may i suggest that i try to briefly answer the various questions that have been put and if you think i am speaking too long, please tell me so.

commission. – in reply to mr zappalà, i should like to say that the current definition of works contracts explicitly provides that such contracts may be for the sole construction or cover of both design and construction. to change that approach would in particular prevent or, at the very least, greatly hamper use of turnkey projects, public/private partnerships, works concessions and competitive dialogues. the commission is, therefore, opposed to imposing a separation between the design and the execution of works. in reply to mrs schörling, the commission has proposed including as possible award criterion the environmental characteristics of a product or service, provided that they present an advantage to the contracting authority. that criterion allows a public purchaser to evaluate the intrinsic qualities of the product or service and to award contracts to the most economically advantageous tender. the proposed amendments go further, in allowing more general environmental considerations such as the long-term effects on the environment of the products or services purchased to be taken into account at the award stage. such considerations are not measurable; they cannot assist in an evaluation of the intrinsic qualities of the product or services and are therefore inappropriate at the award stage. in reply to mr rapkay and mr hughes, the purpose of the public procurement directives is to coordinate the procedures for the award of contracts and not to state which obligations – social or otherwise – private contractors must comply with once a contract is awarded. contractors are in any event required to comply with all applicable laws and obligations, whether social in nature or not. however, the commission is willing to state in the recitals of the directives that tenderers must comply with applicable social rules, including collective agreements of general application in performing public procurement contracts. the commission also agrees that contracting authorities should be required to state in the contract documents the body from which information on applicable social obligations can be obtained. in reply to mrs hautala, i should like to say that regarding the preliminary reference currently before the court of justice, the commission has taken note of the conclusions of the advocate-general. however, those conclusions cannot prejudge the judgment itself. in addition, having regard to the content of the communication on the environment and public contracts, the commission – as it explained at the time of the court hearing – does not see an obstacle to the emissions criterion being taken into account where this involves – as the case of the city of helsinki has shown – an external cost to the purchaser itself. the commission will, therefore, wait for the court's ruling and reconsider interpretation in the light of the judgment and, if necessary, will consider revising its position on the amendments from the european parliament. i should like to reply to mr lehne but, as he has left the chamber, i shall skip that part of my reply.
commission. – mr president, the commission is always pleased to assist members of parliament in forming their opinions. may i therefore say that if mr lehne had been present i would have said the following – and i am, of course, willing say it even though mr lehne is not here. mr lehne stated that social and environmental clauses must be introduced in the tender documents themselves and should not influence the choice at the award stage. therefore, i would support his view that article 53 on award criteria should not be modified. such considerations may be taken into account at the appropriate stage, either in the tender documents or in the contractual clauses. i cannot support amendment no 147 by mr zappalà, since it will not provide any legal certainty to economic operators. may i end my reply to parliament here and conclude by saying that there is now a real need to ensure that our public procurement rules remain relevant to increasingly sophisticated procurement requirements. that is why parliament and the council must now press ahead to ensure that these directives are adopted at the earliest opportunity. mr president, i am sorry for having spoken for fully half an hour, but i feel that parliament is entitled to a complete response to the many amendments tabled. the commission awaits the vote tomorrow.
commission. – mr president, i shall try to be brief. until 1971 the only rules and principles applicable to public procurement were those enshrined in the treaty itself, and in particular the provisions of articles 28 and 49. however, experience has shown that the genuine opening up of markets and the creation of a real and efficient internal market required that those rules and principles be clarified through detailed provisions coordinating national procedures. to revert to the legal situation of the 1970s – and this would be the result of the proposal just made and enshrined in amendment no 147 – is not acceptable, especially in a proposal aimed at modernising the legislation. moreover, to do so would also deprive economic operators of one of the most important advances in the field of public procurement, namely the possibility of enforcing their rights through efficient legal remedies guaranteed through the two specific directives which govern remedies in respect of contracts falling within the scope of the public procurement directives. therefore, the introduction of amendment no 147 simply does not make the amendments aimed at raising thresholds throughout the directive acceptable.

- the next item is the report (a4-0454/2001) by mr davies, on the joint text approved by the conciliation committee for a european parliament and council directive on ozone in ambient air (pe-cons 3658/2001 - c5-0524/2001 - 1999/0068 (cod)).
- mr president, the directive on ozone in ambient air is intended to deal with the problem of tropospheric ozone produced and trapped in the air near the earth's surface, which, as we all know, has harmful effects on human health, vegetation, ecosystems and the environment as a whole. the concentration of ozone - we know - is due to the accumulation in the atmosphere of precursors, but their eradication is of course not an easy solution, since these precursors sometimes act as ozone reducers in the atmosphere. various national measurements have shown that, under climatic conditions such as high light and a stable atmosphere, reduction of precursor agents does not produce the desired effect of decreasing ozone concentration, but quite the opposite. so the solution to the ozone problem is really complex. the simple closure of sources of precursors, such as the chimney of a factory that emits fumes, which are precursors of ozone, into the atmosphere, is not an appropriate measure. the rapporteur and several members of the committee on the environment, including myself, have worked hard for almost two years to improve the commission's proposal - which is certainly necessary - but also to arrive at a balanced proposal which would allow the member states to comply as much as possible. and finally, last october, a joint text was reached which was approved by the conciliation committee. i would like to highlight, as a very positive aspect of the proposal that has been adopted, the combination of long-term objectives with the short-term treatment of risk situations, as well as all the measures aimed at rigorous monitoring and monitoring of ozone levels in the atmosphere in all the member states. i also think it is important to apply the principle of transparency of information, since the public must be better and more informed about the impact of ozone levels in the atmosphere. another important aspect is the consideration of weather conditions and the comparison between the different member states, which should indeed provide data to see how this problem is evolving in the different member states. this directive is an important step in the right direction towards an integrated approach to the problem of pollution and, together with the directive on national emission ceilings, we believe that they will be really very important tools for dealing with environmental problems and, in particular, pollution problems in a horizontal way.
the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. i am of course very pleased that we are now approaching the time when we can adopt the directive on ozone in the air. thanks to this directive we will be able to protect vegetation and human health from the harmful effects of excessive ozone concentrations, except where this cannot be achieved by proportionate measures. i therefore warmly welcome the conciliation committee's joint draft of 11 november 2001. as already noted, the directive has been improved in essential respects during the process from the common position to a final directive. it has become clearer and more consistent, thanks to the high quality of the european parliament's proposals and the successful negotiations during the conciliation. i simply want to take this opportunity to thank in particular the rapporteur, mr chris davies, and all the members of the conciliation committee.

- mr president, i am pleased to say that in this second reading the parties have worked to bring their positions closer together. and if the council and the commission have already made an effort to accept the many amendments at our first reading, i think we can now say that the effort to find positions and converge on common positions has been made by parliament. in that respect, i must emphasize the role of mrs myller. we believe that this is a reasonable programme which allows the commission to work, which allows legislation and which allows countries to move within viable programmes and therefore we understand that we must support it. it is the right framework for combining the development of the peoples of europe into a policy axis of sustainable development and i think that is enough. if this is done, it must be made clear in the conciliation that certain areas are subsidiarity-specific. and i'm also going to talk about principles. the desire to generalize all measures and to implement a uniform policy in all countries is contrary to sustainability and is a principle of globalising mindsets. it's very easy to attack globalization when you're talking about economics and not want to call globalization imposing the same suit on everyone. sustainability attaches great importance to social principles, technological feasibility and the context in which the measures are applied; the first principle of sustainability is to know how to combine general principles with tailor-made clothing for what each people, each place, each climate and each context needs. we must have the greatness to admit the freedom of the rulers to make these suits to measure and adapt the model of the suit - which we do not renounce - to the measures. we also support a scientific policy here and we believe that the role of the people's party and parliament in this case is to support the council and the commission because co-decision is not only a right of parliament but also a responsibility which parliament has to help the governments. that is why we respect the dates of all the agreements which the commission and the council are to conclude with other european countries. we must be serious and support the policy that has cost them so much. we support thematic strategies and a more scientific policy precisely because this means adapting to the state of the matter, to the situation of the countries and the sector and the problem. it is necessary to assess whether or not there are appropriate technologies, whether or not there are applicable technologies, because often, because of the climate, the conditions, the size of the company, etc., the technologies may be different. but the results should be the same. we therefore support the scientific nature and the study of the economic and social impacts of the programme, because if there are no social principles, there is no sustainability. that is precisely why we are not in favour of a simple review of subsidies, that is to say, of setting a deadline whatever the subsidy, and especially for certain sectors which have had to close down because of measures imposed by the commission, which has imposed laws on them - as in the coal sector - and which now face the problem of being subject to stricter criteria than others. we first define the criteria for negative subsidies and then we realise that five years is not enough time for a generation to recover or for some depressed areas to regenerate. we also reject the substitution principle, because it offers no guarantees for industry, citizens or society, and it allows for a very loose interpretation of certain sectors, certain countries or certain officials or experts to establish measures which are harmful to society and have no legal guarantee. and the principle of legal certainty is inherent in the rule of law. i hope that the management can be carried out.

behind the programme was not simply to continue with the same thing, not just to add to a long list of legislative proposals to those already in the fifth action programme which, moreover, as mr jackson very rightly said, are in fact often lacking in implementation. this is something we have to deal with. however, it is also important to emphasize what we actually agree on. it is about the overall structure and priorities. it's about having the courage to say that these four questions are the most important. it is also about the underlying principles of environmental policy in this decade and the need for broad consultation and participation in decision-making on environmental issues. we agree on the issues to be raised. these include climate change, nature and biodiversity, environmental and health measures, the question of how we use our natural resources and the question of waste. we also agree that existing legislation should be implemented in practice, that environmental considerations should be integrated into all other policy areas and that legislators, decision-makers and the public should have access to adequate information. the strategy for the next 10 years is in fact based on the fifth environmental action programme, which has been developed by describing how environmental policy and challenges have changed. today's lifestyles, consumption patterns, the way goods are produced and the way we as individuals live and operate affect environmental problems. the eap is challenging. i'm aware of that and i take responsibility for it. although the criticism has been harsh, i think it is right to dare to do something new and to try to find a new structure. it was important to me to draw up an environmental action programme that everyone, not just the experts, could follow and evaluate when new proposals and initiatives were presented, as was the case with the recent climate package. i therefore naturally do not agree with the rejection of the council's common position. after all this work, let us try to finish it and help one another as best we can! the committee on the environment supports in principle the general approach to the development of future environmental policy contained in the council's common position. this includes the requirement that policy be based on participation and dialogue and on the best available scientific evidence. this means that we will analyse the problems we face and possible solutions very thoroughly, while taking account of current research, using indicators, etc. in this way we create policy through sound work, and this is in line with the strategic direction of this programme. it also means, as i said, that it is pointless to introduce more or less arbitrarily objectives and time limits into the programme. at the same time, i want to avoid any misunderstanding and make it clear that i am of course in favour of using clear targets and time limits. our proposals will also contain such and they will be discussed in both parliament and the council. the few overall objectives now contained in the programme are widely recognised and should be so. i can of course also approve the additional objectives proposed by the commission in its communication on sustainable development for the gothenburg summit, namely amendments nos 11, 15, 16 and 27. this is, however, on condition that they faithfully reflect our message. i cannot accept the inclusion of other objectives in the programme as is done in amendments nos 17, 24, 25, 26, 34 and 42. it is also gratifying that the committee supports the idea and the proposal for thematic strategies and also the proposed content. the committee has added a proposal on the urban environment. it is contained in amendments nos 32 and 33, which are broadly acceptable. we thus have a stable platform for future work and cooperation. the problem is that the proposal to have the strategies ready for implementation within three years clashes with the requirement of best scientific findings, consultation and broad participation. we also have to remember that we have seven thematic strategies to deal with. together with amendment no 12, which requires that all thematic strategies be subject to the codecision procedure, this would mean that the commission would have to present all thematic strategies by the end of the year at the latest in order to allow time for the codecision procedure. we may be able to meet the deadline for some thematic strategies, but not for all. i would therefore urge the european parliament not to push this issue too hard. it will give us the opportunity to develop the strategies and to present a package of measures that is optimally adapted to the problems at hand. we cannot therefore accept amendments nos 12, 13 and 41, but i will keep the european parliament informed of our work on the thematic strategies and we will submit oral reports every year to comply with the requirement of amendment no 14. i must inform the house that i am opposed to most of the amendments relating to chemicals. the problem with these is that there is no agreed definition of the principle of compensation. we should therefore examine it carefully before making it legally binding. of course, i think it is fulfilling its function, but before we make it legally binding we must come up with a definition that is sustainable. as regards the proposal that the reach register should cover all existing substances and that all products, unlike substances and preparations, should be labelled, i can only say that this is practically impossible. however, we can in principle accept amendment no 31 on coordination of work on chemicals and pesticides even if coordination is already under way. as regards the question of voluntary commitments and agreements, we see them as part of a favourable mix of different policy instruments, including legal and economic instruments. according to the oecd, there are more than 300 agreements in the member states of the community. they differ widely because they are flexibly adapted to different situations and objectives. the commission plans to present a communication exploring the possibilities of this instrument. it is too early to determine the nature of the agreements in the programme and therefore we cannot accept amendments nos 9 and 40. on a number of other issues, such as sustainable development and integration, measures relating to tax levels at community level, environmental crime, etc., there is general support from the commission. in addition to the amendments i have mentioned, the commission can support amendments nos 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 18, 19, 21, 39 and 45 and parts of amendments nos 43, 46 and 47. however, i cannot accept the other amendments which have been tabled. mr president, we are approaching an agreement on the environmental action programme for the next ten years. mr müller's contribution as rapporteur at this second reading has been very much appreciated. there is no need for a second debate, because her amendments are carefully selected, which bodes well for the next stage of the procedure. i hope that the council, on the basis of the amendments supported by the commission, will take a positive view of parliament's opinion, so that together, the commission, the council, parliament and the other stakeholders, we can continue to work to preserve and improve our environment. thank you for an interesting debate!

the rapporteur. - mr president, i must confess that it was a pleasure to see you come in, because i almost thought i was going to be alone in the chamber. i am also very grateful to the commissioner for coming here tonight after a hard day's work. the green paper on an integrated product policy should, in my view, be the framework for the formulation of a set of guidelines and proposals which will make it easier for producers and consumers alike to make full use of the instruments and opportunities offered by the market in order to achieve a functioning of the market which is more in line with the practice of sustainable development. this new approach must go beyond the traditional approach - followed so far by the european union - which is based mainly on promoting environmental improvement in the productive sector through rules setting limits on pollution and also through voluntary instruments promoting the differentiation of companies and products incorporating environmental improvements. as regards these voluntary measures, such as the regulation on european co-management and eco-audits and the eco-label, which have been in place since the early 1990s, we must admit that they have not been as successful as expected and, above all, that they have not been as successful in all the member states. only 3 200 companies in europe have been awarded emas certification and 350 products from 70 companies have been awarded the so-called european eco-label. in my view, the main cause of this situation lies in the rigidity of the system and the still weak consumer demand for environmentally friendly products. the commission is aware of this problem and has presented this green paper on an integrated product policy, with varying degrees of success and balance. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is protected. different mechanisms have been proposed to encourage this necessary environmental improvement of products and their consumption. the proposal contains a number of indications which give a foothold to different market policies and instruments, going beyond those which are exclusively environmental, and which i think will pave the way for more detailed and more developed discussion in a future white paper. we are faced with a decisive approach to facilitate the promotion of environmental improvement through the market in the european union, which will make it possible to set more environmentally fair prices for products, stimulate demand in a more correct way and make widespread use of clean production instruments. i also believe that this approach will give greater strength to the integration of environmental policy into other areas, such as economic and social policy, and we will thereby better fulfil the mandate of cardiff and gothenburg. i believe that parliament, through its amendments, has brought greater precision and clarity to the commission's proposal as regards the orientation of the ppi and also as regards the role of each of the actors (business, administration and consumers), and that it clearly addresses the issue of shared responsibility without implying a reduction in the producer's responsibility, but taking into account and emphasizing the responsibility also of the administration and the consumer. the administration, for example, can be a very important driver of a more environmentally sound market through public procurement. it also identifies market instruments useful for implementing the ppi: economic instruments, such as the issue of tax incentives, etc. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'customs' in the definition of the concept of 'commercial vehicle' and to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'vehicle' in the definition of the concept of 'vehicle'. it also stresses the decisive role of information, which must be clearer, more accurate and more fluid. i think i have taken account of most of the amendments tabled in the house. i have accepted them and have only rejected those which i think do not fit into the framework and context of a green paper. in my view, this is a good proposal and deserves the support of the whole of parliament.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report we are voting on today is obviously not the miguélez report. for obvious reasons: the committee on fisheries, by accepting most of the amendments to my report, and myself, by reaching a compromise with some of the amendments on certain points, have made significant changes to the original text. this text is therefore a summary of the different positions in this parliament on the reform of the cfp, and in assessing it there will be those who think that the glass is half full and others who say that it is half empty. in any event, i think that the report contains enough positive elements in relation to the current cap to make me, as rapporteur, ask this house to vote in favour of it. i have to say that the fisheries committee has been more inclined to point out the shortcomings of the current cfp than to put forward concrete proposals for its reform. however, i believe that there are enough positive elements to lay the foundations for a future cfp. the greatest difficulty has been to reconcile the different interests of enterprises, in order to enable them to be economically viable, those of the preservation of resources and the socioeconomic measures capable of defending an activity mainly rooted in backward, peripheral and objective 1 areas. the european commission would have to be able, through a clever policy, to reconcile these three aspects, especially since the failure of one of them would imply that of the other two. we are concerned about the contradiction between the commission's highly critical analysis of the current cfp, which is shared by the european parliament, and the subsequent reform proposals, formulated in the green paper, which are hardly innovative. the book is about immobility, a "more of the same" that no one likes. the report i am presenting to you is clear in defining the fundamental objective of the common fisheries policy: to balance the viability of a strategic economic sector for the european union - which contributes to food supplies and is vital for employment and the economic and social cohesion of the union's peripheral regions - with the maintenance of sustainable marine ecosystems. the committee on fisheries calls for tacs to be fixed in accordance with rational and transparent methods, taking account of scientific advice and information from professionals in the sector, especially as the fixing of tacs will be multiannual and multi-specific. it called for an end to the inconsistencies between the current cfp and the single market by requiring that fishing restricted areas, whether closed areas, boxes or access limits, be based on scientific criteria for the protection of resources. as the report points out, the current cfp is a derogation from the principle of equal access and, in the absence of a council decision, this derogation will end on 31 december 2002. the cfp is bound by the fundamental principles of the treaty, including, ladies and gentlemen, the principle of equal treatment. the relative stability of the highly dependent fishing communities requires a new analysis, as called for in the report, which takes account of the developments in the community over the last 25 years. this analysis is essential in the context of the review of the cfp. the fisheries committee has also rejected the extension of the exclusive fishing zone beyond the current 6/12 mile band. as regards the fleet, the report is clear in pointing out that the multiannual guidance programmes (mags) have not produced the desired results, largely because of a lack of willingness on the part of some member states to implement them properly. fleet reduction is a socioeconomic sacrifice which, if it is to be understood and accepted by the fishing industry, must be carried out in a balanced way in all the member states and must also have sufficient community financial support. the community must continue to contribute to the modernisation of the fleet through structural measures, strengthening safety and habitability aspects without this leading to an increase in fishing effort. it is therefore necessary to continue structural aid. we recognize that the functioning of the monitoring and control mechanisms is unsatisfactory. we believe that all efforts to conserve resources are doomed to failure without a harmonized european system with a high degree of sectoral compliance. it is necessary to extend the powers of community inspectors and to establish a uniform system of penalties. the community must take a firm stand on international relations and link them to the european union's external policy. the union's international relations with regard to fisheries must be viewed primarily from a commercial perspective, aimed at obtaining catch possibilities for our fleet. fisheries agreements are and will remain an essential element of the new cfp. this requires a uniform approach to the conclusion of international agreements, so that operators are subject to the same conditions as regards fishing opportunities, the payment of fees and licences and the use of surplus quotas. the european union's trade relations and market policy must combine respect for the principle of community preference with a reduction in tariffs linked to the establishment of a list of sensitive products, thus facilitating access to raw material supplies for the processing industry. as far as the social aspects are concerned, they were completely absent from the green paper. we call on the commission to fully integrate these economic and social measures which are necessary to ensure the economic and social cohesion of the regions dependent on fisheries. the fisheries sector is characterised by harsh working conditions and the absence of collective agreements, which makes it necessary to increase social dialogue. finally, and in the time allocated to me by my group, i would like to regret what has gone astray in these long months of parliamentary proceedings, especially two points: a community fleet that can operate under one flag and a single body of community inspectors. i am sorry that the european parliament is not, on this occasion, the innovative and cutting-edge institution that all members of this house want. in fisheries we have been decades behind the european path, but just as we already have euros in our pockets and our skies are watched by eurocontrol, sooner or later the european flag will fly over our fisheries.
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. - mr president, as it could not be otherwise, the committee on the environment decided, by an abstention and a large majority in favour, that only the balance of the marine ecosystem - as other colleagues say - will guarantee employment in fishing in the future, and that the fleet should be adapted to existing resources. as the rapporteur said, the failure of the current cfp must be overcome. we all know that biological stops, no-go zones, mesh sizes, tacs, etc. have not improved the situation and that the green paper proposal does not go any further. we in the committee on the environment believe that action must be taken on the sources of pollution, which are many - industrial pollution, the enormous tourist pressure we are all well aware of in our country - action on the extraordinary ecosystems that exist in our own country, such as rivers, and action on hydrocarbon plants and others that go in the opposite direction to what we would like. social, environmental and economic indicators are needed to ensure that actions are effective, as are accompanying social measures and incentives for sustainable fishing practices, such as the artisanal practices that occur on our nearest coasts. the precautionary principle, which is well defined in the fao code of conduct and the un agreement, must be respected. consumer confidence needs to be strengthened by acting not only on traditional fisheries but also on aquaculture. information and awareness-raising, as well as the involvement of citizens and the sectors concerned, must also be ensured if the measures to be taken in those sectors are to be successful, as must the involvement of local and regional authorities. control and monitoring - as the rapporteur said - of the measures taken, otherwise there will be inequality between the different countries. mr president, we believe that it should not be forgotten that increased fleet capacity does not guarantee employment. the loss of jobs in the manufacturing sector is 19%, and in the processing sector it has been 10% in recent years. so we have to act on that contradiction.

in writing. - (es) i voted in favour of the rod report, since i am in favour of the conclusion of the cotonou agreement for a number of reasons. firstly, because with this agreement the eu reaffirms its commitment to the acp countries and its willingness to contribute to their sustainable economic and social development. secondly, because it makes the eradication of poverty through progressive integration into the world economy the main objective of the agreement. thirdly, because the political dimension it includes can go a long way towards addressing the causes which have largely prevented acp-eu cooperation from producing the desired results. without democracy and peace, it is impossible to promote economic development or to ensure that the benefits of development are equitably shared by all. this is why political dialogue, good governance and conflict prevention are so important as part of the agreement. i do not therefore share many of the criticisms contained in the explanatory statement accompanying the rod report. it is true that everything can be improved in this world, but the cotonou agreement represents a step forward in the field of eu development cooperation policy. this is a step which obviously must be followed by many others, particularly as regards parliament's control of edf funds. but this agreement is a step in the right direction.
the rapporteur. - madam president, i should like to begin by expressing my satisfaction - as you have just done - at the initiative of the united kingdom, the french republic and the kingdom of sweden, which we are discussing today. the european union and the existence of a european area of freedom, security and justice mean, in turn, the creation of an area without internal frontiers in which the free movement of goods, persons, services and capital must be guaranteed within the territory of the states of the union, as provided for in article 14 of the treaty establishing the european community. there can be no obstacles to the application of the law in the european union. the tampere summit called for the principle of mutual recognition to become the cornerstone of judicial cooperation in both civil and criminal matters in the european union. the confidence between member states in their legal decisions and their correct application is the minimum required. similarly, greater efforts are needed by the member states to achieve a minimum degree of harmonisation of national criminal laws. until now, the enforcement of financial penalties was governed by two european agreements: the 1970 hague convention and the 1991 convention on the enforcement of foreign judgments in criminal matters. i would point out that the first, even after it had entered into force, had only been ratified by five member states; and the second, the 1991 convention, has not even entered into force. this is clearly an indication of the need for initiatives of this kind in order to accelerate and make a real contribution to the construction of the european area of justice that we agreed on in tampere. while several legal acts are already available in the field of civil law, there has been more hesitation in the field of criminal law, which is much more sensitive. so far, the principle of mutual recognition has been used only for the decision on the pre-emptive seizure and the safeguarding of evidence. the road ahead is still long and greater political will is needed on the part of the council to be able to fulfil the mandate of the tampere summit with the work prepared by the commission, which often encounters barriers and little cooperation from the council. this initiative is a major step forward in removing these barriers. mutual recognition is undoubtedly a key element in the construction of an area of freedom, security and justice. i also welcome the legal instrument chosen, the framework decision, which will undoubtedly avoid the complexity and the long duration of the ratification procedures. i would also like to point out that, as in the conventions mentioned, the principle of double criminality applies and that, therefore, its absence is a reason for non-enforcement. the mechanism we propose in this initiative is a certificate which serves as a guarantee to the competent authority for the legality of the substantive judgment, thus replacing the examination of the content. the difficult question of how the amounts received should be divided between the two participating states is settled in article 10 so that the compensation and costs are borne by the issuing state and all other amounts by the executing state. i therefore welcome the introduction of this initiative and i largely support it. i believe that an area of law, as called for in tampere, presupposes a transfer and a non-bureaucratic execution of criminal judgments and that this initiative is a first step towards a global application of the principle of mutual recognition. i support in particular the provisions on the law applicable to alternative custodial sentences and the reduction or remission of financial penalties. i also support the possibility that the executing state may reduce the financial penalty, if necessary, as provided for in article 5. however, i have considered it appropriate to introduce a minimum amount which, in accordance with the convention implementing the schengen agreement, should be eur 40. in this respect, it is important to clarify that conversion of the financial penalty should only be considered in exceptional cases, since in general the currency of the issuing and executing states will be the euro. i would like to stress that i personally consider the amount of 40 euros to be insufficient and small, but i have proposed it in the interests of consistency with the agreement in the schengen implementation convention, which set that amount. i would like to stress both points and ask the council - which is not here today - to take account of the sensitivity and the proposals of this house and, in particular, of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, and the rapporteur therefore believes that the initiative should include the following in the framework decision: a european area of law must be based on the principle of mutual recognition. it is therefore not enough to simply harmonize the legal systems. the charter of fundamental rights of the european union summarises, for the first time in the history of the union, in a single text, the totality of the civil, political, economic and social rights of european citizens and of all persons living in the territory of the union. it should now be possible to measure all legal acts of the union against it. thirdly, the documents to be translated must be translated into all the official languages of the executing state. if a citizen who is liable to pay the fine or who has been subject to a substitute custodial sentence has knowledge of only one of the various official languages of the executing state, he will not be able to consult documents concerning him, which constitutes a breach of his rights. finally, in cases where the competent authority of the executing state is not known, it is necessary to use the contact points of the european judicial network exclusively instead of designating additional central contact points. the amendments have therefore been made for the most part with the sole aim of improving the original proposal and contributing to the fulfilment of the tampere mandate, as well as adding another element in the construction of a genuine area of justice, freedom and security.

- doc. a5-0465/2001 by mr vidal-quadras roca, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the energy performance of buildings (com (2001) 226 - c5-0203/2001 - 2001/0098 (cod)).
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy supply is not affected by the consequences of the crisis. we are all aware that the main component of the energy bill in the union is buildings: ventilation, cooling, heating, lighting, etc. this chapter concentrates the bulk of the union's energy expenditure. everything done in this area has therefore a special impact from this point of view. mr president, this directive marks the end of the era of voluntarisms or recommendations. we are entering into a firm commitment, into binding action and into a firm will to make such measures a reality. there are three aspects of the directive which i would like to stress. the first is the obligation for all buildings in the union to have a certificate that qualifies them from the point of view of energy efficiency. this certificate will undoubtedly have a great signal value on the markets and will make a significant contribution to energy savings. the second is the obligation for all new buildings to incorporate an energy efficiency study, an indispensable requirement for building permits. the third aspect is the obligation for all buildings of more than 1,000 m2 that are subject to major renovation to improve their energy efficiency. there are other measures envisaged in the directive, but i wanted to highlight these three because they are undoubtedly the ones with the greatest potential. it will not be lost on the honourable members that if - as some studies predict - it is possible to achieve in the coming years a saving of 20% in the energy bill of buildings, 20% of 40% brings us closer to 10% and this, in terms of the bill for oil and co2 emissions, is of importance to no one. mr president, it is time to thank the other groups in the house for their valuable contribution and help in getting parliament's amendments to improve this important piece of legislation. i would like to thank the socialist group and mrs zrihen for their many contributions and, above all, i would like to highlight their interesting suggestion concerning social housing. i would also like to thank the green group and mrs ahern very much for their excellent interest and cooperation and to highlight their very interesting contribution to passive cooling techniques, which are so important in those parts of the union where the climate is very warm and cooling (air conditioning systems) is becoming a determining factor. i would also like to thank the liberal group for its emphasis on the fact that tax incentives are always better than sanctions. as we say in spanish, "it's better to lick than to bite", and this is also true in the economic field. unfortunately, there are two points on which we have not been able to achieve unanimity in this house: firstly, the deadlines for implementing the directive, where we have opted for a reasonable middle ground between too long a period, which would not make it effective, and too narrow requirements, which would make it unworkable. and the second is the limit of 1,000 m2, which the green group has wanted to lower. we understand your intention and share your concern, but if we really want this directive to be published in a timeframe that makes it effective, we must accept the number proposed by the commission. mr president, if it is true that politics is the art of making the necessary possible, this directive will ensure that a very important chapter of the union's energy expenditure will be saved in the next decade, and that this will contribute to the well-being, progress and security of all europeans.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is properly implemented. mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and colleague, mr vidal-quadras, on the excellent work he has done on this important directive. as he has already said, the european union is consuming more and more energy and therefore also importing more and more energy products, because our demand exceeds our capacity to meet it with our own resources. this is why it is important, firstly, to diversify the sources of energy, to look for new sources of energy, including, of course, renewable energy, and, secondly, to promote and pursue energy efficiency. i hope that mr vidal-quadras has welcomed the opinion of the committee on the environment, since i think that the points we have underlined in it contribute to enriching some of the aspects of his excellent proposal. i think that a key reference to increase the receptivity of the member states to the proposal is that they take account of local climatic and particular conditions. another point on which the committee on the environment has insisted is the homogenisation of the certificates for buildings in the different member states, which would make it possible to compare the energy efficiency achieved in each of the buildings. we also wanted to clarify the definition of those buildings which are excluded from the application of energy-saving measures and, also, in order not to have our proposal rejected, we have proposed, as mr vidal-quadras has done, that the commission's proposal to reduce the surface area of the buildings concerned be accepted. i am in favour of that approach, mr vidal, as is my commission, but i also understand your position. i think we will see what the result is eventually, and we will have to respect it. the important thing is that the directive comes through, mr vidal-quadras.
commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by congratulating mr vidal-quadras roca on his excellent work on the proposed directive concerning the energy performance of buildings. i should also like to thank the committee on industry, external trade, research and energy for its thorough and thoughtful discussions and to express my satisfaction with the way in which the debate in parliament has sharpened the focus of the proposal and strengthened it. it will very likely be one of our most important means of meeting the european union's kyoto commitment and of improving our security of supply. as has been pointed out, the buildings sector accounts for over 40% of all eu final energy consumption. it also has a very large cost-effective savings potential. this proposal may lead to a significant improvement in the energy performance of buildings by promoting better minimum standards in member states and in their building codes and by requiring more frequent updating and wider application of these codes. not only would this apply to new buildings but, as has been said this evening, even more importantly to many existing buildings when they undergo major renovations. that is where the real potential for improvement lies. the commission welcomes parliament's report and the proposed changes that will serve to improve, clarify and strengthen the proposal. many amendments do this by enhancing the technical and financial definitions, giving concrete examples and defining the proposal's scope and implementation more exactly. for example, amendments nos 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 19, 23, 24, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31, 35, 36 and 37 are amendments the commission can accept, many as they are, some with minor redrafting. amendments nos 3 and 6 encourage the use of subsidy schemes and incentives to promote the implementation of the proposal, taking into account socio-economic implications, and are thus also acceptable. amendments nos 7 and 22, on individual metering and billing and authorisation of inspectors respectively, can also be accepted if their financial and legal implications are illuminated more clearly in the text. mr adam mentioned amendment no 15. that is a comprehensive amendment, parts of which are acceptable to the commission. the setting of efficiency levels at community level is, however, not yet feasible. amendments nos 18 and 20 are also acceptable in parts, bearing in mind the need to allow co2 indicators to remain optional. amendments nos 1, 12, 13, 16, 17, 21 and 27 are not acceptable to the commission for technical and definitional reasons, including the degree of detail or because of related problems of subsidiarity that would result for example from the setting of efficiency levels at community level. because of the heterogeneous nature of the building sector as a result of differences in climate, culture and building traditions, subsidiarity and flexibility for member states are important in the implementation of this directive. the commission feels that the most effective way to improve energy performance requirements in member states is to provide methods to encourage them to improve their own building codes, set their own performance levels and ensure full application and regular revision of those. while methods of calculation, many norms and a number of standards can be established at community level, the actual efficiency level of energy performance of buildings should remain a member state matter. most of the amendments proposed take these principles into account. another important point is with regard to the threshold for upgrading the energy performance of existing buildings when they undergo major renovation. upgrading existing buildings is an important part of this proposal. for many member states it represents a new area of endeavour which will require new performance standards, new resources and substantial investment. we feel that the proposed threshold of 1 000 m2 for upgrading is therefore the best possible compromise attainable at this early stage. finally, as regards the period for transposition of this directive we feel that it is important to underline that we should avoid an unnecessarily long period if we are to meet the target date for kyoto which is usually set at between 2008 and 2012.

commission. – motor vehicles are indeed, as mrs caullery says, complex and sophisticated. that is one of the reasons why we decided to introduce sector specific rules rather than fall back on the general regulatory framework for vertical restrictions. i would stress the following, however. the proposal in our view improves and does not undermine the safe and reliable servicing of cars. it does not make it more difficult for car manufacturers to fulfil their obligations. the repairer to whom a dealer may subcontract the service if he or she so wishes must be entrusted by the manufacturer with the task of providing the services which dealers provide today. to put it bluntly, the only difference between an official dealer who provides after-sales services today and an official repairer in the proposed regime tomorrow is that the latter may not have a showroom from which to sell cars. technical expertise, training, tooling, and service standards will remain those decided by the manufacturer and applied throughout its network. in these circumstances manufacturers are indeed in a position to comply with their obligations. mr naranjo escobar asked whether there will be undesired consequences and whether it would not be advisable to have a transitional period while keeping the location clause for the time being. the time frame is already sufficiently structured because, after consultation, the final commission regulation will be adopted before the summer of this year. it will probably contain a clause saying that it will be fully effective from october 2003 and we have taken into account also the situation of the existing dealers by introducing in the draft regulation an explicit notice for the termination of the contract. at any rate it is clear that what we have adopted today is a very deeply thought through and structured draft regulation but there is still to be further consultation and if we see important and persuasive arguments coming up in the consultation of course we will take them very seriously into account. in reply to mr berenguer fuster, the commission allows selective systems for many products in line with the policy it applies: the draft regulation neither imposes a particular distribution format nor prescribes in detail how agreements should be drafted. it recognises that other vertical restraints agreed between the parties may trigger economic efficiencies which lead to optimal investment levels by manufacturers, official networks and independent repairers. if i can conclude with a slightly more general point, with this proposal we do two things. on the one hand we bring the forces of competition more vigorously into play. there is an injection of additional competition. on the other hand we free up the choice of modalities by means of fewer rigidities and more flexibility.

commission. – in this area some action concerning taxation is important. the commission has a role to play in this. i would remind you that the commission's position for the nice igc was that there should be a shift to qualified-majority voting in those areas of taxation which are crucial for the functioning of the single market. i would not expect member states to top up with higher taxes. they would face constraints in doing so. will the new system bring about legal uncertainty for dealers? i believe not – on the contrary. we are also confident of avoiding the sometimes-feared economic consequences for dealers and employment. the draft regulation offers former dealers the opportunity to become official repayers within the manufacturers' network and to locate where they wish. at any rate we already know that, this draft regulation aside, several manufacturers are planning to restructure and reduce the number of official network dealers in their systems. as to the european warranty, it remains in the proposal. networks have to provide warranty, irrespective of where a car is bought.

question no 39 by mr trakatellis (h-0030/02) subject: nuclear safety: bulgaria's failure to comply with the partnership agreement with the eu and its commitments concerning the dismantling of the kozloduy reactors with the prospect of the dismantling of units 1 and 2 of the kozloduy nuclear power plant by the end of 2002, bulgaria's energy minister, mr kovachev, stated on 8 january that his country would not respect its commitments to close and dismantle old-type reactors which present risks, contrary to what had been provided for in the revised partnership agreement concluded between the european union and bulgaria, as well as in the sofia memorandum concluded in 1999 between bulgaria and the commission. how does the commission intend to enforce the commitments under the partnership agreement concerning the dismantling of units 3 and 4 of the aforementioned plant, and what is the state of progress with the dismantling of units 1 and 2, all of which are hazardous and cannot be upgraded at a reasonable cost? can bulgaria, in the context of the pre-accession procedure, request the opening of negotiations on energy, even though it refuses to comply with the commitments it has made to the eu on nuclear safety and has not yet defined a new strategy in this area in accordance with the principles of the free market (production and pricing) and the opening of the market to competition?
the commission. - mr president, i have to say that i am not in favour of this. in order to avoid any misunderstanding, i must state clearly once again: there is no binding commitment by the bulgarian government that blocks 3 and 4 will be decommissioned by 2006, but there is an agreement that the decision on the decommissioning of these blocks will be taken earlier than the bulgarian government had originally envisaged. the commission stated in that communiqué that it understood that the shutdown would take place no later than 2006. this still requires formal notification by the bulgarian government, but it will certainly come. i should also like to say, mr president, that the energy supply in bulgaria is a matter for the bulgarian government. the commission is also not directly responsible for energy efficiency in the balkans and the situation in bulgaria on the energy market. i can only reiterate our assessment that the closure of units 1 to 4 will not lead to a shortage of energy in bulgaria, but that there is a considerable overcapacity. i fully agree with you that it is absolutely necessary to inform the bulgarian public precisely about the need for the closure and also precisely about the accompanying measures, because in fact - and you know this very well - large sections of the bulgarian public have no understanding of this demand of the international community. we always pretend that these are the obvious things, and i'm grateful to you for bringing this up. the vast majority of the population in bulgaria does not take for granted that the country's most important and largest power plant is being shut down under pressure from the international community.
the commission. - mr president, the commission has not done that at all, and it cannot do that. this was a political condition which the member states had put before us for the opening of negotiations with bulgaria. this policy condition, formulated by the member states, is the result of an assessment made by the industrialized countries at the beginning of the 1990s, when the safety of nuclear power plants in eastern europe was subject to a review. the commission has also decided to extend the scope of the directive to include the nuclear power stations which, in the opinion of the western industrial countries, cannot be retrofitted at reasonable cost. i am not aware at the moment of the standards applied by the states at that time. if you're interested, i'm happy to do the research for you. the commission has not made any inquiries in this respect, but has done what was its political task, namely to reach a result with the bulgarian government on the fulfilment of a political condition for the opening of negotiations.
the commission is not responsible for the safety standards of nuclear power stations anywhere in the world, including bulgaria. even if i could answer your technical question, i'm not allowed to. the responsibility for the operation of the kosloduy nuclear power plant, for any safety problems associated with it and also for any accidents that may occur, lies solely with the operator, in this case the republic of bulgaria. i must also make it clear that the commission is not in a position to take any responsibility, because we are not in a position to have any influence on the way this nuclear power station is operated. i have no personal judgment on how dangerous or safe this nuclear power plant is. i would like to give you detailed information on how all this is going to be done technically, as soon as i have it myself. we must assume that the time needed to complete such a project of decommissioning a nuclear power plant is not to be calculated in years but in decades. in other words, this is a very long-term task which may involve long-term commitments or burdens on the community budget.
