question no 41 by concepció ferrer (h-0054/02) subject: improvement of the regulatory environment for small and mediumsized enterprises the internal market is a privileged market in which european businesses interact. however, this interaction is hampered by the persistence of some significant barriers to the free movement of goods and services. the need to improve the regulatory environment, highlighted at the lisbon summit and in the european charter for small enterprises, requires follow-up. what action is the commission taking in this regard?
the commission. - mr president, the internal market has brought enormous benefits to businesses, but there is still more to be done. progress in this area is being monitored in the context of the commission's internal market strategy for services adopted in november 1999. the commission shall review the internal market strategy annually in order to assess the results achieved and to propose improvements. the last assessment was in april. one of the objectives is to improve the business environment and many of the measures related to this objective have a particular focus on helping small businesses. the commission also monitors the development of the business environment for small enterprises through the annual report accompanying the european small business act. the 2002 report will be published in the coming days and will assess the measures announced by the member states and the commission to help small businesses. the conclusions of the 2002 report will be reported to the conference of european ministers responsible for sme policy on 23 february in aranjuez, spain, and will be presented to the barcelona european council. at this point, i can say that progress has been made. progress has been made in areas such as access to finance and the exchange of good practice. in addition, in december, an sme ambassador was appointed to enhance contacts with smes and their representative bodies. he works in the enterprise dg and is responsible for acting as a contact person on issues such as smes' access to finance and innovation, as well as on issues related to competitiveness, better regulation, the completion of the internal market and participation in eu programmes, and how to improve consultation procedures.last year, the commission launched the campaign 'smes in the digital age'. the aim is to make smes aware of the opportunities offered by information networks. this year, six events are planned in different member states and a major conference in brussels. the commission's work on better regulation is also progressing. both the white paper on european governance and the laeken communication on improving and simplifying the regulatory environment have proposed a number of measures to improve the situation. the proposals cover the entire life cycle of a community act. the need to strengthen the consultation of stakeholders and civil society, the evaluation of community actions and costs, and the simplification of existing legislation are among the issues raised. the commission will, after consulting the community institutions and other stakeholders, make a proposal by june for a simple action plan to simplify and improve the regulatory environment. the enterprise dg is actively involved in the preparation of this action plan and is drawing on the experience gained from the enterprise impact assessment system and the associated pilot project. the conclusions of this project will be finalised in february.
- mr commissioner, you have given me such a complete answer that i have little hesitation to ask again. i would, however, urge you to ensure that the measures you have announced will be taken, particularly with regard to simplification of the rules, are actually implemented and implemented as quickly as possible. it is very good to have big statements, big words and big policies for existing businesses, but it is essential that those who - driven by the entrepreneurial spirit we want to encourage - decide to set up a new company do not encounter obstacles and difficulties that prevent them from moving forward. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very important one.
commission. – i share mr harbour's view that there is a lot to improve in the impact assessment. for that reason, when i took office i launched a project to create more solid methodologies for business impact assessment. the results of this work are ready now in february. alongside this, the commission proposed at the göteborg summit the need for sustainable impact assessments, which means impact assessments that include economic, social and environmental factors. this work is now proceeding inside the commission and is led by the secretary-general. i fully agree that we must have predictable accepted methodologies so that anybody can assess how we have come to these conclusions. the commission is ready to open the debate on these issues and to appear before the respective committees, for instance, to discuss what we have learned in our business impact assessments. the commission appreciates the importance of both business and sustainable impact assessments and the need to achieve them quickly. secondly, of course it does not mean that measures will not be taken if costs are incurred but we should at least try to assess the costs honestly and then an informed decision can be taken.
mr. crowley arrived just before i gave him the floor. if he wishes to put a question, the commissioner will answer it. question no 40 by brian crowley (h-0025/02) subject: improving the business climate in 2002 and creating an electronic society for all could the commission give an overview of its proposals for 2002 which should improve the business climate, in particular for small and micro enterprises, and could it indicate within what timeframe it intends, as it has committed to, to submit its new initiatives to strengthen the trend towards an electronic society for all?
commission. – the european commission will publish within a week the annual report on the european charter for small enterprises. through the annual report we monitor progress on the environment for small businesses. the 2002 report evaluates actions reported by the member states and the commission in favour of small businesses. the conclusions of the report will be presented to the conference of european ministers responsible for sme policies on 23 february and submitted to the european council. as i have already said, the report shows signs of increasing political commitment and major progress has been made in the field of access to finance. progress has also been made in exchanges of good practice such as cutting red tape in company creation. as regards the efforts of smes to adapt their business practices to the global knowledge-based economy, the commission launched last year the godigital initiative for smes as part of the eeurope action plan. in some countries this report has received a very positive welcome. we are organising campaigns throughout the european countries at the moment. before the end of 2002 a portal to provide smes with legal information, guidance and advice will be set up. the commission has also just today adopted a communication on eeurope benchmarking, where you can follow how smes are being connected and how broadly they use ecommerce. this commission communication highlights new challenges in relation to internet usage: broadband is needed to stimulate new services; schools are connected but the internet is not yet sufficiently part of the pedagogical process; governments online have to move towards full electronic transactions. the indicators include amongst others internet penetration in business and the percentage of companies selling online. while good progress has been made, the take-up of ecommerce is not as fast as expected. this confirms the relevance of actions such as godigital, but also indicates the urgent need to identify obstacles to ecommerce amongst especially small companies as well as consumers. eeurope should be continued beyond 2002 and shift its focus towards effective usage and availability of the internet for all citizens and businesses. the communication on the impact of the e-economy on european enterprises contains proposals to deepen cooperation between all relevant stakeholders to develop a policy agenda for maximising the benefits of the e-economy for european enterprises, taking into account the needs of smes. the industry council endorsed this proposal in december 2001 and invited the commission and the member states to intensify the debate on the e-economy. the spanish presidency has decided to launch a policy debate with member states to agree future priorities for the promotion of the e-economy in europe and to address this topic at the industry council meeting in early june. to this end it will be necessary to identify policy changes at national and european level to adapt to the needs of the e-economy. these activities will be developed in close cooperation with the reflections and the preparatory work relating to the future of the eeurope action plan.
the commission. - mr president, last december - thanks to the swift action of the european parliament - new legislation was adopted covering all electronic communications. it also contains, for the first time, a legal basis for frequencies. it is on this basis that the bodies are now being set up: a committee to consider long-term issues and a working group to consider the current administration. having a common legal basis and common bodies makes it possible to think in advance about common objectives and coordinate actions. this does not guarantee, of course, that everyone will eventually choose the same course of action, but i hope that at least we can agree together on open and transparent procedures and that before the first state starts to allocate frequencies, the rules of the game are known to everyone. the market can act more wisely if it knows at least how different regions in europe are progressing. i don't think the kind of madness we had last time will happen again, but there's no guarantee that everything will go smoothly.

commission. – the two directives on electronic commerce and copyright are extremely important. it is the commission's duty to ensure that member states transpose them into their law. they are both within the remit of my colleague, mr bolkestein, but we are cooperating here and i am ready to contact him after question time. on the matter of copyright, the commission is organising a workshop in the next few weeks on digital rights management technologies. when content is sold on line it is very important to guarantee a system where the copyright holder can receive proper royalties for his production. new technologies like digital rights management are helpful there. my personal wish is that this technology could result in more targeted methods to get proper revenue for copyright holders so that member states would not need to go for these very broad untargeted solutions such as copyright levy. finally, on the follow-up of the member states, there is often a problem that progress is piecemeal and there is not sufficiently strong coordination in member states to guarantee that progress will take place in all areas. that will be one of the issues we will raise at the next informal council and we will pass this challenge to european council in barcelona.

commission. – to be honest, mr rübig, last year was not an easy one for the risk capital market. the venture capital market developed very rapidly in 2000, then we saw the difficulties and it went down. at eu level, the european investment funds invested in venture capital funds in various member states. these investments were well-timed because of the lack of venture financing. we have also been using community budget funds, with part of the multiannual programme credits transferred into the investment funds. through these efforts the public sector has been playing its role. at the same time it is very important to complete the legislation on a genuine internal market for financial services and risk capital. in this regard we hope that the solutions resulting from the lamfalussy report will be very useful. today on the internet i saw some good news: some new venture rounds for wireless applications have been completed. perhaps the worst is over, but the market is still very tight compared to the situation in the past. so all such measures, an active financial market and public support measures, if there is market failure, will be needed.

question no 45 by mihail papayannakis (h-0008/02) subject: employment in greecereading the council recommendation (com (2001) 0512/final) on the implementation of the employment policies of the member states, it is clear that greece still has one of the lowest employment rates in the eu and that the unemployment rate has stabilised at 11%, i.e. well above the average. these figures reflect structural problems affecting the labour market, a situation which is also reflected in the commission's communication on structural indicators. according to the latter, greek indicators for enterprise r & d expenditure, internet access, lifelong learning and public expenditure on education are the lowest among the member states. could the commission state whether, following the council recommendation and the commission communication, greece has taken further specific measures and initiatives in the above areas to promote employability and improve its position?
the commission. - i mentioned the specific indicator because it's too big a difference. we have therefore a growth rate of 150%. there is also an increase in spending on training for research and technology, but there are other indicators which are stable and have not diversified. the first advances have been signed, which i believe are about 10%, and as regards the employment figures for the second community support framework, i would not say that it is possible to give figures, since they would be rather fictitious. what do i mean by that? there are the direct jobs created by the greek programmes, the stages, there are the indirect jobs created by the training and the linking of local development resources, whether in the public or private sector, but which are not measured after the training, i.e. the oaed is not able to give the results of the training, and these are among the important elements requested in the third community support framework, so that there can be monitoring.
question no 46 by mr kratsa-tsagaropoulou (h-0035/02) subject: undeclared work in greece in 1998, the commission published a communication com ((1998) 0219/final). the commission has also proposed that the member states should establish a dialogue to combat undeclared work, which according to the data available at the time represented some 15% of gdp in the european union but more than 20% in greece and italy. recent checks by the greek authorities and other available data indicated that 10.5% of enterprises were not registered with the social security system and that the percentage of unaffiliated workers was between 21 and 30%, which resulted in depriving the public finances and in particular the social insurance funds of several billion euros. what commitments have the member states made following the dialogue launched in 1998? can the commission provide an assessment of the progress that has been made? what are greece's obligations in this case and what recommendations have been made to it? what specific measures does the commission intend to take in the context of both the quality policy at the workplace and the open method of coordination to ensure safe and sustainable pensions?
the commission. - as you said, this is a matter where the european union can intervene very difficultly. the registration of enterprises, which is a top priority for a country both in terms of its tax system, i.e. its revenue, and its insurance system, i.e. its pensions, is obviously a priority for the member states and i do not think that recommendations are needed in this direction. i would like to believe, from the information we have, that the computerization of the social security foundation, the law allowing for peripheral businesses and some reforms in that direction will have an effect.
i call question no 47 by armonia bordes (h-0015/02): subject: transfer of unemployment benefits under the provisions of regulation (eec) no 1408/71 oj l 149, 5.7.1971, p. 2, employees who are nationals of the member states of the european union may be entitled to unemployment benefits in all the states of the union. immigrant workers outside the european community who wish to receive unemployment benefits in a country of the union other than their country of residence are not entitled to them under this regulation, which does not allow them to transfer their rights. how can the commission justify that employees who are not members of the european economic community are not entitled to unemployment benefits when they change their country of residence, when they have paid contributions like other employees? why are they excluded from the e301 and e303 forms which allow the transfer of unemployment benefits?

question no 51 is therefore admissible. question no 52 by maría izquierdo rojo (h-0960/01) subject: spanish presidency and the inhumane living conditions of afghan women
commission. – the commission is very much aware of the need to improve the situation of women in post-taliban afghanistan. our initial eur 57 m commitment to reconstruction in afghanistan includes specific provision for this. the commission services are currently finalising contracts with ngos and un aid agencies to implement 18 projects worth eur 25 m and programmes to support internally displaced afghan people and refugees. gender is a cross-cutting issue in all projects funded from the aid to uprooted people budget. in 2001 more than 50% of the projects directed at health, education and refugee care had specific and significant gender components. the commission is currently assessing project proposals for the 2002 budget for uprooted people. the amount envisaged is eur 24 m. in the new political situation in afghanistan the commission is planning to open an office in kabul in february or march this year. this office will further enhance the commission's ability to oversee the performance and delivery of its aid to afghanistan. echo reopened its office at the beginning of last month. regarding the humanitarian aid provided by echo, women are involved in various types of projects; all medical and nutritional projects funded by echo aim to treat malnutrition among children under five years of age, as well as to monitor the health status of women, in particular lactating and pregnant women. ngos generally organise elementary hygiene education for women. ngos have access to all beneficiaries, women included, and can employ women as local ngo personnel in medically related programmes. medical ngos play a great role in the training of women.
- commissioner, i would like to ask a supplementary question focusing on two aspects. firstly, will women manage a part of this financial support? secondly, since there are specific risks for women - a seven-year-old girl has just been sold into marriage by her family in exchange for the relief of hunger and need - i would like to know whether the commission is providing specific funds to prevent this kind of violation of women's rights. in view of the situation described, which will be repeated tomorrow and the day after tomorrow, i would like a concrete response from the commission. it is also very important to know whether women will manage these funds. the fact that there are many armed men is very detrimental to the progress in improving the situation of women.
commission. – the simple answer to the very important first question that the honourable member asked is an unequivocal yes. not least do we hope that women will be centrally involved in a great deal of our development activity, but there are women in the interim administration. i hope there will be in the transitional administration. women played a crucial role, let us not forget, in the success of the bonn talks in december and we will be doing what we can to support the afghan ministry of women's affairs which will, i hope, be a good example of women managing programmes to help develop society and to help protect the role of women in a society which has abused them for far too long. the honourable member asked a question about the specific security of women and young girls. in the light of recent well-publicised events, i wholly understand that. i hope that the overall improvement in the security situation and the increasing grip of the interim authority with our support will help to prevent things like that happening. but after the ferocious talibanisation of afghan society over the last few years, and given the position of the country where warlordism is still rife, it is going to be some time before we can promote the sort of strong gender policies we would like to see. however, we will do all that we can. i am greatly encouraged by what the honourable member has said.

commission. – as regards the first point, dr buseck is well aware of the problem to which the honourable member referred. the proposals he brings forward on 11 march will reflect that awareness of his. the honourable member will know that he is extremely experienced in dealing with the problems of the region and in particular in mobilising private sector support. i am looking forward very keenly to working with him. he will do an excellent job and he will want to engage with others who are working alongside him in an enthusiastic and transparent way. on implementation, it is fair to say that overall we have established an impressive record as far as the commission is concerned in implementing what we have promised to do in the western balkans and in south-east europe as a whole. what we have been able to achieve in serbia, in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, and in other countries, is impressive. i hope that we will be able to ensure that where there have been any bottlenecks affecting infrastructure projects with the stability pact – and sometimes those bottlenecks are the result of problems in the beneficiary countries – we will be able to resolve them. dr buseck and i are trying to focus on those problem projects and get them moving as rapidly as possible. as for information about what is happening on the ground, that is an issue which dr buseck is well aware of. we will help him to address it, trying to ensure that the publicity for the achievements of the stability pact goes to the pact, rather than to individuals. it is a pleasure to work with dr buseck. i think he will do outstandingly well and he can certainly count on our understanding and support and, i am sure, the understanding and support of parliament, in the efforts he makes in the future.

- madam president, i would like to express my full support for the rapporteur's approach, mrs kauppi, and therefore for the commission's proposal, which mrs kauppi's report supports almost without reservation. the socialists also support this commission proposal without reservation. the proposal deals with two issues of great interest. firstly, tax fraud, particularly in a specific area, such as intra-community and triangular transactions in the field of vat. the second issue - related to the previous one, as a means of combating fraud - is cooperation between administrations to solve or at least reduce the level of fraud we have discussed above. the proposals have been explained perfectly in the previous speech by mrs kauppi and i fully agree with them. that said, i would like to make two additional remarks which are connected with the content of this report. the first concerns the continued application today of the so-called provisional vat system, which was introduced in 1993 with the completion of the single market, with a view to its being provisional, and even with an expiry date, which has been extended and which has not been complied with, as you are well aware. i would like to draw attention to this because, if we are talking today about this report and the fraud cited in it, it is largely because we still have a provisional system of vat - that is, the system established for intra-community transactions - which taxes a number of transactions in the country of destination, but without the border controls established by the regime before the establishment of the single market. obviously, in a definitive vat system, such as the one corresponding to the single market, with taxation at source, we would probably not be talking about this issue, because most of this fraud would be avoided at its source. this is the first point i wanted to make about this report. the second concerns a very important point, which mrs kauppi has mentioned: the legal basis chosen by the commission to present this proposal for a directive. i think it is worth applauding the commission's interpretation of the treaty, in considering that the basis applicable in this case was article 95, that is to say, in interpreting that tax matters are reduced to matters of substantive, substantive tax law, but not to those of adjective law, to those matters - such as those we are dealing with at the moment - of tax administration, of exchange of aid between administrations for tax administration. in these cases, it is not a question of tax law or taxation law in the strict sense of the term, which is reserved to national parliaments and therefore to unanimity, but of a matter which can be dealt with, as now, by the codecision procedure. i would like to conclude, madam president, with a warning from the foregoing reflections, namely that it would be desirable that the next convention and treaty reform should definitively define the scope of taxation and establish a precise area of harmonisation. of course, not all tax matters are subject to harmonization; there are certain matters, such as income tax, which will never be harmonized in full, but others - i am thinking mainly of the basis for calculating corporate income tax - should be established as subject to harmonization and exempt from the unanimity rule, also to give this parliament back the lead in matters as important as the one we are dealing with.

european council in laeken. the european parliament has just issued the report on both decisions with a very high level of technical competence and political sensitivity. i must say that the speed european parliament today. we are of course aware of the european parliament's feeling that it has not had enough time to discuss these issues and i would like to point out in this connection that the closely linked to regulation (ec) no 2580/2001, without any prior consultation of the european parliament, which had expressed its wish to take a position on this matter. it is clear, ladies and treaty on european union. in the specific case of the lists of terrorist organisations, i would stress that the council has dealt with two lists. firstly, a confidential document drawn up by the terrorism group, which was taken up at the meeting on 7 december and which lists 34 terrorist organisations. until 1 june 2001 this list was part of the presidency's 'threat' document, which is confidential and has never been consulted by the european parliament. moreover, under the belgian presidency it was agreed to draw up a declassified document on the threat, to be sent to the european parliament and which the honourable members will receive as soon as the various language versions are completed. it is clear that no provision of the treaty requires the council to consult or inform parliament about this confidential document, which would lose its value if discussed in public, and that its ultimate addressee is the counter-terrorism services of the member states. the other council decision is 2001/927/ec, which contains a public list of terrorist individuals and organisations, linked to regulation (ec) no 2580/2001 and common positions 01/930 and 01/931. the adoption of these instruments responds to an exceptional situation in which the fulfilment of the mandate of the european council and un security council resolution 1373 took precedence over any other considerations. european public opinion demanded that we act quickly, visibly and decisively in the fight against terrorism. despite this urgency, the council consulted this house on regulation (ec) no 2580/2001, but changes in the legislative format, with the council having reserved implementing powers in accordance with article 202 of the treaty, confirmed by the case law of the court of justice, do not require consultation of parliament. the council presidency would nevertheless like to reiterate its willingness to involve the european parliament as far as possible in justice and home affairs within the framework of the treaties and will keep this house informed in the field of police and judicial cooperation. the presence of the first vice-president of the government and minister for the interior and the minister for justice of the presidency in this chamber in recent weeks underlines the willingness of the presidency to work with this parliament. finally, as regards the definition of a terrorist act, the text of common position 01/931 reflects the content of the council framework decision on which parliament was consulted.
- mr president, if we end this debate with a vote confirming the broad consensus we have reached so far on this subject, i would like to call on the groups in parliament not to change the report. we are going to renew our commitment to the fight against terrorism and we are going to complete a process which, as mr de miguel has reminded us, was started in the european parliament. i think that would be one of the most brilliant pages in this house. we now hope that these measures will be transposed quickly so that they become effective, that decisions will be taken to freeze the financial resources of european terrorist groups and that efforts to combat terrorism will be coordinated not only between the member states, as has been the case between spain and france, particularly in recent times, but also between the competent bodies set up within the european union. i am convinced, mr president, that this process is not only a response to a demand expressed very strongly by the citizens of europe, but also an essential contribution to the cause of freedom. there is no greater risk to freedom of thought, expression, to the very right to life, than violence expressed through terrorism. every democratic state has the obligation to put in the hands of the judiciary instruments such as those we are discussing today, which will make its work more effective. in a state governed by the rule of law, democratic dialogue must be based on mutual respect and non-violence, with the aim of defending democracy, as we literally said in one of the recitals of the report on the role of the union in the fight against terrorism. the opposite, ladies and gentlemen, would be to accept that the laws passed by democratically elected parliaments should be changed to give satisfaction to murderers and to stop them from killing; that claim, ladies and gentlemen, mr president, is to be rejected as undemocratic and immoral.

- doc. a5-0023/2002 by mr napolitano, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on relations between the european parliament and the national parliaments in the context of european integration (2001/2023 (ini))
- mr president, my first words are to congratulate president napolitano on his report, which has been rightly praised today and to which my group has not tabled proposals for substantial amendments but essentially for improvements. the report begins by making it clear that the european parliament and the national parliaments, each in its own sphere, fully represent the peoples of the union, who are, mr berthu, the holders of sovereignty, as their constitutions have stated for more than a century. i am grateful to the rapporteur for accepting my amendment, which is intended to recall this point, which is almost always invoked by those who want to strengthen one institution at the expense of other institutions. frankly, that approach is, and you'll forgive the expression, ridiculous. the european citizen needs a european parliament, just as he needs his national parliaments, and relations between them cannot be based on rivalry but on collaboration. the report not only reaffirms the need for this cooperation, but i think it is very realistic to ask that it be organized by means of an interparliamentary agreement in order to make better use of the resources available. the aim is to improve mutual information and to avoid overlapping of the various cooperation activities. the powers of national parliaments are also recalled, not only vis-à-vis the governments of the member states, but also in the application of community law. it turns out that they are powers far greater than what is usually known and said. if the national parliaments do not want to exercise them, then they can do so. mr president, national parliaments and the european parliament must work together, not compete. the report by president napolitano applies, without quoting it, the spanish saying that 'the clear things and the thick chocolate'. from a cordial and sympathetic point of view, it sets out clearly and extends its hand to a broad, solid and substantial partnership. let's give it a yes vote.
- mr president, mr napolitano has put the matter in its proper terms. legislative, budgetary and supervisory powers at national level are vested in the national parliaments. at the supranational level, these powers can only be exercised by a supranational parliament, whatever structure the convention or the future intergovernmental conference may give to that supranational parliament. mr napolitano stressed the importance of maintaining this difference of powers and, above all, pointed out the real danger that certain powers would escape the competence of national parliaments, as in the field of external relations and the third pillar, and that they would not be entrusted to a supranational parliament. there is another, much more subtle, way of eroding parliamentary power, which we are now analysing, and that is the emergence of the so-called open method of coordination of comitology, as applied, for example, in the lamfalussy report, with little possibility of parliamentary control, of self-regulation or co-regulation. i think that is something which the napolitano report has also mentioned and which we should pay attention to.
- mr president, i would first like to say that i agree with the rapporteur's congratulations on this excellent report. it is clear that the union must be constitutionalised, that the existing democratic deficit must be eliminated, that a division of powers must be established, with its own characteristics, and that this of course means parliamentarising the union by increasing the powers of the european parliament and the national parliaments. but in what areas? the powers of the european parliament, of course, in the control of community legislation and those of the national parliaments in the control of their own governments. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. but there is another point: in the debate on the future of europe, i believe that the role of the autonomous communities with legislative powers should also be addressed, in order to define their role in the union in a coherent and constructive way, with the aim, among other things, of bringing the process of european integration closer to the citizens and making it more effective. i think that is also how the role of the parliaments of the communities with legislative powers should be seen.
the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the maastricht treaty for the first time since the treaty of amsterdam. i would even say a new state of mind. i would like to thank you, mr napolitano, and congratulate you on behalf of the commission. the question of national parliaments, of the role they must play, the role they may be called upon to play in the future architecture of the union, is linked to the question of subsidiarity. it is also linked to the question of this shared legitimacy that goes along with shared sovereignty. in this respect, through the question of national parliaments and through the delimitation of powers on which your colleague alain lamassoure is working, the problem of subsidiarity is indeed being raised and will be one of the key issues of the convention through the constitutional process which will begin in a few days. it is therefore very useful, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, that we now have this very high-quality reflection from the european parliament which tells us why and how we should take better account of the national parliaments. why would you do that ? perhaps because this issue, from both its national and regional perspectives, has not been sufficiently taken into account, has not been sufficiently taken seriously by the union in the past years. i say this with the backwardness and the look i can have myself since i sat for 22 years in a national parliament. i can testify, as many of you will no doubt, to a certain sense of impotence on the part of national parliamentarians in the face of so many texts coming from brussels, only to be implemented and not to be discussed. in this sense of the accomplished fact, the frustration of national parliamentarians - the word was used by one of you - is not only directed at the commission, but equally at the council and the european parliament. the desire of parliament, as you express it forcefully, mr napolitano, to open a new stage in its relations with the national parliaments is an important and courageous gesture. this has been demonstrated for some time now by the active role played by your assembly in cosac, by the increase in formal and informal contacts between european and national parliamentarians - i can testify to this in connection with the preparation of the treaty of nice - and by the increase in administrative cooperation. the commission is naturally in favour of this new stage, because it is aware of the contribution that national parliaments can make to the building of the union. the more progress this construction makes, and we hope it will make, in sensitive areas of national sovereignty, particularly the second and third pillars, the more the question of the legitimacy of the whole system will be raised. objectively, for example, there is a shared interest in better monitoring of what is happening in the third pillar, which is of such interest to the citizens, and this monitoring could be strengthened by the communitization which the commission and parliament want together. i therefore believe that the approach of the union's institutions must respect two main principles. first, let us not oppose the two, because universal suffrage irrigates the european construction in many ways, directly for your assembly, indirectly for the council and the european council. i think that's a fortune. secondly, it is necessary to take account of the distribution of powers which is specific to each state, since the prerogatives and needs of each national parliament differ from one country to another. you are asking how the national parliaments can be better involved. the forthcoming opening of the convention, which many of you have mentioned, is in itself a first response to the wishes expressed by the national parliaments. it follows, as i said, the joint efforts of parliament and the commission and the will expressed by the 23rd cosac in versailles in october 2000. however, ladies and gentlemen, while no one disputes the importance or nature of the contribution of the national parliaments, there is no consensus, at least not yet, on the form that it could take. the recent report by mr chevalier and mr mahou to the european council in laeken says so unequivocally. we therefore know that two avenues can be opened: either indirectly, by improving the prerogatives of each national parliament in each of the member states, or directly, by introducing new procedures enabling national parliaments to intervene more directly in european decision-making. it is clear that the national and indirect path must be emphasized and strengthened and it is also clear that it is the preferred path for the majority. the commission does not have to judge the value of each institutional system. on the other hand, it can express its interest in the dissemination of all good practices - and we know that some practices in some member states are better than others - in the field of information and consultation. it can say that it is ready to consider an amendment to the amsterdam treaty protocol to take account of these good practices. the european way is more direct and probably more difficult to follow, because there are at the moment certain disagreements between the national parliaments themselves. but we shall have to think about this european and more direct approach, ladies and gentlemen, when we talk, for example, about the clarification of the council's legislative tasks, or when we take stock of the experiences which have already been shared in the framework of work with the european parliament and with the national parliaments. the commission, like your assembly, does not approve of the idea of a new chamber, which would in fact be a third chamber. the european decisionmaking process is already complicated enough as it is, not to mention, of course, the risks of institutional conflicts between this house and your own assembly, with which the commission has long shared and defended a certain vision and ambition for the community model. in conclusion, and you have said it very well, mr napolitano, the convention, which has not yet begun, will deal in particular with this key issue which is the subject of your report. some subjects can therefore be raised now and, without intending to express a specific opinion on subjects so closely linked to the institutional autonomy of each member state, antonio vitorino and i, who will be representing the commission in the convention, would like to say that we are ready to contribute our ideas and our help to this deepening. this could be the case, for example, with regard to the role of the constituent power of national parliaments or their role in the interpretation of the principle of subsidiarity. almost all of you, ladies and gentlemen, have spoken about this convention, which will keep us very busy from 28 february onwards. in any case, i repeat, one of the key issues for the success of this convention, to raise it to the highest possible level of ambition, will be our common capacity to convince, to engage, to work sincerely with the national parliaments and in this respect, mr president, i think that your report is not only courageous but that it will be very useful.

- report (a5-0006/2002) by mr pohjamo, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the management of regional policy and the structural funds (2001/2066 (ini))
- mr president, i begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mr pohjamo, on his initiative and work, because i do not think we are dealing with a joint report. it is an own-initiative report from parliament itself, in which we try to introduce new ideas to improve the management of the structural funds at a crucial moment for the whole of the european union and for the future of the fund. this report arises from the clear need to improve the management of regional policy as a whole and of the structural funds, the management of which requires greater flexibility and also responds to a general malaise in the european parliament. the margin of manoeuvre and influence of this parliament when the commission presents its reports is practically nil. we therefore believe that the time has come to give the funds and parliament a greater political role. it is time to make sure that the delays in the management of these important funds are not overlooked, that they are corrected and that new elements are introduced. we must distinguish between the budgetary efficiency of the funds and their real effectiveness. flexibility is certainly one element that will increase the real impact of the structural funds on society and on the greater cohesion we all seek. new elements must be introduced into the evaluation of these funds and more socioeconomic parameters, good practice, visibility and, of course, greater monitoring of the principle of additionality. we believe that with initiatives like this, when we vote on them tomorrow, we are bringing in new ideas that will improve the management of the structural funds and regional policy as a whole. we will thus arrive at the new agenda 2006 with a significant added value for all.
- we now adjourn the debate on this point to allow for question time. the debate will resume at 9 p.m.
- the agenda calls for question time in the council (b5-0002/2002)
- question no 1 by mr alexandros alavanos (h-0950/01) subject: inhuman conditions of detention in egyptian prisons mr kostas kastanias has been held since 1989 in an egyptian high security prison, where he is serving a sentence of life imprisonment with hard labour following the thanasis boat case. he is the only survivor, as the other two greek nationals who had been convicted and imprisoned in the same case succumbed to the ill-treatment and inhumane conditions of egyptian prisons. the last to die was mr tassos kontoyiannis: the circumstances in which he died are controversial. the council has been consulted on this matter in the past. the case has caused a stir in greek public opinion: the conditions prevailing in egyptian prisons are inhuman (three-meter-by-four-meter cells, where twenty prisoners are crouched) and mr kostas kastanias' health has been irreversibly damaged. could the council state whether it will use its influence to ensure that this prisoner can serve the remainder of his sentence in a greek prison?
the council has already taken note of the repeated request by mr alavanos and i would like to inform him that this will be submitted to the council to see if the presidency of the council of the european union can make an immediate visit to cairo, taking into account the state of health of the prisoner kostas kastanias, to whom mr alavanos refers.
- question no 2 by mr carlos carnero gonzález (h-0952/01): the commission has not yet decided on the matter. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. in the opinion of the author of this question, the essential collaboration between the eu and the us in the fight against terrorism is through strict respect for the basic principles and values of the rule of law. in the case of the countries of the union, these values include the abolition of the death penalty. the author of this question, in agreement with the main human rights organisations, therefore considers it absolutely necessary that any future agreement between the eu and washington should respect the letter and spirit of article 19 of the charter of fundamental rights, since the us continues to apply the death penalty and will also set up military courts. could the council undertake to consider article 19 (2) of the charter of fundamental rights as fully binding in any extradition agreement with the united states?
council. - the council would remind the honourable member that in the conclusions of the action plan of the extraordinary european council of 21 september, point 2 states that the european council calls for the implementation as soon as possible of all existing international conventions on the fight against terrorism, that is to say all those in the framework of the united nations and the oecd and other international bodies. the european union supports india's proposal to draw up a comprehensive convention on international terrorism within the united nations, which should reinforce the impact of the actions carried out over the past 25 years under the auspices of the united nations. in the context of its programme, the presidency considered it essential to achieve a common area in which the fight against all forms of crime, in particular the most serious forms of crime such as terrorism, trafficking in human beings, drug trafficking and money laundering, is articulated through common regulatory criteria and activities and shared by all member states. in this context, the presidency proposes that such important objectives as the european arrest warrant and the abolition of formal extradition procedures be defined. the presidency also considers it essential and a priority to strengthen relations between the european union and the united states, particularly in the context of judicial cooperation in criminal matters in the fight against terrorism. the council would like to recall that the question of the status of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union must be resolved in the context of the debate on the future of the union. the european council meeting in laeken on 14 and 15 december 2001 entrusted a convention with the task of answering the questions raised in this debate, in particular as to whether the charter of fundamental rights should be incorporated into the basic treaty and as to the accession of the european community to the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. without prejudice to the answer to this question, the council would also remind the honourable member that article 6 (2) of the treaty on european union states that 'the union shall respect fundamental rights as guaranteed by the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms signed in rome on 4 november 1950'. article 3 of the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, as it appears from the case-law of the european court of human rights, provides that no one may be removed, expelled or extradited to a state where he may be subjected to the death penalty, torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
- mr president-in-office of the council, i appreciate your answer, but i would like to reiterate the question. we all know that the necessary cooperation between democracies, and therefore between the european union and the united states, is under way in the fight against terrorism, but that cannot be an obstacle to the european union fully defending the values which are fundamental to it: in this case, the defence of the abolition of the death penalty. unfortunately, in the united states, as we all know, the death penalty is still in force. we also know that the convention will deal with the incorporation of the charter of fundamental rights into the future european constitution, but the charter was also proclaimed by the european council in nice and i believe that what is proclaimed has a binding political value for those who do so. in that context, mr president-in-office of the council, and in the light of your reference to the european convention on human rights, i ask you: will the european union extradite anyone accused of serious crimes, including terrorism, if there is a possibility that in the united states they will be sentenced to death or executed?
the council was in parliament's seat in the committee on foreign affairs when i said, in a very clear and definitive way, and i have the honour to repeat, that the european union will never - i repeat - never allow the extradition of any european citizen, under any kind of agreement with the united states, as long as there is no guarantee of two things - not one, but two - that the death penalty will never be applied and that he will never be tried by a military court of the kind that has just been introduced, precisely after 11 september. i said that in committee and i say it again in the house today. and, by the way, on the abolition of the death penalty, in a debate which took place in this very room a short while ago on the position of the european union in the commission on human rights, we also said that one of the flags of the position of the delegation of the european union and its member states in the commission on human rights is precisely to fight for the abolition of the death penalty in all countries of the world, without distinction of religion, culture, etc.
- question no 3 is therefore inadmissible.
council. - the european parliament is well aware of the dialogue between the european union and cuba, which was interrupted by the cuban authorities when they cancelled the meeting with the european union troika scheduled for april 2000. this dialogue was resumed on 1 and 2 december with the troika's visit to havana. the resumption of the dialogue was the result of the great activity of the presidency, on which the council has had the opportunity to inform this house extensively, particularly at its meetings in november and december. the council also had the opportunity to address this issue at the meeting of the acp-eu joint assembly held in brussels from 29 october to 1 november 2001. the council recalled, among other things, that it had never vetoed cuba's accession to the cotonou agreement but that it was cuba which withdrew its application for accession in may 2000. the council announced that it was prepared to consider the matter when cuba had formally submitted its candidacy in accordance with the provisions of the agreement. on 10 and 11 december the general affairs council carried out its tenth assessment of the union's common position and considered that it remained valid and formed the basis of the european union's policy towards cuba. the council also considered that it was essential to continue the dialogue initiated in order to achieve tangible results. in particular, with regard to future cooperation based on respect for the democratic principles of human rights, fundamental freedoms and the rule of law. in this context, the council recalled that it expected significant signals from the cuban government towards the achievement of the objectives of the common position. the council also reiterated that the objectives of the european union with regard to cuba remain to promote a process of transition towards democratic pluralism and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, a lasting economic recovery and an improvement in the living standards of the cuban people. after a detailed study and exchanges of information, the council also noted serious shortcomings in the recognition and implementation of civil and political freedoms and a refusal by the cuban authorities to consider the possibility of introducing reforms leading to a political system based on these values. the council nevertheless noted some positive signs: greater religious freedom, the non-application of the death penalty for two years, which brings us to the consideration which was the subject of the previous question, which is one of the union's policies. where the death penalty cannot be abolished, it is at least necessary to achieve the non-application of the death penalty, as well as a considerable reduction in the number of political prisoners and an increase in the ratification of un human rights instruments. these are the positive signs. the council also welcomed the decision of the cuban government to approve the country's accession to all the united nations conventions against terrorism, which was adopted at its meeting on 4 october. the council also recalled the importance which the european union attaches to cuba's adherence to the principles contained in the united nations pact on civil and political rights and the pact on economic, social and cultural rights, and expressed its wish that cuba should be able to sign both pacts as soon as possible. finally, i think it is important to note that in the context of the tenth evaluation of the european union's common position on cuba, the german delegation issued a statement in which it endorses the council's conclusions but calls on the commission to draw up an effective framework for cooperation in the short term. the council intends to assess its common position on cuba in the next six months in the light of the developments which have taken place during this period.
- we reiterate our friendship and personal esteem for the president-in-office of the council, but we understand that it was clumsy to ratify the common position. we believe that the common position is a negative thing, that in cuba everyone regards it as such, from the authorities to the opposition and the church, and that practically all the ambassadors of the countries of the european union in havana regard it as ineffective and even counterproductive. i think that the ratification of the common position has certainly produced a significant slowdown in the process of reopening dialogue, which we, like you, hoped for and for. the question i have to ask is: what is your response, what is the council's response to the repeated requests from the acp countries that cuba be treated like everyone else and be offered a place with guarantees as a signatory to cotonou? that is the question and i want to tell you, mr president-in-office of the council, in all sincerity, that we will put it again to you in a month's time in cape town, in the joint assembly, before all the acp partners, who have unanimously and repeatedly called for cuba to be included as a member of their community. thank you and welcome again, mr. de miguel.
counsel. - your honor, dear friend, when you ask me this question in cape town i will answer you the same way i'm answering you now. the european union has always taken a favourable position. i have told you, mr president, that when the cotonou agreement, which is now in force, was negotiated in february 2000, if i remember correctly, there was already a formal proposal from the acp committee to include cuba at the time the new convention was signed, with the full agreement of the council of the european union. to the surprise of the council and the acp countries, the cuban delegate - who was then the minister of industry - disappeared from the meeting, and there was no way to formalize this matter because cuba was not there to give its consent. when cuba is ready to accept not only the benefits but also the obligations of the cotonou convention, i can assure you that the presidency of the union and the council will be in full agreement. we'll have plenty of opportunities. you speak to me of the joint assembly and i speak to you of the ministerial meeting scheduled for the spanish presidency between the acp countries and the ministers of the council of the european union to be held in santo domingo. that can be as good an occasion as any. we will always be ready to give a positive response, as long as cuba can commit itself not only to the benefits but also to the obligations arising from the cotonou agreement.
- mr president-in-office of the council, my colleague miguel ángel martínez and i, who have been following political life together since 1977, have discussed these matters a lot and i would like to make a few points. firstly, what cuba wants - and this was expressed by foreign minister pérez roque to the parliamentary delegation - is for the european union to guarantee that if it asks for acp membership there will be no opposition on its part. before submitting your application, you want a formal assurance that there will be no opposition. secondly, mr martinez and i do not share the same perceptions of cuba. i was with members of the opposition, with dissidents, who literally told me that if you are not inside the regime, you simply do not exist. secondly, as regards the assessments of the ambassadors, there was a friendly discussion - at least at the meeting i attended - but i would like to know how it is possible that the opinion of all the governments, with the nuanced reservation of germany, is contrary to that which, according to mr martinez, was expressed by the ambassadors: the latter, in favour of establishing a dialogue without conditions, the governments, in favour of maintaining the common position as far back as december. i would ask the president-in-office of the council if he agrees with me that the cuban government still has a long way to go to fulfil its obligations under the democratic clause, both for an association agreement and for establishing other links with the european union, and i would like to see it extended to the issue of economic freedom, fundamental rights - what used to be called formal democracy, which we all now share - and political pluralism, which are the conditions of the common position.
- mr de miguel, i do not encourage you to give a general answer as the honourable member is asking, but to answer this question with the brevity to which we are accustomed.
the council has not yet taken a decision on the matter, and i would like to ask the commissioner to take a decision on the matter. i have already said in my reply that the european union is in a positive mood, provided that cuba is prepared to accept the obligations of the cotonou convention and a relationship with the european union which has its conditions, as everyone knows.
question no 5 by mrs maría izquierdo rojo (h-0959/01) subject: spanish presidency and the inhumane living conditions of afghan women
the council has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the conclusions of the european council in madrid. at its meeting on 10 december, the council welcomed the petersberg agreement, which defines the interim arrangements applicable in afghanistan, and reiterated its commitment to play an important role in the international effort to contribute to the reconstruction of afghan society and economy. the ministers also stressed the special need to promote the role of women in afghan society. during the recent ministerial conference on the reconstruction of afghanistan held in tokyo on 21 and 22 january, the presidency of the european commission, in its capacity as co-chairmen of the union in the steering group on the reconstruction of afghanistan, explained the union's position to the other international donors and the afghan interim authority. the union delegation stated, inter alia, that the european union's assistance would be conditional on all afghan groups fully implementing the spirit and letter of the petersberg agreement, the aim of which is the establishment of a broad-based, multi-ethnic, fully representative government committed to gender equality and the improvement of the situation of women. the european union also stressed in tokyo the importance of afghanistan taking over the emergency aid, rehabilitation and development tasks, and of involving people from all regions and ethnic groups, and especially women. the council will continue to monitor closely compliance with these criteria in the months and years ahead. in this connection, the council would recall that the european union's special representative in afghanistan, ambassador kleiber, has already started his work in kabul, assisted by a special representative of the presidency, ambassador lópez nadal. the council will take particular care to ensure that women can participate and participate fully in shaping the future of the country. in this same context, the council also refers to the answer to oral question h-0897/2001.
- in recent years, taliban fundamentalism has preyed on women, and even today its effects continue to ruin the lives of afghan women. the men are still armed and this poses a clear threat. the day before yesterday, mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, a seven-year-old girl was sold into marriage to satisfy her family's hunger and needs. the president-in-office of the council has given me a very firm answer, which was already known. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is prepared to take any further action to ensure that the sale of seven-year-old girls for marriage does not continue. would you at least be prepared to convey the urgency of taking some kind of measures to prevent this horror?
council. - mr president, i would like to reply to mrs izquierdo rojo that the union's policy on afghanistan is absolutely indivisible and applies to all violations of human rights, and particularly women's rights. the case you mention is just one more in the list of horrors and outrages suffered by many human beings in afghanistan, children and adults, men and women. and so the union's policy on all these issues has been and will always be the same. i can assure you that we will take action and try to strengthen our political action in afghanistan and will make all assistance conditional on the safeguarding of these rights, including also preventing the sale of minors for marriage.
council. - what we are trying to do is a comprehensive development plan for afghanistan, which we have just begun. we now have the financial means, which are, of course, considerable, since the european union's contribution has been, as the honourable member knows, very important, the most important of the international community. but there are also other members of the international community who have contributed. we now have the resources to carry out the necessary development programmes and, of course, the development of small and mediumsized enterprises is, in the eyes of the whole world, one of the fundamental elements of the development of afghanistan, where, in the short term, it cannot be expected that there will be major investments in large industries and large projects, and we will therefore begin to coordinate all these programmes with the commission. we are of course very aware that in small and medium-sized enterprises women have a very important role and that will revalue the role of women within afghanistan.
- mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, during the taliban presence in afghanistan and before, the situation of women has been deplorable. they've been marginalized, humiliated, persecuted. they have even been taught to believe and think that this is normal, making it difficult for them to change. we cannot accept the sale of girls, the fact that women are still marginalised and that their human rights are not recognised. that is why parliament thinks that the spanish presidency of the union could do something more, some special programme of support for these women who have suffered a particular marginalization, because the current situation in afghanistan cannot really be compared with the reconstruction of other countries at war. could you elaborate on the answer already given by the president-in-office on this situation?
the council has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the conclusions of the tokyo summit, and it is therefore important that the commission should be able to take a decision on the matter. the total marginalisation of women in the afghan education system is well known; by depriving them of education they have been totally marginalized from access to all the goods of society. i know that commissioner patten and the relevant directorate-general of the commission are coordinating all these programmes, one of whose fundamental objectives - i repeat - is the recovery of women in afghan society. i am not in a position to give you details at the moment, but i will of course convey to the commission the concern here expressed by the european parliament that there should be a special dedication of the funds to programmes directly aimed at the recovery of the role of afghan women in society.
- question no 6 by mrs rosa miguélez ramos (h-0963/01): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the victims of the floods in the canary islands. subject: attendance of regional governments at council meetings the federal, regional or decentralised structure of several member states has led them to include representatives of their regions or länder in their delegations to meetings of the council of ministers, as the treaty on european union has allowed them to do since the reform of the treaty in maastricht ten years ago. regional representations are now at the head of the member state delegation; during the belgian presidency they even chaired councils of ministers when the subject fell within their competence. in other member states, such as spain, where there are regions or autonomous communities with broad legislative powers, the central government prevents the regions or autonomous communities from being part of its delegations to the various council meetings, even when the competence lies exclusively with those regions and not with the central government. what is the council's position on this situation ? which member states, whose federal or autonomous political structure is similar to that of spain, include representatives of their nations and regions in their delegations? which member states do not do this? does the spanish presidency intend to promote the participation of these regions or autonomous communities now that the regions have been recognised at the laeken summit?
council. - the council would remind the honourable member that article 203 of the treaty establishing the european community provides that the council shall be composed of a representative of each member state, of ministerial rank, empowered to commit the government of that member state. under this provision, it is the sole responsibility of each state to decide how it will be represented at council meetings and who will be part of its delegation. this decision will inevitably depend on national constitutional arrangements which differ from one member state to another, because each member state has its own constitution and its own territorial organisation. the council cannot therefore comment on representation decisions taken individually by a member state.
- mr president, it is a temple-like truth that the representative of the council has just reminded us: each member state is sovereign to decide, of course, on the composition of its delegation at each council meeting. however, i believe that when a national delegation does not have representatives of the regional governments, who have, in some cases, exclusive competence, at these council meetings, this creates a distance between the community and the citizens on the one hand and their representatives on the other. some will call it distancing, others will call it a democratic deficit, and even more so when some communities do have the possibility of being represented in the regions and others do not. in certain member states, such as mine, the regions, the autonomous communities, are as much a state as the central government, as reflected in the constitution. the president of my region, galicia, is himself a strong supporter of this regional involvement. however, it is argued that it is the government of the nation that has the representation in foreign policy, and i ask you: does the council believe that decisions on internal community policies, such as fisheries, agricultural or consumer policy, are part of international or foreign foreign policy or does it believe that these are internal community matters?
the council has already taken a decision on the matter, and i am sure that the council will take a decision on it in due course. the regions may have their powers within a framework of decentralisation and the transfer of powers from the state to the local authorities. the transfer of powers varies from one state to another and in many countries is entirely different. even in countries which have made a major transfer of powers, such as germany, austria or spain, the systems are completely different. you cannot compare the german federal system with the system of the autonomous regions of the spanish state. the representation of the state is therefore mainly achieved through internal cooperation and each state can, within the framework of this cooperation, represent the interests of the territorial entities in its territory in the way that best suits the general interests of the country as a whole. i will tell you that community policies are not matters of foreign policy but of community policy, but i would remind you that in community policy the representatives in the council are the member states of the european union and it is for them to defend the positions which affect all those countries according to their own constitutional system. we therefore assume that each country applies the constitution as it is written, and that does not mean that the quality of the representation of the interests of the territorial communities depends on this or that system.
- i am grateful for the council's reply, because it shows that the council cannot break the principle of institutional autonomy by which we govern ourselves. secondly, i would like to point out that spain has been a member of the european union since 1986 and that this institutional framework has been respected since then. also during the whole period of socialist governments. thirdly, i would say that there are no homogeneous positions on this debate, not even in the academic field, in the positions that the different autonomous communities can defend. i would therefore like to ask you whether you do not think it would be more fruitful to improve the role of the committee of the regions in the work of the union.
the council. - the european convention is about to begin its work. it will be attended by representatives of governments, national parliaments, the european parliament and the commission. representatives of the committee of the regions and the economic and social committee are also invited. nothing prevents any country from accrediting, within the parliamentary delegation or the government delegation, persons who are sensitive to the problems of the regions. therefore, your honour, each country is free to accredit to that convention whomever it wishes. neither the presidency nor the council intend to influence the debate within the convention. the debate will be open and free. all issues concerning the regions may be dealt with within the convention and the convention shall make such recommendations as it deems appropriate to the intergovernmental conference on the importance of the role of the regions in the decision-making process of the union. the intergovernmental conference will decide on this in due course.
- you know very well that only one supplementary question can be asked. there have been procedural motions, and i will accept them, but i ask you not to abuse them.

beyond state and regional governments, i.e. local communities, ngos, private entities, etc. - is beneficial to the achievement of economic, social and territorial cohesion in the union, we do not consider that such cooperation has been satisfactorily respected in all member states, but has been applied unevenly. we therefore urge the commission to ensure that socioeconomic and environmental cooperation is regularly implemented in all regions receiving community funds and to ensure that the programming of projects is consulted with the parliaments and governments of the constitutional regions with legislative powers. we also demand that it develop clear indicators to assess the application of this principle of cooperation. we also hope that, in the framework of the guidelines for the mid-term evaluation of september 2002, the commission will define indicators for the allocation of the efficiency reserve which, in addition to financial management, will take account of other aspects of management, such as cooperation, additionality and the quality of expenditure. at the same time, we ask that, in the event of reallocation of unspent resources, unused appropriations be allocated to the most active and innovative disadvantaged regions and to measures to promote sustainable development. finally, supporting the rapporteur's idea of including the quality aspect in the annual monitoring of programmes subsidised by the commission, we propose that the contribution of these programmes to the implementation of the union's strategies for sustainable development and employment be assessed. we hope that our amendments will have the support of the majority of parliament, because they will serve to improve our community economic and social objectives.

- the next item is the report (a5-0007/2002) by mr musotto, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the second report from the commission to the council, the european parliament, the economic and social committee and the committee of the regions on economic and social cohesion (com (2001) 24 - c5-0527/2001 - 2001/2207 (cos)).
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, there is a differential feature in european regional policy, marked by geography, which defines the outermost regions. they are remote, isolated, fragmented and highly dependent on the outside world, and have developed unevenly since the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, which allowed specific measures to be taken to correct their backwardness. the authorities of these regions have recently met in the canary islands to discuss, with the representatives of the european commission and the three states concerned, the situation of economic and social cohesion in these unique regions. i am sure that, in addition to asking for special treatment, they have asked for some of the measures that mr musotto is asking for today in his report - which i also congratulate - in which he stresses the need to differentiate between statistical convergence and real convergence, and the need to use alternative indicators to income per capita, such as unemployment, the lack of infrastructure, the shortage of transport and energy, dual insularity, the formation of human resources and the ozone index in the outermost regions. i am sure that this will not limit its economic and social development and that europe will have made a clear demonstration of solidarity between its peoples.

located in the future member states (and that is almost all the regions of the future member states) or in the member states of the present union. so priority and focus on the regions that are really lagging behind. second point of convergence: cohesion, as many of you have mentioned, is not a matter for a single policy, but for all community policies, which, as the treaty provides, must energy, competition, research, employment and many other policies. more than ever before, each of these policies must contribute to greater economic and social cohesion, if only because of the challenge that the great enlargement will bring, which, as we see in our second interim report, will increase disparities and inequalities. thirdly, we must go beyond a minimum cohesion policy and or islands; the commission's proposals are based on the following principles: i'm waiting for your ideas on this, but i've already told you where i'm going. fourth point of convergence: to meet all
