is undoubtedly the credibility threshold below which i believe we cannot go down without calling into question the very essence of this cohesion policy. the fact that parliament and the commission are giving a common response to these four points is for me an important and useful political element in the debate on the future of cohesion policy. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we must therefore - i am thinking of the question put to mr izquierdo collado earlier - prove, prove again, that this cohesion policy has worked, that it has borne fruit, that it has helped to create greater cohesion, but that we still need it. i can't do this demonstration alone. you can count on me to do it at commission level, with all my colleagues; but i cannot do it if the regions, the member states and the elected members of parliament do not contribute to this demonstration. it is also normal at this stage that we do not have complete agreement on all the subjects raised in mr musotto's report. there are points of debate or discussion between us: this is the case, for example, with regard to the instruments of this future cohesion policy, the place of the community initiatives, that of the cohesion fund or a possible single fund for regional development. all this will of course depend on the level of ambition we can give to this policy. another point of discussion is the choice of eligibility criteria. the commission has long used the criterion of gdp per capita and per region to determine which regions are lagging behind in development. it seems to me that this is a reliable, simple and transparent indicator, accepted by all member states; and it is in order to maintain objectivity and impartiality in this approach that we do not propose at this stage to add any other criteria to the per capita gdp criterion. however, ladies and gentlemen, this does not mean that the commission will remain deaf to the appeals of regions which could be affected by enlargement, by a statistical effect, which many of you have mentioned, that of the mathematical fall in the community average of gdp per capita or the fall, also mathematical, of the eligibility threshold, which would mean that certain regions which still have great problems (not only in southern europe, but in east germany, england and elsewhere) would be mechanically, artificially, above the threshold, even though they still have real difficulties. i am committed, as i said, to proposing a fair and community solution when the time comes to continue to support the regions which would thus be just above the new threshold of eligibility. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use and the development of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use is a good one. i have noticed that in the current programmes - those which i have signed and which are being launched - there are more programmes which are directly focused on quality rather than quantity than in the previous period. finally, i do not forget and will not forget the special attention that is due (not only under article 299 of the treaty, but also because of the reality of their problems and an unbearable rate of unemployment) to the seven outermost regions of the union. i hope, ladies and gentlemen, that these few explanations will have helped to further advance the level of consensus between parliament and the commission, so that we can together preserve and promote this model of european society, at the heart of which is cohesion. one of you mentioned - and i would like to finish on this point - the appropriations we have proposed for the countries that will join the union, probably in 2004. i do not share the very harsh judgment expressed by mrs schroedter earlier. i don't think that's fair. i know. we have proposed a phasing-in. these countries already benefit from the cohesion fund and they have - i regret that mrs schroedter is no longer here to hear my answer - great difficulty in using these funds. and it is for this reason of realism that i have proposed, together with my colleagues, that we should enter gradually into cohesion policy. i'm not looking for a gimmick or a display. i do not want the european money for the candidate countries which will join the union in 2004 to remain in brussels or to return to brussels. that is why we are proposing more money, ambitiously, beyond what was proposed in the berlin agenda for the first year of accession, but not to the extent that this money cannot be used by countries which do not yet have the administrative equipment to manage these appropriations. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i will stop here. finally, i confirm that the commission should adopt the third report on cohesion in december 2003 and that this report should be able to indicate the commission's orientations for the future agenda. this would therefore be done much earlier than usual, so that we can, as i said earlier, start the actual implementation of the new programming on the ground at the beginning of this new agenda, in 2007, and not two years later. we still have a few months to conduct and succeed in this political debate on cohesion policy so that, if we manage to conduct this debate (and i need you to do so), we will arrive, in due course, at a decision by the heads of state and government which will not only be faithful to the cohesion at the heart of a certain model of european society, but which will enable these heads of state to take on board the political and strategic choice they made in budgetary and financial terms when they decided to proceed with the reunification of the european continent with the great enlargement which is being prepared in a very few years. we will accompany them and i personally hope that from the next agenda, in 2007, they will be able to benefit, like all the other member states, from the full range of cohesion policy.
- doc. a5-0012/2002 by mr hatzidakis, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 92/6/eec on the installation and use of speed limitation devices on certain categories of motor vehicles in the community (com (2001) 318 - c5-0267/2001 - 2001/0135 (cod)).
the commission's proposal is based on the principle of subsidiarity, which is the basis of the directive, and it is therefore in line with the principle of subsidiarity. the proposal aims to extend the scope of the mandatory installation and use of speed limitation devices to vehicles in categories lighter than those currently affected by these limitations. this measure is the implementation of the priorities set out in march 2000 in the commission's communication on road safety, which was also explicitly supported by this parliament. the proposal will contribute to improving road safety, protecting the environment and maintaining conditions of fair and equal competition between all operators within the european union. i should like to make a few comments on the report to which your attention is drawn. there are several amendments which we can support: amendments nos 4, 6 and 7 can be accepted in their entirety; nos 5 and 10 are acceptable in principle, although pending an adjustment of dates, and so is amendment no 6, which i referred to earlier. the commission would prefer the following timetable: two years for new vehicles, three years for international transport and four years for domestic transport. i think that this answers some of mr jarzembowski's questions about the effects on small and mediumsized enterprises, which are the ones that use these types of vehicles the most. there is a time for adaptation and, if we take into account the turnover of these types of vehicles, the time for the directive to come into force, etc., we see that it is no longer so out of place. as regards amendment no 9, the commission could accept a study in the context of road safety by 2010, provided that it is not a separate report. in any case, the 18-month period is too short to carry out such a study, we need at least two years. in this connection, i would like to stress the great importance for the commission of intelligent speed adaptation systems, which will be a subject of study to which the greatest attention will be paid. amendments nos 8 and 11 are conceptually unacceptable to the commission. the acceptance of higher maximum speeds for a limited period of time not only raises technical problems for which there is no solution, at least at present, but would also make the implementation of the measure more difficult. the commission considers that there is no advantage at present in applying this directive to m1 and n1 vehicles. the commission cannot accept amendment no 12, which was supported by mr jarzembowski, among others, because the directive's triple objective - road safety, environmental protection and competition on equal terms - cannot be achieved if the same speed limit is not imposed on all vehicles. finally, we will examine carefully amendments nos 1, 2 and 3, which refer to the textual differences between the language versions, as regards the definition of vehicles. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and all the members who have spoken in this debate. i hope that the implementation of this directive will improve road safety, which is what is intended, because the figure of 42 000 deaths a year is totally unacceptable to all of us.
- this debate is over. the vote will take place on thursday at 12 noon.
- the next item is the report (a5-0001/2002) by mr marques, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposals for council decisions authorising france to extend the application of a reduced rate of excise duty on 'traditional' rum produced in its overseas departments (com (2001) 347 - c5-0401/2001 - 2001/0142 (cns)) 2. authorising portugal to apply a reduced rate of excise duty in the autonomous regions of madeira to rum and liqueurs produced and consumed there, and in the autonomous region of the azores to liqueurs and spirits produced and consumed there (com (2001) 442 - c5-0422/2001 - 2001/0169 (cns)).
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. as indicated in these reports and in the commission's proposals, these measures are absolutely necessary to maintain local production of rum, traditional in the french overseas departments, and of rum, liqueurs and spirits, traditional in madeira and the azores. these traditional activities are very important for the economy of these regions and their maintenance is essential to ensure the economic, social and territorial balance of these regions of the european union. i would like to say something about the legal basis of the proposals, as they have been the subject of some controversy and have been referred to by the rapporteur himself, mr marques. both are based on the application of the second paragraph of article 299 of the ec treaty, which is, in fact, the one which refers to the outermost regions. this provision allows the council to adopt specific measures, which may derogate from other fundamental provisions of the treaty, and establishes the conditions for the application of the treaty to regions which - it must be said very clearly - have very different specificities, due precisely to their ultraperipheral nature. i would point out, ladies and gentlemen, that this provision was included in the treaty of amsterdam in order to create a common legal basis for action in favour of these regions. these measures should allow for the full integration of these regions into the union, while recognising their specific characteristics, such as their remoteness and the dependence of their economies on a small number of products, many of which are related to traditional and craft activities. the commission therefore considers that this second paragraph of article 299 of the treaty is the legal basis for the formulation of these proposals and others which may come at some future time.

- the next item is the report (a5-0005/2002) by mr glante, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the proposal for a council regulation on the establishment of a galileo joint undertaking (com (2001) 336 - c5-0329/2001 - 2001/0136 (cns)).
commission. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr glante for his report. i would also like to thank mr savary and mr chichester, the whole sky and space team and all the members of the european parliament who signed a document supporting the galileo programme for the european council in laeken. unfortunately, we did not succeed on that occasion, but let us hope that we will succeed next time. we must not be discouraged and we still have a margin of time, albeit a very short one, to try once and for all to carry forward a project which i believe is absolutely crucial for europe and which, moreover, will be a reflection of europe's real will to be and to be in the international arena. i shall concentrate on only three aspects of the report which have been mentioned here. we all think it is crucial that the private sector should be involved. the differences lie in how and from what moment, if i understand correctly. i would like to say in that connection - as mr savary and mrs langenhagen have said - that, regardless of the outcome of the amendments to mr glante's report, i hope that the report as it stands after the amendments or without them will have the greatest possible support, regardless of my preference for one formula or another. we believe that the private sector should be involved from the outset, not only because of the limited funds it will provide during the development phase from 2002 to 2005, but also because in the medium term it is up to the private sector to make a substantial contribution in the next phase, not only in the deployment phase but also in the operational phase. a substantial increase in the financial participation of the private sector is an essential condition for securing the necessary public funding in the subsequent phases under the future financial perspective. i would like to say that the involvement of the private sector is not something that is improvised, but something that must be prepared now, and that was reflected in the resolution of the council of ministers in april last year. the commission proposal which is being tabled today merely puts this principle into practice. it is true that there is a suggestion, the one put forward by mr glante, whereby that direct participation is replaced by the creation of the joint venture, by the creation of a development company parallel to the joint venture, which to us, as i have said, does not seem sufficient. we believe that participation must take place within the company and that there is also a clear will, not only from the space sector but also from the applications sector, to enter this phase already, in this public or private participation. i would also like to say that by participating in the capital of the joint venture, industry is already taking on a minimum of risk, and i think that is desirable, because it must also participate in the final definitions of the architecture of the whole system. some in the council and in parliament fear that conflicts of interest will arise. i believe that national legislation today provides for formulas to avoid such conflicts of interest. as i have said on several occasions, we are giving aid and financing programmes, while there is a bank which acts as a financial adviser on the aid, while, linked to that bank, there is a non-governmental organisation which is the one who makes the programme and while, also linked to that bank, there is a study group which assesses the reality of the programme. and we say that all of that is correct and that there are enough barriers to ensure that no interrelationship of interests is possible. i think that in this case there are even more concrete and clearer ways, the famous chinese wall, that would allow us to avoid this kind of problem. article 9 of the statute states that, in the proposal we are making, the executive committee must act in matters of procurement with complete independence from the board of directors on which the companies participating in the joint venture would be represented, that is to say, the executive committee acts outside the companies which may possibly participate in the tenders. to avoid worrying, there are formulas that can give greater guarantees. as regards the role of the member states, we fully support the approach in mr glante's report, namely the creation of a monitoring committee composed of representatives of the member states, so that they can closely and continuously monitor the activities of the joint venture. that is why we have proposed to the council, and the council has approved it, that in the regulation - not in the statutes of the joint venture, but in the regulation - a supervisory board be set up, composed of representatives of the states. it shall meet before each meeting of the governing board of the joint undertaking to decide on the positions which the commission intends to take on the various items on the agenda. these operating rules seem to us the most appropriate to achieve our objective, since they maintain the autonomy of the operation of the joint venture while allowing the states to monitor the action of the commission, which represents the european community on the board of directors of the joint venture. as regards the military dimension, i would say that galileo is a system designed for civilian purposes, which must be managed by civilians and that, moreover, is one of the essential differences with gps. that said, it's true that there is a service reserved for public administrations, which is intended for applications like firefighters and security, which at a given time can be used for other purposes, but it is that today the open gps is being used in some applications and in some military uses. we can hardly prevent them from carrying a device synchronized with galileo. i would like to say, ladies and gentlemen, that these systems are always dual-use. secondly, as the honourable members know, there is a free access signal, totally free of charge, and another access signal, which is paid for, with some services, coded, but which is also free. and a third signal reserved for the public sector, but - i insist - that is intended, not for military use but for civilian use as i have indicated. ladies and gentlemen, with regard to galileo, all the elements for a decision are now on the table of the council of ministers, the funding for the whole development phase, without any eu country having to put in one more euro to carry the project forward. it must be made very clear that the current financial perspective covers the whole development phase of galileo. no state would have to put in an extra euro. galileo is essential for european industry, for technological capacity, for european space technology, but also for a number of other elements, such as autonomy, sovereignty and the ability to offer an alternative service to gps, which would strengthen it, because, as we have consistently said, galileo will be and should always be compatible with gps, both should be mutually reinforcing, and, in the event of failure of one of the two, the other should serve as an alternative for all users. the only thing to be seen is whether or not there is the political will, and i think this is one of those occasions when we will know whether or not there is the political will to go forward with a europe that counts in the world. the ball, as we say in spain, is in the ministers' court and i hope they will decide to do so.

republic of congo, a situation of poverty aggravated by the war that has ravaged the country since 1996. data have already been presented: it has been said that over 300,000 people need assistance, that 30% of the population is homeless and that 12,000 homes need to be rebuilt. in this respect, the resolution we adopted this week, which establishes links between emergency aid, rehabilitation and what development policy is, has been very timely. the second reality is the hatred that has been growing between the people of the east and the population of neighbouring rwanda, hatred that has been demonstrated by the rejection by the population of goma of the hospitality offered by rwanda and the mass return of this population to their lands, already invaded by the volcano, despite the risks of a new eruption. these two realities should lead us to a strategy and action by the european union that will enable us to get involved in this region. it is true that a good policy is needed to rebuild goma, to anticipate possible new eruptions and to control the miragongo volcano. however, this whole strategy will not achieve effective results unless the foundations of a democratic regime with a broad social consensus are consolidated in the country, guaranteeing stability and peace. nor will it be of any use if there is no confidence in that stability among the whole region. it is therefore important that this inter-congolese dialogue which is being resumed in south africa in sun city put an end to this conflict. we also believe that it is important to organise a regional conference to reconcile the countries of the great lakes region and to restore the lost confidence of the various peoples of the region. the resolution we are presenting is a set of wills, principles and strategies which we want to see applied to deal with the eruption of the miragongo volcano, without losing sight of the above. we support the overall plan for 2000 managed by eco and we ask that this plan, which is very important for the african region and for the achievement of the objectives set out above, be speeded up and that this aid does not arrive late, as has unfortunately happened many times. - mr president, commissioner, i wish to point out that i am speaking in place of my colleague, mr pérez álvarez, who was the alternative rapporteur for this report on behalf of my group and who was unable to be present at this sitting. i would like to thank the rapporteur, on his behalf and on my own, first of all for the work he has done and for the positive attitude he has taken to the amendments tabled by my colleague. directive 93/104/ec is a continuation of directive 89/391/ec on the introduction of measures to encourage improvements in the safety and health of workers at work, with the idea that the completion of the internal market should lead to an improvement in working, living and working conditions through the approximation of legislation. in this sense, the commission's report provides an overview of how the member states have transposed and applied the directive, with results that clearly indicate that the method and the result can be improved. it was not only possible to verify the temporary delay in complying with the deadline for transposition and, consequently, the failure to apply the directive within the deadline, but also that the exclusions and exceptions were due to criteria which were not always clear. the transposition of the directive by means of collective agreements has not always been accompanied by the success desired for this instrument of social dialogue. the amendments tabled by mr pérez álvarez were intended to highlight and remedy these shortcomings, and the amendments i am now going to comment on are also designed to do so. the first is that the confusion of the concepts of 'exclusion' and 'exception', the latter always singular, must not lead to the possibility of circumventing the mandatory nature of the terms of the directive. the commission has also proposed a clarifying addition, which is not intended to replace but to clarify and extend the content of the paragraph, including through concepts and definitions that ensure the application of the directive, in keeping with the idea that things are what they are and not what they are called. we believe it is important to emphasize these two points in order to improve the living and working conditions of workers. all this in the terms of article 31 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union 'fair and equal working conditions'. first, that 'every worker has the right to work in conditions which respect his health, safety and dignity', and secondly, that 'every worker has the right to limitation of maximum working hours and to daily and weekly rest periods, as well as to a period of paid annual leave', both aspects - occupational health and working time - clearly linked, all aimed at a fairer society in which respect for the individual and collective rights of workers prevails.

mediterranean countries to work together with our men. we therefore turned to the bank, but we have understood its concern, mr president, the concern of all the people here and of the member states, and so the commission's proposal is a bank, the majority of which is in the hands of the european investment bank, the commission, the various shareholder countries and, above all, the southern mediterranean countries, which will start, yes, with a modest share but which will then increase their presence in the bank itself. as regards the last question, i do not think the commission needs to special assessment. we have stuck to what is our great obligation to obey the mandates we have. and we will continue to do so in the future.

- mr president, i wish to address the house precisely to discuss the subject of sustainable development at the barcelona european council. the commission's resolution obviously has many interesting points, but with regard to amendment no 10, which deals with the information and sustainability reports it has to issue to grant the structural funds and with regard to the spanish national hydrological plan, i want to say that i am very concerned because the sustainability criteria are not well defined today. what we consider sustainable is not well defined and this lends itself to subjective views, to propaganda and to unfair views. i believe that the criteria for defining sustainability must be developed with an open mind, because comprehensive policy requires that the multifaceted nature of sustainability be integrated. but territorial criteria must also be taken into account. objective and territorial parameters must therefore be used, with the understanding that sustainable development always affects a specific territory. in this sense, climate change, for example, cannot be applied only to gas emissions, it must also be applied to desertification, which is perfectly quantifiable, to rainfall. but i'm also worried about something else. if we have managed to make sustainability and the environment a transversal project, the environment must also open the door to social and economic criteria. there is no sustainability without an assessment of the social impact, the habitability of the territories, the negative economic impact and the costs. so either we enrich the criteria for sustainable development or we create situations of asymmetry, of injustice, making it even more difficult to develop energy and water policies in the future.

of quality and security of supply, which cannot be reduced. i think that economic experience does not in any way indicate that competition in the market economy has made countries that have it worse off than those that do not have it, but the opposite. however, efficiency in allocating resources and thus prices to consumers can be extraordinarily beneficial. spain is a good example of this. the spanish household consumers have saved €2.4 billion since 1996 as a result of the liberalisation of the electricity market, and the same could be said for telecommunications and other markets. i will continue with the same example, highlighting the efforts made by spanish society in terms of modernising the labour market, which has enabled the unemployment rate in spain to fall from 23% in 1995 to 12% in 2002, and which will bring the unemployment rate to 9% during the current spanish legislature, that is to say, by the year 2004, in the european context. so liberalisation and competition are not a risk to citizens, but quite the opposite, there is a considerable saving in what is paid for public services, and there is a considerable increase in employment, and it is undoubtedly the responsibility of public authorities, of regulators, to ensure issues such as the quality of service or the sufficiency of supply. i believe that the experience, not only of spain but of many other countries in the union, supports this point. what is certain, ladies and gentlemen, is that we are now fortunately at the end of a recession which has been very intense and relatively rapid, as the chairman of the federal reserve, mr greenspan, assures us this afternoon, and what europe needs is capacity for economic growth. many of the objectives which you have set out, such as environmental, social, health, education and quality of life objectives, require economies to grow to their potential, and i would remind the european parliament that in the last ten years the european economy as a whole has only grown by more than 3% a year, and that in the other years it has not been able to grow by 3%. an economy in such conditions has to take comfort in a structural unemployment rate of around 9 or 10%, and i am convinced that no group in this house considers that to be good policy, not economic but social policy. i believe that the introduction of the euro has indeed shown that - the agenda calls for the council statement on the international criminal court. i must remind members that, given the lack of time, they must scrupulously observe the speaking time allotted to them.
the council. - mr president, i am very pleased to appear before you today to set out the position of the presidency of the council on the steps the european union is taking to achieve the forthcoming establishment of the international criminal court. the european union has strongly supported the historic project of creating a permanent international criminal court with universal jurisdiction. this parliament knows this well, since it has always been at the forefront of the effort to push european union action towards this transcendent goal for human rights and justice. i would therefore like to reiterate to you that the creation of the international criminal court is an important part of the union's foreign policy and is therefore on the agenda of the spanish presidency. the european union welcomes in particular the imminent achievement of this objective, which we have been waiting for so long and which we all have confidence will be achieved in the course of this year. it is difficult to overstate the importance of this fact, which has been fought for by so many eminent jurists, human rights defenders and political leaders, and which is now truly within our grasp. it will be a victory for all mankind, which will be due, in no small measure, to the resolute and consistent action of the european union. the collective experience of our continent, which has been mired in conflict and horror for the past century, makes us europeans particularly sensitive to the urgent need to develop and strengthen international criminal justice as an instrument for human rights and humanitarian standards throughout the world. it is therefore no surprise that european countries and the european union as a whole are at the forefront of this movement for the international criminal court, a truly universal, independent and effective court. the european union is firmly convinced that the establishment of the international criminal court will be a step of great significance for the whole world. when very serious crimes are committed which offend every civilized conscience, when collective values are attacked head-on, the international community must react with the full force of law and justice. the most serious violations of human rights and international law must be vigorously combated and adequately punished, using the mechanisms agreed within the community of states. the international criminal court will be a valuable instrument in that struggle for justice and against impunity for the most heinous crimes, which are war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. in a broader context, the creation of the international criminal court is part of a movement which has characterized the evolution of our world in recent years, i am referring to the emergence and consolidation of an international criminal justice system which pursues particularly serious behaviour beyond the borders of states because it constitutes a serious threat to the security of all peoples. in such cases, which affect us all, action must be taken by the national justice systems, through mechanisms of close cooperation between them, by duly constituted international tribunals such as those already in existence for the former yugoslavia and for rwanda, set up by the security council, or in the near future by the international criminal court, which is already a reality. the trial of former president milosevic which has recently begun in the hague is just one more example of this trend which is gaining momentum all over the world because public opinion in all our countries demands it and because it must be seen as the logical outcome of the processes of globalisation and globalisation which are under way. the important thing is that a culture of impunity is being overcome, a culture that was based on silence and oblivion and is being replaced by a culture of demanding responsibility for particularly serious acts. in the same way, we are moving from an attitude of looking the other way when our neighbour's house is on fire to an attitude of feeling concerned and looking for effective ways of acting and working together to deal with situations that are intolerable. it is not a question of seeking revenge and retaliation but of ensuring that justice prevails as an indispensable condition for opening the doors to lasting peace and reconciliation in every situation in which a serious conflict has been experienced. mr president, as you know, the preparatory work for the establishment of the international criminal court is well under way. on the basis of the statute adopted in rome in 1998, the preparatory commission has already drawn up most of the instruments that the court will need to function effectively. in this process, which is undoubtedly technical but of fundamental scope and importance, the countries of the european union continue to play a very important role, i would even say a leading role, within the collective work that brings together countries from all over the world. what is even more important, the process of ratifying the rome statute is proceeding at a faster pace than we expected. while 120 states voted in favour of its adoption at the rome diplomatic conference, the treaty has now been signed by a total of 139 states, an overwhelming majority of the world community. as you know, 60 ratifications or accessions are required for the statute to enter into force and the international criminal court to be launched. the european parliament has already ratified the treaty of rome, and the council has also ratified the treaty of rome. as you know, all the member states of the union have either ratified the statute or have put in place the constitutional mechanisms necessary to ratify it as soon as possible. we are confident that all the member states will be among those countries which, by participating in the assembly of states parties, the first of which may be held later this year, will put into effect the concrete decisions which will open the way to the effective functioning of the court. in accordance with the common position adopted by the council on 11 june 2001, the european union urges all states which have not yet done so to ratify or accede to the statute as soon as possible, so that the international criminal court can soon become a reality. i would like to point out that 15 candidate or associated countries have recently joined the common position and are cooperating closely with us in this endeavour. it is also worth noting the work carried out by a large number of non-governmental organisations, often with the help and collaboration of the european union. in line with this call, the union has been working with third countries and groups of countries to speed up the internal procedures necessary to proceed to an early ratification of the statute. the commission has also been able to provide technical assistance in this area. in the coming weeks we intend to intensify these efforts on several continents with a view not only to achieving the swift entry into force of the statute but also to ensuring that the assembly of states parties reflects as closely as possible the varied composition of the international community. the legitimacy and effectiveness of the future court will depend crucially on its composition and the support it receives being interpreted as a genuine reflection of the international community as a whole. it is extremely important that all the continents, all the legal systems, are duly represented at the court and that it includes equally men and women judges, as the rome statute specifies. it is the pursuit of this broad support for the court that should inspire our efforts. we are encouraged in this endeavour by the fact that among the ratifications registered and those expected in the coming months are countries belonging to all continents, predominantly so far from europe, africa and latin america, and with different legal systems and degrees of economic and social development. no one can say that the international criminal court is going to be a court of the western world or of the developed countries. it will be a judicial body of the international community as a whole, fully independent and linked to the united nations system. it is important to emphasise that all countries, whether or not they have signed the statute, can play an active part in the process of establishing the international criminal court by participating in the work of the preparatory commission and then, if they so wish, as observers in the assembly of states parties. and that the doors will remain permanently open to all countries wishing to ratify or accede to the statute in the future. the european union has maintained a constant and sustained dialogue with some countries with doubts, some of our strongest allies - i am referring in particular to the united states - and we will always be ready to continue these exchanges in order to clarify our respective positions and foster a spirit of cooperation in the future. it is clear that the task will not end with the entry into force of the statute and the decisions adopted at the first meeting of the assembly of states parties. all necessary steps will have to be taken to ensure that the establishment of the new institution at its permanent seat in the hague is as rapid and efficient as possible. the preparatory committee and the host country, the netherlands, are already preparing the implementation of these measures and the european union is cooperating with them. the new institution must then be given the means to ensure that it is fully effective both at headquarters and on the ground. the experience of the tribunals for the former yugoslavia and rwanda has taught us that international criminal justice, to be effective, must be equipped with important personal, material and functional resources. the court, with its potentially universal jurisdiction, will not require less; it will certainly require more. the european union and its member states must also be prepared to provide any assistance that may be necessary. the court, whose action is guided by the principles of complementarity and cooperation with the national judicial systems, can only operate effectively if it has the cooperation of the judicial and administrative authorities of the states. this makes it a very important part of the implementation of the statute to adopt measures at national level to make such cooperation possible. this is a matter for each state according to its constitutional procedures, but the european union can help this process by exchanging information or, where appropriate, offering technical assistance to countries in need. all this is being done on the basis of the common position of june 2001, which i mentioned earlier, and which could be supplemented if necessary by a more detailed action plan or, in due course, by updating and clarifying its terms in the light of the progress of the process. i can assure you, ladies and gentlemen, that the presidency of the member states will take very much into account the ideas that emerge from this debate when it takes decisions. we share, mr president, a firm commitment to the early and effective establishment of the international criminal court as an independent and impartial institution dedicated to bringing justice to the most serious cases of human rights and humanitarian law in the world. on this issue, we are all, the european parliament, the council, the member states and the commission, closely united and determined to continue to act with determination and tenacity. this conviction and determination is what has enabled the european union to play a leading role in this process, along with other countries that are characterized by their commitment to democracy and human rights. we are already very close to achieving our objective with the entry into force of the rome statute and the opening up of the court. she will mark a before and after in the history of mankind's efforts to bring justice to the world. we can then be proud of europe's contribution to this advance of the international community, but we can in no way afford to let our arms drop; it will be time to move on to another phase in the same struggle for justice, in which europe's role will be equally indispensable. i am sure, mr president, that we will have the will and the determination to persevere in this endeavour and i certainly do not believe that we will ever lack the support of this parliament. (applause) i would like to thank

the commission. - mr president, mr president-in-office, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. the fight against impunity for serious crimes and the fight for international justice are an integral part of the eu's human rights and democratisation policy. the statute of the international criminal court, agreed in rome, is probably the most important achievement of international law since the founding of the united nations. the european union has always supported the international criminal court and continues to give its full support to this project, as reflected in the common position adopted by the eu in june 2001. in this common position we support the entry into force as soon as possible of the agreed statute and the establishment of the court of justice. the commission fully agrees with the approach developed in this common position, and i also fully agree with what mr ramón de miguel has just said as president of the council. the commission welcomes the fact that the central and eastern european countries associated with the european union and the associated countries cyprus and malta, as well as the efta countries belonging to the european economic area, officially declared in january 2002 that they share the objectives of the common position. the eu budget supports projects by non-governmental organisations to raise awareness worldwide of the need to establish the court. since 1995, the european initiative for democracy and human rights has spent some eur 6.9 million on such projects. in 2001, eur 2.1 million was allocated to three complementary projects by non-governmental organisations in support of the international criminal court. the ngo coalition for the criminal court project aims to facilitate the participation of civil society and its cooperation with governments in the framework of the united nations preparatory commission for the criminal court, to promote and facilitate technical cooperation in order to adopt binding national legislation implementing the rome statute after its ratification. the 'parliamentarians for global action' project is running a parliamentary campaign for the ratification and effective implementation of the statute of the criminal court and the promotion of the rule of law, and the 'no peace without justice' project is focusing on public awareness campaigns and the organisation of conferences to promote the criminal court. the commission communication on the role of human rights and democratisation in third countries of may 2001 identified the fight against impunity as a priority action to be promoted. the commission will therefore continue to support the establishment of the international criminal court. the special budget line for the international criminal court, which also includes the ad hoc tribunals for the former yugoslavia and rwanda and the recently established tribunal for sierra leone, has a budget of eur 5 million for 2002. in 2002, the commission will focus its efforts on two aspects. firstly, to raise awareness of the criminal court, by calling on more countries than the 60 required to ratify the statute so that it can enter into force. at the same time, we want to ensure that all geographical regions are represented. secondly, we want to focus on the adoption of binding national legislation to implement the project, including the training of the relevant professionals who can contribute to the work of the court, i.e. judges, lawyers, law enforcement officials and parliamentarians. a limited contribution may also be made towards the main costs of the court of justice. a call for proposals to achieve these objectives will be issued in march this year.

the commission. thank you, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this house has taken the initiative to draw up a report on the impact of transport on health. it is a difficult task for mrs lucas to undertake, and i want to thank her for the work she has done. the white paper on european transport policy for 2010 puts the citizen, the user, at the centre of our policies. one of the objectives we have set is simply to halve the number of fatalities on our roads by the year 2010; from the present 40 000 people, less than 20 000 will be victims by that date. i would like to recall some of the recent measures we have put forward to improve safety, such as the recently adopted directive on working time in road transport, which will have clear implications for safety. the commission has also presented parliament with a number of specific measures - some of which will be coming shortly - all aimed at the same objective: the amendment of the regulation on driving and rest periods, the introduction of speed limiters for small lorries, the compulsory use of seat belts in all vehicles - including buses - and the introduction of the digital tachograph. the second element is road pollution. the commission is obliged to acknowledge that considerable progress has been made in relation to vehicle emissions and noise levels. in the space of a few years, the euro standards have made it possible to reduce considerably these pollutants from road traffic; however, there is still room for improvement. the commission has embarked on an ambitious strategy to combat air pollution and its negative effects through the sixth environmental action programme, the cafe (clean air for europe) programme on air quality. among the initiatives that need to be taken in the future, i would like to mention two that are perhaps the most important: the first, which i consider to be far-reaching, is to replace 20% of conventional fuels by 2020 with cleaner alternative fuels, whether biofuels or even hydrogen, with an intermediate stage on the use of biofuels by 2010, with the ambitious target of 5.75% of all fuels used in the union by that date. the second initiative is aimed at supporting european cities that are committed to an ambitious strategy for sustainable, long-term mobility. this is the civitas project, which has been allocated eur 50 million to support cities that are pioneers in seeking to rationalise car use in favour of greater use of public transport, not to mention collateral initiatives aimed at promoting the use of cycling or even walking. the examination of the health implications is an element which i think is of great importance. the commission has already taken steps to advance the development of health impact assessment methodologies and their application in the community context. given the need to further improve methods and pilot projects, funding from the new health action programme will be available to develop and test health impact assessment methodologies. the programme is currently being discussed in the european parliament and the council - in the european parliament, mr trakatellis is the rapporteur - and it is expected to enter into force in the near future. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have tried to give some examples of how we take account of health aspects in our transport policy, without wishing to be exhaustive in any way; - doc. a5-0461/2001 by mr mayol i raynal, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the labour cost index (com (2001) 418 - c5-0348/2001 - 2001/0166 (cod)). i call mr mayol i raynal to speak.
the rapporteur. mr president, i am responsible for presenting to you, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, a proposal for a regulation on the labour cost index. this proposal is based on the new article 285 of the treaty, a new provision introduced by the treaty of amsterdam. this article provides in particular that the council, acting in accordance with the procedure laid down in article 251, shall adopt measures for the compilation of statistics where this is necessary for the performance of the activities of the community. secondly, this article provides that community statistics will be drawn up in accordance with the principles of impartiality, reliability, objectivity, scientific independence, cost-effectiveness, confidentiality, and without entailing excessive burdens for economic operators. we are in the framework of a codecision procedure. and this statistical tool, this labour cost index, is required by the european central bank as an element to be taken into account in setting monetary policy. the ecofin council of 29 september 2000 adopted an action plan on the statistical needs of the economic and monetary union. the action plan includes the establishment of a draft of short-term statistics on labour costs. i ask that this bill be tabled quickly. we have, at present, a clue that exists on this matter. this index was developed in the 1990s by the statistical programme committee, but it has no legal basis and its method of calculation is lacking in terms of timeliness, coverage and comparability. the idea behind the central bank's request and the commission's proposal is that labour costs would be a cause of inflation. the european institutions responsible for the economy, employment and monetary affairs must therefore be provided with regular and reliable indices on this subject. that opinion is questionable. i believe that there is a committee in the commission which agrees with this and another which does not. as regards low wages, the relevance of this position may be questioned, since in several member states there is a minimum wage which changes with the cost of living, and not the other way around. it is nevertheless useful for the union to have a macroeconomic indicator on this data which can be used by the social partners in particular when discussing the establishment of conventions, etc. the aim of the proposal is to establish a common framework for the development, transmission and evaluation of comparable labour cost indices. this is the subject of the first article. this cost is defined as the total of the employer's quarterly costs of employment (article 2). the data should be broken down by economic category. four indices are to be established: the total labour cost index, another index covering the total cost excluding irregularly paid bonuses, then wages and salaries, and finally social contributions and employer taxes minus subsidies paid to offset direct labour costs. it should also be noted that on this last point it is often the state which decides the amount of these contributions and that, therefore, it cannot be said that wages are fully covered by these possible inflationary surges. data for this index must be calculated on a quarterly basis (article 5 (1)) and must be reported in the form of indices within 70 days of the end of the reference period (article 6 (1)). transitional periods may not exceed two years from entry into force (article 9 (1)). in the application of the regulation, including the decision on derogation, the commission shall be assisted by the statistical programme committee. a few thoughts. the analysis of labour costs is undoubtedly an important element, as i have already said, from a macroeconomic point of view. however, some questions may arise. this index will have to be specified later by creating a separate index for total cost and excluding the expenditure on vocational training borne by the employer. there is also the possibility that we have envisaged in the context of an amendment tabled by my group - for technical reasons, this issue was not raised at commission level, so we were obliged to table this amendment later. this is the possibility of taking into account hourly productivity and then the possibility of postponing the first deadline for the presentation of the evaluation report to 31 december 2003, in order to allow an analysis based on an operating period which takes into account the possible transitional period. i apologize, but i see that time is running out and that, not being used to these timed reports, i have exceeded my allotted time by one minute and eleven seconds. at this late hour, i understand that this abuse is reprehensible. again, i apologize for that.
the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been asked to make a statement on the subject of the european social fund, and that the commission has been asked to make a statement on the subject of the european social fund. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i think that the concern that some of you have expressed about the interrelationship between wages and inflation, which could be a debate for another time, has little to do with what is said verbatim in the preamble to the proposal for a regulation. it states that a set of statistics, of which labour cost indices form an essential part, is a relevant element for the understanding of inflationary processes and the dynamics of the labour market. i think that's a hard statement to refute. of course, the other subject could be discussed in greater detail. as for the debate itself, i would refer only to mr mayol's two concerns. to what extent, on the one hand, can indexes be drawn up in the future which do not take into account training costs and exclude such costs? the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. these total costs are very insignificant. in the end, they account for less than 2% of total costs, and yet the calculation of these vocational training costs would or would require a very significant cost from the point of view of the overall compilation of the statistics. for this reason, until we have more information to enable us to do so at a lower cost, we are not in favour of making progress in this direction. we are also not in favour of not carrying out the report which is due at the end of 2002. and i understand mr mayol's argument that we are still in a transitional period and that not all the regulations will be applied 100 per cent. but we will have some experience of the application of the rules and will also be able to highlight more clearly the shortcomings and the difficulties. if the report is intended to identify the difficulties in implementing the regulation and to take the necessary measures to ensure that it is implemented as efficiently as possible, we think that keeping the date of 2002 is still correct, irrespective of the fact that if parliament wants further information on the application of the regulation at a later stage, it is of course within its rights to ask for it and eurostat, and i for my part, will be happy to provide it. that's all i have to say, your honours. i thank you very much for your cooperation in the adoption of this regulation, which is important in statistical terms and important for defining the future of monetary policy.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to welcome the excellent report by mr andreasen, which invites us to reflect on the development of our new information policy. the report you have just discussed directly echoes the commission's work to invite all the institutions to draw up a comprehensive information policy for the european union. the commission sees this as support for its action and welcomes it. i would like to respond to the andreasen report and the debate that has just taken place by presenting the main objectives of our strategy and then to elaborate on some aspects of its implementation. beyond the framework for interinstitutional cooperation set out in the communication of 27 june 2001, the commission is now examining the objectives that a genuine information and communication policy of the european union should pursue. as the andreasen report very well points out, interinstitutional cooperation is not an end in itself. it is essential that we develop a better understanding of the citizen and of the existence and role of the european union as such. this is not just about spreading factual information. the aim, i believe, must be to develop genuine communication capable of engaging in a dialogue with national public opinion. i wonder whether a genuinely comprehensive information and communication policy of the european union should not also aim at greater participation of citizens in european debates. these questions call for a greater awareness of the need for the european union to take better control of its own image. this control is achieved by the development of its own message body. it should be able to adapt to its different priority or specific information actions. as your rapporteur has said, these messages will have to be tailored to local realities and the concrete concerns of citizens. the question is to define the most credible information on the local area. the commission fully shares the principles of action adopted by mr andreasen. firstly, decentralisation: it must not only apply to the implementation of the strategy, but also to the adaptation of messages to the needs of different types of public, whether adaptation to different national realities in the fifteen member states, or adaptation of messages to the different target groups of information and communication policy. but it also requires better coordination and greater capacity for direction on the part of our institutions. i fully support the rapporteur's idea of strengthening the coordinating and guiding role of the interinstitutional information group chaired by vice-president vidal-quadras, whom i welcome and thank for his recent reference to cooperation with the commission. secondly, interinstitutional cooperation: it should eventually be possible to put it into practice in a multiannual action programme which would give our information and communication activities a better perspective and visibility. the commission can only welcome your proposal to hold an annual plenary debate with the council on the information and communication policy of the european union, and i welcome the council's decision to take part in the meetings of the interinstitutional information group. i hope that other bodies, in the capacity of observers, will also be able to join the work of the gii. third: partnership with civil society. as you rightly point out, the strengthening of this partnership requires us to rationalise the networks and links we have developed with the member states at national, regional and local level. as you can see, the reflection on the strategy itself is useful and necessary, but it must go hand in hand with a better organisation of our means of action, and that is why the commission is currently working on assessing the effective capacity of the tools at our disposal. it is clear that the coherence of our message depends on greater synergy between our different means of action. the rapporteur stresses the need to develop common european union houses in the candidate countries as well as in all the member states. as you know, that is the commission's policy. your idea of developing a kind of one-stop shop for the citizen in each country is very much in line with our concerns as the commission. in this connection, the commission is looking forward to the greatest possible coordination between the institutions and the member states, which you are calling for. this should contribute to better complementarity between their respective activities. in the same vein, the commission is also seeking to develop a better synergy between the networks and the relays with the offices and representations of our institutions, which you call the houses of the european union. i believe that this coordination is already a reality on the ground today. in addition, to address your concern about the visibility of these houses of commons, the commission is considering ways of making information from the european union more easily recognisable by the recipients. beyond the definition of common themes and messages, should the european union not seek to develop its own identity around a logo or a unique presentation of these different channels, a kind of branding? finally, you are right to insist on the need to develop a more comprehensive and systematic audiovisual policy as the privileged vehicle for information and communication in the european union. first of all, let me stress that the responsibility for this lies to a large extent with the member states themselves. the council itself has recognised this. the commission will nevertheless have to give this matter serious thought in order to systematize its partnerships with all the national, regional and local audiovisual media. the commission has always regarded europe by satellite as a privileged instrument for interinstitutional information, which it will seek to develop in the light of the budgetary resources made available to it. as regards the budget, i would point out that we are now closing the campaign on the euro, which is freeing up some funds. in the future, i think we will have to agree on priorities for the next few years: the future of europe, no doubt, and globalisation, as well as the continuation of the enlargement campaign. i hope that i can count on the support of the european parliament in defining the budgetary priorities needed to fulfil the new tasks of the european union's information and communication policy. the commission also takes note of your wish to consider the establishment of a european public channel to provide the public with relevant information on the initiatives and functioning of the european union on a continuous basis. the commission will endeavour to present a first analysis of the feasibility of this project by the end of this year. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the task we are undertaking together is vast, but it is also exciting. the commission welcomes the political will and awareness which are driving our institutions today. this shared political will will enable us to develop a coherent and comprehensive information and communication strategy for the european union for the benefit of our citizens. i welcome the excellent spirit of collaboration that has been at the forefront of the development of our new information strategy. this will be the subject of a new communication which the commission is expected to adopt towards the end of june. it is with pleasure that, following the debate we will have tomorrow in the interinstitutional group, a brainstorming debate on the priorities of the substance of information and communication policy, i will come back to you to present our conclusions during the july plenary session.

commission. – mr president, thank you for giving me the floor on this subject, which is of the highest importance, even though it may not attract publicly the attention which it deserves. i should like to start by thanking parliament for the interest it has shown in this report, and in particular the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and its rapporteur, lord inglewood, and also and the commission hopes that indeed will be the case. if we succeed in this it will give a strong political signal that the european union is not only serious about achieving an integrated capital market by the year 2005, as requested by the european council in lisbon two years ago, but also ready to lead on the development of international accounting standards. comparable, transparent financial reporting is an essential building block for the realisation of integrated, competitive and attractive eu capital markets to complement the single currency and so strengthen the european economy. that will also show, in particular in our relationship with the united states, how determined we are about the way we want to see things develop in future. it should pave the way for the united states to accept international accounting standards for listing purposes. i shall certainly be pressing the case when i visit washington in the second half of may. after the collapse of enron, concern has grown, certainly in the united states but also in europe, about the quality of financial reporting by listed companies. one must of course avoid knock-on effects that might lead to a loss of confidence among investors, shareholders and other stakeholders, including employees, in the functioning of our capital markets. long before enron started to make headlines in the press, europe made the choice of international accounting standards of high quality with the potential to become truly global standards. high-quality accounting standards are the bedrock of good financial reporting and the principles-based approach of ias will ensure that accounts reflect economic reality, thus restoring investors' confidence that things are really the way they look. the aim of the international accounting standards board (iasb) to minimise detailed rules and exemptions will defeat a culture that boils down to "where does it say that i cannot?", one which the many thousands of pages of rules-based standards of the u.s. gaap have fostered. ias will also provide the relevant and reliable information which investors and other stakeholders need to make meaningful cross-border and cross-sector comparisons throughout the european union. listed european companies have long been awaiting the signal which this parliament is now ready to give, and for eu companies it clearly means that things have started in earnest and that they must start preparing a switch-over to international accounting standards without wasting any time. this major achievement also demonstrates that our institutions can work closely together when the time comes to deliver, and i greatly welcome this. in this respect, and in response to the remarks made by lord inglewood and mrs thyssen and also, i believe, by mr lehne, may i underline that the commitments undertaken by the commission on 5 february, 2002 in president romano prodi's declaration to this parliament on the implementation of financial services legislation fully apply to the present proposals as well. that is the case and will remain so. those commitments apply as well to the present proposal and a clear reference to this is made in amendment no 4 as adopted by the committee on legal affairs and the internal market on 26 february 2002. the commission can accept all the amendments adopted unanimously by the legal affairs committee, notwithstanding the repeal of amendment no 6, which amounts more or less to the repetition of a recital. before i conclude, may i reply to three specific points made this evening. firstly, on languages, it is indeed important that the ias endorsed by the european union are made available in all official languages – at the moment 11, but pretty soon 19 – and then become part of community law. secondly, with regard to smes, a point raised in particular by mrs thyssen, the commission will engage in a debate about the accounting requirements for small and medium enterprises in the context of the modernisation of the accounting directives, for which the commission will officially present a proposal before the summer. lastly, there is the question of the consequences of the enron debacle. i am planning to engage in a debate about the consequences of that debacle for auditing and we are, at present, discussing with member states a document on auditor independence which i am sure mr lehne will be interested to read. as soon it is available we will make it available to members of this parliament. in conclusion, mr president, a strong vote in favour of this proposal would constitute a major contribution to international and european harmonisation in the accounting field by promoting a single set of accounting standards, namely the ias. adopting ias for europe would offer increased comparability of financial information to investors and shareholders and would contribute to a return of confidence in the efficiency and effectiveness of our financial markets. it is an opportunity for european leadership which i am sure parliament will want to seize, as do the commission and council.

- mr president, two years ago the commission put forward two proposals for amendments, one to the sixth directive and the other to the regulation on administrative cooperation. the aim of both was to put an end to the discrimination suffered by european companies in relation to those of third countries, particularly american ones, in the provision of services. this discrimination is due to the fact that companies from outside the union do not pay vat when providing electronic services, whereas european companies are obliged to pay vat. the urgency of the matter meant that parliament quickly withdrew both reports. at the moment the council is asking us to change the legal basis exclusively for the administrative cooperation regulation. i'm not going to go into this, but i want to say that these are two different things. the commission believes that the legal basis should not be changed, but that the matter should be studied with the utmost urgency, in order to put an end to this discrimination and, in addition, as parliament has requested, to facilitate the use of electronic means for identifying customers, thus eliminating the costs borne, in particular, by small and mediumsized enterprises. i would therefore advise this house, mr president, to accede to the council's request for urgent procedure and not to agree to a change of legal basis on this subject. it is one thing to refuse the material request and another to refuse it as a matter of urgency so that these two proposals can be put to the vote very soon.

the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all i would like to express my appreciation to this house for having accepted the proposal to draw up a report on this subject, women and fundamentalism, thus allowing us to tackle this serious problem and making this debate and the subsequent vote possible despite the difficulties involved and the pressures that exist. on behalf of the hundreds of millions of people who are deprived of their rights or who are restricted by fundamentalist pressures, i thank the european parliament very much. today the european union must defend the universality of human rights in a globalised world where fundamentalists pose serious threats to freedoms, human rights and peace. this report makes useful proposals to combat them. the first of these, mr president, is that we must not make religious fundamentalism a taboo subject, because problems are not solved by silencing or concealing them, but by knowing them and facing them. secondly, fundamentalists should not be fought against by other fundamentalists; human history is full of such failures. fundamentalism, on the other hand, is being pushed back by the promotion and exercise of democratic freedoms, by the promotion of women's emancipation, by pluralism and ideological and cultural diversity, by the promotion of openness and acceptance of differences and by economic and social well-being. mr president, one of the keys to combating fundamentalism has been modernity in the plural and multicultural sense. there is no social modernity without the human. the attempts to modernise a society by marginalizing women from democracy are failing; hence the denunciation of the partial modernisation processes of state leaders who intend to modernise only economic and technological issues, while keeping intact the basic axes of obsolete patriarchal societies. today women are the main bearers of social modernity. however, mr president, there is not a single emancipated female. women's identity must be personal and individual, distinct from religions, traditions and cultures. stereotypes, dress, values, life patterns and habits of behavior should be a matter of free personal choice. mr president, another key to preserving society from fundamentalism is secularization, or the separation between public affairs, which belong to the political sphere, and religious convictions and beliefs, which must be free and respected and which belong to the private sphere of individuals. the place of religion in a social and political context can be very wide. mr president, the accusations being made against this report, which clearly and respectfully distinguishes fundamentalism from the normal practice of religion, even though in some periods of time there has been no such distinction, are unfair. in short, mr president, we are facing a human rights scourge of enormous proportions. applied to women alone and only in the present, we can count hundreds of millions of people whose rights and freedoms are being deprived, restricted, violated or annulled. due to time constraints, i have not been able to stop at the death sentence for stoning of safiya huseini in human life is worth in the european union.

the commission. - mr president, i should like to congratulate mrs izquierdo rojo because her report touches on a very important and difficult problem. first, as regards fundamentalism, i think we should look at the analysis of the concept outside the european union. the european union, according to the treaty, is a union of independent states. religion is a purely private matter for citizens european union. recently, on women's day, we had the discussion about muslim women in europe. islam is now the second largest religion in the european union. the speakers, european muslim women,
