but also of understanding other people who, perhaps by different roads, are seeking the same truth, the same harmony and the same solidarity as we are.
- mr president, allow me to begin by expressing my satisfaction that this parliament has reached unanimous consensus on a euro-mediterranean policy, which is summed up in a very positive and concrete way in mr esteve's report. but at the same time i must express a feeling, no longer of dissatisfaction, but of bitterness, because of the feeling - which i am sure practically everyone shares - that in this euro-mediterranean process we are climbing up a ladder which is at the moment descending at a speed clearly superior to our upward march: we are going backwards. in the economic and social spheres - and there are shared responsibilities, but also european responsibilities - there is a clear tendency towards an increase in the distance, the rift, between the european union and our mediterranean partners. but above all, it is in the political sphere that circumstances, as a result of the appalling situation in the middle east, are really putting the euro-mediterranean process, if not in danger, then in a very delicate situation. i take this opportunity to say that the valencia ministerial conference will undoubtedly be an important occasion for israeli and palestinian representatives to sit around a table, but that the significant presence of the palestinian authority - it should be recalled that president arafat was present at the previous conference - must be a sine qua non condition for this conference to take place, because the european union could not participate in the 'dishonor ceremony' which would mean bringing together the mediterranean countries leaving the chair of the palestinian authority empty.
- mr president, commissioner, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr esteve, on his comprehensive and thorough work, which covers all the concerns and questions of euro-mediterranean cooperation one after the other. the relaunch of the barcelona process is more necessary than ever for peace and stability. it must be achieved by intensifying political and mediterranean dialogue, addressing fundamental issues such as the necessary promotion of democratic values, the most fundamental rights - which are also so seriously undermined in the middle east conflict - the terrorist threat or issues related to economic cooperation, the environmental aspects of development, migration or drug trafficking. in the short time i have, i shall concentrate on a few aspects: it seems obvious that the creation of a free trade area will boost the economy and prevent some people on one side of the border from dying of hunger while others on the other side die of cholesterol; but we must ensure that this free trade area does not become a time bomb that will blow up the efforts of the southern european territories to achieve the true convergence, the true cohesion that they do not yet enjoy. the establishment of a free trade area must also take account of the profound changes that are going to take place in the european union, such as the reform of the common agricultural policy and enlargement, so we must be very careful about agricultural trade, which is also necessary and useful. political dialogue should not be promoted exclusively between the european union and its mediterranean partners, but also between them. it does not seem logical that an increase in the association agreement should not be accompanied by a broader south-south dialogue, and that there should still be situations of closed borders in diplomatic relations. the european union is also calling for the establishment of a european union-wide network of border controls and for the establishment of a european union-wide network of border controls. on the other hand, the necessary fight against terrorism must not be used as a weapon or a pretext to make the political adversary or the enemy disappear; in order to find peace, it is a priority to preserve yasser arafat as a valid interlocutor. dialogue and mutual understanding are necessary elements after the attacks of 11 september, and after these attacks, a deep gap has opened up between the two cultures that must disappear. to this end, cultural and social exchange should be encouraged by enhancing mutual information through common, mutual means of communication, such as euro-mediterranean television. finally, we must not forget the important role that the regions of southern europe are playing and will play in the future in euro-mediterranean cooperation.
- mr president, probably the most important thing about the valencia summit is that it can be celebrated. it is obvious - the commission and the rapporteur say so - that the barcelona process should not be confused with the middle east peace process. but it is true that without peace in the middle east there will be no barcelona process. i would therefore like to congratulate the spanish presidency on the efforts it has made to achieve peace. the barcelona declaration is the most firm statement i know of on this subject. the presence of the president of the council of the union at the arab league summit is a first. the mission in the middle east, firstly, was carried out and, secondly, it was right to maintain its dignity: there was no arafat, but there was no sharon either. i also welcome the convening of the eu-israel association council and the meeting in madrid. in this process, it is necessary to guarantee the security and viability of the two states: the palestinian state and the israeli state. once the issue of the peace process has been clarified in the barcelona process, i think the commission's self-praise is exaggerated. it is true that some progress has been made in the association agreement, that the agadir process has been launched and that a development process has been tentatively initiated, but these efforts seem to me to be absolutely insufficient in view of what remains to be done. the commission rightly says that 45 million new jobs will have to be created in the southern mediterranean over the next decade to maintain the current levels of unemployment and poverty. if this is not done, the external security of our southern border will be jeopardized by the growth of fundamentalism - as mr morillon and other speakers have pointed out - and our own internal security, because illegal immigration flows will increase. i therefore think that the points made by the rapporteur, mr esteve, in the various sections of his report are very correct, and i also think that in order to make this happen, to move from the muse to the theatre, it is absolutely essential that a euro-mediterranean assembly should serve as a spearhead, to give impetus and speed up the process, which is a matter of great urgency. i am also pleased that there are more speakers from non-mediterranean countries - something which has not been frequent when we have been dealing with these issues - because it shows that the european union is beginning to realise that, in addition to looking to the east, it must also look to the south to ensure its own survival.
commission. – mr president, firstly i would like to congratulate mr esteve on his excellent report, as many others have done in this debate. it clearly shows the importance that parliament gives to the mediterranean region. i noted mr swoboda's remark about his being the only non-mediterranean participant in the debate – there is in fact more than one, but it can be looked upon as a strength of this parliament that we have such commitment to and identification with an issue like this. from the outset, let me just reiterate, if need be, the strategic importance of the mediterranean for the eu. on the eve of the next enlargement and in the face of the developing political situation this is truer than ever. after a careful reading i must confess my satisfaction with the convergent approach between this report and the commission’s communication. more has to be done, but the commission and parliament are in broad agreement on the way we understand our political, economic and social relations with our southern neighbours. despite the serious political setbacks in the region – the current dramatic situation in the middle east being one of them – and a certain scepticism at the end of the 1990s as to whether the barcelona process constituted the right means to make the euro-mediterranean partnership move forward, the process has stood the test of time. we cannot ignore the implications for the process of the tragic development of the situation in israel, gaza and the west bank. this is not the occasion today to debate europe’s role in bringing an end to that conflict but the situation as it is, and the continuation of this dreadful violence, stresses even further the need to continue with the development of the barcelona process as a means for europe to make its contribution to the peace, stability and prosperity of the region. one can always discuss how strong an instrument the barcelona process really is, but it is beyond discussion that this process is part of the solution and definitely not part of the problem, so we had better strengthen it. in substance, substantial progress has been accomplished since 1996. all euro-mediterranean partners are now used to having a permanent dialogue and to working together. the barcelona process is the only place where we can hold a 27-member discussion and, more importantly, where the 12 mediterranean partners can regularly discuss and meet. in the present circumstances, this is a meaningful indication of the resilience of the process. we have also made substantial progress towards introducing a free trade area. most of the association agreements are already ratified, signed or initialled. intra-regional agreements, such as the agadir process, are being negotiated. yet, although our euro-mediterranean trade relations are progressing steadily in north/south terms, south/south trade is still stagnating at a mere 5% of mediterranean trade. macroeconomic stabilisation has indeed taken place successfully in most mediterranean countries, but reforms related to the business environment are not progressing at a sufficient pace. the challenge for the mediterranean partners is to unleash the full potential of their economic forces, and in this regard the barcelona process has become the framework of reference for all international donors to relate to and further pursue. in the cultural sphere, substantial work has been accomplished. some hundreds of regional projects have been financed and have promoted a dense network of human exchanges. so what is the way ahead? how can we raise the profile of the partnership? how can it better be used to guarantee a common area of peace and stability? politically, we must pursue and reinforce our support for the barcelona process as a tool for promoting understanding and political dialogue. the road is well-paved, despite some potholes on its way. a clear example of this dialogue is the senior officials' meeting on terrorism just held on 27 march. by the same token, the 27 partners have been able to come a long way towards an agreement around a set of priority actions on an issue as sensitive as justice and home affairs. we hope to reach a final consensus in valencia. based on these priorities the commission will launch this year a regional programme on judicial cooperation, the fight against terrorism and organised crime, and migration. this success marks a milestone for the partnership and demonstrates its political capabilities and potential. in particular, as far as migration issues are concerned, several of the requests by parliament (observatory on migration flows, network of contacts) will be included in the coming regional programme. at an institutional level, further efforts need to be made in order to promote the "co-ownership" of the barcelona process. a feeling that the eu "imposes its agenda" exists among the southern partners and needs to be alleviated. in this sense your proposal of launching a euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly is more than welcome. economically, signs are encouraging. the grid of association agreements is almost completed; south/south trade integration progresses, notably in the framework of the agadir process – even if not as fast as we would like. the meda programme has dramatically improved its delivery – though given the starting point one might say that improvement had to happen – but still, it is happening with a ratio of payments to commitments of 53% in 2001 compared to a mere 26% for the 1995-1999 period. we are catching up. yet the economic situation of the region remains uncertain and demands supplementary efforts from everybody. i am glad that parliament supports our proposals to further this process, in particular in areas such as investments, environment, transport, infrastructures and energy. as you know, the idea of launching a euro-mediterranean bank did not receive the full assent of the member states at the barcelona european council. nonetheless, a new european investment bank facility will be launched and a representative office of the eib in the region will be created. finally, the social and human aspects of the partnership show today, more than ever, its relevance, creating bridges across the mediterranean and promoting a better understanding of each other’s cultures and societies. i noted that this aspect was given prominence in many of the contributions in the debate here today. the barcelona process allows a unique and structured framework that allows this social and cultural dialogue at regional level – not only north/south, but also south/south and indeed south/north. the european commission has put forward a set of new proposals. i am happy to see that they are very well taken by parliament, in particular the euromed foundation and the cooperation between universities (the tempus programme). as regards the launching of a new euromed foundation, the commission is persuaded that it would contribute to the enhancement of the partnership. however, some member states do not seem to be as convinced as we are. some efforts of political persuasion will be required in the coming weeks. the commission has also proposed the enlargement of the tempus programme on university cooperation to the mediterranean. the approval of this extension will be obtained at the council of education ministers on 30 may. moreover, all existing regional programmes in this area (heritage, audiovisual, youth) will be pursued in the near future.

in writing. - i did not vote for the community patent: as a fervent 'europeanist' i wished i could have done so but was prevented from doing so by the linguistic discrimination contained in the draft. respect for cultural and linguistic diversity is now one of the fundamental principles of community law. but in law and in fact this principle is not respected in this draft nor in the union's institutions in general. the principle presupposes the equality of all languages in law. the technical adjustment of this equality is undoubtedly necessary, but this adjustment must not contradict the principle. as a catalan, i cannot accept that my language does not enjoy the same rights as those that are now official.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating mr carlo fatuzzo on his excellent work and, above all, on his efforts to incorporate the many amendments tabled to his report. in my opinion, it is true that the classical image of old age has become old and outdated, out of time and out of place. the image of the over-60 or 65-year-old no longer corresponds to a person who is sickly and whose physical and mental capacity has been dramatically reduced. the extension of life, which far exceeds 65 years, is a cultural, social, health and economic achievement. but that achievement can become a problem if we are not able to understand its deeper meaning and to adapt to it, extracting its positive potentials, of course. ageing has been described as the most important social phenomenon of the beginning of this century. the ratio - as mrs hermange has already said here - between the potentially active population and those over 65, which is currently about 4 to 1 in many member states of the union, will be 2 to 1 by 2050. changes like this therefore require to be addressed to minimise their negative aspects. this cultural, social, health and economic achievement requires that the older individual can also enjoy a quality of life at this stage, and that society takes advantage of their experience and wisdom. this will require a combination of public pensions and the possibility of working for older people who wish to do so by promoting flexible working life and equality policies, which are so important in this sector. often the woman has worked or is working part-time, has entered the workforce late, has had numerous periods of inactivity during certain periods of her life, such as child rearing, etc. i think that the appropriate method is open coordination, which makes it possible to approximate the social legislation of the member states and also makes it possible to facilitate the exclusion of people from poverty at this stage of life, and to promote mobility by recognising the exportable nature of pensions, as the barcelona european council decided quite recently. it also makes it possible to take advantage of the capacities of those who are part of the so-called elderly, although perhaps not preferably, for social needs, volunteering, etc. and above all, it makes it possible to encourage their participation in active working life, all this - i repeat - also from the impetus of a policy of gender equality.
the commission. - mr president, i would like to thank mr fatuzzo for his report, but at the same time to bow to his passion and obsession with the specific issue of pension reforms. monetary union and the increasing integration of economic policy in the countries of the european union are undoubtedly giving a european dimension to all policies, even those which until a few years ago were strictly national. in december both the economic and social affairs councils agreed on common objectives and working methods for pensions. i think it is an important political step that both councils, not only ecofin but also the social affairs and employment council, are addressing the issue of pensions with the same emphasis and the same intensity. we have said many times in this chamber that this is not an economic issue, it is a social issue with economic dimensions. today, with its report, parliament is, i think, completing an optimistic step in the cooperation of the council, the commission and parliament on a new, ambitious cooperation programme on pensions. the commission presented its report on pensions in june 2001. i think it is very important to repeat what is stated in both the commission report and the parliament's report. the reform of pension systems cannot be done in a vacuum. it's not a matter of legislation. it is a matter of a set of policies, the effects of which will be felt in pension systems. i would like to refer to the policies which are concerned with solving europe's demographic problem. the debate on demography has been brought up to date by the madrid conference on population ageing and, of course, concerns on the one hand the increase in life expectancy and on the other the inability of european countries to replenish their populations. the second major area is employment, and i would remind you of the important steps taken by the european council on the specific objectives for the participation of older workers in the labour market. i would like to make a special point here. it is not enough to deal with the increase in the age limit, which is justified both by the increase in life expectancy and by economic problems. but it's not enough. we must simultaneously present and implement a set of policies that retain and incentivise older workers to remain in the labour market. today, in the private sector and in a large number of sectors, it is extremely difficult for people over 50 to stay or to find work. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to mention the poverty and social exclusion policies. many members have made clear the link between poverty policies and pension reforms and the commission is currently working particularly on the identification of indicators of pension adequacy in relation to poverty data. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the european union has not expressed the will, and i think it would be impossible, to intervene in national systems or to give directives on which system is the best or which is the worst. however, it is clear that, both because of mobility - many meps have referred to the new but many problems of workers' mobility in the european union - and because of the common causes of sustainability problems, there is a need for cooperation. this need seems to be covered by the open method of cooperation. this method is a new tool, we have tried it in employment policies, in poverty and exclusion policies and now there is a major effort on pensions. are there democratic gaps? there are! is there more scope for cooperation with parliament? there is! i would like to remind you of the role of the european parliament in implementing the open method of cooperation for employment. the european parliament is becoming more and more visible every year, your proposals for guidelines are being taken more and more into account and parliament has a very important role to play in this implementation. the cooperative method for pensions is just beginning. the member states will submit their first reports in september. parliament will be able to intervene in the commission's joint report. i would say, however, that i have no objection to the whole of the report going to the committee on social affairs so that we can have more substantial cooperation from the outset. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the first is that the gender equality dimension, because of the european acquis and european legislation, cannot but be taken into account in all reforms. the second point is that, as has been very rightly emphasized, enlargement and the candidate countries should be part of the planning. the meeting you have organized for may with the authorities of the candidate countries is a good starting point for this cooperation, since in two years' time the candidate countries will have to take part in this joint exercise. i believe that the joint report we have agreed on, which has three main axes and eleven points on which all countries must work to move forward with reform, has two important victories: the first is that the economic and social dimensions coexist and the second is that we give the greatest european added value to national policies.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank mrs damião for her work on a particularly sensitive subject within the occupational health chapter. usually, when we talk about job improvements, higher quality employment, in the culture that made job stability a general principle of labour law, we are thinking more about stable employment than in the aspect of what we now call occupational health, and more about safety and hygiene at work, and we are forgetting an intrinsic aspect of work: work is risky, zero risk does not exist and, what is worse, sometimes the risk is hidden, it is not obvious, it does not hurt our senses and it is made more difficult to perceive. i think that is the situation of those who work with asbestos, an agent whose use can be dangerous and which can cause very serious diseases such as pulmonary and pleural fibrosis or peritoneal mesothelioma. it is an agent, moreover, which offers peculiarities in the form of doubts, of questions to be solved: the effect, for example, of inhaling small doses on the risk of cancer, the limits below which it is certain not to contract cancer, the carcinogenic power of the various types of amphibolic or chrysotile asbestos and to add to all this the fact that often work developed where asbestos is used or has been used is carried out by small and mediumsized enterprises with poor, incomplete or poorly used personal protective equipment: tasks such as the maintenance, repair, overhaul or renovation of buildings or the repair or scrapping of ships or automobiles or industrial equipment. another important and not least important point is the incubation period of the disease and, therefore, the determination of responsibilities in relation to it, as well as the need for prior or periodic medical examinations of workers who work at risk of asbestos, and precautions - as already mentioned here - for those who simply live in the environment and may be indirectly affected. in this connection, i would like to say that we do not share the rapporteur's position that the directive should go beyond the protection of workers and - i mean specifically - all types of workers exposed to the risk of contracting diseases caused by asbestos, because we believe that it would correspond to another legal basis. nor do we agree that, in the event of doubt about the proof of the cause of the pathology, the inversion of the burden of proof is simply established. we are in complete agreement with you, madam rapporteur, on the need for a change in the culture of protection against risks at work in general and against the risks caused by asbestos in particular. we share the need for awareness-raising for all - states, employers and workers - and the opportunity and need for more training and more information; for a change of culture which, of course, madam commissioner, from the commission and from the council, must be promoted and strengthened. we also share the importance of social dialogue as an instrument for an effective policy on occupational health and for the collaboration of administrations with each other, and perhaps a lesser reliance on a third party, the so-called state, because i am aware that the state already has many tasks and that the most important thing here is not to dictate a large number of rules, except in cases of the emergence of new risks. in short, action at the non-regulatory level is going to be much more important and i think that in this action, madam commissioner, the commission has a lot to say.
commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by welcoming and thanking mr de miguel, state secretary for european affairs of the spanish presidency. i would like to thank him for his understanding. we ran out of time, but sometimes things are very difficult. i want to congratulate mrs damião on her excellent report on such a sensitive and technically difficult dossier as asbestos. in order to complement the prohibition of marketing in the use of asbestos and products containing it, it is necessary to amend and update the provisions of the existing directive in order to focus the preventive measures on today's most exposed workers, namely those carrying out repairs, demolition and maintenance activities. i would like to congratulate the house on the quality of its amendments. i very much understand why you so much insist on the need to increase the levels of protection, not only for workers but also for the general population and the environment. unfortunately, this is not possible within the scope of article 137 of the treaty, which is the basis of this proposal. i am going to reply to the members' proposals through my comments and my justification for rejection or approval of the amendments. the commission can accept in full amendments nos 1, 11, 17, 18, 19, 22, 31, 32, 34 and 39, since they improve on the quality of the text and/or clarify its meaning. although i can agree to the ideas behind amendments nos 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13 and 14, the commission cannot accept them for reasons of legal coherence and legislative technique. the commission has to reject amendment no 16 and the second part of amendment no 25, because the employers' responsibility is clearly established in the framework of directive 89/391 and any further qualification would introduce legal uncertainties as regards where this responsibility lies. as regards the limit value, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 15, 21 and 42, because they would introduce two different limit values, implying different protection levels for workers carrying out different activities. in addition, the expression of the limit values as a time-weighted average in a period of four hours instead of eight hours has to be rejected because it would create confusion when compared to the same values in international standards which use a reference period of eight hours. amendments nos 5, 10, 27, 38 and 40 cannot be accepted by the commission because article 137, on which the proposal for a directive is based, does not allow for the recognition of and financial compensation for occupational diseases and concerns only the protection of workers. in any case the compensation issue is a subject of subsidiarity. in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 30, 33, 35, 36 and 37. amendment no 29 cannot be accepted since directive 89/391 imposes an obligation on the employer to provide adequate training for workers and not merely to make training available. amendment no 41, cannot be followed by the commission because it would introduce, in the case of activities involving sporadic and low-intensity exposures, unnecessary additional bureaucratic burden on enterprises and national administrations without any additional benefit. finally, the commission considers that amendments nos 3, 6, the second part of amendment no 23, amendments nos 24, 26 and 28 are already contained in substance in the different articles of the proposal and therefore cannot be accepted. before summing up, there is a real political question: will this directive as it stands now prohibit any export to third countries after 2005? the answer, unfortunately, is clear: no, it cannot. it is one of the main issues of discussion between the commission and the council. a total ban could be the answer but, in that case – and the commission has no objections to this approach – you must admit that it is a very complicated problem because in the case of a total ban we must take into account not only the problems of demolition or maintenance – and the workers who are exposed to these activities – but also the fact that there is a list of different products which contain very small amounts of asbestos which is not dangerous, and we must see how we can solve this very complicated internal market problem. there was a question about the exclusion of asbestos cement. as my colleague, who is an expert on this issue, tells me there is a real problem with this product so we cannot exclude it. at least it is not something less dangerous than the others which we exclude. finally, to sum up, the commission can accept in full amendments nos 1, 11, 17, 18, 19, 22, 31, 32, 34 and 39. it can accept in part amendments nos 20, 23 and 25. it rejects amendments nos 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 21, 24, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 33, 35, 36, 37, 38, 40, 41 and 42. it was a very interesting debate and there is no need for me to refer to the substance of the directive because everybody agrees that this is one of the most important directives concerning health and safety in our legislation. - question no 6 by mr richard corbett (h-0183/02): does the council agree that recent events show the urgency of finding a solution to the kashmir conflict? what steps does the european union intend to take to bring the parties concerned together to negotiate a solution?
the council. - mr president, the presidency is well aware that the kashmir conflict is one of those conflicts which is lasting or has lasted longer than would be desirable. unfortunately, the adjustments of modern society that have emerged in the 20th century in the international context have caused foci of tension to flourish in various places on different continents, which have not been able to be resolved, because they have great political and emotional burdens. it is clear that kashmir does not attract all our attention, not because the problem is not serious, but precisely because - and this is to be commended - of the efforts made by both india and pakistan so that this hot spot, which has been on the verge of unleashing a war that could have had incalculable consequences, has been contained thanks to a spirit of dialogue which, despite the many problems, still exists between india and pakistan. i think the council has greatly appreciated the spirit of conciliation that has been shown by the indian and pakistani governments, particularly in recent months, when very serious events have taken place with terrorist attacks that have been able to destabilize the region, which was already sufficiently destabilized by the conflict in afghanistan. the presidency has certainly offered its good offices to the parties from day one. i think pakistan and india are countries of great culture and long tradition. they think they're capable of resolving the conflict on their own. if you need us, you can be sure that we will be at your disposal, but at the moment the spirit of dialogue between the two powers, pakistan and india, suggests that they are willing, albeit slowly, to resolve this conflict, which is a case similar to what happened on the occasion of the partition of india when the independence of pakistan took place and which triggered great frustrations.

- the next item is the report (a5-0020/2002) by mr skinner, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on the implementation of the action plan on private equity (paci) (com (2001) 605 - c5-0015/2002 - 2001/2213 (cns)).
commission. – mr president, i should like to begin by saying that the commission welcomes this report and would like to thank the rapporteur, mr skinner, for preparing the report on implementing the risk capital action plan. the report is clearly supportive of the community strategy to develop the eu risk capital market. as has been said a number of times this evening in this parliament, risk capital provides a vital source of financing for new and innovative enterprises, and in that way it contributes significantly to economic growth and to the creation of jobs. the development of a large and efficient eu risk capital market is a key element in the so-called lisbon strategy to create a more dynamic and prosperous european union. the period since the launch of the risk capital action plan has seen a rapid growth in the eu risk capital market. investment almost tripled between 1998 and 2000. growth then slowed in 2001 as the "dot.com bubble" burst and the global economy weakened, but nonetheless the market remains fundamentally sound. indeed the slowdown in growth may be seen as a necessary consolidation after the rather exuberant behaviour of previous years. but despite the real progress that has been made, there are still important barriers to development of the eu risk capital market. as the report points out, these barriers affect both the supply side and the demand side of the market. the risk capital action plan is designed to address those barriers, and in order to meet the deadline of 2003 for implementation of the rcap a number of key actions are required. perhaps i may mention four of them. firstly, the relevant measures in the financial services action plan must be adopted urgently. those measures include the proposed directive on prospectuses, the proposed directive on occupational pension funds, about which a number of members have spoken tonight, and the proposed regulation on international accounting standards. the commitment by the barcelona european council to have those proposals adopted as early as possible in 2002 is very welcome. may i say in reply to mr karas, on the matter of occupational pension funds, that the commission is not in the business of making life more difficult for those pension funds that are in operation and that operate efficiently and satisfactorily. why should the commission place an increased burden of regulation on those pension funds? that is why i recently said that if the council were to insist on further restrictions on those pension funds which operate satisfactorily – and basically they are found in the united kingdom and ireland, in the netherlands and denmark: together those countries account for maybe two thirds or 75% of total capital assembled and saved for the purpose of defraying pension fund obligations – why should the commission place further restrictions on those pension funds? that is why i have said that if the council wants to do that then the commission will have no alternative but to withdraw the proposal. that is the first way in which the commission aims at increasing the risk capital action plan market. the second way is that member states must maintain, and improve where necessary, the pace of structural reform. the objective of reform must be to create an environment in which the risk capital market can flourish. progress has been made but much remains to be done. the commission's broad economic policy guidelines for the year 2002/2003 will again call for intensified efforts in this area. thirdly, entrepreneurship must be encouraged. measures to promote a culture of enterprise in the eu have been taken at community and national levels, but members of parliament will appreciate that to change a culture is not easy. cultural barriers can indeed be particularly difficult to overcome but our efforts in this field must continue and, if possible, be intensified. fourthly and lastly the efficiency of public funding for risk capital activities must be improved and it is important that public funding should not crowd out private sector investment. we do not want to see that happen. based on that consideration the commission has clarified its policy on state aid to risk capital activities. i regard the report from the committee on economic and monetary affairs as another important building block in our efforts to develop the eu risk capital market. it is encouraging that the recommendations from the committee correspond fully to the measures proposed in the risk capital action plan, and the commission would very much like to once again thank the rapporteur for his work. before i end my contribution to this debate i should like to say, in reply to a question put by mr karas, that the commission is actively following the negotiations at basle. as mr karas knows, the commission is an observer in those negotiations. we are now entering a third consultation round. more time has been allotted for those negotiations and one of the prime objectives of the commission is to see to such a development as will ensure that small- and medium-sized enterprises will have the same possibilities of attracting capital as larger companies. again, why would the commission approve something which would harm the possibilities for small and medium-sized enterprises to get capital? after all, all we want to do is to facilitate capital going to smes since we all know that smes play a very important part in creating jobs; of course they also they play a very important part in the creation of high-tech industries, or rather, activities which may lead to high-tech industries. in conclusion, i would like to say something about the five amendments which have been proposed by mr goebbels. unfortunately he is not here, but i would like to say that on the first amendment the commission has difficulties because we fear that his amendment would send the wrong signal to the market. we are particularly concerned that state aid discipline should not be weakened, and therefore the commission does not really like the first amendment and hopes that it will not be accepted by parliament. the second amendment states that a shortage of appropriate finance is the major obstacle to starting a business. the commission begs to differ. the commission does not agree that the shortage of funds is the major obstacle. there are a number of obstacles and it would be difficult to say which one is the major obstacle. therefore the commission regrets it cannot accept this amendment. the other three amendments – amendments nos 3, 4 and 5 – are acceptable to the commission and no doubt mr goebbels will be informed about the opinions of the commission. we therefore once again accept the fact that those three amendments will be approved by parliament.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the presidency will of course convey your views to mr goebbels, but in this debate, mr goebbels was represented by mr santos anyway. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.
- the next item is the report (a5-0073/2002) by mrs ayuso gonzález, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation on the common organisation of the market in ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin (com (2001) 101 - c5-0095/2001 - 2001/0055 (cns)).
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the european union produces approximately 20 million hectolitres of alcohol a year, of which 13 million are of agricultural origin and the rest of the production is so-called synthetic alcohol. the main processing industries using ethyl alcohol are those producing spirits, which account for about 30% of the european alcohol market and can only use alcohol of agricultural origin, and the chemical, pharmaceutical and cosmetic industries, which account for the remaining 70% and can source either from alcohol of agricultural origin or from synthetic alcohol. i mean, both alcoholics compete in the same field. in the past, there have been five successive attempts by the commission to create a common market organization for alcohol, but all of them have failed in the council and the reasons for this failure lie in the divergence of the national alcohol regimes traditionally existing in the various member states. in particular, the main reason is that a com would in principle involve the dismantling of national aid as set out in article 10 of the proposal. however, this type of aid linked to rural development can and must be maintained, because it does not distort the market in the current europe of the fifteen. the reasons for a regulatory framework are: the functioning of the single market, fair competition between operators, facilitating greater transparency and knowledge of trade flows in view of globalisation. the main threat to european alcohol producers is the global process of opening up and globalisation. alcohol from third countries is gaining access to the european union market more easily, either as a result of new preferential arrangements, gatt commitments to reduce tariffs or bilateral negotiations with certain third countries with strong alcohol production. in addition, other factors which could affect the future of the european alcohol sector at the moment include the large alcohol production of the candidate countries, the future wto negotiations which may lead to further reductions in border protection and the foreseeable increase in the bioethanol fuel market in the european union which could significantly alter the map of traditional uses and destinations of european ethyl alcohol. in the light of these developments, the council of agriculture ministers of 17 june 2000 invited the commission to examine the desirability of a regulatory framework for agricultural alcohol with a view to improving statistical information for greater market transparency, as well as introducing a system of import and export licences and creating an appropriate management committee for the sector. the commission has proposed a smaller-scale cmo, since it does not include intervention measures or eaggf expenditure, but it goes far beyond the council's own invitation, in that, in addition to definitions, statistics, the system of import-export licences and the establishment of the management committee, it offers us the possibility of establishing tariff quotas, safeguard clauses, prohibiting or restricting the use of inward processing arrangements and a specific provision on state aid. the problem is that a com can only apply to products listed in annex i to the treaty, so it can only cover ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin, but not synthetic alcohol. given the high degree of substitution and competition between agricultural and synthetic alcohol for most uses, the fact that only alcohol of agricultural origin is covered raises the legitimate question of the meaning and usefulness of a regulation which is supposedly designed to organise the european alcohol market as a whole. so when i started to draw up the report on behalf of the committee on agriculture, a difficulty arose: what to do with synthetic alcohol? the addition of synthetic alcohol involved consultation of the committee on legal affairs, as the legal basis of the commission proposal was to be changed. the committee on legal affairs held that the dual legal basis (articles 37 and 95) is impossible, since the procedures under both articles are incompatible. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include synthetic alcohol, which is not covered by the directive. this will ensure that the whole market in ethyl alcohol is regulated at community level. you will understand why the committee on agriculture voted unanimously in favour of this proposal. a com may not be the appropriate instrument, but it must be borne in mind that the commission has the power of legislative initiative. i would like to conclude by asking the commission three questions: can it tell us what the state of play is in the negotiations in the council? does the commission intend to withdraw the proposal? if so, do you intend to submit a new one?
commission. – i would like to thank all members of parliament who have spoken for the work they have put into considering the proposal for a common market organisation for alcohol. in particular, my thanks go to the rapporteur, mrs ayuso, for her analysis of the proposal and efforts to understand its objectives. as you know, this is another proposal to establish a set of common rules for the alcohol sector, after several attempts in the past that all failed for different reasons, as has been mentioned tonight by several members. the commission is of the opinion that the actual market situation in this sector made it necessary to propose at least a minimal set of rules and that, under those circumstances, the chances of succeeding this time were fairly good. that was also the opinion of a large majority of member states that invited the commission to come forward with such a proposal. the commission is therefore somewhat surprised that, despite the hard work of the rapporteur, who initially came forward with a series of amendments which might well have been considered, parliament now proposes rejecting the whole proposal. in the draft resolution parliament has asked the commission to withdraw its proposal as it does not fulfil its objectives of regulating the whole market of alcohol in the european union. i presume this amendment refers to the non-inclusion of synthetic alcohol in the proposal for agricultural alcohol. the commission cannot, at this stage, agree with parliament's position, as is understandable. parliament's position would imply considering the proposal to be the result of a lack of reflection and lack of analysis of the real situation of the sector. if, from an economic point of view, there are good reasons to extend the proposal to synthetic alcohol, there are legal and practical reasons why the commission did not do this, when it established the proposal. synthetic alcohol is a non-annex i product and therefore not covered by cap. inserting it into the proposal would mean that we would have to find another legal basis other than the cap articles 36 and 37 of the treaty. more importantly, the smoothest way to make a proposal was to limit it to agricultural alcohol because the production and trade in synthetic alcohol in the european union is more limited. most of the problems the sector faces are linked to agricultural alcohol and not so much to synthetic alcohol. if, once this regulation is applied, serious problems arise in relation to synthetic alcohol, insertion of synthetic alcohol into this instrument could always be envisaged. the commission is well aware of the fact that the major part of the alcohol market is accessible to both types of alcohol, which therefore compete for the same outlets. in order to realise its objective of better market information and transparency, the insertion of synthetic alcohol in the article on data collection to establish a yearly market balance of the sector and therefore to increase market knowledge might be considered. the commission is working on that. this would also be defensible without a change of legal base provided that it could be shown that it was genuinely necessary, in order to manage the cmo for agricultural alcohol, that we should have the data for synthetic alcohol. the case-law of the court of justice permits the use of article 37 for provisions that have an ancillary effect on non-annex i products, where this is necessary for the proper functioning of the cmo. for the rest, the commission is of the opinion that all other provisions proposed are necessary to establish a set of common rules for the alcohol sector, including the provisions on the application of the rules on state aid. without a fair application of those rules there would not be a common market for agricultural alcohol, as already exists for synthetic alcohol. i should like to say something about the german market in answer to members who have made reference to that particular aspect. the commission is well aware of the functioning of the german alcohol monopoly. the purpose of this proposal for a common market organisation for alcohol is not to put an end to the existence of the german monopoly. if the production of alcohol by german farmers, under the rules of the monopoly, including federal payments, is necessary for the maintenance of precious eco-systems or to cover the additional costs of environmentally-friendly production methods, there would be no problems, as current state aid rules offer substantial possibilities for member states to grant aid for those purposes. if, on the contrary, the aid in germany is not given for such reasons but is simple operating assistance, paid for other reasons, then the application of the state aid rules would cause a problem. on the other hand, those small distillers who produce not only alcohol but also a spirit, could benefit from the de minimis rules on state aid for non-agricultural products. i hope that these comments which i have also made on behalf of my colleague, mr fischler, have clarified the commission’s position on the proposal. moreover, i would like to thank members of parliament for their constructive suggestions, which the commission will consider. in answer to the question put to me by the rapporteur, if this amendment is accepted – which the commission would regret – then mr fischler and my other colleagues will reassess the situation and reflect on a further course of action. again i thank all members that have spoken and others who have dealt with this subject. i thank them for the time they have given to this proposal. in particular i thank the rapporteur, mrs ayuso gonzález, for her efforts.
- thank you very much, mr bolkestein. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon. the next item is the report (doc. (the sitting was closed at 10.25 p.m.)
- mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr beazley. the reality is that the dangers facing children and young people today are very different from those facing us. television and the internet have undoubtedly contributed greatly to this, giving them too many ideas of situations that are not real at all. a study recently published in a spanish media quoted the fact that young people see, for example, how a person jumps from a fourth floor and runs away unharmed or holds a bullet that has just been fired, without suffering any consequences, contributed to the fact that many young people were not aware of the real danger of these situations. moreover, it is thought that they are given too many ideas and that, sadly, this is contributing to the increase in violence both among youth and among children. that said, i would like to express my full support for the rapporteur when he calls on the member states to classify video games through self-regulatory mechanisms set up by the industry and also to set up abuse detection departments. i would also like to congratulate the commission on its intention to carry out a study on the classification of films distributed in cinemas, on television, on dvd and on videotape. ladies and gentlemen, we must be aware that we cannot aspire to a world without violence when our future adults spend their days watching increasingly violent cartoons, films and news reports.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate our colleague mrs de sarnez on the excellent work she has done on a subject of such importance to all europeans. i am not saying that education is not a community competence; in fact, in the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, of which i am a member, whenever we talk about education, a colleague of ours is counting how many times the word 'subsidiarity' appears in the debate. however, one of the fundamental rights of citizens of the european union is the free movement of persons, a right which we are denying to european citizens insofar as there is no recognition of qualifications so that they can go to work in another country of the european union. at present, many erasmus students who spend a year of their studies in another member state lose that year in their home country because the year spent in the first country is not recognised on their return. i find this really unacceptable, especially since, in these conditions, many of the students, instead of going to another country in the european union, prefer to go to the united states or canada and spend a year there and learn the language well. i think we have to avoid this situation by improving conditions within the european union. it is very important that students have the option of spending a year outside their own country, both for the coexistence and the training that this experience offers them and for the possibility it also offers them of learning and perfecting another european language, which is so important to us as citizens of the union. i would therefore like to join the rapporteur, mrs de sarnez, in advocating the creation of a european university label, the improvement of student mobility, the encouragement of the learning of more languages and, above all, the harmonization of higher education which will undoubtedly have to lead to the recognition of qualifications.
the commission has already made a number of proposals, and i am sure that the commission will be able to make a number of proposals. it is very important that parliament and the commission work hand in hand. as has been pointed out, in areas such as our education, it is sometimes not easy, in the absence of legislation, to establish direct collaboration with parliament. i regret it and wish it would change. i have already made it clear to parliament on several occasions when i visited the committee responsible that i would inform it whenever there was any new information and that i would invite members to take initiatives so that the commission could take account of parliament's proposals, which are very important in the area that is so important to us. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the communication adopted by the commission last july was intended to launch the debate on cooperation with third countries, taking into account the observations made by the honourable members: globalisation, increasing international mobility, europe's lack of competitiveness on the international education market, the need to encourage cultural understanding among our young people and those of third countries. the commission recalled that this cooperation with third countries was based on article 149 of the treaty. i would also add that, beyond the treaty, this cooperation is one of the means of promoting dialogue between civilizations. on this basis, the commission has drawn two conclusions, firstly, that if we are building bridges between universities within the european union, which we are doing, we must also build bridges between these european universities and those on other continents. that is the subject of the report under consideration. secondly, we must make our work in this area more visible, in order to promote europe as a centre of excellence and to attract students seeking international education. we've identified two targets. first, to train high-quality human resources in the partner countries and within the community through mutual development of human resources. we do not want to create a brain drain, but we want these students who have been trained in our countries - not in one country but in several, because that is where the european added value we have to offer lies - to return to their countries and, in a globalised context, to know what it means when, as adults, they are called upon to make decisions in the private or public sphere. secondly, we want to promote the community as a world centre of excellence for studies. we have centres of excellence, they exist, we have to link them together and make them more competitive because they will be known. we are making progress, ladies and gentlemen, through concrete action. the first of these concrete actions is the tempus programme, which is extended to the meda partners. this initiative is of course in the context of the barcelona process, but it also responds to the notion of strengthening cooperation in higher education contained in the communication. the rapporteur has mentioned the alfa programme. i can tell him that we are developing alfa plus for the countries of central and south america. alfa plus plans to award, within the institutional framework of university-to-university relations, more than three thousand scholarships to postgraduate students who will be hosted at our universities. you can see that, very concretely, we are developing pilot actions on other continents. we intend to continue to work in this direction. we fully agree with the basic analysis provided by the european parliament and the member states. in this sense, there is for once a good deal of unanimity on the subject at hand. the commission also took note of the requests for the preparation of a framework proposal to respond to the analyses that have been made. we are already working on it and i might even be able to launch the proposal this year. you will understand, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, that i cannot go into details today, but we will certainly take account of the many ideas contained in mrs de sarnez's report. i will of course keep the relevant parliamentary committee informed. mr president, if i may, i should now like to reply very briefly to some of the proposals made by mrs de sarnez. i think i have already answered the question about pilot actions: alfa, tempus and others. the rapporteur calls for a quality analysis to be carried out in universities and for joint study cycles to be built up with joint degrees using ects validation. well, that's what we're doing. we are building pilot projects where three or four universities from three or four different countries are collaborating on the basis of a common curriculum leading to a european master's degree. it is planned that in 2003 the university rectors will meet in berlin for a major conference to present the pilot actions that have been launched, some of which have already been launched during the current academic year, but most of which will be launched during the 2002-03 academic year. so we'll analyze the first results in berlin, and i hope that the initiative will snowball and that seeing that it's very positive, many universities will jump into this new system. as regards the precise location of international mobility, i believe, mrs de sarnez, that this is an analysis which must be made primarily by the oecd and unesco. we are in talks with these two institutions, which, in order to carry out these analyses, have a problem with the comparability of statistics and statistics which are too old and therefore outdated. but we think that these institutions should do it. we will work closely with them. this time, as regards the quality of reception, the administrative procedures, housing and grants, i would remind you that under the french presidency there was a large meeting of the ministers of education at the sorbonne to discuss the obstacles to mobility for a whole day. all this was put on paper and signed by our heads of state and government at the nice summit. the political decision at the highest level exists. the problem we have is that things are not moving fast enough on the ground, because these are issues that have to be dealt with by national governments. and i am not even talking about ministers, because often it is the ministers of social security, the ministers of the interior, who have to get their hands on the dough. we must therefore exert friendly pressure on governments to remove these obstacles to mobility, which are often not important. but we are also making progress in this area. i will give you an example: in some countries, the scholarships awarded by these countries to their students were not exportable, which seriously hampered mobility. however, most of the ministers concerned have taken measures to ensure that their students can continue to receive a scholarship when they continue their studies in another state. the last point is languages. you know that 2001 was the european year of languages. it did indeed make a difference. i say this with great admiration for the rapid reaction of many ministers of education who have undertaken school reforms so that children learn one or more foreign languages from an early age. i can tell you that the heads of state and government at the barcelona summit adopted our slogan: mother tongue plus two. so things are moving, they are moving, not fast enough, but in the right direction. with the help of parliament, i am sure we can make faster progress towards this common vision that we have.

- the agenda calls for the debate on the commission's declaration on the second united nations world assembly on ageing (madrid, 8-12 april 2002).
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, last saturday i spoke in madrid at one of the many round tables organized within the ngo forum which accompanied the second united nations world assembly on ageing. it was pointed out that ageing is affecting both the north and the south, despite the growing duality and inequality that is being established between the societies of the developed world and those of countries struggling to overcome underdevelopment. perhaps most interesting is to understand that, regardless of the location, three specific needs arise for older people. the first concerns health care at an age when health requires more and more expensive care; the second is the guarantee of economic security so that the elderly can continue to live independently when, because of their age, they stop working; and the third is the social consideration, respect and valuation of the elderly by society, not only as recognition for the services provided - which must also be done - but also for the role and function that these elderly people should find and fulfill in our social fabric. the satisfactory response to these three needs is what will allow older people to, fortunately, live in dignity for an increasing number of years. in general, the first two requirements - health care and economic security - have been met in a generally acceptable way in the countries of the european union, although the services are still very inadequate and can therefore be improved, and we must be alert to any threats to their survival. on the other hand, little or no progress has been made on the third need, that of consideration and responsibility for the elderly in our societies. the picture in the developing world is even worse. the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter, but it is not yet clear whether the council will take a decision on the matter. within the demographic perspectives that daily alter migration flows, these are other challenges we must face. the second united nations world assembly on ageing in madrid has done just that, setting out a new strategy which the european union must support decisively, as we do in parliament today by approving the excellent draft presented by mr podestà. we must do so for our future and for the future of a world which should be increasingly supportive and therefore fairer also to the elderly.

commission. - mr president, as we all know, the european union is strongly and consistently opposed to the death penalty and in the countries where it still exists, we call for the use of the death penalty to be phased out and insist that it be applied according to minimum standards. we all now have a common practice of lobbying for the adoption of moratoriums. we are particularly concerned, as the union and as the commission, at the cruel punishments and executions which are carried out in accordance with the sharia law in a number of countries. a hanging in january this year ended a de facto moratorium on the death penalty in nigeria. we took part in the eu's approach to the nigerian authorities on this issue last february. we have also intervened on several fronts in the case of safiya husaini, including when president prodi made a direct appeal to president obasanyo. we are currently following closely the case of amina lawal, cited by mr ainardi, mr karamanou and mr gihlardotti, for which an appeal procedure is currently under way. now, as to the impact of all this on the relations between the union and nigeria, the framework of which is set out in the cotonou agreement. one of the essential elements of this agreement is respect for human rights and in this context equality between men and women is part of the same subject. we welcome the official declaration by the nigerian minister of justice that the federal states must amend their criminal laws to exclude the imposition of punishments that go against the rights of citizens guaranteed by the nigerian constitution. it also appears that the federal government is concerned about the incompatibility between the criminal application of sharia on the one hand and the international conventions signed by nigeria on the other. we funded the nigerian implementation of a sharia study which indicates that sharia laws were poorly drafted and actually contradict other federal laws. the application of these laws is also somewhat inconsistent because of the lack of training of judges. the solution seems to us to be for the moment still on the side of dialogue and in particular on the respect of the obligations contracted by this country in the framework of the cotonou agreement. you know as well as we do that this agreement contains procedures which can be applied in the event of human rights violations. this is the point that we need to assess together in order to put the necessary pressure but to avoid punishing all the states of nigeria indiscriminately or jeopardizing the creation of an environment conducive to change because it is this change that will be the result of our collective pressure and efforts.

the commission is aware of the difficulties which the safety, the proper functioning of the rail transport network and the movement of goods are facing as a result of the repeated intrusions of illegal immigrants into the transport facilities which allow the passage from calais, france, to the united kingdom. this phenomenon, as i believe your various speeches have shown, is the result of a rather complex combination of factors and, in any case, in my view, it demonstrates once again that the union needs common immigration and asylum policies more than ever. i agree with mrs ludford and mrs roure on this point. in this context, the commission has already taken all the appropriate initiatives, by submitting to the council and to your parliament all the proposals necessary to ensure a kind of equality of treatment between the member states on matters which are obviously difficult. as regards asylum policy, the commission's proposals seek to create a fair, efficient and rapid european asylum system. we proposed a council directive on asylum procedures in september 2000. you know that many member states are opposed to the introduction of binding time limits for completing procedures. so we are going to table a revised proposal in the next few weeks, as the laeken european council has asked us to do. in the next fortnight or so, your parliament should be taking a decision on the proposal for a directive which was tabled by the commission a year ago and which aims to harmonize the conditions for the reception of asylum seekers. this priority of the spanish presidency could be the subject of political agreement in the council in the coming weeks. of course, the task will be made easier if parliament itself takes a stand. another proposal for a directive adopted last september aims to harmonise the concepts of refugee and person in need of international protection. it should be negotiated by 2003. all these proposals aim in particular at reducing what might be called pressure differences between member states, which produce incentives for what is bureaucratically agreed to be called 'secondary movements due to differences in practical and legal frameworks in asylum law'. all these initiatives also aim to ensure access to protection for those who need it, which is particularly evident in this case - in full compliance with the 1951 geneva convention on refugees. finally, the commission has also proposed a regulation on the responsibility for examining asylum applications which, as mr berthu rightly pointed out, contains a clause whereby a member state which has knowingly tolerated the illegal stay of third-country nationals on its territory for more than two months is responsible for examining the asylum application concerning them. the negotiations on this subject are not yet completed, although parliament itself has been working on it, and should be concluded during the danish presidency. so we are still in the drafting stage on this point, mr berthu. the commission fully supports the objective of developing a comprehensive approach to the management of migration, including its external dimension. this is one of the objectives of the common asylum and immigration policy which was set at the tampere european council. we shall come back to this on monday in luxembourg, with particular reference to the fight against illegal immigration. a thorough reflection on the links between development and migration will also have to be initiated. as regards the fight against illegal immigration, the council adopted an action plan on 28 february, which is very much based on our proposal and which stresses the importance of cooperation with countries of origin and transit. the fight against human trafficking and illegal immigration networks is obviously a priority and must be accompanied by assistance to victims who want to participate in the criminal prosecution of traffickers. and on the basis of a green paper on the return policy for illegal residents which the commission adopted yesterday, we will very shortly be launching a very broad consultation on this aspect of a comprehensive migration policy. finally, and this is a sign of the complexity of the subject, we are preparing a communication on guidelines for integrated management of the external borders. the responsibility of carriers is governed by the schengen convention and has been clarified by the adoption of a directive aimed at harmonizing the penalties applicable in this field. we are aware, however, that the problem is much wider and have taken various initiatives to bring together professionals, administrations and humanitarian organisations. finally, as regards the specific situation at the scnf terminal in fréthun, we have approached the french authorities, in accordance with community legislation, to ask them to take all the necessary measures to ensure the free movement of goods travelling by train. the french authorities have informed us that the work to secure the fréthun site is now almost complete, and that the extension of the fence, the installation of video cameras and various other equipment are being completed. they undertook to complete the work in time for the june 2002 traffic to resume the normal course of traffic before october 2001. we also made sure that the staff assigned to the surveillance of the sncf site was reinforced. at the transport council on 26 march the commission, following a number of parliamentary interventions, put this item on the council's agenda to allow the two ministers most concerned to express their views, and this is a euphemism i am not using without some caution. the two delegations, the french and the british, indicated that they had agreed on the measures to be taken to ensure a return to normal traffic under normal safety conditions. the commission has now concluded that it is up to them, having done its own vigilance work, to take all the necessary measures to ensure the free movement of goods. you will note that i have only touched on this aspect of the matter - important though it is - after having touched on the aspects of asylum and immigration policy, which are obviously the main context of this case.

the council. - mr president, i would like to thank all those who have spoken for their views and contributions, which now exempt me from going into too much detail, because i think that all the process will demonstrate all its virtuality, all its potential, all its effectiveness, and at that time, moreover, it will demonstrate that it is more necessary than ever. a stable peace can only be based on prosperity, cooperation, economic integration, mobility between peoples, the exchange of ideas, the exchange of their educational systems, the exchange of their peoples, and for that all that the barcelona process implies, in the political aspects, in the economic aspects and in the cultural and social aspects, is of extreme importance. i therefore conclude from today's debate that we all
