middle east, many members have referred to the policy of mr sharon, the current prime minister of israel. i would remind you that mr sharon has been prime minister for a little over a year, not even two years, and that he is prime minister because he is responding to the will of israeli society. i would also like to remind you that mr sharon's government is a government of national unity in which the labour party and several other parties are represented, and therefore when we talk about mr sharon's policy - we should not forget these things - we are talking about the policy of many others. it is the policy that all those in your government have adopted, because otherwise they would have resigned, or been sacked if they showed their disagreement. i think we often make the mistake of over-personalizing the causes of conflict. the middle east conflict, in its modern form, is over 50 years old, and at that time there was no mr sharon. i want to remind you that the second intifada began before mr sharon became prime minister. so we have to take all of this into account and get to the root of the conflict. it is true, however, that there are specific policies which are particularly objectionable and objectionable, and as such have been very clearly denounced by commissioner patten and myself, not only today but on many, many other occasions. but the problem is not only with the individual, but with something much deeper, namely that when a conflict lasts for a long time with its various oscillations, it is because there is no genuine majority will for peace on the part of the parties; because there is no sincerity and honesty in the peace manifestations made by one side and the other; because when some express their will for peace, but in their innermost being they are wishing for the destruction of the state of israel, they do not want peace, and when others say they want peace, but in their innermost being what they are trying to do is to make the great myth of israel a reality and therefore the consolidation of a state of israel over the present occupied territories, they do not really want peace. as these two attitudes come from their respective historical dreams, and these historical dreams are not compatible with each other, until there is an explicit, sincere and honest renunciation of these historical dreams, there will be no peace no matter how much we try to impose sanctions, no matter how much the international community does everything it can do. and it is in this context that the action of the international community must be situated, because our role at the moment is particularly clear, and consists in conveying to the parties that there must be a sincere and honest renunciation on the part of israel to increase its territories on the basis of occupation and there must be a sincere and honest renunciation on the part of the palestinians and the entire arab world to the destruction of israel. then we can actually build on a completely solid foundation. it's a work of persuasion. i am not at all sure that this is a work done on the basis of sanctions, i am not at all sure. it must be a work of genuine persuasion that reaches the political leaders of both parties and that reaches the respective public opinions. because the israeli public, which has now voted - a little over a year ago - for mr sharon, had previously voted for mr barak to make peace, and had previously voted for mr netanyahu, and previously, in a space of five or six years, for mr rabin. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the negotiations on the new treaty of rome, and it is not only the european parliament that has been involved in the negotiations, but also the european parliament itself. i don't mean that we agree with all of their positions. what i am saying is that we should go together, because that is very important and, if you read the madrid declaration correctly, it says what the european union has been saying for a long time, and those who have come to the positions of the european union have been others, including, to a large extent, the united states. i am very glad about that, and we shall continue to pursue this policy because i think it is absolutely essential. it is in this context of the international community, the whole of it, that it makes sense to speak of observers; it is then that it makes sense to speak of forces of intervention, because otherwise it would not be possible; and it is then that it makes sense to speak of marshall plans and economic contributions - which will have to be very important, by the way - and to speak also of everything that is meant by the rapprochement of peoples on the basis, among other things, of educational systems. the presence of the historical dreams i referred to earlier is clearly reflected in the educational content of both sides; the respective youths have been educated not in conciliation or coexistence, but in hatred. we therefore have a great deal of work ahead of us, but the road is clear. we know what the final horizon is and what is needed is to continue working in that direction. - the agenda calls for joint debate on the reports by mr johan van hecke (a5-0106/2002) on human rights in the world in 2001 and the european union's human rights policy, on the one hand, and by mrs díez gonzález (a5-0084/2002) on the commission communication on the role of the european union in promoting human rights and democratisation in third countries, on the other, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy.
the rapporteur. - mr president, we have drawn up this report which i am presenting today in the light of the fact that the commission's communication stresses the importance which the union attaches to human rights in the development of its foreign policy, which in our opinion deserves a very positive assessment. but i would like to stress that, although this communication contains important proposals and suggestions, it does not, in our view, offer any concrete instruments which will enable us to meet successfully the new challenges arising from a new vision which we share, and in which human rights and their promotion are fully integrated into the union's external policy. it is true that there are no substantial differences in approach between the union's institutions in theory when it comes to defining how to approach the development of human rights and the consolidation of democracy in the world, but it is also true that the differences and responsibilities between the union's institutions begin when it comes to moving from the realm of rhetoric to the realm of concrete achievements. it is not unusual to see that the democratic demands on our partners are too often overshadowed by the economic and commercial interests of the union or its individual member states. i would add to this a further paradox: although there is only one doctrine, different policies are being applied. if not, look at the paradigmatic case of cuba, and i quote it only as an example. the council is blocking it, while the member states maintain bilateral, commercial and other relations with the island. in this context, the aim of this report is not to reiterate the well-known doctrine of the union but to present concrete proposals for action, both in relation to the negotiation phase of all types of agreements between the union and third states and in relation to the implementation of such agreements or their possible suspension. the proposals contained in this report are intended to bring greater coherence to the work of the various community institutions, putting an end to the factual contradictions and the special preponderance of the political will of the council in this area, because in our opinion the absence of a uniquely unified union position leads us to act on the international scene guided by necessity or under the changing leadership of others, who do not always share our interests in this area. we have drawn up this report with ambition and responsibility, with the ambition required to commit ourselves to the defence of human rights in the world and with the responsibility that comes from knowing that the challenge of integrating human rights into the union's foreign policy is truly complicated. but also bearing in mind that the contradictions between institutions, the lack of unanimity, coordination and unity in action are the worst enemies of human rights and democratization in the world. the proposals in this report must therefore be seen as a contribution to overcoming this situation, to overcoming our own contradictions. as mr patten said in his speech this afternoon, we like to give lectures on human rights, but sometimes it is worthwhile to look a little at ourselves. my first proposal is therefore to ask the commission to draw up an interinstitutional code of conduct to make the union's external action in this area more consistent and fair. this code should govern relations between the union and the more than 120 states to which the democratic clause is currently applicable. a code, ladies and gentlemen, which will be an instrument for knowing in what terms, internal and external, dialogue is taking place; a code to bring the union's discourse and actions together, but never to mortgage dialogue; a code as a political instrument, not a legal and ethical one, which systematically collects the values and political thinking of the union and its rules of application. i would like to stress that this code should not be based on the punitive and suspensive nature of the human rights clause, but on mutual respect between the parties, incorporating as many positive incentives as possible and including generous cooperation programmes, which will make it possible to improve respect for human rights at all levels. our objectives must not only be to assess the progress made by the various partner countries in the field of human rights but to achieve a coherent approach between countries and regions, avoiding above all, as we saw in geneva, unfair outcomes, comparative harms and double standards in dealing with them. the code is, after all, the abc of parliamentary democracy. the second proposal in this report, which i would like to highlight, is the recommendation that the parliament elected in 2004 should set up a committee on human rights, with responsibilities for human rights and democratisation in third countries and responsible for relations with international organisations working in this field. thirdly and lastly, i would like to refer to the commission's proposal for the creation of a union agency for human rights, a suggestion already made by the european council in cologne. this agency, ladies and gentlemen, would be a body whose objective would be to establish common criteria and parameters for the analysis of the human rights situation in the world, by producing an annual assessment which would enable interinstitutional action to be taken in accordance with the elements constituting the code. the commission will of course have to define the areas of action of the agency, but it would be very useful to carry out a more effective and coordinated work, which could, for example, include the impact assessment of structural measures, given their great importance in the reconciliation processes after an armed conflict. in short, it is a useful instrument, which does not take away powers from anyone but adds up own and external efforts and resources. finally, as regards the five amendments tabled by mrs malmström, i must say that i will not accept them, that i will ask the house to vote on the report adopted by a large majority in committee, with three abstentions and no votes against. i am grateful, however, to mrs malmström and to the other members of parliament from all political groups who have amended and reflected with us on this report, because their work has helped to enrich it. i would also ask the house to take into account that the original text is in spanish and to check the other versions, because i think there are differences in the nuances.
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs rosa diez, for her report. the european union's commitment to the defence of human rights and democratic principles requires effective action, but above all consistent action. without consistency, there is no credibility, and without credibility, there is no authority to promote and enforce respect for human rights. i therefore share the commission's strategic and comprehensive approach to mainstreaming human rights in the union's external policy and to ensuring that all community policies, programmes and projects take account of this issue. finally, i agree with the approach of humanitarian aid based on human rights, which is very important for conflict prevention, or that country strategy papers should propose concrete measures for the promotion of human rights, and that these measures should be considered as a priority. the fight for human rights is inseparable from the fight against poverty and development cooperation policy, insofar as both promote the establishment of the economic and social conditions necessary to guarantee peace and to ensure that every person can live in dignity; conditions without which respect for fundamental rights is nothing more than an entelechy. i therefore ask the commission in particular to consider universal access to education as a priority topic in the framework of political dialogue and the discussion of country strategy papers, because education is indispensable for the development of peoples and without development it is difficult to speak of full respect for human rights.
- mr president, human rights are a subject on which spanish socialists are particularly sensitive, and that is that, while for the vast majority of men and women in the countries making up the european union these rights already constituted one of the main bases of their system of coexistence, we still had to put in decades of effort and suffering before we achieved an acceptable situation of dignity in terms of human rights in our society. the rapporteur, mrs rosa diaz, is well aware of all this. he knows it even better than others, because, as a basque and a democrat, he belongs to a category of spaniards and europeans who still today must continue to fight against ultra-nationalist terrorism in order to consolidate fundamental rights which are the hallmarks of the european union. i shall be speaking in support of what mrs diez and mr van hecke are saying and proposing, and i shall add only a few comments. the first is that the various excellent initiatives proposed should not be interpreted in a restrictive way. for example, it is not so much a question of a very high level of respect for human rights being an unjustifiable precondition for the european union to establish cooperation relations with third countries, but rather that the objective and result of such cooperation is to raise the level of respect for human rights in each country with which it cooperates. my second comment is in line with some of the criticisms we have already heard, namely that we make many demands in the field of human rights when we talk about third countries and, in particular, developing countries, and that we are much more conciliatory when we talk about the frankly unsatisfactory human rights situation in the countries of the european union itself. that's not the case. the fact is that these reports refer specifically to third countries, but i take it for granted that the moral and political authority of our discourse in cooperation with the world around the european union, with which we want to interact consistently, will be all the more credible and effective the more we preach by example and the more what we ask of others is backed up by our own conduct and by our self-assertion to keep moving forward, day after day, improving everything that concerns the protection of human rights in the territory of the union.
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. i should like to thank mrs díez gonzález and mr van hecke on behalf of the commission, and in particular on behalf of my colleague mr patten, who cannot take part in the debate today, for their reports which are very complementary. in your report on the commission's communication on human rights, mrs díez gonzález, you call on the institutions to draw up a common code of conduct to guide the union's relations with third countries. the commission reiterates the importance of a constructive and dynamic approach to the european union's relations with other states, based on critical partnership and cooperation. the council also reaffirmed this approach in the guidelines for human rights dialogues. this dialogue is particularly promising when respect for human rights and democratic principles is an essential element of agreements concluded with third countries and these agreements contain a human rights clause. the cotonou agreement is one such step forward - and it has been mentioned here. the commission is ready to discuss the future form and proper application of this clause and will continue to attach great importance to parliament's views. in her report, mrs díaz gonzález also advocates the establishment of a european agency for human rights and democracy, which would have a reporting and advisory role. however, as the commission stated in its communication, it is of the opinion that the european union does not lack consultation opportunities or sources of information. the european union can rely on reports from the united nations, the council of europe and, not least, a large number of international non-governmental organisations. the real challenge for any institution is to use the information available quickly and fully and then to build the political will to make difficult decisions. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. it would also be extremely difficult for the commission to delegate powers to such a body in the sensitive field of human rights. mr van hecke's report focuses on two main issues: the fight against terrorism and the fight against modern forms of slavery. the european union strongly condemns slavery in all its forms, a term which today includes, in addition to traditional slavery and the slave trade, serious violations of children's rights and women's rights, the exploitation of certain situations of dependency and apartheid. millions of people in many parts of the world are still affected. the european union has just made a statement on this subject in the committee on human rights. the european union welcomed the various international instruments, in particular those of the ilo, to combat these forms of slavery. it also called for a more active approach to human trafficking. in the field of basic labour standards, the commission presented a comprehensive strategy in its communication of last year entitled 'promoting basic labour standards and a more social approach to policy in the context of globalisation' to provide incentives and empower countries to implement and comply with basic labour standards. one concrete step was the adoption by the council of a revised scheme of generalised preferences - the social incentives scheme - which provides for additional preferences for countries which meet basic labour standards. in addition, serious breaches of one of the fundamental agreements with the ilo will now be among the grounds for temporary withdrawal of generalised preferences. the eu has suspended the generalised system of preferences for burma for these reasons in particular. in many countries the commission has now increasingly supported projects against trafficking in human beings, against trafficking in women, against child labour or slavery. for example, projects against the exploitation of minors in gabon, benin, togo and nigeria, or projects under the stop or daphne programmes, which are aimed at combating human trafficking and sexual exploitation. in his report, mr van hecke rightly emphasizes that the events of 11 september represent new forms of terrorism. i now come to this part of the report. the fight against terrorism has rightly permeated the whole of the political debate. human rights considerations are involved at different levels. the european union maintains the important legal distinction that it is states that can violate human rights, whereas terrorist acts are legally classified as crimes, as a crime. in all aspects of the fight against terrorism, it is of the utmost importance that we and our allies, despite the urgency of the action, strictly respect the values of international human rights and humanitarian law. the report by mr van hecke also refers to the european initiative for democracy and human rights. the commission is actively pursuing the implementation of its new strategy. this includes a longer-term approach, which involves the selection of a limited number of priority areas to which it attaches central importance and where the community's contribution can make a real difference. as in the past, the commission will continue to involve the european parliament in the discussion on the way in which the european initiative for democracy and human rights is being implemented. i would like to congratulate mrs díez gonzález and mr van hecke again on their reports. the commission welcomes cooperation with parliament to further advance our common concerns for democracy and human rights. the european union is founded on respect for human rights, and this foundation applies to europe's internal policy as well as to our european foreign policy. - the next item is the report (a5-0109/2002) by mr wynn, on behalf of the committee on budgets, on the draft amending budget no 2/2002 of the european union for the financial year 2002 (7033/2002 - c5-0131/2002 - 2002/2043 ((bud)).
- mr president, i do not think i can improvise for five minutes an intervention on budgetary matters. in any case, mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen of the committee on budgets and other interested parties, the wynn report - which was previously the costa neves report and will shortly be the podestà report, so that we can say that it has been one of the most followed and be returned to the member states for under-utilization. a budget surplus in national budgetary policy is a good thing, it is a saving. it often involves a budgetary effort not to make a expenditure the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. i am very pleased to see that the commission has taken the initiative in this matter. the member states not only want their money back, but they are entitled to it under the treaty, and the commission has presented the supplementary and amending budget accordingly. the money from the member states' contributions to the european budget which we did not use last year should be returned to the member states as soon as possible, in accordance with the legal provisions, for purely economic reasons, because everything else is an economic loss. we had a very large surplus last year and i will come back to the various components in a moment. the supplementary and amending budget now also includes several components, namely, firstly, the surplus from last year and, secondly, the implementation of the new own resources decision, which includes several components. the new own resources decision, as agreed in berlin, was to enter into force on 1 january 2002. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use (emah) in order to ensure that the agency is able to carry out its tasks in the field of medicinal products for human use. in concrete terms, this means that the current member states will have to pay in some cases higher contributions than they would have to pay under the new own resources decision. the new own resources decision has several components: 25% of customs revenue may remain with the member states, the share of vat revenue decreases while the share of gnp increases; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it's been decided. this is something that has to be implemented now and the commission has therefore linked it to the surplus. the reimbursement of the customs duties, which means that member states can retain 25% of the customs revenue, will apply from 1 january 2001. the money that would be needed for this, of course, we have set off against the surplus, because otherwise it would have been returned and then called again. the commission's annual report for 2000 analyses the progress made in the european union in the area of equality between men and women. we welcome the fact that the female employment rate has increased, albeit slightly, but we still find that women's jobs are often part-time, more precarious and with lower career expectations. we have not achieved equal pay for equal work. the differences are still very significant, and although we have made some progress in reconciling work and family life, we have not yet achieved a greater division of labour within the family, which would enable women to devote themselves more professionally to their work. when we think that women need help, we mean mothers, young women with small children, and we believe that we can solve this problem by creating day nurseries. another very common phenomenon is that in families there are elderly people, people who are in charge of these same women, disabled people who represent an added work for the housewife, for the woman. it is not generally taken into account that social aids are also necessary, such as day centres to facilitate women's entry into the workforce. we can see that women are not making enough progress in the society of the future, that is to say, in the new technologies, the information society. only 20% of women are in this sector and that is something we should encourage, by giving them access to lifelong training, because the jobs of the future will necessarily be in the new technology society. there is still a very marked absence of women in management positions, in companies, associations, political parties and public institutions. we have repeatedly called for a greater presence of women, a greater balance between men and women, but we have seen the difficulty of achieving the presence of women in decision-making positions. we therefore call for innovative measures, specific measures aimed specifically at ensuring that women are more represented in all areas, in the professional sphere, with a greater division of tasks between men and women, and with a better reconciliation of professional and family life. we must ensure that the community objective of equality between men and women is met in programmes financed from european funds, in accordance with the treaty, and we must promote greater participation of women in decision-making positions. these objectives will also be taken into account in the process of enlargement of the european union, with the aim of ensuring that the acquis communautaire is incorporated into the national legislation of the candidate countries. domestic violence and the trafficking and exploitation of women remain a serious problem and we must continue to work to help the victims and, where possible, to eradicate the causes that provoke it, such as poverty and insecurity. as we can see, there is still a lot of work to be done, there is still a low presence of women in management positions, there is still a low representation of women in the workplace and, above all, equal pay for equal work is not achieved for women. i believe that we must therefore call on the commission and the institutions to exercise greater vigilance so that the objective of equality becomes a reality as soon as possible. - mr president, commissioner, rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, in most normal situations the main - and often the only - source of the resources necessary for the maintenance of the wage-earner and his family is the income from his work, that is to say his salary. therefore, within the system of wage protection, in addition to the mechanisms that facilitate the collection of wages on the real estate of the debtor entrepreneur in a privileged way, the legislator builds a specific guarantee of the collection of wages by a public system, often structured around a public administration body, for the cases of insolvency of the entrepreneur. this was the main objective of directive 80/987/eec: to ensure a minimum level of protection in the community in the event of the insolvency of the employer. it is true that the implementation of this directive encountered many difficulties, both because of the concept of insolvency for the purposes of the directive, the need to set limits on the time and amount of liability and the increasingly frequent consequences of transnationality - as the rapporteur has already said - and of globality, as well as the need to adapt this directive to other subsequent directives or the need to simplify the rules on the payment of wages due, all of which are difficulties which the amendment seeks to overcome. the amendments to the text of the common position reinforce the objective of protecting workers, which is the aim of the directive, and i believe that they represent important progress. it remains to be clarified, with the clarity that would be desirable, some concepts which require greater precision (possibly because social reality is almost always ahead of legal-positive reality), such as the concept of worker, so that it covers all the real modalities, the problems arising from the decentralisation of production or outsourcing, the concept of the role of wage or labour dependency in relation to economic dependency, or even the concept of the proper use of the guarantee institution. but, in substance, we should be happy that we have reached this point. i believe that the concern of the commission, parliament and the council during the spanish presidency shows that it is possible and feasible to achieve 'more europe' and, moreover, points out to the candidate countries the path they must follow to achieve a more social europe. i think, therefore, that i must end by congratulating the rapporteur, even though, in theory, not all the objectives that would be desirable have been achieved. however, the possible is the enemy of the optimal, and now that we are so close to the 52nd anniversary of the date on which europe began to move, it may be appropriate to say that europe is becoming more and more slowly, step by step, but it is also worth stressing, madam commissioner, that social issues are finally taking their rightful place in the europe we want.

concerning the new forms of employment, i would like to confirm to members of this house that the commission is aware of the problem and is dealing with it in a new way and in a much broader context than in the directive with which we are dealing today. indeed the forms of the employment and the way in which work is organised are undergoing rapid and far-reaching changes. new types of employment are emerging. there are new types of worker, half-way between the traditional models of the employee and the self-employed worker. various terms have been used to describe or designate these workers. the terms used most often are economically dependent workers or para-subordinate workers and persons who perform work similar to that of an employee. what these workers have in common is that they resemble self-employed workers in the autonomy they have to organise their work and/or the fact that they take an economic risk. at the same time, they are economically dependent in the sense that they depend more or less on just one client firm and are very often highly integrated into the internal organisation of the company. the commission raised the problem of these economically dependent workers with the social partners. there was a consultation with the social partners, and they revealed their sensitivity to the problem, but it was obvious that they did not have a concrete approach or a concrete proposal. it was clear that there was a need for further information about the phenomenon in all member states. i must reassure you that in the existing text we take into account the concrete forms of employment which have already been legislated for – i mean part-time work, temporary employment contracts and fixed contracts. but there are other forms of employment, to which i have already referred, that cannot be covered by this directive. in order to take into account your concerns, and after our consultation with the social partners, i confirm that the commission has launched a study which should provide an overview of the legal, social and economic position of economically dependent people in the 15 member states. once this study has been finalised, the commission will organise a joint hearing with the european parliament for three reasons: to exchange views and practices, to evaluate the results of the study and to raise the awareness of all concerned. consideration could be given to inviting representatives of the accession countries to participate in this joint hearing. after this joint hearing, the question is whether we will go further: is the commission going to propose concrete community action? after all this information and the reactions, the commission will consider the forms of community action needed. we will propose them to establish a broader framework and then see how it might be done.

- the next item is the report (a5-0127/2002) by mr ojeda sanz, on behalf of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, on the proposal for a council decision amending decision 1999/311/ec adopting the third phase of the transeuropean cooperation programme in higher education (tempus iii) (2000-06) (com (2002) 47 - c5-0096/2002 - 2002/0037 (cns)).
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr president, and the commissioner for their help in drafting this report, and for the goodwill shown by the commission's officials in this area. the tempus programme - in this particular case, the extension of the tempus programme proposed by the council - must be seen in the context of a strategy which is primarily intended to strengthen dialogue and understanding between the peoples and cultures of the european union and the mediterranean. some asked why an existing programme was being extended rather than creating its own. if the question is good, the answer is easy. if an existing programme is extended, avoiding the usual problems of setting up a new programme, the experience and experience of the tempus programme can be used, supplemented by the improvements which have been introduced gradually and which will undoubtedly encourage the rapid diversification of university offerings and cooperation between the euro-mediterranean partners. as you know, the tempus programme is inspired by the events which followed the fall of the berlin wall in 1989. this programme was set up in 1990 to meet the needs of higher education reform in the countries of central and eastern europe and at the same time to promote transeuropean mobility in higher education. funding for this programme was included in the phare budgetary framework, and in 1993 it was extended to include all the newly independent states such as armenia, azerbaijan, belarus, georgia, kazakhstan, kyrgyzstan, the republic of moldova and the russian federation, among others. the second phase of this cooperation programme in the field of education already covered a total of 13 associated countries for a period of 4 years and from 1997 the 10 countries of central and eastern europe in the pre-accession process gradually left the tempus programme to participate in socrates (the general community programme in the field of education). however, the council decision was amended to extend tempus ii for a further two years. this decision provided for an evaluation by the commission to consider tempus programming. the aim of tempus iii is now to extend this cooperation to the mediterranean partners, thus meeting the needs for cooperation in higher education in this area. it is proposed to extend the tempus programme to morocco, algeria, tunisia, egypt, israel, jordan, palestine, syria and lebanon. this cooperation aims to strengthen the structural mechanisms enabling universities to carry out sustainable cooperation beyond assistance granted through cooperation programmes and to better prepare the institutions of the european community and the institutions of the associated countries and territories to develop and consolidate partnerships. this will have a multiplier effect, beyond the participating institutions and a lasting impact on education systems, which is what this is all about. it is also important to broaden the range of participants, which will go beyond the traditional academic community, involve public administration officials and civil society in general, and encourage cooperation in higher education which can play a key role in changing attitudes by enabling younger generations to compare their respective national values and cultures. the aim is to go beyond purely academic issues to those dedicated to strengthening civil society mechanisms in the mediterranean partners and to contributing to a better understanding of different cultures and respect for human rights and minorities in these countries. the various evaluations of the tempus programme have shown that it is perceived as a valuable instrument for promoting mutual understanding and it is on this scale of values that the participants should place emphasis when planning their activities. these are the substantial changes in the tempus programme for the mediterranean partners which we fully share in this report. otherwise, this programme remains unchanged in substance. i would therefore like to reiterate that the main objectives of the tempus programme are to facilitate the development of higher education, to respond better to the socioeconomic and cultural needs of the target countries, and to promote understanding and rapprochement between cultures and the development of free and flourishing societies. these objectives should be achieved through joint european projects, which are the main inter-university cooperation instruments of the tempus programme. in addition to the jeps, the tempus programme also offers individual grants to teachers, researchers, etc. for a range of complementary activities in support of the overall objectives of the programme. with this report we have sought to underline the need for the tempus programme to extend well beyond the university community, so that the latter, which will remain its main focus, can contribute to the transformation of civil society.

policy, which i believe is the treatment of immigration and asylum. within the area of freedom, security and justice which we europeans have set ourselves the task of building up, in accordance with the premises of the treaty of amsterdam, the progressive formulation of a common immigration and asylum policy occupies an essential place. a policy on immigration and asylum which must be based on a comprehensive and balanced approach. this overall framework, according to the tampere european council conclusions, must be based on four essential premises: proper management of migration flows, the pursuit of fair treatment of third-country nationals, cooperation with countries of origin and the establishment of a european asylum system. progress in these four areas has inspired the preparation of the spanish programme of objectives and priorities for the presidency of the council of the european union. this is all the more so given the renewed impetus given by the laeken european council of 14 and 16 december 2001, which stressed the need to strike a balance between the protection of refugees in accordance with the principles of the 1951 geneva convention, the legitimate aspiration for a better life and the reception capacity of the union and its member states. we have also tried to give priority to those instruments which the laeken conclusions themselves identified as being most urgently needed for their adoption, such as the global action plan against illegal immigration. in line with these ideas, i shall try to systematize my presentation of the progress made in recent immigration and trafficking in human beings. on the establishment of a common european asylum system, we have taken very important steps in these last two formal councils of ministers of justice and home affairs. i would like to highlight the directive laying down minimum standards for the reception of asylum seekers in the member states. this proposal seeks to ensure that asylum seekers who arrive in our states enjoy a minimum status of rights essential to the development of a dignified life, including residence and free movement, family reunification, schooling and education for minors, access to employment and vocational training. the council, after its meeting on 25 april, has reached a general political orientation on the text of the directive and we must now examine the proposals instrument, which we adopted on 28 february and which i believe is of particular importance: the council regulation laying down certain detailed rules for the implementation of regulation no 2725/2000 on the establishment of the eurodac system. once eurodac was set up in december 2000, an implementing regulation was needed to establish procedures for identifying asylum seekers by means of an electronic comparison of their fingerprints. this will facilitate the application of the dublin convention, which, as the honourable members are well aware, determines the member state responsible for examining asylum applications. in the second part of my report on the progress made so far in the six months of our presidency, i shall focus on the milestones of our immigration policy, which is guided by the idea of proper management of migration flows, which includes both the idea of their legal regulation under the fair treatment of third country nationals and the fight against illegal immigration, in particular against trafficking in human beings, all of which is guided by the idea of cooperation with the countries of origin. in this connection, we have tried to move forward with the progressive unification of our visa systems. to this end, the general affairs council of 18 february adopted two regulations establishing a uniform model for visas and a uniform model for the visa sheet issued by the member states to holders of travel documents not recognised by the member state issuing the form. at the last jha council on 24 april we supplemented these rules with the council decision approving a uniform model for visa applications. alongside this unification, we have also reached a general approach to the regulation establishing a uniform model for residence permits for third country nationals. among other advantages, this standard will facilitate the recognition of documents by police and border control authorities, which will benefit the holders of documents and help to detect counterfeits more easily. secondly, in order to provide financial support for certain measures proposed by the member states, aimed at promoting cooperation and coordination between national administrations and the transparent application of community legislation in the field of immigration, asylum and borders, at the council meeting in april all the member states reached a general agreement on the approval of the argo programme, which will run for five years and is endowed with 25 million euro. thirdly, there is no doubt that proper management of flows requires effective measures to combat illegal immigration, in particular trafficking in human beings. the conclusions of the laeken european council called for the adoption of a global plan in this respect, which we had the opportunity to discuss at the informal ministerial meeting in santiago de compostela and which we formally adopted at our ministerial meeting on 28 february. the plan, which is closely inspired by the commission's november 2001 communication, is conceived as a programmatic guide to help plan the actions that can be implemented to effectively combat the phenomenon of illegal immigration. let me briefly outline the main actions and measures covered by this plan. first, visa policy; second, enhancing the exchange and analysis of information on the problem of illegal immigration; third, the plan addresses a series of pre-crossing measures; fourth, the plan focuses on improving the quality and effectiveness of border controls; fifth, another aspect addressed by the plan is readmission and repatriation policies; sixth, the operational role of europol in the fight against trafficking in human beings will be enhanced; and finally, the plan addresses repressive measures against repressive measures against these crimes. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the necessary protection and assistance is provided to victims, to combat employers who employ illegally, to seize the proceeds of trafficking and to confiscate the means of transport used, and to make it effective to oblige carriers to bear the costs of repatriating foreign nationals who do not meet the requirements for legal entry. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the council of ministers for justice and home affairs, following its approval, has already taken some measures to implement it. the council conclusions on illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings by sea are therefore welcome. these conclusions seek a comprehensive european union response to the mass arrival of migrants by sea, on the basis that migration issues should be a relevant part of the eu's external relations. i think this is a major issue which we must be aware of and above all we must act accordingly and as quickly as possible. i repeat, migration issues must be given a prominent place in the european union's external relations. as regards the jha issues, we will give priority to measures such as the carrying out of a study to improve the control of maritime borders, the prevention and adoption of operational measures, especially the exchange of information, which is already bearing very good fruit, and the firm appeal to the states of origin and transit to combat human trafficking and to readmit illegal immigrants leaving their coasts, among others. secondly, as requested by our heads of state and government at laeken, we have determined the list of third countries with which new readmission agreements should be negotiated, and the general criteria for this determination have been laid down. in april we also carried out a risk assessment operation at the main european union airports, known as operation rio, the results of which, which i had the opportunity to present at the council on 25 april, will enable us to deepen cooperation between the border control authorities of the member states and europol and to learn about the methods, routes and other procedures used to smuggle migrants into the territory of the european union. in the same spirit of cooperation, the strategic committee on immigration, borders and asylum (scifa) met for the first time this semester, with the participation of the heads of the external border control services. this meeting, which will take place every six months, has served to set out a strategy for improving operational cooperation between member states in external border control, in areas such as risk assessment systems, the situation at our maritime borders, and specific training for our border control officers. we have also developed mechanisms to deal with the situation of foreigners who do not fulfil or no longer fulfil the conditions for entry or residence, through conclusions on the obtaining of travel documents for the purpose of repatriation. on the other hand, as i said at the beginning of this speech, it is essential to encourage cooperation between the countries of origin, transit and destination of these movements of people if we are to manage migration flows properly. in recent months we have intensified the union's external relations in this area. i should like to briefly describe the contacts we have made. as a conclusion to the meeting of the council of ministers of justice and home affairs on 28 february, we held a meeting with the candidate countries for enlargement, during which we discussed, among other issues, the control of external borders. at this meeting we handed over a catalogue of recommendations and best practices on external border control and on admission and expulsion procedures in the schengen area, which we had approved the same day. for the first time in the union, we also held a meeting of the 15 member states with the ministers of justice and the minister of the interior of russia, during which we were able to discuss, among other issues, the issue of migration, border management and readmission policy, and also handed over to the russian representatives the catalogue of recommendations to which i referred earlier. thirdly, at the euro-mediterranean ministerial conference held in valencia on 22 and 23 april, cooperation in the fields of social integration of immigrants, migration and the movement of persons was discussed and a regional programme in this field was adopted within the framework of the valencia action plan. the plan also reflects the parties' intention to hold a euro-mediterranean ministerial conference on migration and the social integration of immigrants in the second half of 2003. finally, i would like to focus on the conference on migration, held in the framework of the asem process in lanzarote on 4 and 5 april. this initiative, which started with the asem heads of state summit in beijing in october 2000, has served to lay the foundations for dialogue and cooperation between both parts of the world on the general situation of immigration, the management of migration flows and the fight against illegal immigration. the meeting resulted in the adoption of a declaration underlining the need for cooperation between europe and asia to organise migration flows in a comprehensive manner and setting out, inter alia, the establishment of a network of national contact points to continue the dialogue and develop future actions. so far, my presentation has focused on the concrete results achieved in recent months. i would also like to stress the important impetus given to various regulatory instruments in the various working groups, both in the area of asylum and in the area of immigration. i can say that work has made considerable progress on the proposal for a council regulation laying down the criteria and mechanisms for determining the member state responsible for an application for asylum, known as dublin ii, or the directive laying down minimum standards on the status of refugees. similarly, and in accordance with the amended proposals on minimum procedural standards for granting and withdrawing refugee status and on family reunification, which the commission presented on 30 april, we will push forward with the continuation of work to make progress in these areas. as you know, the commission has recently presented the green paper on a community policy on the return of illegal residents and the communication on 'guidelines for an integrated management of the external borders', and we will endeavour to encourage the relevant council bodies to study them. in the area of regular immigration, considerable progress has been made in the discussion of the proposal for a directive on the status of longterm foreigners and the proposal for a directive on the conditions of entry and residence for the purposes of employment and selfemployment. under our presidency, a study has been initiated on a proposal for a directive on the issue of short-term residence permits to victims of trafficking in human beings who cooperate with the competent authorities. finally, in this section on progress, i would like to refer to the impetus given to the european union's action plans with third countries. in particular, as regards the dialogue with morocco, the work of the social affairs and migration group, which held its second meeting on 12 march this year in rabat, has made progress. i would also like to point out that the high level group on asylum and immigration has agreed to send a mission of experts to morocco to assess a border control programme. to conclude, i would like to briefly outline our work prospects until 30 june 2002. the spanish presidency will be discussing the creation of the visa data bank, on which we have already consulted the guidelines for the common system for the exchange of visa data, before the last meeting of the council of ministers on 13 and 14 june. we intend to submit for approval in june a draft council conclusions which will indicate to the commission what aspects should be considered and examined in the feasibility study. this system is a further step in the implementation of the global plan against illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings and will make it possible to avoid issuing a visa in a consulate of a country of the union if it has already been refused in another consulate of another member state. the results of the feasibility study on european border police, which is being carried out under the auspices of italy by a working group including representatives from germany, belgium, france and spain, are due to be presented at the end of this month. we also plan to submit to the council the proposal for a decision on the signing of the readmission agreement negotiated with hong kong and the draft mandate for the commission to negotiate such an agreement with ukraine. if the proposal for a regulation known as dublin ii is sufficiently developed during these months, we shall submit it for discussion in this last council of our presidency. i would like to conclude by thanking once again the commission and commissioner vitorino for the key role they have played in these efforts, without whose help they would not have been possible. i would also like to thank parliament for its dedication and cooperation, which have given a very important boost to the european union's policy on immigration and asylum during the almost five months of the spanish presidency of the council of the union. i believe that the balance of results and prospects is positive and i can say that we are largely achieving the objectives which were part of our work programme and which i had the opportunity to present to the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs on 4 february. ladies and gentlemen, thank you very much, and, in a very special way, thank you very much, mr president. - mr president, immigration is certainly an inexcusable duty of solidarity on the part of the more developed countries. it is also an essential instrument in the fight against poverty and social imbalances in the world and, moreover - and this must be said and explained bluntly - it is a necessity for maintaining growth and prosperity in our countries. but it is true that migration flows to the european union have increased dramatically in recent times and the capacity to receive them is not unlimited. it is therefore no exaggeration to say, as the council has said here, that the proper management of immigration is europe's greatest challenge today. we must ensure that the immigrants we are able to welcome are protected and subject to the law, that they assume the rights and obligations that this entails and are fully integrated into the society that receives them, sharing with other citizens the values on which it is based. it is proven that illegality is the breeding ground for marginalization. we must therefore make it a priority to combat illegal trafficking in human beings, that is to say, the mafia and organised crime, in close cooperation with third countries of origin and transit for migratory flows, some of which must be required to make greater commitments. i ask the commission to draw up and report to this house on this matter, because the sensitivity to sign readmission agreements is fundamental in this area. i agree with commissioner vitorino when he says that there is a link between foreign and immigration policy. both the spanish presidency and the commission are pushing for greater cooperation in the police and diplomatic fields, including, of course, visa policy, which i believe - commission. - these two questions refer to the publication by certain non-governmental organisations and some newspapers of draft requests from the european union for services in the wto negotiations. these leaks, because they are leaks, are regrettable because they disrupt our own internal preparation for the negotiation; the community consultation processes are not yet completed; we are only at the initial stage of discussing projects and have not yet reached a final position at union level. in fact, we are in the process, as the procedures require, of consulting our member states so that they have the opportunity to study these initial requests, to conduct their own internal consultations and to offer us their comments, all of this process resulting, at a certain point, which has not yet been reached, in the transmission of these draft requests to geneva. these leaks are also regrettable because they are not beneficial to our own negotiating position. the publication of such negotiating proposals clearly puts pressure on the third countries to which they are addressed, which themselves have had to deal with a number of questions on what we regarded as still only draft proposals: all of which, of course, do not facilitate negotiation. finally, they are regrettable because, for once, the european parliament was not informed before the others, or at any rate immediately after the council, which is not in accordance with the rules we have established together. i would remind you that within the limits set by the treaty, which clearly gives priority to the council, we have adopted informal information and consultation processes between us which have worked well so far and which, moreover, i have no reason to believe will not continue to work well in the future. the final reason why these leaks are unfortunate is that they give a kind of strange signal, as if it were a scoop, in which interesting discoveries, in the sense of detective novels, would have been made. however, this is not the case, since the outlines of these proposals are public, have been on our website since the end of 2000 and do not contain any new elements compared to what we had posted in the political principles. in any negotiation, there is a first time for reflection, a second time for transparency, and a third time for negotiation away from the spotlight. we are at the stage of reflection. we have consulted each other extensively before we have sent our initial drafts to the member states. i can assure you that parliament's positions on the negotiations on services, in which it has placed great emphasis on the need to ensure respect for public services, a concern which is also the concern of the commission and which we have incorporated into our proposals, are not at all different from what we have indicated. we have indeed consulted and taken into account the views of a number of professional circles and the views of a number of non-governmental organizations: none of these organizations has received any special treatment from us. in short, these leaks are indeed very regrettable, but they are also, as regrettable as they are, positive: once these secret documents have been made public, everyone who is carefully interested in them and who now has the opportunity to look at them closely will see that these so-called secret proposals are entirely in line with the objectives we have proclaimed publicly and that there is no hidden agenda, contrary to what has been written here and there. they will find, in particular, that we have no intention of promoting or calling for the privatisation of public services, or their dismantling, in any sector or in any country. in fact, this publication has, so far, only one victim, and that victim is the myth of the hidden agenda. this victim is so badly hurt that i am even now sometimes personally suspected of having organized this leak myself to show how much what we were doing in secret was consistent with what we announced in public. i deny, of course, any such statement. in conclusion, let us briefly recall that the wto agreement on services is the most flexible agreement in existence, that it provides for each country to draw up a list of activities for which it is prepared to offer access to its market and to offer national treatment to foreign suppliers, that each country may exclude from its commitments activities which it considers politically sensitive and that, as a consequence, the problems of diversity of the economic and social situations of the participating countries are respected. in addition, wto members retain the sovereign right to regulate, in accordance with specific public objectives, the commercial and non-commercial activities that are carried out in their territories. that's the general principle. the draft requests in question, in accordance with the negotiating proposals we had submitted previously and in line with the objectives we have already set out, concern a number of sectors, which i will mention briefly: the professions, business services, courier services, postal services, telecommunications, construction and engineering services, distribution, environmental services, financial services, tourism, travel, transport and energy. it is not a question - as you will have seen when you listened to this list - of health or education, and we have not made any requests to third countries in the health or education sectors, and we have no intention, i must say, at this stage, of making any offers in this area. there is one other question, to which mr van den berg has drawn our attention: the question of water in developing countries, which is indeed a complex one. the commission is convinced that in this water matter we have good reasons for making demands on third countries in the matter of water distribution. i am referring specifically to 'water distribution', to distinguish it from the problem of access to water resources, which is outside the scope of the wto agreement on services. we consider, following a number of international works, that if the billion or one and a half billion people on earth who do not have access to water today are to have access to it in the next ten years, then we need private financing. the current volume of capital to be invested in such infrastructure is something in the order of 200 billion dollars. today the level is something in the order of 70 to 80 billion dollars. the gap cannot be filled by public funds alone. we therefore believe that, if properly steered, the gats negotiations could make a useful contribution to an international effort which has been undertaken to achieve the un millennium water goals. the last point is raised by mr van den berg. this is the question of the relationship between the imf's requirements, or conditions, for the developing countries and the wto negotiations. the answer to this is that the services negotiations and the imf's structural adjustment programmes are not linked. however, developing countries which have made or are said to have made commitments under structural adjustment programmes have an interest in having these countries, if i may say so, take credit for them in international negotiations. as long as these conditions are not consolidated in the wto, they are not considered binding from the wto's point of view and therefore countries which for one reason or another have been forced to accept, or have accepted, such conditions from the imf can use this credit in the wto negotiations. we are prepared to look at this in a very positive light.
- i ask you, commissioner, and members, to be very brief because we have exceeded all the time limits imaginable for this question.
commission - very briefly, let us make a clear distinction between the community regimes for services and the wto regimes. we have community regimes which we adopt for our own reasons and we adopt positions within the wto which are sometimes distinct. we cannot, of course, not go no further than we have done internally, but we can go no further than we have done internally, and that is still our policy. on your second specific question: are we asking others to make efforts to liberalize in areas where we are not prepared to make commitments? this is not our policy, the instructions i have given and what i have said publicly are that, in case we do so, we will do so only as an exception and therefore, at that time, with the necessary consultations and consultations.
commission. - the mandate i have as commissioner is the one adopted by the council, and by parliament for that matter, in 1999 for seattle. so the extension of that mandate and the reservations i have are in this document which is a public document. as regards services, i would remind you that the gats negotiations operate in stages: first the requests - everyone makes requests to everyone - then the offers - everyone makes offers to everyone. the deadline for applications is june of this year and for tenders march of next year, and it is only at the end that, after comparing the applications and the tenders, everyone takes a stand. so it is then, probably around the beginning or the middle of 2004, that we will know exactly what we are prepared to offer and i will do so, as i have done so far, in consultation with the council, with parliament and with a number of other sectors of civil society - professional and non-professional - who are interested in these issues.
commission - i don't think there are any relationships like that. the agricultural negotiations which are being conducted jointly by my colleague fischler, as the main negotiator, and myself, as the secondary negotiator, are negotiations whose terms were set in doha and we all committed ourselves, around the table, to improving our market access, to reducing our internal support and also to reducing export support. this is the general line that was agreed by everyone in doha. then comes the question of quantity: how much ? it is precisely this that is being negotiated and there is, to my knowledge, no link of the kind you are referring to between deregulation on the one hand and reduction of subsidies on the other.
commission - i have indicated the priority sectors. in general, they correspond to those in which the european union has a clear comparative advantage. financial services, telecommunications, distribution and construction services are the most frequently mentioned in bilateral negotiations or visits. in general, these sectors account for about 70% of the european union's gnp and still only account for 25% of our exports, which shows that we have a very large potential to exploit.

- question no 30 is therefore inadmissible in the absence of its author. question no 31 by mr göran färm (h-0343/02): subject: implementation of the budget the european union's budget has been in a large surplus for several years. this is a negative development since it implies that the funds committed are not being used where they should be. in the long run, this situation may undermine the union's credibility. what does the commission intend to do to solve this serious problem? is the commission in contact with the council of the european union and the member states in order to improve the implementation of the union budget?
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. the answer to mr färm's question is as follows: in 2001, the total commitment appropriations were used to 97%. this was a significant improvement on the figure for the previous year, when we had a commitment appropriation utilisation rate of 82%. the situation was different with regard to payment authorizations. in 2001, the budget was used up to 82% of the available funds, below the already low figure of 88% in 2000. the surpluses in 2001 were mainly due to the under-utilisation of the structural funds ( 9.4 billion), the cohesion fund and the ispa, sapard and phare pre-accession instruments. however, savings in the agricultural sector, amounting to eur 1.9 billion, also contributed significantly to the 2001 budget surplus. in the case of the structural funds, the main reason for the under-utilisation is the late introduction of the programmes for the new programming period 2000 to 2006. in the case of sapard and ispa, it was the combination of two factors, firstly the difficulties encountered in starting up new activities, and secondly the establishment of the necessary administrative structures in the applicant countries. the commission is very concerned about this development and has already taken a number of measures to give substance to the measures taken in 2001. among other things, the member states, which are responsible for the implementation of the programmes, were asked to strictly respect the implementation timetable for the period 2000 to 2006, including the n+2 rule laid down in article 31 of regulation 1260/1999. the rules apply to each programme from 31 december 2002 and to the others from 31 december 2003. in a letter of 21 november last year, my colleague mr barnier specifically drew the attention of the member states to this rule. the commission services shall regularly inform the member states of the status of all commitments which are liable to be affected by this rule. the last notification was made in april 2002. the member states were given until 31 march 2003 to submit their final payment applications for the programmes of the last planning period, i.e. the 1994 to 1999 planning period. for the cohesion fund, each financing decision shall set a mandatory deadline for the submission of these payment applications. the commission has informed the member states that it is opposed in principle to any extension of those time limits. the implementation of the structural funds will be monitored more closely throughout the year, in particular by means of the new payment estimates to be drawn up by the member states. these estimates are now also communicated to the budgetary authority in the course of the budgetary procedure. the commission will also alert the relevant member states to the risk of automatic decommitment of commitments which have been outstanding for too long. the estimated needs of the member states for payments to be made under the structural funds in 2001 (excluding advances) were 15 billion higher than the actual amounts of payment claims received by the member states. for the other budget lines, the commission is endeavouring to refine its forecasts of needs and to further develop the implementation plan for the 2002 budget, in order to present in good time, thanks to an early warning function, any discrepancies between the needs for implementation and the available funds. this plan is intended to monitor the implementation of the budget throughout the year and will be reported to the budgetary authority in september and november 2002, as we have promised you.
commission. - mr president, i would first like to point out that implementation in the area of external aid you mentioned has improved considerably over the last two years. in the last year, 2001, almost all available funds were spent. this is a very serious change from previous years. the reform and, above all, the measures taken by my colleagues chris patten and poul nielson have a very positive effect here. as regards the second part of your question, i can say that the member states are now interested in spending the funds in the structural funds. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the budget for the financial year in question. on the one hand, we have the anticipation and the huge discrepancy with what is then realized, and on the other hand, of course, the fact that the return is welcomed. we are here to consider how we can use instruments to make these forecasts, on which we will then build our proposal, more concrete and perhaps even more binding. i would point out that the rule in rural development measures is that if the member states' forecasts of what they need differ by a certain percentage from what is actually achieved, this is, as it were, punished negatively in the form of a deduction next year. this is a very far-reaching regulation, but it has nevertheless been shown to work. my colleague barnier is also working to improve the current imbalance in the structural funds.
- mr president, commissioner, i'm not going to tell you about the big numbers you're handling. we all know that 1.27% is committed to 1.14% and approximately 1% is spent. but we always blame the member states for this and say that they commit more than they are then able to spend. i am going to ask you a very specific question about a programme which is entirely and exclusively the responsibility of the commission, the life programme. the life programme, which last year had approximately 100 million euros, committed 20 million less than it had, despite having more than enough well-assessed and well-ranked projects to have committed the 100 million. this year, when this programme is about to be awarded - if it has not already been awarded, because it was to be awarded in the next few days - will the commission do the same? what are you going to do to ensure that the commission actually allocates 100% of the appropriations it has and that it also leaves some projects in reserve, since in its implementation these programmes reached the normal level you have mentioned, of 70% or 80%, which is then spent in the commission? commissioner, this is a matter for the commission alone and not for the member states.
the commission. you are right that the structural funds are essentially a means of repaying what the member states have spent. in this respect, if there are no invoices, no payments can be made, whereas the live programme is a direct implementation. we had a delay in certain tenders last year. i'm afraid i can't tell you the current call volume. i would like to give you a concrete and very precise and detailed explanation in writing.

- question no 32 by mr staes (h-0266/02): subject: european budget and support for the arms industryaccording to the institute for security studies, the european union spent between 1.5 and 2 billion euros on arms-related expenditure in 1999. the bulk of this money is going to the framework programme for research and technological development through the structural funds and the research and technology budget. can the commission confirm this and say to what extent european union funds are used to support the arms industry, directly or indirectly? could it also say how much of the european union's budget has been devoted to measures aimed at the conversion of the arms industry?
commission. - i would therefore like to reply to mr staes on both points. firstly, as regards the research programme, the treaty and the texts relating to the fifth framework programme are clear: the commission has no legal competence in the field of specific military research, since this area falls within the scope of intergovernmental cooperation and the weu. i refer to article 17 of the treaty. the decision on the fifth framework programme stipulates that community financial assistance for research projects under the framework programme will be used exclusively for civilian purposes. it therefore does not allow for explicit support for both civilian and military research. the proposal for the sixth framework programme is in the same vein. it is also quite clear that it is not always easy to assess the proportion of civilian research which may be applied in the military field. for example, there are computer research programmes which may at some time, even if they are for civilian purposes, have military applications. but we only do research programs for civilian purposes. that's it for the research programme. as regards konver, i told you that actions financed by konver are still possible under objective 1 and 2 programmes, which are the responsibility of my colleague mr barnier. i have no other information to give you on the current share of actions financed by konver under objectives 1 and 2. i would point out, however, that the konver programmes are aimed at converting the employment pools most affected by the reduction in armaments activities or the closure of military sites. so the purpose of these programmes is a socioeconomic purpose which goes in the direction i think you want.
