question no 36 by sarah ludford (h-0280/02) subject: cyprus what does the commission propose to do to lift or ease the trade and economic embargo on the northern part of cyprus, within the limits of european and international law, in order to help alleviate the current isolation of the turkish cypriot people and to participate in a political settlement of the situation on the island, with a view to eu accession?
the commission. in accordance with the judgment of the european court of justice of 5 july 1994 in the anastasiou case, cypriot products enjoy privileged access to the eu market when accompanied by a certificate of origin issued by the competent authorities of the republic of cyprus. at present, turkish cypriot exporters resident in northern cyprus are required to use stamps of the turkish republic of northern cyprus. this turkish republic of northern cyprus is not recognised by any state in the world under international law, with the exception of turkey. the commission has not received any comments from interested parties. on 5 august 1994 the president of cyprus, mr kleridis, sent the following letter to the secretary-general of the united nations: provided that the procedures provided for by national, european and international law are respected, turkish cypriots may export their goods under the same conditions as the rest of the population of cyprus. the letter thus contains the clear political commitment of the republic of cyprus to issue certificates of origin at the request of turkish cypriot exporters. it is therefore for the cypriots to agree on the practical arrangements for turkish cypriots to obtain certificates of origin issued by the republic of cyprus. madam president, i am sure that we both agree with all the members of this house that this extremely difficult question can probably only be solved and will be solved in the context of the solution of the cyprus question as a whole. it is therefore our aim to put an end to this situation, which is very sad for the turkish cypriots, by settling the cyprus question as planned this year before we take the accession decisions.
commission. - mr president, we are not refusing to trade with the turkish cypriots. i agree with you that the commission considers that it is highly desirable to increase the involvement of the northern part of cyprus in trade, because it is a regrettable situation that the greek part of the island is developing positively and rapidly, while the turkish part is sinking ever deeper into poverty. we're not denying the deal. the problem is that the turkish cypriots are prevented by their own authorities - i say authorities in quotation marks - from fulfilling the necessary conditions, and these are the certificates of origin which cannot be issued by the turkish republic of northern cyprus but only by the internationally recognised republic of cyprus. the commission cannot change this perfectly clear legal situation. we would be clearly in breach of the law if we acted otherwise here.

- mr president, to understand the discussion we are having about the two magnificent reports presented by mr trentin and mr marinos, it would be useful to recall that maastricht was not just another european council; it was, in fact, a council where two dogmas were enshrined: the dogma of price stability and the dogma of budgetary balance. lisbon and barcelona add a new dogma, a clarification of the doctrine, and point to reform as the only way of salvation, understanding salvation as closing the gap that separates us from the united states. the defence of the dogma is entrusted to the european central bank - the guardian of the faith in monetary policy - although in the field of budgetary and macroeconomic policy, where the risk of dispersion is greater, it is difficult to know who has this role. we are now witnessing the resurgence of deviant and perverse behaviour and - what is worse - the emergence of doctrines which seek to justify this kind of perversion, not so much in monetary policy as in budgetary and macroeconomic policy. the documents are repeated in succession, reaffirming the dogmas, but there is a lack of coordination and a lack of firmness. that is why, at a time when we are tackling the reform of the treaties, when the convention is in progress, i would like to say, in the same vein as for the employment guidelines, that they should serve to share the diagnosis, to establish clear lines of conduct and clear mechanisms for sanctioning or repressing deviant behaviour. i would also like - as mrs randzio-plath will probably explain - for the commission to remain the driving force, to retain the monopoly of initiative and for the principle of qualified majority to be extended in parallel with the principle of co-decision in most macroeconomic matters. mr solbes is not a simple altar boy; he is a prince of the church, and he has a fundamental role, spearheading like st vincent ferrer, in this reform process.
- the good dr. duisenberg has been telling us for months about the economic recovery. so are the followers of the good dr coué. they see the signs everywhere, like the fortune teller who sees happiness in coffee grounds. in fact, we have to ask ourselves if we're not in recession. in the face of this reality, the liberal conceptions which govern the economic policy of the european union reveal a certain harmfulness. the so-called stability and growth pact and the independence of the central bank deprive the public authorities of the means to cope with the crisis. in the face of this reality, the famous lisbon declaration is more a charm than a policy, and the commission's recommendation on the broad guidelines of the economic policies of the member states and the community for 2002 is the same charm. when the invisible hand of the market works, all of this is pretty much fine. in a sense, because the gap between rich and poor is growing. it is a tragic fact that in the world as well as in our own country, and we see, with the example of the french republic, that the demagogues are watching the corner of the wood to take advantage of this situation. i should like to congratulate the handful of colleagues who have just organized the summit of the poorest in europe with the ngo quarter-world. this europe now represents 17% of the population, that is to say 60 million people living on an income 60% below the average. but let us return, if you will, to that invisible hand. when that hand has ants, itches, rheumatism, which seems to be the case today, nothing is right. member states will find it increasingly difficult to respect liberal prohibitions such as the 3% threshold. and what about the budget balance for 2004! several countries are experiencing difficulties: germany, for example, is now in this situation. and it is the strongest economy of the 15 countries. when berlin sneezes, europe catches a cold. we have an example from the other side of the atlantic: with their usual pragmatism, the united states of north america, these champions of liberalism, have just proved once again that sometimes it is necessary to resort to anti-liberal measures. we could use some inspiration from this side of the atlantic. the rapporteur is timidly, too timidly - i conclude, mr president - introducing homeopathic amendments to the commission's liberal creed. despite all the respect i have for bruno trentin...
- mr president, i think it would be unfair not to commend the work done by the commission to achieve the white paper's objective of simplifying and clarifying legislation, removing all the drawbacks of legislation scattered over seventeen directives. the proposals he has put before us are also reasonably good and very well thought out, and i think that all the sectors involved have recognised this. i would also like to highlight the work done by the two rapporteurs, because the food chain is long and therefore there was a lot of material to be studied and they had to study and agree on a number of amendments which i am sure will improve the project. these legislative rules are based on the control of food safety from farm to fork in order to offer the highest guarantees to the consumer. i support everything that both speakers have said. one of the key points of the future legislation is the mandatory application of haccp in all food businesses including the primary sector. risk analysis and control of critical points was designed to be applied in the food industry and has certainly been a great advance in food hygiene. but the reality is that many small businesses have not yet been able to put this into practice. it is precisely because it has not yet been applied to the whole of the manufacturing sector and because the system has been designed for industry alone that it should not be extended to the primary sector for the time being. the primary sector is already obliged to comply with the so-called guidelines for good practice, a system which has the same purpose as that pursued by haccp and which is more adapted to the characteristics of this economic sector. and if there have been problems, it has not been for lack of rules, but for lack of compliance with them. i am not saying that the primary sector should be required to comply with haccp standards in the future, but they should be adapted to the versatility of agriculture and livestock farming. the application of these rules should be considered an essential measure of food safety, but it can never replace controls. i think that they must be insisted on and that they must be made methodically the same in all countries. economic operators should take responsibility for the safety of food, ensure the viability of food and its ingredients and establish emergency withdrawal procedures. finally, i would point out that exports and, above all, imports must comply with hygiene standards, otherwise insecurity may come from outside, and our companies will lose competitiveness in relation to those which do not meet the same requirements.

- mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the commission on the very balanced proposal it has put forward, both in the directive and in the regulation on the control and surveillance of zoonoses, which will be voted on here in this parliament tomorrow. these are matters of great importance to all the countries of the european union. and for some of the countries of the european union they are not of great importance, but of paramount importance. i would like to express my deep concern about the outcome of the vote on the report presented to the committee on the environment, since, in my view, it takes our concern for consumer health to an irrational extreme. we are all concerned about the health consequences of salmonella - and our rapporteur has just said so - and much more so about countries such as spain, greece, italy, portugal and france, which are exposed to this danger because of the volume of livestock susceptible to infection by the average temperatures which are favourable to their development and by a number of other circumstances which are not to be taken into account. however, i do not understand why, under the pretext of defending consumer interests, some countries in the european union support the extension of control and surveillance measures to agents not transmissible to humans, that is to say, non-zoonotic agents, which do not fall within the scope of these regulations. the only types of salmonella that affect humans are enteritic salmonella and salmonella tifimurium, so extending community regulations to other types - there are up to more than a dozen - can only bring, in my view, commercial consequences that would punish these countries of the european union and small producers. the production in the north, where the incidence of salmonella is almost zero due to its climatic conditions, would not be affected. i therefore ask all honourable members to support the amendment tabled by the group of the european people's party, which reflects the sentiments of many of the countries which have expressed themselves in this regard in all the discussions taking place, both in the working groups of the council of ministers and in the working groups of the commission. this amendment guarantees consumer safety, since it includes all the advances proposed by the european commission and does not penalise anyone. i regret that the report adopted by the committee on the environment has not taken account at all of the main countries concerned and i hope that this situation will be resolved, if not in tomorrow's plenary session, then in the negotiations at the next progress council, in the negotiations which will have to be undertaken in the codecision process, since the measures will be difficult to achieve. i also regret that there are a number of loopholes which have not been sufficiently analysed in this parliament, such as that in article 9 of the regulation, which provides for the freezing of trade in those countries whose national control programmes are not approved. this initiative may lead to a situation of clear commercial discrimination. the report adopted by the committee on the environment has not, in my view, been sufficiently calibrated by all the countries and, moreover, it repeats this error. the first summit of heads of state or government between the european union and latin america and the caribbean was held in rio de janeiro in june 1999 on the initiative of the french and spanish governments. during the meeting, spain offered to host the second summit agreed at the time, which also coincided with the spanish presidency of the european union. the summit will therefore take place in madrid on 17 and 18 december, as planned, that is to say on friday and saturday of this week. the profound changes in the european and american regions during the 1990s and the mutual desire to establish a general framework for bi-regional relations were the main reasons for the rio summit. at the end of the meeting, the heads of state or government adopted two important documents: the rio declaration, which set out the general principles to be applied to relations between europe and latin america and the caribbean, and a second document, the plan of action, which identified 55 priority areas in the political, economic, cultural, educational and social fields, among others, which were to lay the foundations for a bi-regional strategic partnership between both sides of the atlantic. with this madrid summit, the european union and latin america and the caribbean commit themselves to deepening this partnership so that both regions can unitedly face the challenges and better take advantage of the opportunities offered by the young 21st century. in madrid, the heads of state and government intend to adopt three documents: an evaluation report on the work done since the rio summit, a document setting out the increasingly numerous common positions and values we share, and finally a political declaration which, in addition to proclaiming the consolidation of our bi-regional strategic partnership, will list the firm commitments made by the highest officials of both regions in the political, economic and cooperation fields, going beyond what was adopted at the first summit. until 1999, relations between the european union and latin america and the caribbean had been based on a mainly subregional approach. political dialogue and cooperation were adapted to the different subregional realities, i.e. the dialogue was subdivided. the san josé dialogue for central america was established, the dialogue with the andean community, mercosur, icaricom and, with a few exceptions, such as mexico and chile, which had some specific relationship, practically all the dialogue focused on various subregional units. the rio summit was the introduction of this new bi-regional approach, which has certainly added weight to the european union's relations with the subregions and with the individual countries. in the run-up to this second summit, the spanish presidency has worked hard to make substantial progress in the three strategic dimensions i have mentioned. in addition, and this should be emphasized, the european union's strategic relationship with latin america and the caribbean has been intended to be the framework or the minimum reference standard on which the european union's relations with each of the subregional areas or individual countries of latin america and the caribbean are to be built. from the point of view of political dialogue, the european union's priorities with latin america and the caribbean during this short period from the rio summit to the present day have been mainly the strengthening of democracy and the rule of law, the defence of human rights, the fight against drug trafficking, as well as the promotion of regional integration and coordination between the different positions of both regions on the international agenda in the framework of international organisations and conferences. the madrid summit is a step forward, not only in terms of quantity but also in terms of quality, in the form of a better structuring of the political dialogue and a wider range of topics to be discussed, including those which do not relate to regional problems. it is hoped that this leap will lead to the development of a common vision of world affairs. from an economic point of view, it should be stressed that the european union and latin america and the caribbean are two regions with very different economic and social characteristics. the population of latin america and the caribbean is larger than that of the fifteen - i do not mean the enlarged europe, because naturally we will have more inhabitants there than they do - and for the most part it is very young, that is to say, it is composed of very young age groups. the average per capita income in latin america and the caribbean is just over eur 3 000 a year, while the eu average is seven times higher. the bi-regional market continues to offer ample opportunities for trade. from 1990 to 2000, european exports have increased from approximately eur 17 billion to eur 54 billion, i.e. we are talking about a figure that is almost three times as high. as for european imports from latin american and caribbean countries during the same period, they have increased from about 27 billion to 58 billion, that is to say, we are talking about a doubling. despite this dramatic increase in volume, imports from latin america and the caribbean have fallen from 24% of the total in 1990 to just 12% of the total in 2000. in relative terms, trade between the two atlantic coasts is declining, but within the americas it is increasing. there has also been a marked increase in european direct investment in latin america and the caribbean. the european union is now the largest investor in the region. investment rose from eur 66 billion in 1997 to eur 122 billion in 1999, representing almost 11% of total european investment abroad and almost two thirds of european investment in non-oecd countries. this investment, mr president, is a major reflection of the european union's confidence and commitment to the whole of latin america and the caribbean and is undoubtedly a major contribution to the growth of economic activity and job creation in that region. the europe of the fifteen also shares, and above all shares, deep historical, political and cultural roots with latin america and the caribbean, which facilitate the development of a true identity and a true strategic partnership. these common positions and values are creating important links in terms of identity and solidarity and are encouraging both regions to increasingly exchange their own experiences and combine their forces to solve common problems. among the challenges facing the european union and the countries of latin america and the caribbean is the need to modernise education systems, create an economic and social climate conducive to sustainable development and establish mechanisms for good governance. the promotion of a strategic partnership cannot be based on a common identity, be it historical, cultural or political, but must be the result of a shared interest in translating principles, values and objectives into practical mechanisms for dialogue and cooperation, so that both regions can face together all the major challenges of this new millennium. on 17 and 18 december in madrid, the heads of state and government of the 48 countries of latin america and the caribbean and of the european union attending the summit - we should note that this summit of heads of state and government is the largest and most comprehensive ever held in the union, because we are talking about 48 heads of state and government - will try to give a major boost to the bi-regional strategic partnership, which, as i have already said, began in rio de janeiro in 1999. in each of the strategic pillars on which this partnership is based, the political, economic and cooperation in the social, educational and cultural fields, both regions have wanted to take an important step forward. the joint fight against terrorism, by acceding to all the relevant international conventions and implementing all the relevant un resolutions, will be particularly worth mentioning. efforts to strengthen democratic institutions and the rule of law, with particular attention to human rights and the strengthening of judicial systems, in order to ensure equal treatment of all persons before the law, will be continued. it also notes the entry into force of the rome statute of the international criminal court, which, as you know, has been ratified by a very large number of countries in latin america and the caribbean. it is planned to strengthen political dialogue and consultation in the united nations system, as well as in other international fora, on the most important issues on the international agenda. on the economic and commercial front, it should be noted that the negotiating process for the association agreement between the european union and chile was successfully concluded on 25 april. it is a free trade agreement between the two parties. it is a truly innovative economic agreement, the most advanced of all those concluded between the european union and other third countries, and it has not hesitated to be called a fourth generation agreement. it is a free trade agreement which has perhaps reached the highest level, in terms of the number of issues that have been discussed and the considerations that have been made, which undoubtedly opens the door to other agreements of this kind, both in the region and in other parts of the world, but let us remember that, precisely in the region, we are trying to establish a free trade agreement between two areas of economic integration such as the european union and mercosur and, therefore, the agreement established with chile already sets a precedent for establishing something that will be historic, which is a free trade agreement between two common markets or between two areas of economic integration. i would also like to mention, for its relevance, the recent approval by the general affairs council of a proposal for future relations of the european union with the andean community and central america which opens the door for consideration to be given to the creation of free trade areas between the european union and both areas and for intensification not only of cooperation but also of political dialogue, which is an added value that did not exist before in the agreements with these countries. we all know that the difficult internal situation in some countries of the south american bloc has made the complex negotiations for the association agreement between the european union and mercosur, to which i have referred, difficult. the summit is in fact seeking to take stock of the results of the negotiations in which the political, institutional and cooperation chapters have been completed and to record the small progress made in the areas of trade and trade facilitation measures with the idea of not abandoning this important project of a future free trade agreement between mercosur and the european union. both regions - i mean the european union and latin america and the caribbean in general - have committed themselves to working together to ensure the success of the world conference on sustainable development to be held in johannesburg next august, and to making a mutual commitment to success in something that is very important and in which latin american countries have a lot to say, which is the millennium round, with the trade issues that have recently been launched in doha. education, culture and access to knowledge are undoubtedly important keys to success in the 21st century. i would like to highlight the launch of the @lis programme for cooperation with latin america on the information society, recently approved at the meeting of science and technology ministers in seville, and the alcue programme for scientific and technological cooperation and a new postgraduate scholarship programme which aims to help 4 000 students from across the atlantic to benefit from the advantages of studying at european universities. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to reiterate that this madrid summit, which is to be attended by - as i have already said - 48 heads of state or government, is to consolidate a bi-regional process on the basis of a strategic partnership. i am convinced that at the end of the summit we will be able to congratulate ourselves on the progress made in a process which began only three years ago.
commission. – mr president, the day after tomorrow, as the presidency has just pointed out, the second summit between the european union, latin america and the caribbean will take place in madrid. the fundamental aims of this summit are: to reinforce the bi-regional strategic partnership that was launched nearly three years ago at the first summit in río de janeiro, and to set out new objectives for the next two years. i will not repeat all the reasons for the importance of this relationship, which was set out so cogently by the presidency – economic, political and cultural – but we all know how important it is. rather than repeat what has been said so eloquently already, i would like to address two main questions regarding the summit. firstly, what has the commission done to ensure the success of madrid? and secondly, what results do we expect from the summit? it goes without saying that the commission is strongly committed to ensuring the success of the meeting in madrid. and, we are equally committed to ensuring that the bi-regional process initiated at rio succeeds. indeed, what is at stake in madrid is the fundamental credibility of this whole process. as parliament knows, public opinion has been increasingly critical of summits in recent years. we look back to the controversy surrounding the g8 meetings last year. these summits are frequently derided as high-level talking shops that too often produce little more than hot air. the summits’ grandiloquent final declarations are frequently, and perhaps rather embarrassingly, contrasted with the paucity of the results they actually achieved. as the commission has repeatedly emphasised, we are determined that madrid will not just be a talking shop like that. it has to be credible, and in order for it to be so, we need to demonstrate clearly that the ambitious objectives defined at rio have been achieved. i do not want to launch into a long-winded overview of everything that has stemmed from rio. nor am i the right person to outline everything that others have achieved since then. instead, i shall concentrate on the commission’s accomplishments in the priority areas of cooperation that it committed itself to work on. i firmly believe that we have fulfilled our part of the bargain and we can go to madrid with our heads held high. firstly, the commission has launched several programmes aimed at supporting and strengthening those institutions that explicitly defend human rights. these include a regional programme in support of ombudsmen in latin america and two multi-annual programmes on democracy and human rights. in addition, the commission has co-financed a bi-regional conference on the work and cooperation of ombudsmen and national human rights institutions, as well as an inter-continental conference on human rights protection. moving on to information society, which the presidency referred to, our most notable achievement has been the adoption of the @lis programme. aimed at reinforcing cooperation between the european union and latin america, it was officially launched at the eu-latin america and caribbean ministerial meeting in seville a few weeks ago. in the social sphere, the commission also goes to madrid with a positive balance sheet. we have promoted the participation of different civil society groups and have financed a series of meetings that will submit their conclusions to the summit. we have co-financed an academic seminar on social equity, an ngos forum as well as a civil society meeting. this is on top of the recent business forum held last month in mexico. as evidence of our ongoing commitment in this area, it is worth noting that in programming cooperation for the period 2000-2006 the commission has allocated a substantial part of its existing financial resources to the social area. in addition, the commission is currently working on all initiatives aimed at increasing public administration capacity in social policies, through exchanges of experience, best practice and know-how. finally, in the field of education, the commission has approved an ambitious scholarship programme under the name of alban. over a period of nine years, 4 000 scholarships will be awarded to latin american graduates wishing to complete their studies at european universities. i want to emphasise to parliament how much importance i personally attach to this programme. as we all know, too often latin american students feel that they have no choice other than to head directly north to continue their studies. we have to give them another option: the option of coming to study at european universities. that would be good for us, and i hope it would be good for the next generation of leaders in latin america. these are scholarships which will be generous – worth about eur 19 000 each year. they will be managed by, i hope, a network of higher education institutions. if we can make a success of this scholarship scheme, we can look at developing similar schemes in other areas, because i believe profoundly – a point made by mr iglesias on a number of occasions – that one of the most important ways in which we can help our partners around the world is by opening our own universities to as many of them as possible. let me move on to my second main question: what does the commission expect from the summit? first of all, madrid should be an opportunity to enhance the political dimension of our bi-regional strategic partnership. this partnership is about more than just developing cooperation projects: indeed, 48 heads of state and government have not come together simply to endorse a new list of projects. i am convinced that what is really important is the opportunity that madrid presents us with to give political weight to fresh and bold initiatives. in particular, we need to bring our political dialogue into sharper focus. by doing so, we will come closer together on issues of common concern, such as climate change, the development agenda agreed at doha, the international criminal court and human rights. we must also commit ourselves increasingly to assert these convergent positions in international fora. this will result in the strengthening of the multilateral system. europe has a particular responsibility, through our actions and cooperation with others, to make it clear that, in our judgment, the only way in which we can tackle international problems is through international cooperation. we should look in particular for partners in making multilateralism work in latin america and the caribbean. secondly, the commission expects the summit to address what is one of the most important questions for the people of latin america and the caribbean: the fight against social inequities and the search for social cohesion. we know – some of the figures were given by the presidency – that latin america faces a potential problem of political instability because of social inequity. this issue needs to be addressed, and the summit should concentrate on the search for solutions to this problem. lastly, we expect madrid to represent a milestone in a number of sub-regional negotiation processes – again, as the presidency pointed out. perhaps most significantly, the summit will mark the conclusions of our negotiations with chile. this is indeed a considerable achievement. it constitutes a major strengthening of bilateral relations and i endorse everything that the presidency said about the extraordinary depth and breadth of the agreement we have concluded with chile. it is one of the most important agreements we have ever concluded with any country. elsewhere, the summit should welcome the fact that the negotiation of the political, institutional and cooperation chapters with mercosur is practically finished. i hope it also encourages the efforts being made to conclude the outstanding negotiations in due course. with regard to central america and the andean community, the european union has been particularly sensitive to the requests of these two regions significantly to enhance their relations with us. the general affairs council conclusions of 15 april have paved the way for the negotiation of a political dialogue and cooperation agreement with both regions. these negotiated agreements will seek to enhance our trade and investment relations and prepare the ground for still closer cooperation in the future. by doing this, the european union has satisfactorily responded to the legitimate aspirations of these countries, and i hope the madrid summit will wholeheartedly support this move. before concluding, i would like to extend my congratulations to the spanish presidency for the excellent work it has carried out regarding the preparation of the summit. i would also like to pay tribute to the european parliament’s extraordinary commitment to the future of our relations with latin america, and to one or two individual members who have played a particularly constructive role, one of whom is going to speak as soon as i have sat down. i should like to congratulate parliament in particular on the ambitious and far-reaching initiatives contained in the resolution of 15 november 2001. we in the commission have been working hard with the spanish government and others to make this summit a success. we have been working for almost 18 months with that objective in mind. we have been able, not without some difficulty, to bring to fruition schemes like the scholarship programme and the programme on the information society. we have concluded negotiations with chile on an extremely wide-ranging agreement, as we said, which many faint hearts thought impossible. we have made more progress with mercosur than most would have predicted. now we want to raise the level of our relations with the other subregional groupings as well. this provides the basis for a good summit, which will further strengthen our bi-regional relationship and prepare us to take things forward even further when we next meet – probably in two years' time – almost certainly with a larger european union. (applause)
- mr president, by including this item on the agenda in a very difficult international context and coinciding with the visit of president fox and a large delegation of mexican parliamentarians, we wanted to underline the interest that this parliament attaches to relations with the countries of latin america on the eve of the summit. i agree with mr patten that such meetings have been criticised because the grand declarations made at them often do not translate into concrete objectives, and i understand that summits really do help to be the ritual staging of an underlying political will to generate the political energy needed to make the machinery work. the question now is to give substance to the ambitious objective of strategic and regional partnership which the heads of state and government set out in rio de janeiro. and i agree with mr patten that the european union is coming to this summit with a number of very positive signs. firstly - and i think this is the merit of all the political groups in this parliament - with a clear and ambitious report aimed at establishing a bi-regional association which would try to devise a common european union strategy for latin america. secondly, with a will expressed in the budgets which allows the european union to present itself in madrid with a decent amount in the 2002 budget. and thirdly, with an ambitious association agreement negotiated with chile - for which the european commission must be congratulated for its negotiating effort and the presidency-in-office for its impetus - with negotiations with mercosur which must also receive a new impetus, because it is in times of crisis that this type of agreement may be most needed, and also with negotiating directives, presented by the commission, for new agreements with the andean community and central america which, in the opinion of this parliament, must give - i do not say at this moment - a horizon of association, as the president of the european parliament has reflected in a recent letter to the president of the commission; and also with an ambitious commission programme which includes a whole series of initiatives which, although they are not just one additional euro, are very important for the establishment of this bi-regional association. among all these compliments, commissioner, i would like to make a small criticism: you will understand that we do not think that the eur 30 million cut proposed by the commission in its preliminary draft budget for 2003 is the best presentation letter for the summit at the moment. having said that, i think it is important that the summit takes into account the fact that the great and profound social inequalities in latin america can jeopardize the progress achieved with so much effort in the fields of coexistence and democratization and that, therefore, a very clear message must be sent in support of the normalization and consolidation of democracy in countries such as venezuela and argentina, the inclusion of the farc and the ln in the list of terrorist organizations, as well as the tendency to normalize relations with cuba, on the basis of the premises of the democratic clause, and its progressive insertion into the cotonou agreement. and i understand that it is very necessary for the european union to face up, without any complexes, to an ambitious global relationship with latin america, so as not to leave the entire protagonism to the united states, which does not ask too many questions about the degree of regional integration in latin america. i therefore hope, mr president, that at this madrid summit a clear message will be sent, at a definite level, to constitute a common space that can be expressed in a great transatlantic axis that can give a channel to relations between the european union and latin america for the next millennium. - mr president, we must recognize that the world is in turmoil and out of balance, not only because of globalisation or the new international order resulting from 9/11, but also because of exclusion, privilege, corruption and favouritism. europe, latin america and the caribbean are not exempt from this situation. we must therefore take advantage of the madrid summit to reflect honestly and draw pragmatic conclusions, and to convince ourselves of the need to work together to ensure that society as a whole functions properly and raises its quality of life, as well as the road to peace and stability on the planet, particularly in these two geographical blocs united by history, the european union and latin america and the caribbean. in these, respect for human rights and the rejection of political impunity and intolerance, as well as the deepening of the exercise of democracy and the incorporation of civil society into political decision-making, must be the priority axes of our future joint action, within the framework of respect for the sovereignty and independence of peoples. in madrid we must therefore strengthen the interinstitutional political dialogue in order to ensure a climate of confidence and to achieve appropriate relations.

commission. – mr president, i should like to follow very directly what the high representative has just said, but note at the outset that once again we are faced with reciprocated terror in the middle east. israeli civilians were brutally murdered again last week when a suicide bomber blew himself up in rishon-le-zion. i know we all condemn this wholeheartedly. there is no possible justification for such acts. i am glad that arab leaders are now publicly condemning these terrible suicide bombings. they must end, and palestinian leaders must, as we have said repeatedly, do all in their power to control and prevent terrorism. violence against civilians can never be justified as an expression of political aspirations or frustrations. we continue to demand that the palestinians should dismantle terrorist networks and end the armed intifada. there will be no settlement in the middle east without the creation of a viable palestinian state and an israel that can live securely within recognised borders with the assurance that it will not be overwhelmed by returning refugees. we should also be clear that a palestinian state will require a return to the 1967 borders, or something very close to them, and it cannot be divided up into parcels of land separated by settlements. without the creation of such a viable palestinian state and a state of israel that is recognised by the entire international community, the madness will continue, children will be murdered, blood will flow. sunday's decision by likud against the very idea of a palestinian state – to which the high representative referred and which has also been condemned by mr peres and others – if maintained against the wish of the whole international community, including the united states administration, would bring us, in the words of the israeli labour party chairman benjamin ben-eliezer “to an era of continuing confrontation and bloody battles". let me focus for a moment on the palestinian authority, as the high representative did. the palestinian administration that rises from the ashes of the old, must be more open, more democratic and more transparent. we have been saying this for a long time and we have actively worked for it together with many palestinians and the international community. i commend to the house an article in today's international herald tribune by a palestinian academic now at cambridge university in which he sets out the case for reform of the palestinian authority extremely clearly. we know that reform is difficult. look at the brave decisions and periods of hardship that the candidate countries and our balkan neighbours have endured. but reform there must be. i have no doubt that it can be achieved if the palestinians can be confident that their institution-building efforts will be rewarded with a state and not with destruction. the commission, as parliament knows, has been funding a project on these reform issues under the chairmanship of michel rocard – who is a distinguished member of this house – and with henry siegman as project director. that work has already informed the commission’s efforts to apply strict conditionality to european union budgetary support. we have been one of the only donors which has attached clear, concrete and tangible conditions to its assistance, obliging the palestinian authority to carry out concrete reform measures. for example, firstly, we reinforced transparency in the palestinian authority's public finances. secondly, we helped to consolidate all sources of palestinian authority revenue in a single treasury account, which was closely monitored by the international monetary fund. thirdly, we insisted that the finance ministry should take full responsibility for managing the palestinian authority payroll. we demanded as well a freeze on public sector hiring and a strict ceiling for expenditures under an austerity budget. | we are already doing a great deal, in other words. but we must redouble those efforts, in order to drive forward a fundamental reform process. i repeat that no one has done more than us in trying to establish reformed, viable and transparent institutions in the palestinian territories. we want to see the rapid establishment of a body responsible for the reform process. we want to see the financial control mechanism strengthened. we want to see palestinian authority auditors who are answerable to the legislature. we want more detailed reporting on palestinian authority budget execution and public debts. we want the development of a unified pension system covering all public employees and we want the integration of the palestinian authority’s donor-funded investment budget into the overall budget for 2003, bringing the investment budget under the direct control of the ministry of finance. what the high representative said is absolutely right: the palestinian authority has to look and act more like a government, and that covers not only the ordinary areas of government activity but also the security services in particular. we also want to see a reform of the palestinian judiciary system. the overdue promulgation of the law on the independence of the judiciary is a condition for further european union budget support. if this law is promulgated, we will contribute with technical advice and support for a judicial reform programme helping to instil good governance and respect for the rule of law. according to the world bank, the physical damage caused by israeli military operations to palestinian infrastructure and institutions amounts to roughly usd 300 million, increasing emergency needs this year to a total of usd 2 billion. the gap between the support already pledged and estimated needs is now approximately usd 800 million. with the rest of the international donor community, including the united states, we are committed to supporting the palestinian authority in its reform and reconstruction efforts. a team from the commission is currently conducting an infrastructure damage assessment, and assessing the institutional capacity of the palestinian authorities and of the municipalities. this report will guide us in our repair and reconstruction efforts. in the short term we need to work on a quick-start package to get administrative services running again. there is a very simple reason for that: with the destruction of computers, records, payrolls and simple accountancy information, unless we are able to put something very quickly in place, i will not be able to come before this house and say that the money we invest in the future of the people of palestine is money that is being properly spent. so we need something and something quickly in order to establish the bare bones of decent government in palestine. in this work we face a serious dilemma. not just the palestinians, but the israelis too, want us to reconstruct infrastructures and institutions which have already been paid for by the international community and destroyed by the israeli defence forces. how can we be sure that this will not happen again? the answer is that we cannot give that guarantee. however, it is equally the case that i do not believe that we can renege on our responsibilities. meanwhile, our resources are stretched to the limit. we are already providing eur 230 million this year to the palestinians through the palestinian authority, through unrwa, and in humanitarian assistance. once the needs assessment is completed, we will come back to inform the house and the council of the full financial implications and to ask for your help in providing an appropriate european union response. i want to make this point: reconstruction will not be cheap, and it is not going to be cheap for us to live up to the rhetoric that we have used with passion, eloquence and, i am sure, good intentions. if we are going to live up to what we have promised, it is going to cost money. over the past few weeks there have been allegations of misuse of european union monies by the palestinian authority. the israeli government has prepared a dossier claiming that yasser arafat and the palestinian authority secretly used budgetary support provided by the arab states, norway and the european union to finance supporters of terrorism or even directly to fund acts of terrorism. similar charges have been made about the cia – so we are in interesting company. these are extremely serious allegations. we are obviously examining them very thoroughly. so far we have found no new evidence of european union funds being used for purposes other than those agreed between the european union and the palestinian authority. at this stage, the allegations appear to be groundless – rather like the allegations that were made a short while ago about textbooks. this has been reflected in the tone of media reporting. the first headlines in the european and israeli press were: "eu finances terror". now the news stories say only that "eu funds may have been misused inadvertently". these allegations should be seen in the context of efforts to delegitimise president arafat and the palestinian authority and to weaken donors’ support at a time when the international community is putting pressure on israel to engage in serious negotiations. we nevertheless take the israeli allegations extremely seriously, and as i have said, we shall continue thoroughly to examine any evidence of misuse of european union funds. such misuse could not be condoned, any more than we can condone israel’s destruction of eur 20 million worth of eu-funded projects. we will ask the palestinian authority to cooperate fully in clearing up any allegations regarding the use of european union funds. we need to be confident that funds are properly used. that is my responsibility to this parliament, and it is both my responsibility and our responsibility to all european union taxpayers. what is needed now is a strong and concerted effort by the international community to reform and rebuild the palestinian authority as the legitimate governing body in the palestinian territories, and as the only valid interlocutor in the forthcoming peace talks, about which the high representative has spoken. there have been so many debates on the middle east when we have all expressed our horror at the descent into the abyss and our shared approach to political recovery and the building of a durable peace. today, rather than repeat what has been said so often before, and what is widely reported in the media, i thought it right to focus on a practical role that the european union can and must play as effectively or even more effectively than any one else in constructing a better future. i just hope that we get the chance to rise to this challenge. finally, i should like to associate myself wholeheartedly with the remarks the high representative made at the end of his speech. any act of anti-semitism is intolerable, any act of anti-semitism should be condemned out of hand in democratic pluralist societies, just as any act of racism anywhere should be condemned. but it is not anti-semitic to find oneself in disagreement with mr ariel sharon, or with likud party resolutions, or with some of the things done by an existing government. i am sure that, like other members of this house, we all want to see a viable, secure israeli state living in peace with its neighbours. i find it perverse to suggest that it is anti-semitic to argue that. counsel. - as you know, and i assume you know as a member of the european parliament, the council only acts and adopts rules on a proposal from the european commission. it is up to the european commission to make the necessary proposals which we will adopt. if what we have approved is then in contradiction with the domestic laws of any country, then it is up to the commission to open an infringement procedure and take that country to the court of justice if necessary. and it will be the court of justice that will decide. the council does not settle disputes between countries and you should know that. we are talking here about a very delicate institutional balance and about rules which are written in the treaties and on which our coexistence has been based since 1956. i would therefore say that what the presidency is going to do is to ensure that this institutional balance is maintained and that the prerogatives of each institution are respected. so if a country has internal legislation which is not in line with the acquis communautaire or the rules of the treaty, it is for the european commission to initiate an infringement procedure against it and for the court of justice to condemn it.

- question no 13 by mr cercas (h-0296/02): subject: the lisbon strategy and full employment the conclusions of the recent european summit in barcelona state that full employment in the european union is the central element of the lisbon strategy and the main objective of economic and social policies, which requires the creation of more and better jobs. they also indicate that particular attention should therefore continue to be paid to the reform of employment and labour market policies. the presidency of the council has stated in its programme that the creation of more and better jobs is one of its top priorities. however, according to official eu estimates, unemployment in the eu stands at 7.8%, with spain having the highest unemployment rate (12.9%, according to eurostat figures published in february 2002) and the most precarious employment situation, despite the economic growth phase it has experienced. in view of these results, what initiatives will the presidency of the council take to ensure that the national employment plans actually reduce the number of unemployed and actually promote the creation of quality jobs in all the member states?
council. - the council considers that in order to achieve the objective of full employment in the european union, set at the lisbon european council and reiterated at the barcelona spring council this year, particular attention must continue to be paid to reforms of employment policies and the labour market. in this context, it is essential to remove barriers to integration into the labour market and to promote active employment policies, while maintaining the preventive approach and individual attention to the unemployed to prevent them from falling into long-term unemployment and to help improve their vocational integration skills. the council also stressed that, in order to achieve the objectives set out in lisbon, the european employment strategy should pay particular attention to the long-term challenges facing the european union, especially those affecting the progressive ageing of the population. the european employment strategy should contribute to the creation of a dynamic and efficient labour market, where motivated and trained workers can perform high-quality and high-productivity tasks. the strategy should therefore give adequate consideration to policies that improve both the supply of and demand for labour. in the context of the implementation of the employment strategy, the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states in 2002, formally adopted by the council at the beginning of this year, largely reflect the new political messages endorsed by the last european councils which examined the issue of full employment in europe. it is now up to the member states to implement employment policy in accordance with the employment guidelines, while respecting the principle of subsidiarity and the member states' powers in the field of employment.

the council has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the commission's proposals, and i am sure that the council will take the necessary steps to ensure that the commission's proposals are implemented. but as you know, there is no better way of forcing member states to come forward with employment plans of real substance than by making that political weight and insistence which is part of the debate we are having here. the countries must be made aware that the commitments of the councils are truly binding and that, moreover, the issue of employment is the first objective of the lisbon strategy. the other aspects of the lisbon strategy are conditional on job creation. i shall certainly convey this concern to the spanish minister for labour and social affairs to see if, at some new session of the social affairs council - which is still to hold a meeting before the end of the presidency - it can be reiterated. but the presentation of the national employment plans is precisely at the beginning of the year. we made an effort at the beginning of the year, everything was presented to the barcelona european council, there were new indications in barcelona, but i think it is never a bad thing to remember, even at a time when plans do not have to be presented - but when they have to be drawn up - that the european council has given very clear guidelines with regard to national employment plans and that it would be appropriate for the countries to be already, in a more concrete way, making forecasts and greater precision when preparing their employment plans for the beginning of next year.

- question no 15 by anne e.m. van lancker (h-0304/02): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the united kingdom for the construction of the railway line between london and london. subject: accessibility of documents relating to meetings of the council and committees since the opening of the lisbon process, the council and the commission have become the focal points of a set of coordination procedures. the economic policy committee, responsible for employment, labour market and social protection matters, carries out important work which the council discusses and approves without parliament's involvement (joint reports by the council and the commission on employment, exclusion, pensions or on the objectives and indicators of the fight against poverty). the european council itself sometimes mentions these documents without them being accessible. is the council prepared to forward these documents from the commission and the committees to parliament? could the documents adopted by the council be disseminated through the jo and the internet sites? is the council prepared to define a method which would involve parliament more in the decision-making process surrounding the procedures in question?
council. - apart from the existing provisions on public access to documents of the three institutions - council, parliament and commission - there is currently no specific procedure for the official transmission to the european parliament of documents relating to the lisbon objectives. that said, in the context of transparency, all reports and other documents adopted by the council on these matters, in particular with a view to the coordination of economic policies, are, as a general rule, published on the council's website once adopted and are therefore accessible to the general public.
the council has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the commission's proposals. of course, first of all, to parliament, which, as you say, is the body representing the peoples of europe. but it is also true that we live in a normative system in which there are obligations on the council to send documents to parliament when this is required in the legislative decision-making process. there are some documents which do not involve a legislative decision-making process, which are the responsibility of the member states, and in which it is not specified that these documents should be transmitted. the truth is that today the world of the union is a world with a glass ceiling because virtually all the documents of the member states are published on the internet and it is really hard for me to remember that there is a council, even in the case of the most sensitive councils, which are the foreign affairs councils, where documents have been secret or not accessible to the public. i think there are some documents which are sent to parliament ex officio. and there are other documents which, if they do not come to parliament of their own accord, are simply requested by members who are interested in them, because they are normally accessible; they are not secret and are available within the member states. i'll tell you, the internet system today makes things extraordinarily easy. i am, however, aware of this interest - which, by the way, is not the first time that parliament has expressed to me - that it should have a greater involvement in all that is the lisbon strategy; of course, to have a greater involvement, more information is needed and i will therefore pass it on so that the transmission of documents to parliament can be improved.

mr president, i am not going to say that the council has not taken the necessary steps to ensure that the community's development policy is not disrupted by the economic crisis. you know that very often in development aid mechanisms there are a number of special appropriations which are devoted to financing development aid projects provided that they encourage the establishment or establishment of contacts by companies in the countries concerned. without going into whether this is good or bad, it has been a very powerful instrument for countries to allocate large sums of money to development aid and it has also been a very powerful instrument for many companies, helped by these specific credits, to get involved in carrying out projects in countries where, if they did not have these privileged credits, it would have been extraordinarily risky to start different projects. naturally, my ideal would be that there should be no such link, and this was advocated by some countries and, of course, by the commission, but the reality of the weight of a custom, of a practice which has been carried out for many years, has been imposed, and no agreement has been reached to dissociate the issue of development aid from the trade issue. that's all i can tell you.

the council has already adopted a directive on the establishment of a european works council in order to strengthen the position of employees of multinational companies operating at european level by means of their own mechanisms in decision-making procedures. in relation to the more specific issue of mitigating the negative effects of mass job cuts, the council adopted in 1975 the directive on collective redundancies, amended in 1992 and consolidated in 1998, which also lays down certain information and consultation requirements for employers. in any event, it is not for the council, as a commission. – the main problems in the existing financial regulation are the constraints on how we are allowed to spend money. we asked to have this modified when working with the un family and the red cross, but not others. we do not want to engage in core funding because we are not a nation. but we want to do multiannual programme-based funding – up to three years, say – and to have the accounting and auditing done in the same way as the member states when channelled through the un or red cross. this will make it possible for them to make better use of us. sometimes we are not invited to participate in a consortium because of this problem and end up doing less interesting things. that is a real problem. it would also make more sense for reasons of efficiency, not to mention in terms of influence. there are other problems, including the very large number of budget lines and instruments that we have with the absolute dividing-line between european development fund resources and budgetary sources, which cannot be mixed. this has created enormous problems in our decision-making and reporting back to parliament. for instance, when we are funding the agriculture research network, which is working globally, we have to find some of the money under the edf, and some in the budget. this is legally and technically incredibly difficult. the same applies to our contribution to the global health fund on aids, malaria and tb. our colleagues cannot understand why we are so difficult to work with. this is why we have asked member states for the changes in my area of work. i do not know why progress with the member states is so slow. this has been slower than i could ever have imagined, and i do not look forward to celebrating the two-year anniversary in july. i know parliament is supporting the commission on this issue, and we have to make an effort to get it sorted out with the member states.

commission. – the commission shares the concerns of parliament on the situation in madagascar. it deplores the dramatic impact that the current crisis is having on the population and is alarmed that the political dispute may degenerate into ethnic conflict. the commission is monitoring developments in madagascar closely. it supports and welcomes the mediation efforts of president wade of the organisation of african unity and of the united nations to encourage a democratic dialogue between the parties with a view to achieving a peaceful, global and lasting solution to the crisis. in line with this objective, the union has welcomed the agreement signed by the two leaders in dakar on 18 april, aiming at national reconciliation. the commission deplores that, notwithstanding the dakar agreement, the confrontation continues. the commission is convinced of the importance of a comprehensive dialogue between the two leaders. it considers that only an agreement between the parties, and national reconciliation, will make it possible to resolve the present crisis and to preserve the integrity and unity of the country. the commission is convinced that the dakar agreement remains the appropriate framework for a democratic dialogue and for the achievement of a solution. we welcome the renewed efforts of president wade and of the oau to organise a new meeting between the two leaders in order encourage the implementation of the objectives of the dakar agreement. the union is prepared to offer political and technical support in order to restore civil peace and the principle of democracy and to find a political solution to the crisis. moreover, the implementation of the substantial community co-operation programme will help resolve the economic crisis facing the country. the commission has already envisaged the re-establishment of the free movement of essential goods and persons through the rehabilitation of roads and bridges. moreover the commission has taken measures, together with some member states, in order to supply food and medicines and establish a food safety net. furthermore the commission is considering the “urgent budget support programme” on the basis of a world bank analysis of the current situation and in cooperation with the bank and some member states. in addition the 9th edf foresees eur 327 million for co-operation with madagascar which is an important resource as a basis to meet priority needs in the future. at this stage the organisation of relations or a referendum does not seem appropriate. i agree with what has been expressed here that we must be careful not to be one-sided. only a political solution and national reconciliation can restore civil peace and enable economic activity to resume. my analysis may not appear very strong or active, but can be summarised as follows: no matter how one examines the issues of an election referendum or the decision of the high constitutional court, efforts must focus on conciliation. this is a meaningful message for us to stress at the moment.

commission. – mr president, the commission fully shares with honourable members their concerns about the continued violence in parts of indonesia. together with the eu diplomatic missions in jakarta, we have been monitoring the situation in the moluccas since early1999 and we have participated in two fact-finding missions in late 2000 and early 2001. the commission has also participated in several eu démarches to the indonesian authorities to express our concerns about situations of continuing conflict in different parts of the country. in addition, the commission has provided more than eur 4.6 million in humanitarian assistance to the people of the moluccas since may 1999. we have joined with the member states in a declaration welcoming the malino ii peace agreement and urging its full implementation. at the same time, we have urged the government of indonesia to take appropriate measures to support the peace process. since then, we have followed closely the efforts of the government to deal with new outbreaks of violence, including the arrest on 4 may of ja’far umar thalib on charges of incitement to violence. the situation in aceh has also preoccupied us for some time now and has also been the subject of eu démarches to the indonesian authorities. eu heads of mission visited the region in october 2001. i am therefore particularly happy to welcome the joint statement issued on 10 may by the indonesian government and the free aceh movement (gam), following two days of consultations facilitated by the henri dunant centre in geneva. the joint statement recognised the special autonomy law as the starting-point for further negotiations in an all-inclusive dialogue and confirmed the intention of both parties to work on an agreement for the cessation of hostilities. it has been our view for some time that the full implementation of the special autonomy legislation will be the key to a durable resolution of the present situation. papua has equally been a matter of continued concern and the subject of eu démarches. the eu condemned the kidnapping and murder of theys eluay in november 2001 and called on the government of indonesia to ensure a full investigation of this dreadful incident and to bring its perpetrators to justice. eu heads of mission in jakarta also visited papua in february this year. in the case of papua, too, it is clear that full implementation of the special autonomy legislation will be key to the resolution of the situation. the commission has included in its country strategy paper for indonesia, which is now in the final stages of preparation, a particular emphasis on institutional capacity building, good governance and the rule of law, as well as conflict prevention. financial support has already been committed to the undp-managed partnership for governance reform, and technical assistance has been provided to the attorney general’s office. provision has been made in the draft national indicative programme for 2002-2004 for a specific programme to support the implementation of the government’s policy for decentralisation in indonesia and to promote good governance at local government level. in the meantime, we have also taken steps to support the processes of conflict resolution more directly. following discussions between commissioner patten and the indonesian foreign minister, mr wirajuda, last november, and in the context of the commission’s rapid reaction mechanism, an independent mission on conflict prevention in indonesia visited the moluccas, sulawesi and papua in february 2002. the expert mission met a wide range of central and local government representatives, as well as ngos operating in these areas. on the basis of the mission’s report, a package of projects is now in preparation for the moluccas and papua. the project in the moluccas will focus particularly on support for the participation of civil society. the projects in papua will support both the authorities and civil society. all of these measures are consistent with the commission’s support for the eu’s stated position, which firmly supports the territorial integrity of indonesia, while encouraging the government to make urgent efforts to address and resolve peacefully indonesia’s internal conflicts, whether separatist or sectarian in character. we will continue to follow this approach and to provide all possible support for constructive action to deal with these very difficult situations.

- mr president, the climate of confrontation between religions, ethnic groups and civilizations, which is worsening all over the world and, in particular, in the indian region, is worrying. the implication of the powers that be in the narrowing of this climate is also very worrying, as it points out that it is not a completely spontaneous phenomenon or the simple fruit of confrontations, but that it is being orchestrated to hide, many times, the real social problems that hit both sides. we must take into account the climate of extreme tension and violence that we are experiencing, which has increased - i believe - since 9/11, and this alleged clash between civilizations, with the war in afghanistan and all that accompanies it, because it indicates that we are seeing the consequences of the process called 'globalization' which is gradually increasing inequalities and tensions, and, as a consequence, clashes between communities are emerging. i therefore believe that the european union must - as the commissioner has already said - be attentive to these phenomena, must redouble its efforts and not only turn to the appropriate places, but also to the united nations, in order to be able to deal with the problem in all its dimensions. these types of events are going to increase and we, the european union, as an international body, have a greater responsibility and the possibility of acting, not only with economic aid but also by changing - as i said earlier - the effect and the process of globalisation, which is affecting so many people all over the world.
- mr president, india is a state whose independence and foundation in the middle of the last century, was possible on the basis of a massive social mobilization and globally respected and that was articulated on a doctrine of passive resistance as a political resource. mahatma gandhi led the indians with the message of non-violence, tolerance and overcoming religious differences in an epic that has remained among the most emblematic victories of peaceful methods in politics since it established the world's most populous democracy and a society considered as a model of coexistence of races, languages and, in short, civilizations. however, clashes based on religious fanaticism have never ceased to occur in india. if these clashes had already one of its most significant victims in the mahatma himself, the list continued later with other assassinations, such as that of prime minister indira gandhi, that of his own son - also prime minister - and others. and beyond those we know as important characters, thousands of innocent people have fallen there victims of intransigence and fanaticism. it is a paradox that precisely where material and social needs are greatest, religious extremism and intolerance arise and are built up among them. we are talking about a country where inequalities are widespread and where the physical environment and natural disasters often make life even more difficult for the population, and it is precisely in this territory that clashes between the followers of the major religions and those of other less numerous communities have permanently marked and stained the history of the largest democracy on the planet. the international community must call on the government of india to guarantee the safety of its citizens and to do so with the same commitment with which it is facing other development challenges in which it is not unsuccessful. the government of india must continue its efforts by devoting sufficient resources to allow the return of displaced persons to their places of origin and to restore coexistence in gujarat and other areas affected by the recent clashes which have motivated our debate and must also clear up those cases of connivance of the security forces in episodes of religious and political violence. the european union must support these efforts and bring as much humanitarian aid as possible to the area as a matter of urgency.

findings were deeply worrying. violence was not only widespread, but in many cases extreme brutality was used. unofficial figures set the death toll at 2000, most of them muslims. the mission also national level. i am confident that india's commitment to democracy and the rule of law will ensure that those who were responsible for these atrocities will be held to account, and that the victims
