bringing us a new proposal for a regulation which, in my view, is going in the right direction. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. i don't think any of this is real. however, i am sure that the proposed measures will require manufacturers in certain countries to maintain unjustifiably high prices because of anti-competitive practices. the main point of the proposal is the disappearance of the dealer location clause, and that is a step in the right direction. it is true that it may affect the structure of the distribution market, and i can therefore agree to a transitional period. on the contrary, not approving this measure until a study has been carried out and a new decision has been taken is, let us not be mistaken, a ploy by those who do not want this measure to be approved. not now, not ever.
- mr president, commissioner, i will go straight to the point, i will go straight to the point and rightly so in the debate on the location clause which is the focus of the debate and discussion in this house. i fully understand the commission's objective in advocating the abolition of this clause. the commission considers that the abolition of this clause would increase competition between distributors and that this would result in a reduction in prices. the people's party group, which is characterized by the defence of freedom and the defence of consumers, can only be praised for this. but as the commissioner has put it, there are some issues that should be cleared up before a surgical solution is found. it seems clear that the current level between brands is sufficient. if the location clause is abruptly removed, do we not run the risk of hindering the manufacturers' ability to organise their distribution network? is there not a risk that it will be the larger manufacturers who will eat up the smaller manufacturers and thus reduce competition? secondly, the commission's proposals, many of which are interesting, contain sufficient elements to enhance intra-brand competition within a single brand. wouldn't it be wise to wait and see how it works before shooting fleas out of the sky? thirdly, does it not seem clear that the investments made by distributors are jeopardized and jeopardized the smaller they are, which would increase the market share for the very largest, contrary to the commission's intention? the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the new rules are applied in a way that is compatible with the common market.
the commission - mr president, this draft regulation is the result of a long process of in-depth analysis of the situation in the motor vehicle sector. in its november 2000 evaluation report, the commission concluded that the current scheme had not produced the results it was intended to achieve and therefore could not be confirmed in its current form. the main objectives of the future system are therefore clear: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's internal market is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. the draft regulation also aims to ensure the functioning of the internal market for new cars. it is unacceptable that in the internal market the car, ladies and gentlemen, the very symbol of mobility, should continue to be one of the least mobile goods. in the past, the commission has had to fine car manufacturers for hindering parallel trade. these concrete cases show how much consumers have been deprived of the advantage, the right to buy cars where they preferred. in this connection i would like to stress that the commission's objective is not price harmonization as such but the deeper, more fundamental objective of ensuring the functioning of the internal market and, in particular, of allowing consumers to buy cars, directly or indirectly, where they are most convenient. finally, independent retailers and repairers will also benefit from the new set of rules because it strengthens their economic independence and opens up new business opportunities for them. the commission's draft regulation has been very well received by consumer associations, motorists, spare parts manufacturers and independent repairers. they believe that such a reform is clearly in the interest of european consumers. some of their reactions, in fact, say that the proposal for a regulation is not brave enough. european industry leaders are continually calling on the european institutions to promote liberalisation and flexibility as key ingredients for a more competitive economy that boosts growth and jobs. this draft regulation was drafted in this spirit, which is always promoted by european industry, and which the commission fully shares. we are therefore surprised at the heavy lobbying against the draft regulation by some industry interest groups. it is regrettable that at times there have been real forcing and simply wrong statements about the draft regulation. this is in contrast to the openness and willingness to dialogue which the commission has shown towards all the parties concerned. we are fully convinced of the benefits that will flow from the new regulation. it takes account of the fact that motor vehicles are special products. the new regulation aims to ensure that motor vehicles are produced safely, benefit from highly reliable after-sales services and meet environmental standards. we must have confidence - we have confidence - in the many highly qualified retailers who will make the right commercial decisions. they are, after all, the ones who know the needs of consumers and who bear the commercial risks. i am glad that this draft commission regulation has been the subject of extensive debate in the european parliament, particularly in the context of the debate on mr konrad's report in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, and i too found the dialogue we had very useful and constructive. i note and welcome the fact that the report adopted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs is broadly in favour of the general line indicated by the commission, in particular on the need for changes to the current system. i shall now briefly consider the most important amendments contained in the report of the committee on economic and monetary affairs. one of the most important elements of the new system is the prohibition of the location clause. this is the key to ensuring that the other measures are also fully effective. the abolition of this clause for the sale of motor vehicles, which will allow dealers to open secondary sales or delivery points in other areas, including other member states, is a key element in facilitating consumer access to cars sold by dealers in other member states at lower prices. this will increase competition between dealers of the same car brand and will promote market integration, also ensuring the possibility of a multi-brand sales activity. the committee on economic and monetary affairs proposes that this measure, i.e. the abolition of the localisation clause, be subject to a transitional period until 1 october 2005 and that the abolition of the localisation clause be made subject to the results of an evaluation. i understand that the transitional period would allow both producers and retailers to prepare, to adapt to the new system, but i think it would be harmful, really harmful, to postpone a decision on the abolition of the location clause until a future assessment. it is not appropriate to prolong a state of uncertainty about the future regime; we should instead have clear rules from the start, otherwise the transition period itself - let us say - would be meaningless: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are applied in the community. it wouldn 't be a transition . the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. as one of you said, a ruse to never decide. the commission believes that we must take this responsibility now. we cannot always say that we want a european union closer to the citizens - how many times have i heard this in this house and how much i agree with it! - and not act accordingly when we take decisions. that said, as i said before the committee on economic and monetary affairs, i am prepared, with regard to the location clause alone, to consider the usefulness of a longer transitional period than that provided for in the draft regulation. however, it should not be forgotten that the extension of the transitional period will also delay the benefits which consumers will be able to enjoy under the new system. multi-brand activities one of the central objectives of the project is that retailers should actually be able to sell different brands if they want to. the project aims to make multi-brand business easier for retailers, while protecting the brand image in which manufacturers have invested: this will encourage consumer choice and increase competition between brands. i agree that brand image is an important competitive tool for car manufacturers. the taxation of separate car dealerships or separate sales staff is however not justified and would render the multi-brand sales activity economically unattractive for retailers. i would also like to stress that multi-brand is of particular importance for small dealers, because it can facilitate their presence and survival in rural areas. leaving this element to bargaining between the two parties is not appropriate as long as retailers are economically wholly dependent on their producers. to strengthen the position of dealers, therefore, they must be able to decide whether to display cars of different brands in separate sales areas of the same motor show, or in separate showrooms, and whether to employ separate sales staff for each brand. i also think that parliament should agree to the need to protect retailers, as proposed by the commission: the minimum notice period and the obligation to provide detailed justification for termination of the contract are intended to strengthen the position of dealers. the draft regulation also aims to reorganise the link, which is currently very close, between the sale of new passenger cars and after-sales services. a dealer may choose to concentrate its business solely on sales of motor vehicles or to provide after-sales services as well: this right strengthens its independence. as after-sales services can only be subcontracted to authorised repairers, a high level of quality and safety is ensured. the commission's original proposal, in my view, already ensures the proximity of a service point to the concessionaire in the event that the latter subcontracts this activity; however, in the light of the amendments proposed in this connection, a solution could be found in imposing an obligation on the dealer not only to inform the consumer of the location of the authorized repairer but also of the distance of the authorized repairer from the point of sale. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the market is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. dealers whose agreements are terminated can now remain on the market as authorised repairers. in view of this and in order to protect the interests of the consumer in a wide network of service centres, it would be wrong to limit the number of authorised repairers. finally, i am generally in favour of amendments to improve access to technical information and to clarify the definition of spare parts. in conclusion, mr president, i note and welcome the favourable attitude of the committee on economic and monetary affairs to the commission's line. i have expressed my views on the main amendments it has suggested and i would ask the honourable members to take these considerations into account when they vote, if they wish. the very fact that the report of the economic committee broadly supports the commission's line shows that this parliament does not believe in the bleak scenarios put forward by those lobbyists who had presented the commission's draft as a kind of catastrophe. you will recall that the same kind of reaction was given when the commission opposed the proposal to continue duty free. there was talk then of 140,000 unemployed that we would create. even then, considerable political pressure was exerted at high levels and a great deal of lobbying was done. the commission was not swayed by the pressure. duty free has been abolished for the benefit of the taxpayer. no aspect of the catastrophe has occurred. i thank the honourable members for this dialogue. i also personally thank them for the appreciation they have shown. some of you said we were brave. thank you, but i don't think it's courageous to act in the public interest. if i may express a personal opinion, i am sure that the citizens, your voters, expect parliament to be at least as courageous. - the agenda calls for the debate on the council and commission statements on the eu-latin america summit in madrid on 17 and 18 may 2002.
the council has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the conclusions of the madrid summit, and the council has also taken a number of decisions on the basis of the conclusions of the madrid summit. after a long preparation, since the preparatory work for the summit began a year ago under the swedish presidency and continued during the belgian presidency, it must be said that the summit has produced remarkable results, in line with the objectives set by the spanish presidency for this six-month period. as the house is aware, the theme chosen for the summit was 'european union, latin america and the caribbean, promoting a strategic partnership for the 21st century', which i believe sums up what is being defined between the two geographical areas: a common space and joint action in the international arena between two regions of the world that share principles and values as deep as democracy, the rule of law, respect for human rights, equality between men and women, the market economy, rational thinking and so many others that underpin what we understand as the western world. the preparations for this summit, mr president, had defined three thematic areas: political dialogue, economic and commercial cooperation, and cooperation in the fields of culture, education and social policy. the working sessions were adapted to these areas, with the following points introduced by different countries: the political session dealt with the strengthening and modernisation of the state, cooperation in the fight against terrorism, cooperation in the fight against drug trafficking, multilateralism and the promotion of democracy, human rights and the rule of law. the session on social policy and cooperation in cultural and educational matters covered cultural diversity, the danger of technological backwardness, education, equity and social cohesion, sustainable development and the environment. the economic session also covered international financial architecture, bi-regional trade, international cooperation for sustainable development and development finance, measures to stimulate economic growth and development and, finally, regional integration processes. the president of the european central bank and the president of the inter-american development bank also had a working lunch. i would now like to point out to the house, mr president, what the presidency considers to be the most important results of this summit in the three areas to which i have referred. firstly, and in relation to the political field, where we have clearly achieved remarkable results, the firm commitment to combat terrorism and drug trafficking, which are perceived as threats to the whole world, by strengthening the mechanisms of cooperation between governments. secondly, the strengthening of the bi-regional political dialogue by means of consultation in international forums, especially the united nations. this consultation will enable us to join forces among those of us who share the same principles and values in order to tackle the main issues on the international agenda. the renewed commitment to cooperate in strengthening democratic institutions is therefore fully justified. the second aspect, the economic and trade area, is where more substantial progress has been made compared with the situation resulting from the first rio de janeiro summit in june 1999. on the one hand, the entry into force of the agreement with mexico, which has had a very positive impact on trade flows between the european union and mexico. the conclusion of the association agreement with chile is undoubtedly the most important event. all the participants pointed out the importance of this event, after complex and sometimes difficult negotiations which will lead us, as has happened with mexico, to a privileged relationship with social and economic benefits directly for chile, but which transcend this country to be a message of confidence throughout the continent in these times of economic uncertainty, especially in some subregions. the negotiations with mercosur have made progress and the political and cooperation chapters and the trade facilitation chapter are virtually complete. it was also agreed to continue trade negotiations with a ministerial meeting in july, which means that the negotiations will be supported despite the adverse circumstances arising from the situation in argentina. the community has also made progress in the negotiation of the association agreements with the andean community of nations and central america. in the meantime, political dialogue and cooperation agreements are being negotiated, while cooperation on trade, investment and economic relations is being deepened. the aim is to prepare the ground for the conclusion of the doha round and the negotiation of association agreements with these two latin american subregions. in view of the experience with mercosur, it is essential that both integration processes be deepened to facilitate the agreements we are aiming for. i can inform parliament that the central american side has gladly accepted this formula, although it would have preferred a more precise timetable starting from the madrid summit. the andean community was less satisfied with the agreement reached, although it acknowledged that the formula obtained opened the door to a future association agreement which would allow it to overcome the unilateral concessions it currently enjoys under the system of generalized preferences linked to the fight against drug trafficking. in conclusion, i would like to mention the decision of the caribbean countries, together with all the acp countries, to open negotiations for economic association with the european union in cotonou next september. as you can see, with these decisions and agreements there is a broad perspective, of fluid and intense relations, between the two sides of the atlantic in the not too distant future and which, as i have said, will be to the benefit of the societies of america and europe. i would also like to stress three other points in this economic field: on the one hand, the decision to cooperate in eradicating poverty through, among other instruments, institutional strengthening. important decisions were taken on this and its consequences at the monterrey conference in march, which were reflected in its final document, the monterrey consensus. secondly, the creation of better conditions for development and macroeconomic balance, to which efforts will be added by both the inter-american development bank and the european investment bank. the two financial institutions are thus incorporated into the process of strengthening the strategic partnership with all their experience and capacity, which is a remarkable innovation. it is also worth noting the support for the introduction of the euro, recognising its positive effects, as both the council and the european central bank did at the madrid summit. new elements of interest are also emerging in the field of cooperation. i would like to refer to the following: the alis programme for the development of the information society, a four-year programme which will have a budget of 85 million euro, of which the commission will finance 63.5 million euro and the latin american countries the rest, until that figure is reached. although the commission will be able to give more details, i would simply point out that the objectives of the programme include the standardisation of the regulatory framework and the interconnection of networks. in the area of education, which was given particular attention at the summit, the new alban scholarship programme stands out. this programme was presented by the commissioner for external relations, mr patten, in the context of the cultural forum parallel to the summit, which brought together cultural foundations and bodies from european and latin american countries. the programme consists of the financing of 3900 grants for postgraduate studies, with the commission providing €75 million and the european universities participating in the programme providing €38 million. i think this is a milestone which deserves to be highlighted, because it will give a decisive boost to cooperation in the field of education between europe and latin america and will enable the training of latin american postgraduate students at the highest level, with all that this implies in terms of aid to development in those countries and of overcoming an almost one-way relationship between these societies and the united states of america. i think it is a very far-reaching programme, and i take this opportunity to congratulate the commission on the work it has done through commissioner patten. the summit also supported the 2002-04 action plan on higher education, with the objectives of improving the quality of teaching and facilitating student mobility. mr president, the second european union-latin america and the caribbean summit took place at a time when the international environment was not the most favourable, either for one side or the other of the atlantic. in addition to the economic difficulties following the attacks of 11 september, the difficult situation in several south american countries - the particular situation in venezuela one month after the serious crisis in april, the peace process interrupted in an electoral climate very much affected by the unacceptable terrorist violence in colombia, the deep crisis in which argentina is found - all this, together with european attention to enlargement and the various electoral processes taking place in these months in some countries of the european union, did not augur the best for the development of the summit. however, the madrid summit had a very high participation rate, very significant concrete results and a very positive assessment both by the participants and by public opinion in general. the agreements and decisions adopted at the summit, which were set out in a 33-point political declaration known as the madrid commitment, mark the beginning of a new stage in bi-regional relations, which represents an important step in the process of consolidating the strategic partnership. the convening of the next summit in mexico in 2004 guarantees continuity in this process of consolidating and strengthening the bi-regional partnership. to this end, the commitments made in the madrid declaration must be followed up in an appropriate way so that the mexico summit can be a significant new step in this process of alliance between the european union, latin america and the caribbean, a process which has always been encouraged by this parliament. the rapporteur. - mr president, one of the essential functions of modern states is the police function and, within it, it is of paramount importance to guarantee the citizens' security as a basic premise for a free coexistence. however, the exponential development of activities in contemporary societies has generated new needs for the provision of surveillance and security services for persons and property, carried out by private individuals or legal entities, and states have had to react to integrate functionally private security into the monopoly that corresponds to the state because this is a complementary and subordinate activity with respect to the public security service. the member states of the european union have successively adopted legislative provisions to establish administrative controls which differ from one state to another. freedom, security and justice are elements which must be guaranteed by the states. it is the responsibility of the states to guarantee the safety of their citizens. the creation of the single market and the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice certainly require the harmonization of private security services in the european union. however, this is not an easy subject. the studies which have been carried out on this subject show that there are a number of difficulties in completing this process. firstly, there are major differences between the national laws governing the matter. secondly, the existence of strong legal barriers between the member states which restrict or impede the free provision of services in the private security sector. thirdly, the need to harmonize the essential aspects of the various national regulations relating to the sector. these problems are what determine the need to harmonize the legislation of the member states of the european union in the field of private security, thus guaranteeing the free provision of services in a european area of freedom, security and justice. but, having said that, i feel the need to ask this house to support the report of the committee on civil liberties tomorrow, in the vote, which calls on the council to withdraw this initiative, not because of its opportunity, but because the legal form chosen is that of a decision, and because of the legal bases chosen by the current presidency of the council - the spanish presidency - to be able to regulate this matter, based on article 29 (a) and article 30 (1) of the treaty on european union. it is essential - and this has already been stated by the legal affairs committee of this parliament and by myself in the committee on civil liberties - to determine whether the matter covered by the spanish initiative falls within the sphere of community competence or within the sphere of union competence. i would therefore like to stress that there have already been at least three judgments of the court of justice in which spain, belgium and italy have been condemned for maintaining in their legislation certain conditions for the exercise of the provision of private security services which violated the principle of non-discrimination provided for in the treaty on european union. i am against the provision of private security services as part of a public service, as the court of justice has said, and so the exception for public employment under article 39 (4) of the ec treaty does not apply to the free movement of workers. i also believe that private security activities do not constitute an exercise of official authority and that when they act to assist the public security forces they do so only as auxiliary functions. i must also stress that the private security sector - as the court of justice has said - is an economic sector and that the legislative provisions governing its activity in the member states must therefore be subject to the measures laid down by the community with a view to establishing a single market without internal frontiers within the territory of the european union. i would also point out that the community has not yet adopted any directive regulating the private security sector. but i do not think that this will be an obstacle to future harmonization in this sector. the rapporteur therefore considers that adoption of the present initiative would be contrary to article 47 of the treaty on european union, which requires the union to respect the community's capacity to act in a given area of competence conferred on it by the treaty on european union and prevents it from legislating on that matter. for the reasons i have just given, i therefore propose that the content of the initiative, which is timely and of great interest, be reconsidered and that, in accordance with article 208 of the community treaty, the council ask the commission to examine the need for joint action in the sector of natural or legal persons providing private security services and, if necessary, to propose the adoption of the relevant provisions. i therefore propose, mr president, that the initiative of the kingdom of spain be rejected because it is not legally possible to regulate matters falling within the scope of the first pillar of the treaty on european union from the scope of the third pillar regulated by the treaty on european union. if it did, it would be in breach of, among other things, article 47 of the treaty on european union. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. - mr president, i shall confine my remarks to the initiative on the declaration of basic salaries and allowances of europol staff, which i dealt with as rapporteur for the committee on budgets. in principle, it is a minor matter, with a routine appearance. however, as it stands, it lacks the necessary rigor. this parliament has already spoken about the appropriateness of including europol's budget in the community budget. europol has indeed been widening its field of competence in recent years and this has not been accompanied by a change in its legal framework to allow parliament to exercise its democratic control function. the decision to adjust wages must be entered in the budget. this area, which of course includes its financial regulation, operates without parliament having a say on these matters, and in this context we are consulted on the adjustment of salaries and allowances, as provided for in article 44 of the present convention. as mr deprez has already pointed out, the decision does not take account of the reason why the salary adjustment is fixed at 5.2%; for the same period, the salary adjustment for community officials in the netherlands is 4.3%, a figure based on the statistical information provided by the oecd for all community institutions. it is true that article 44 of the convention does not link adaptation to a procedure comparable to that used for other officials, but i sincerely believe that the absence of justification does not seem to be very much in line with the principles of sound financial management applicable to the community budget. the rejection of this initiative does not therefore call into question the level of remuneration for europol officials, but the lack of justification in the procedure followed. we want europol to be strengthened, to carry out its tasks effectively so that citizens feel protected, and this is perfectly compatible with the democratic control that this parliament has been demanding every time that the legal status of this instrument of police cooperation is discussed.
commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the house for being able to address them at this point in the debate as i will have to leave for rome to participate in the launch of a feasibility study on the external border guard. so let us say that i am allowed to speak because i have to leave for the front. the five initiatives that were presented by the member states have different scope but all relate to police cooperation. i will start with the initiatives concerning europol. the first one, initiated by belgium, aims to adjust the basic salaries and allowances of europol staff. it is a formality since it results from the application of the europol regulation and the commission has nothing against such an initiative. concerning the second initiative of belgium and spain for a council act drawing up a protocol amending the europol convention, this is a significant step to implement the provisions regarding europol as laid down in article 30(2) of the treaty of the european union, which, as you know, foresees europol's participation in joint teams and the possibility to ask member states to conduct and coordinate investigations. it also directly follows up to the tampere conclusions 43 and 45 on the subject. the commission is therefore pleased that the justice and home affairs council of last april arrived at a political agreement on this part of the initiative while awaiting the opinion of parliament. regarding the part of the initiative on the simplification of the procedure for amending the europol convention, the council is currently considering two different alternatives. the commission's firm opinion, and there i follow mr deprez' arguments, is that the europol convention should be replaced by a council decision pursuant to article 34(2)(c) of the treaty of the european union. on this point, the commission fully agrees on the draft recommendations of parliament on the future development of europol and its formal integration into the institutional framework of the union as introduced by mr deprez' report. a council decision will not only allow the amendment of articles of the convention through a simplified procedure but also the adoption of implementing measures with a qualified majority in accordance with article 34(2). if europol were to be established today, it would probably be based on a council decision, this being the modern legal instrument. furthermore, the legal basis of europol will then be in line with the one chosen for eurojust. finally, a council decision would bring the role of the court of justice into line with that which has been provided for in the amsterdam treaty. i will now comment on the draft recommendation. we are in full agreement with recommendation no 6 on the cooperation with eurojust and olaf and with almost all of no 4 of the recommendation regarding democratic control. regarding the latter, i am pleased that parliament agrees with what the commission proposed in the communication that we have launched on the democratic control of europol. we have some misgivings with the proposal to have representatives of parliament on europol's management board. i believe there are alternative forms of parliamentary control that are more appropriate to the specific nature of europol. concerning recommendation no 2 on the budget, the commission feels, as it has explained in the communication that i have mentioned above, that the question of community financing should be settled in the context of europol's possible future operational competences. as regards recommendation no 3, the tasks, we can agree with everything except the first two points: participation in joint teams and asking member states to open investigations. from a commission perspective, these latter two points are superfluous since the council arrived at political agreement on them last april. as regards the three initiatives submitted by the spanish presidency, i would like to express to the spanish presidency the commission's gratitude for putting this subject on the agenda as they meet a real need for progress in police cooperation in the european union. with respect to police studies, the commission has on different occasions underlined its interest in advancing cooperation in an area in which knowledge at european level is often insufficient. at the same time, however, we have warned against a multiplication of networks, the functioning of which, according to the experience gained the european police college may prove difficult. the commission has, therefore, suggested a more pragmatic formula proposing to amend the council decision of 22 december 2000 creating the european police college to allow the police studies institutes of the member states, where these institutes are separate from police training institutions, to participate as full members of the european police college network. i am pleased that this suggestion, which is very much in line with the suggestion of mr sousa pinto, has found an echo in a number of member states and now seems to be the most favoured option in the council. regarding the initiative for a council decision setting up a network of contact points for national authorities with responsibility for private security, the commission agrees that the growth of the private security sector in our countries, as well as in the candidate countries, requires a general policy discussion about division of responsibility between the public authorities and the private sector in providing security to our citizens. however, as much we would like to see a serious policy discussion taking place at european union level on this subject, we must totally respect the division of competences established by the treaties. the commission has pointed out on several occasions that even though it would be positive to establish contacts between the responsible authorities dealing with private security in the member states, it should be underlined that, according to the jurisprudence of the european court of justice, private security is a service as any other service. as such it falls within the remit of the european community, as mrs cerdeira morterero has just emphasised, and creating a network based on title 6 would violate article 47 of the treaty of the european union, which states that "nothing in this treaty shall affect the treaties establishing the european communities or the subsequent treaties and acts modifying or supplementing them". the commission has therefore taken the necessary steps to proceed within the context of the first pillar to a study of the need for common measures to regulate the provision of security services by private providers in the european union. in addition, the commission would like to reiterate its argument on the inconvenience of creating another network with the administrative and budgetary consequences this implies. finally, concerning the proposal to set up a network for the protection of public figures, the commission welcomes this initiative which identifies an area where the need for strengthened cooperation in the european union has become evident. although we must question the basic convenience of creating yet another network, it seems obvious that this initiative responds to a real need confirmed by experts in the field. an important point made by the rapporteur, lord stockton, and shared by the commission, is that the network should not be competent to harmonise member states legislation and regulations. the network should have no power of decision but should only function as an advisory body and should have not budgetary implications. there is only one caveat to the support by the commission for this initiative and this is linked to the question of the commission's participation in the network: we should be more involved. in conclusion, i would like thank the rapporteur, lord stockton, whose work is a valuable contribution to this initiative as regards its legal basis but also as regards the added value this network will bring to police cooperation.

the rapporteur. - mr president, this is indeed an own-initiative report on the mid-term review of agenda 2000 in relation to the second pillar - rural development. we believe that rural development must consolidate multifunctional agriculture throughout the union and that it is therefore necessary to make rural development one of the priorities of the european union. the first and second pillars are two inseparable instruments of the common agricultural policy and must therefore be complemented and put at the service of a multifunctional agriculture which allows the maintenance of numerous agricultural holdings throughout the territory of the european union. we believe that this complementarity between the first and second pillars is the only way to prevent the creation of a dual agriculture within the european union: one that looks only at markets and depends exclusively on market support, and another that turns its back on agricultural markets and depends on support that is disconnected from production. it is not a good model, it would not be a good model, if the first and second pillars were like two watertight, incommunicado compartments, if all the multifunctionality were concentrated on the second pillar, rural development. mr fiori, since you have just referred to my report, i have to say that i think your view is wrong and ultimately ineffective. multifunctional agriculture should enable us to make market management compatible with the management of rural areas and to make possible the existence and viability of farmers on agricultural holdings throughout the territory of the present and the enlarged union. it is true that agenda 2000 created the second pillar of the cap, rural development, and we welcome that. but we must point out that it is true that it has a meagre budget: 10% of the cap budget is devoted to rural development. we therefore call for a larger budgetary allocation, a budgetary reinforcement of this pillar, so that it can meet the challenges it faces. we have also noted, with some regret, that the uneven application of rural development measures by the member states does not always produce a positive result for the rural areas of the union, especially those which are deeply rural, more backward and more peripheral, and which do not find a genuine satisfactory solution to these problems. we therefore propose that, without prejudice to the powers of the national authorities, we should be able to define priorities in the second pillar of the cap in order to make progress in defining a core of priority actions at community level to ensure sustainable development in the union. we also propose that the commission define a new type of rural area which should facilitate the setting of priority measures for each territory and, in turn, allow us to apply different cofinancing rates depending on the various rural problems in the union. we are asking that, in the context of the mid-term review of agenda 2000, we should introduce a mandatory and uniform modulation of aid under the first pillar. mr. fiori said that the will has already been a failure. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we believe that within this measure and in the mid-term review we must strengthen the cross-compliance of aid and establish a link between the implementation of direct payments and the services provided in the area of multi-functionality, extending the cross-compliance measures in favour of sustainable rural development. we also call for the community support framework for rural development to be simplified by creating a single agricultural and rural fund for the whole of the cap, based on the two sections of the eaggf guarantee section and the eaggf guidance section. and on the occasion of this report in favour of a multifunctional agriculture, of a different multifunctional agricultural policy, i would like to end by asking for co-decision for this parliament in the field of agricultural policy.
- mr president, the berlin council limited the interim reform of agenda 2000 - and the two own-initiative reports referred precisely to the commission's future proposals for the revision of agenda 2000 - to respecting the limits of the financial perspective and to the possible revision of intervention prices for cereals and milk quotas. the financial perspective has been respected, and expenditure has been far below the budget. as far as the price of cereals is concerned, in my view the real need would be to restore the price differential for oilseeds in order to correct the strategic deficit in vegetable protein. however, it would be necessary not to carry out experiments with durum wheat or rice to avoid the risk of crop disappearance. and as regards the milk quota system, we should refrain from carrying out experiments which could have disastrous consequences in mountain areas. i therefore believe that the interim content of agenda 2000 should in no case be translated into what i would call a radical reform, with budgetary restrictions, in view of enlargement. however, certain aspects of agenda 2000 which have shown themselves to be dysfunctional or ineffective could be reformed. for example, the application of modulation should be compulsory and uniform in all member states, and the scope of the funds released for its application should be considerably extended. in relation to rural development issues, here are some notes: political patronage can compromise the achievement of objectives entrusted to rural development. the co-financing requirement, as currently designed, creates a deficit of rural development actions in the poorest regions, which are the most in need, and the predominant actions in some countries often have little to do with sustainable rural development. i think mrs rodriguez ramos' report addresses these problems very well and will therefore receive the full support of my group. as regards mr fiori's report, it must be acknowledged that it still has some structural problems, possibly arising from the large number of amendments it received. now, mr fiori knows that my group - and i personally - made a considerable effort to reach agreement on certain aspects of the amendments i had tabled, and it seemed to me that the final result of the vote in the committee on agriculture reflected certain commitments among all the members of the committee. i was surprised by mr fiori's final amendments which will be voted on tomorrow, and i would like to say with all my heart that i do not share the view he has just explained to us, that we must confront an economic, business-like vision, which must also exist in a large part of agriculture, with modulation policies. i believe that public policies should be policies which are aimed at specific objectives - sustainable development, job creation, social criteria - and which should in no way be incompatible with this business and economic vision of agriculture. i have a difference of opinion with mr fiori on this and if his amendments to abolish modulation are adopted i shall advise my group not to vote in favour of his report.
- commissioner, when agenda 2000 was signed in berlin in 1999, we all breathed a sigh of relief, because it opened a period of budgetary tranquility in which multifunctionality had firmly established its foundations and guaranteed the survival of a sustainable rural environment, where quality, safety and respect for the environment had found their place. its mid-term review is therefore key. the common agricultural policy is currently undergoing a major change, due to the challenges facing the european union, particularly in its challenges of enlargement to the east and the world trade organisation negotiations. the european union is preparing to launch the review of the cap in 2003, which could be the prelude to a more thorough reform planned for 2006. one of the keys to this debate is the modulation of market policy support to channel funds to the second pillar, rural development, where we have fallen short; in this way we would achieve a policy, in the opinion of many, more consistent with the commitments made in the wto, and also facilitate the path to accession. but what seems like a laudable goal can also be a double-edged sword. we all want farmers to contribute to the sustainable maintenance of rural areas, but rural areas cannot live without farmers, and if we try to achieve the ultimate objective at all costs, we run the risk of making a mistake in the means used, because we all want greater rural development, but this cannot be achieved by jeopardizing the profitability of agricultural activity. any adjustment made by the european union to direct income support must be made without prejudice to farmers' incomes. if we accept the modulation of cap aid, it should be done in a way that does not compromise the competitiveness of farms and takes account of the economic disparities in the european union. we must therefore be extremely cautious in conveying this message to society. this prudent attitude is, i believe, what inspired the european commission to postpone the presentation of its proposal for the revision of the cap for 2003 until 10 july, once the united states has passed its new agricultural law. this new law represents a 180-degree turn in us policy by reintroducing clear price support, which could put community producers at a clear disadvantage. the european union cannot go along with the vagaries of any country when the future of its farmers is at stake. i would like the european commission to present its proposals to this european parliament and to calibrate very carefully the impact that the farm bill is going to have. we demand that the community executive report on this impact in order to have a clear accounting. if we are to opt for modulation, it must be approached carefully, along a prudent line, so that we do not end up in a situation where there is no return for our farmers.
- mr president, commissioner, in the proposal before us, the european commission asks the parliament and the council to give their opinion on the extension until 2008 of the evaluation period for active substances which should have ended in july 2003. there are 834 substances left to be evaluated. the commission is trying to be realistic and we certainly support it, but i would call its position optimistic, since less than 100 have been examined in the previous period. i will point out the most sensitive points for our group in the european people's party: firstly, we must maintain the possibility of essential uses, because their disappearance could be traumatic for some crops and regions. we must support and support those amendments which propose it. secondly, i cannot share the philosophy that substances are harmful in themselves, because it depends on what concentrations, what situations, what forms of use. so our goal should be the smallest risk, not identified with the smallest amount. thirdly, preliminary evaluation - as proposed in some amendments which we do not support - should not be carried out by industry, ngos, etc., but by those who are legally required to do so. however, these - industry, ngos, etc. - should have access to all the information and can provide studies and trials for these evaluations. the new integrated agricultural policy which is making its way through the european union has led to a considerable decline in the consumption of plant protection products, for example in some crops such as extensive grassland crops. this has not been sufficiently appreciated or known by public opinion. this public opinion is increasingly sensitive to ecological theories, the defence of which could produce unintended effects against biodiversity by accumulations, without protection in smaller crops, which would present us with serious problems of shortage and dependence, could lead to not looking for solutions for essential uses, to setting parameters that exceed the limits of analytical determination or to having plant protection products evaluated by ngos interested in this. interested in what, i wonder. technical assessments are made by scientists and discussed among scientists. i would ask the european commission and the commissioner and all the political groups in this parliament to exercise responsibility when voting, bearing in mind that without agriculture there is no sustainable development. there may be agriculture without sustainable development, but the opposite is not true.

- mr president, as my colleagues have already mentioned, the lisbon, stockholm and nice summits set common objectives to combat poverty and social exclusion. this was done because it was found that since 1995 poverty levels had remained at the same level. in other words, 60 million europeans - 18% of the population - remain below the poverty line, the threshold measuring 50% of the average income of the countries. and with the added complication that 50% of luxembourg's income is not the same as that of portugal. it is also found that those countries which have social expenditure above the eu average, such as finland, denmark or germany, have much lower poverty levels, sometimes half, than those countries which have their social expenditure below the eu average and these include the countries of the south and the united kingdom. i think that a lot has been said at this stage of the debate about the need for plans in each of the countries and the need for the european institutions to be involved in them too. i therefore believe, mr president, that some of the proposed amendments cannot be voted on tomorrow, because that would break the philosophy of the report. i would remind you, mr president, that one of the amendments proposes to remove the eight challenges mentioned by my colleague, mrs ilda figueiredo, including the right to work, housing, education and health. if some of these amendments were to be adopted as they are now, the philosophy of the report would be broken. i therefore ask my colleagues to vote for the report as it stands, because it is a good report which correctly addresses the problems of poverty and social exclusion.

the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the draft council decision which is being tabled in this house today is the culmination of a long process. a moment ago we were discussing whether it was 25 or 30 years. in any case, it's a long process. since 1960, when the draft convention on the election of the european parliament by universal suffrage was adopted, our house has produced up to five reports which have ended up on the council's table. the spanish presidency has finally reached a painstaking agreement within the council. we must welcome this and congratulate the presidency on this package of measures. this text contains most of the proposals which the european parliament had made in the anastasopoulos report. in particular, it introduces the principle of proportional representation with a preferential list as chosen by each member state, the incompatibility between the status of member of the national parliament and that of member of the european parliament, with exceptions for the united kingdom and ireland until the 2009 elections, the right of each member state to set a ceiling for the electoral expenses of candidates and the right of each member state to constitute territorial constituencies which do not affect the overall proportionality of the election. the 1976 act is also adapted to the changes introduced by successive treaties in the institutions and bodies of the union and a clever solution is found for the implementation of the matthews judgment on the gibraltar electorate vote. it is true that other proposals from parliament have not been accepted, such as the single constituency for the whole of the european union, the transfer of elections to may or the objective of equal representation of men and women on the electoral roll. there will therefore be those who say that this is a minimum agreement, but the rapporteur believes that it is better to take a step forward, moving towards a more homogeneous electoral system, than to remain in the dead end in which we were stuck. the european union has done so, moving cautiously, sometimes too cautiously, but moving forward in any case, like the turtles, slowly but surely. the report as requested does not, of course, mean that parliament's positions are being abandoned. the rapporteur has chosen to reaffirm them in the recitals, enriched by the contributions of the members of the committee, to whom he expressly and warmly wishes to thank for their cooperation. these are not purely rhetorical demands. the draft decision provides for a further revision of the minutes before 2009, at which time parliament's demands could be incorporated. i therefore ask for a favourable opinion on the draft decision. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i the union a face and eyes. i have included this proposal in the recitals, with the support of the committee on constitutional affairs, because i firmly believe that it is time for citizens to - question time to the commission (b5-0252/2002): the agenda is closed. part one
question no 3 by mr paulo casaca (h-0401/02) subject: commission encouragement of cartels in the european sugar refining sector article 81 (1) of the treaty prohibits cartels in europe, in particular where they prevent or distort competition within the common market. however, as pointed out in paragraph 91 of special report no 20/2000 of the court of auditors, there is no real common market for sugar and no competition between the various sugar refineries. the flows, or rather the absence of international flows, in the field of trade in sugar and raw sugar and the level of sugar prices within the european market fully confirm the court of auditors' suspicions about cartel formation in the sector - encouraged by the european institutions. the commission, by prohibiting the export of sugar to europe to refineries which have not concluded agreements with the european cartel, is contributing to a significant increase in the latter's power. why have the competition departments of the commission not yet opened any investigation - both internal and external to the commission - into these practices which clearly promote market-sharing, price fixing and dumping in uncontrolled territories and for which the cartel of the european sugar industry is customary? does the commission not consider that its inaction is a clear breach of the treaty?
the commission mr president, contrary to the criticisms made by the honourable member, the commission is convinced that it has exercised its powers fully in the sugar sector, which has been the subject of several competition proceedings. in this connection, the commission would point out that, over the course of almost thirty years, it has investigated a number of practices in this field and has imposed sanctions on cartels at european level and on cartels at national level or on abuse of a dominant position. all these decisions were reviewed by the court of justice, which largely upheld their validity. in 2001, a new investigation was launched following a complaint, but the investigation did not provide any evidence of the alleged facts. the sugar sector was also the subject of specific investigations under the merger regulation. moreover, as the honourable member is aware, the commission presented a first reform of the common organization of the market in sugar over a year ago. the aim of this reform was to open up the sector to competition. the european parliament and the council, however, rejected the commission's proposals by a large majority. the commission has, however, published a call for tenders for an external study on the situation of competition in the sugar sector and the impact of the common organization of the markets in this sector. the results of this study should be known in early 2003.
mr president, i would like to say that the commission has been very active in the sugar sector. without claiming to be exhaustive, i would like to recall that as early as the beginning of the 1970s the commission adopted a decision sanctioning no less than 16 undertakings for infringement of article 81 of the treaty. in 1988, the commission imposed sanctions on british sugar for abuse of a dominant position; in 1997, the commission also sanctioned irish sugar for abuse of a dominant position. in 1998, the commission imposed sanctions on a price cartel on the uk industrial sugar market which had lasted for nearly four years. in 2001, the commission received a complaint concerning a collective refusal to sell by sugar producers established in a member state. the investigation, as i have just said, has not, however, been able to establish the existence of such a concerted refusal. all parties were informed of the closure of the proceedings and the complainant withdrew his complaint. finally, i would also like to point out that the commission pays particular attention to these problems in the context of merger control. finally, it is regrettable from the commission's point of view that the european parliament and the council, as i have said, rejected by a large majority the proposals put forward by the commission over a year ago, proposals which were specifically aimed at introducing greater levels of competition in this market.

- question no 5 by mr jorge salvador hernández mollar (h-0404/02) subject: illegal immigration into the european union from morocco the association agreement with morocco makes the need for dialogue to deal with 'illegal immigration' and 'conditions of return', as well as 'reduction of migratory pressure', one of the priority actions to be implemented. the asylum and immigration action plan for morocco highlights that the fact that morocco does not require visas for immigrants to transit through its territory facilitates the entry of illegal immigrants into the european union and complicates readmission in the absence of proof. the general affairs council of 18 september 2000 gave the commission a mandate to negotiate a general readmission agreement between the european union and morocco. can the commission state what initiatives have been taken for dialogue in the context of the association agreement? does it consider it feasible to use financial cooperation for morocco as a means of pressure to ensure compliance with title vi of the agreement? does it intend to press for morocco to impose visa requirements on third country nationals in the near future, thereby slowing down the arrival of illegal immigrants in the european union? can it state at what stage the negotiations on the abovementioned readmission agreement are at? can it guarantee that the member states and the european parliament are and will be regularly informed of the progress made in these negotiations? second part
commission. – as you can see: at the fifty-fifth minute of this question time we are on question 5 and the honourable member has asked five distinct questions in his question. i shall respond to them all. on question 1, in the framework of the agreement the parties have established a working group on migration and social affairs. it has met twice so far and migration issues have been discussed in three categories: socio-economic development, support for legal migration and combating illegal migration. a series of informal thematic meetings on specific issues in these categories is anticipated this year and next year. in addition, a dialogue to prepare the meda-funded projects related to migration has been established. on question 2, the commission continually monitors the implementation of projects and programmes to ensure fulfilment of the said objectives. the dialogue on migration is making good progress and there are no indications that cooperation will not sustain progress in future. the commission will of course take the satisfactory implementation of the association agreement into account when it decides on the allocation of future funds. on question 3, the introduction of visas for third country nationals is a measure that the moroccan authorities will need to consider. we can discuss that in the dialogue under the association agreement. if a visa system did help to curb the influx of illegal migrants through morocco's southern and eastern borders the commission could look favourably at supporting moroccan initiatives for introducing such arrangements. on question 4, in september 2000 the council approved negotiating directives for a community re-admission agreement with morocco. after several high-level meetings last year, the moroccans eventually agreed to enter into an informal dialogue on re-admission. the commission has suggested formal negotiations being launched before the end of next month. finally, on question 5, whenever the commission is authorised or mandated by the council to negotiate a community re-admission agreement with a third country it conducts negotiations in accordance with the relevant directives and in full compliance with the procedures set down in article 300 of the treaty. that makes provision for parliament to be comprehensively informed about, and consulted on, the final outcome of negotiations. in addition, of course, the commission is manifestly ready to inform the relevant parliamentary committees whenever it is invited to do so.

commission. – i am grateful to the honourable member as he points out the consequences of efforts to reach the continent of europe are often terribly tragic, involving large numbers of casualties and deaths. the pressures on the system in spain and other countries are self-evident. there is, however, a dilemma in seeking to use a financial framework for the purposes of moving the moroccan authorities more in the direction that the honourable member would want. i am sure he is conscious of that dilemma and aware that any risk or threat to financial support could weaken the system even further, and that would simply exacerbate the problem we are dealing with. i can reassure him that the commission is very actively engaged in trying to ensure that the best standards are set and maintained and will use all its endeavours to that end.

commission. – the honourable member is right to indicate that the spur for migration – indeed including legal migration – is frequently poverty and the sense of hopelessness about the future that makes people desperate enough to uproot themselves and to seek to move to countries with which they have no familiarity either in terms of language or custom. it is true to say that development policies must be partly geared to trying to combat poverty to provide people with a workable, reasonable alternative to moving themselves and their families to other parts of the world. it is important, however, that when the community allocates funds for trying to combat poverty and provide the basis for sustainable development, those funds are fully and effectively spent. upon examination, what the honourable member will see is not any meanness or narrowness in the attitude taken to the meda programme. on the contrary, the attitude towards financing the meda programme has much more to do with a desire to ensure efficient, value-for-money spending with proper, generous effects for the people who should be the recipients of such development support, rather than simply having figures on a budget which can look impressive but have less impressive consequences.

- question no 7 is therefore inadmissible. question no 8 by mr pat the cope gallagher (h-0383/02) for the committee on transport and tourism, subject: measures to boost the european tourism industry following the last informal meeting of tourism ministers and the seminar organised by the spanish presidency for those concerned, can the commission indicate what concrete measures it intends to propose to boost the european tourism industry, given the particular importance of this sector and its potential for job creation in regions which, due to their peripheral location, do not have many other sources of economic growth and prosperity?
commission. – in its communication "working together for the future of european tourism", the commission proposed an operational framework with the aim of strengthening european tourism. this communication and the parliament resolution on european tourism, and the council resolution on the future of european tourism, provide the basis for concrete measures to be undertaken. but first of all, i would like to thank the european parliament for its high involvement in promoting tourism as is shown by this question from the honourable member. recently, just in may, we had an opportunity to debate tourism, when the european parliament adopted the report of ms torres marques. the resolution supports our proposals and encourages us to implement and follow them up carefully. let me now turn to some of the concrete measures which will be taken. the main objective is to incorporate tourism in community policies and measures favouring an integrated approach. we need to improve cooperation between tourism stakeholders, notably social partners, including an annual european tourism forum. we will organise this forum for the first time in december this year in brussels. we want to promote stakeholder access to community instruments, involving also local authorities and the private sector. we are mobilising existing survey, analysis, competence and support centres for the development of knowledge and observation regarding tourism. this has been a major request by the european parliament. more specifically, we will look at tourism satellite accounts to measure the economic impact of tourism, and on a european agenda 21 for tourism to promote the sustainable development of tourism. finally, we need to strengthen the position and image of europe as a diverse and attractive set of destinations. this was a major discussion point at the informal meeting of the tourism ministers, to which the honourable member refers in his question. these measures benefit all types of regions in europe, also those with a peripheral location. a considerable share of structural funds made available to the member states supports tourism, both directly and indirectly. less densely-populated, rural or peripheral regions can therefore make good use of the possibility offered in this context to create jobs and to generate economic growth. for the mainstream programmes which represent over 90 % of the financial envelope available in the structural funds, the commission has set clear guidelines which explicitly encourage the support of a balanced and sustainable development of tourism, in particular through three activities: firstly, the modernisation of tourism-related infrastructures and the improvement of their efficiency;secondly, upgrading skills and professional profiles in order to respond better to the expectations of tourists and the needs of the industry;thirdly, encouraging business-to-business partnerships, public-private cooperation and networking in order to improve the integration of the different services involved in the “tourism chain”. in the context of the diversification of activities in rural areas, there are also funds allocated in the framework of rural development programmes by the european agriculture guarantee and guidance funds. these measures try to improve the attractiveness of the villages and rural areas, protecting nature and historical and cultural heritage. tourism related measures are also financed with the funds allocated to the community initiative leader+ improving the quality of life of the rural areas. in conclusion, tourism development should be carefully planned so as to take into consideration the carrying capacity of the site with regard to environmental, social and economic impacts.
commission. – in reply to the honourable member, i would say this: first of all, we discussed in a ministerial meeting – and since that we have included in the europe action plan 2005 – a possibility to create a european-wide portal which would provide easy access to all european destinations. if this were to be done as a project between the member states, of course according to their choice, these kinds of peripheral, lesser-known but exciting areas would be better marketed. secondly, i agree with you that in those areas where there is a rural population it is easier to guarantee sustainable development. if the marketing is well done there are a lot of tourists who will chose these types of destinations. but it is difficult for companies to reach rural populations. concentrated internet marketing would be the cheapest way. finally, on the investment issue, i should know more of the details of the fund which the member is talking about. i am sure that we can come back to this issue later.
commission. – as far as basle ii is concerned, thanks to the great attention paid to this issue by parliament – and mr rübig in particular – the commission is carefully following and participating in the preparations. before any decisions are made, we will have open consultation with all the stakeholders so that nobody will be taken by surprise. the interests of european smes have indeed been communicated for inclusion in that preparatory work. i fully agree with you that smes in general and tourism enterprises in particular, which often do not have much equity capital, are most vulnerable if borrowing or lending become too tight. we need to pay particular attention to that. the problem is that real banking activities are run in member states by private financial institutions. our scope is therefore limited.
question no 9 by astrid thors (h-0449/02) subject: migration to an open ipa how does the commission intend to encourage and organise the migration of existing ipas to a single and open ipa in the coming months? how does it intend to organise dialogue on this subject? will it simply consult industry and technical experts, or is it prepared to include consumer groups and members of the european parliament in the dialogue?
the commission. the member's question on the transition to an open application interface concerns the interoperability of interactive tv services. the question has three parts. part one: how does the commission intend to promote and organise the transition from the current interface to a single interface? the provisions of article 18 of directive 2002/21/ec of the european parliament and of the council on a common regulatory framework for electronic communications networks and services (framework directive) impose a legal requirement on member states to promote transparency in the provision of application programming interfaces. the provisions do not require any specific interface technology or a single interface. the standard for home multimedia platforms, mhp, meets the requirements for interoperability and transparency in this area. we therefore encourage industry to introduce this standard on a voluntary basis. the mhp standard will be included in the list of standards published in the oj in accordance with the directive. member states are obliged to encourage the use of the standards included in the list. we expect the list to be published in the autumn. the directive also requires member states to review interoperability and user choice by july 2004. the directive contains a procedure for making the use of a standard compulsory. this is one of the issues that will be addressed in the proposed review. the second part: how does the commission intend to organise the dialogue in connection with such a transition? the directorate-general for the information society has initiated a dialogue with industry on the interoperability of interactive television services. the commission has set up a european network of national standards bodies to ensure the interoperability of the european rail system. there is no consensus in the industry on what interoperability actually means. we have therefore taken steps to move the dialogue forward. firstly, we have asked the digital video broadcasting group, the dvb group, to examine the technical compatibility of interactive services. secondly, we have started a study of the strategic aspects of interoperability in order to have access to an independent analysis later this year. the analysis includes consumer issues. finally, we have asked the cenelec standardisation body to carry out a preliminary study on the standardisation of digital tv and interactive tv services. the task will be to analyse the current state of the art and make recommendations. in the third part, the commission will limit the dialogue to industry and technical aspects only. it is also willing to open the dialogue to consumer groups and members of the european parliament. i am very much in favour of the involvement of members of parliament and consumer groups. however, the dialogue must have a sound technical basis, and that is what we are currently focusing on. the political debate must be preceded by careful studies on issues such as interoperability. decision-makers need to understand the options available and their implications. it is a process which shows that the commission is following up its commitment from the december plenary.
the commission. i want to give you two answers. as regards the seville summit, digital television is included in the europe 2005 action plan. i personally believe that digital television will play a major role in the information society in the long term because if we really want the whole population to be able to access the internet, the internet must also be made available via television. we decided in december that industry would have one year after the directive had entered into force, and we must stick to this commitment. however, i very well understand that we may have to do more in the meantime to ensure that all those involved in the process know that if a solution is not reached on a voluntary basis, the commission has a mandate to act.

the commission - your honor, we don't know the exact percentage. we have only projections and forecasts and, as i said in my first speech, the forecast is for an increase in road transport of around 50% - between 40% and 50% - in the next ten years, that is to say, between now and 2010. that is the overall forecast, but obviously there is a very high probability that there will be a greater incidence in some areas. the background is the recent enlargements that have taken place: for example, the iberian peninsula - in its exchange through the pyrenees with france - or the incorporation of the scandinavian countries, in exchanges with the rest of the continent, or austria. there is no doubt that an enlargement automatically leads to a qualitative and quantitative jump in trade, but i cannot give you any more specific data, except for the overall forecasts of about 50% for 2010.
