very important dimension, and, of course, the elements of prevention. in the same way, we will not forget diabetes with the new perspectives that are opening up in this respect, as mr van velzen has just emphasized. i would like to say to mr liese, who tabled an amendment in the sitting, that for me, as far as palliative care is concerned, it is quite clear that this point can be taken up in the context of what is called the coordination of european policies and support for research in the field of diseases, which must in any case be seen in a global way. so there will be no problem in incorporating this idea which you have developed in plenary. however, i can assure you that the commission is not in a position to accept the amendments on life sciences which have just been tabled in plenary, which would compromise the balance between the genomic and non-genomic aspects that has been jointly achieved in the sixth framework programme. for the other thematic priorities, the commission can accept all amendments in general, except for those which go into too much detail for specific programmes, such as food safety and quality. we are now entering into details and issues which are not covered by the specific programmes as they result from the sixth framework programme. as regards an amendment which has just been tabled in plenary by mr van velzen, i believe that there is a need to develop thinking and research on space and satellites, but this must also be done in collaboration with the european space agency, which is also the operational element of space policy. if there is understanding in substance, then there should be a way of working together in form. i think that in general i can say that everything in mr van velzen's report reflects exactly the common wishes we have expressed, even if, on certain points, there are obviously details which we may not be able to take as such, but the general philosophy is certainly the same and i can only be pleased about that. the same applies, of course, to mrs zorba's amendments. they are quite acceptable and have even given an extra dimension to the debate by linking the concept of multidisciplinarity, by placing greater emphasis on the mobility of researchers, and i share what your neighbour, mrs zrihen, has just said about the concept of europe, because the main wealth of europe is the human potential of researchers, which we must exploit, by ensuring a better link between the research process and the bologna process, so that we arrive at a europe of knowledge, as was said at the barcelona summit. because the great problem for europe will be to maintain a high-quality human potential, and i will also come back to this with regard to the dimension of science and society and the attraction of young people to research. there is of course also, as you said, support for the creation of the european education area. i also think that in the debate on the rules of participation we are also integrating this idea of science and education, which is obviously an important point, but we also think that complementarities with differences and similar actions are needed within the framework of the thematic priorities. as regards mr purvis's intervention, which referred to a problem of reformulation in the text of an amendment tabled in plenary, which seeks to clarify the eligibility criteria for experienced researchers, i would like to say that, in the spirit of our text, it is four years of experience or the doctorate that must be understood. the text as originally formulated is therefore not satisfactory, so we are proposing a much simpler text, namely four years' experience or a doctorate, which would be in line with the amendment you tabled in plenary, because that is the sensitive point, and i think you have done well in emphasizing that our inclusion was perhaps not clear enough and that, therefore, it is better to have gold rather than including, which would be simpler. that is a very specific answer to an amendment which is going to be voted on in plenary. on the other hand, mrs zorba, we have difficulty accepting the amendment to fix a predetermined amount for international grants, because i think that giving predetermined amounts introduces a notion of rigidity which is not entirely compatible, but we can assure you that we will follow up positively the philosophy of your amendment on individual grants, since this is obviously one of the opening points of the framework programme. but we cannot say that we should, say, start classifying all mobility actions in too rigid a way, because that would ultimately prove to be harmful. on the other hand, with regard to the amendments on science and society, we fully agree with your amendments which call for the involvement of citizens and stakeholders, such as patient associations or environmental protection, in the debate on science and society, and with the amendments which stress the important role of teachers and the media in a better understanding of science. however, we do not think it would be appropriate to introduce an explicit mention of science and society issues in the thematic priorities, as this is a subject which goes beyond thematic priorities because it covers the whole field of science and society. and so it would seem a bit reductive to put it only in the thematic priorities. however, these are details in relation to the general philosophy you propose. secondly, and this is important, i note that parliament has made sure that 'science and society' is a stronger priority. it is true that this is the first time that this subject has been dealt with as such in a framework programme, and you have made sure that it is budgetarily strengthened, which i think is a good decision. as regards the report by mr alyssandrakis and what mrs matikainen has added: i think that all your amendments, mr alyssandrakis, add useful details to the commission's proposal. the commission agrees to take them up, sometimes with a slight reformulation, but without touching their 'philosophy'. this is the case, for example, with all the amendments relating to radiation protection, which is obviously an important problem. as regards nuclear fusion, we support the majority of the amendments supporting the financing of the activities concerned, but we would point out that the iter project is a new step. i think that mrs matikainen and you are saying a bit the same thing, but the iter project really needs to be considered as the next step and therefore it must also appear in the specific programme because it is part of the great prospects of nuclear fusion. this does not prevent basic research and research in general from continuing in other contexts than the one of the implementation of iter, as you have just pointed out, with jet and other types of tokamak, stellerator, for example. but we have to make it our goal to make iter the important. the commission attaches great importance to the management of radioactive waste. the proposed amendments, however, tend to introduce time limits which are too restrictive for research. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the waste is not disposed of in a manner which would be contrary to the interests of the community. as regards mr piétrasanta's report, we would like to thank you, mr piétrasanta, and through you, the whole of parliament. we thank you, as mrs mcnally has reminded us, for your interest in the joint research centre and for the support objectives. it is a useful instrument for contributing to the realisation of the european research area by creating a common base of knowledge and measures and also, as you have pointed out, mr piétrasanta, by creating links with national centres. i think that's an interesting point you've made. in this connection, i should like to point out that the commission intends to include in the council minutes a statement welcoming parliament's intention to set up an ad hoc group of members of parliament to act as an interface with the joint research centre, a monitoring committee of sorts. i think this is an idea which was already in the avignon report, but you have done very well to take it up. institutionally, we will see to it that a declaration is made to the council to put it into effect. this is a good idea and one which parliament supports. we think that the amendments are acceptable, including those which emphasize the priority of environmental issues, in particular the protection of ecosystems and food security. you know that the joint research centre has expertise in the field of traceability, for example of gmos, which is considered to be one of the best in europe. it is therefore an important tool in the context of the enlargement of the centre and its opening up to new members: i will come back to this in connection with mr schwaiger's report. mr schwaiger, i should like to say how timely your amendments are, which is normal since you are well aware of the matter and have been keen to visit the jrc. we don't have any problems. on the contrary. we believe that your report provides additional elements which emphasize the need to integrate the joint research centre into european cooperation networks, particularly networks of excellence, and we share the principles you have mentioned, whether they concern ethics or openness. i would point out, however, that the same is true of research to support the harmonization of nuclear safety standards area which can be put to good use. i think that is how i have dealt with the various reports and i would like to conclude by commenting on some of the points made. i have already told mr purvis that we will make the correction in the spirit you have indicated. i would stress that you are right to say how important 'science and society' is for young people. how can we encourage young people to study science, as mrs mcnally said? it is therefore in this respect that there must be convergence of action. you know that we have developed a "science and society" action plan. we'll have to see how - mr president, as has been made clear both in the speeches of the presidency and the spokesmen who have already spoken, seville will be the last summit of the spanish presidency and, although it is not the time for the final balance sheet, it is time to take a brief look at the way things are going and to see whether we are in time to approve or, if possible, to take a good note. it could be said that these five months have been characterized by an excess of noise on most of the issues raised as priorities for the semester. there is a lot of noise about enlargement, about immigration, about mediterranean policy, about fisheries policy and the reform of agricultural policy, about foreign policy, about transatlantic relations, etc. it is true, mr president, that we have spoken about everything: sustainable development, the spirit of lisbon, the institutionalisation of the union, the peripheral regions - but if we look at the progress made - on any of the issues mentioned - we will come to the conclusion that there is a great asymmetry between what is said and what is done. as they say, mr. president, there's been a lot of noise and a few nuts. i know that on some issues - perhaps on many of them - the presidency has alibis, but the truth is that we have come to the end with a more complicated agenda than when we started it and with a greater degree of confusion. on the subject of immigration and asylum, for example, we have been repeating the conclusions of the tampere council for over a month, commitments which the council has been unable to implement because of a lack of political will. nothing new is being said. everything has been said and agreed, but there is such a drum circle that it seems that we are inventing something for the seville summit. as far as employment policy is concerned, the only thing that can be said with any justice is that barcelona has diverted the spirit of lisbon. it was not taken into account that lisbon's strategic objective was not only to create a more prosperous and competitive economic area, but also to achieve full employment and greater social cohesion, and that is where the backsliding took place. what about the great challenge of the swedish presidency, sustainable development? this is a paradigmatic example of what has not been done. now, in the barcelona summit resolution, sustainability was mentioned 103 times. anybody want more? the valencia summit was a success because it took place. yes, i know that the climate in the middle east was not the most favourable, but we were not even able to carry out one of the few concrete priorities of the spanish presidency, the euro-mediterranean bank. as regards transatlantic relations, it has already been said - mr poettering himself has said this - that we have never had so many open disputes with the united states, for example on trade and industrial issues, the non-ratification of the kyoto protocol, the divergent positions on the middle east, the belligerent position of the united states in relation to the international criminal court, which leads them to allow themselves the luxury of threatening us, of threatening to intervene if an american military man is tried in the netherlands. we don't seem to have the most respect in the world. i would like to conclude, mr president, with a note on institutional reforms: the world has become very complicated, globalisation requires ever more strengthened global institutions and policies closer to the citizens, but the spanish presidency - and i am sorry to say this - has been characterized by giving contradictory and wrong answers to these challenges in this area: more renationalisation, less european government; and this is not the way to solve any of the problems europe has to face. the reduction of the powers of our common institutions is a defensive reaction which can only lead to failure. it is, mr president, nationalism of the most stale kind, and 'more europe' is less nationalism, of the old and also of the new. in conclusion, we could say that we are reasonably dissatisfied today, but we would like nothing more than to change our minds and, in these remaining days, in the final race, to have a surprise from you, to have more lights on and some shadows disappear. as i said to president aznar on 16 january in this very house, i would like nothing more than to be able to congratulate you at the end.

the committee on fisheries has adopted a number of amendments. mr president, the committee on fisheries has voted in favour of the commission's proposal which we are now discussing along the lines of previous resolutions adopted by this house. as regards fisheries, the proposal concerns fresh and chilled fish of certain species such as sea bream, hake and bass. also smoked fish and salmon. the authorized exceptions - as those who have spoken before me have already said - must be part of a strategy for the economic and social development of the canary islands and thus contribute to the promotion and diversification of local activities. these tax measures are exceptional, specific and designed to compensate for the disadvantages of the peripheral situation and therefore fall fully within the scope of article 299 (2) of the treaty. this is a legal basis intended to enable local economic activities in the outermost regions to compete, despite the considerable disadvantages arising from their isolation, remoteness and the small size of their local market. it is a legal framework which is not exhausted by this type of tax measures. in the fisheries sector, for example, the specific features of this ultraperiphery should be taken into account when reforming the common fisheries policy, in the context of article 299 (2), as the commission's own proposal already states.
- mr president, my first words are to express my congratulations and my thanks to the rapporteur, mr marques. i congratulate him on his excellent report, which responds to a demand from the canary islands - one of the outermost regions of the union with unique fiscal specialties, backed by a solid legal basis (article 299 (2) of the treaty) - and i thank him for his excellent work and flexibility, which have enabled him to build around it a solid parliamentary majority, which makes it possible to approve this report within a few hours, thus ending a long parliamentary journey that began almost two years ago. the economic and fiscal regime of the islands is the backbone of the statute of autonomy and self-government of the canary islands, the current version of which has its origins in the treaty on european union and in the treaty of accession of spain to the european communities, but which - over the centuries, since our incorporation into the crown of castile, before castile was spain - has undergone various adaptations, depending on what happens at each moment. it is therefore a matter of historical rights whose rank is no less important than the tax peculiarities of luxembourg or some of the british isles, to mention only the case of countries where the handling of this matter has met with opposition, even obstinate opposition, paradoxically. the members who have tried - and still try - to amend the rapporteur's text with their amendments are defending legitimate interests, no doubt, but they are linked above all to the tobacco and alcoholic beverage and spirits lobbies, and they do not now coincide with the interests of the canaries, the vast majority of whom, through their legitimate representatives, have expressed themselves in the line of the report presented to us by mr marques. as the spanish government has done, by virtue of its constitution, as does the european commission itself - which has understood that this draft is in accordance with, and does not contradict, community law - and as reflected in the broad agreement within the council, which will probably approve it in a few days' time, once this parliament has pronounced itself. the canary islands will thus have a good economic policy instrument to diversify their resources and boost their economic and social development, to halt the decline of their already weak industrial sector and, if possible, to stimulate its development, especially in the agro-food processing sector, which - if it happens - will allow the maintenance and creation of new jobs in a region with a high unemployment rate, while providing alternatives to a dangerous dependence on the tourist sector. the canary islands cannot continue to grow solely at the expense of receiving a few hundred thousand more tourists each year. this year we will have received 12 million visitors, with the benefits that this will undoubtedly bring, but with the sometimes devastating effects that this will have on our sustainable development: in some islands the annual number of tourists far exceeds the number of permanent residents, which now creates a number of problems, which will increase in the future if we do not help to correct this trend, which is what this regulation is aiming at. for all these reasons and others mentioned by the rapporteur and some of the speakers, this report must be adopted, and that is what i hope as a member of the european people's party.

commission. – mr president, the programme that we have been discussing tonight, known as the fiscalis 2007 programme, will continue and extend the existing fiscalis programme which has been in place since 1998. before the commission decided to propose the fiscalis 2007 programme, it evaluated the activities and the results of the existing fiscalis programme. that evaluation was based on member states' reports on their experience with that programme. the evaluation indicated that member states viewed the programme as being an essential tool in fostering administrative cooperation between administrations responsible for indirect taxation. accordingly, the commission decided that the existing programme activities should continue to be funded by a community programme. the commission also felt that it was necessary, particularly taking into account the conclusion of the council's ad hoc working party on tax fraud, to propose the extension of the programme to direct taxation. that will mean in future that direct tax administrations will have a tool to help them to work closer together in a manner which has become second nature to indirect tax administrations by means of the fiscalis programme. the commission also believes that it is important to give as much support as possible to the countries preparing for the enlargement of the european union. for that reason, candidate countries are put on an equal footing with member states in this programme, which has special objectives to meet the needs of those administrations. i should like to add it is very important that this programme is adopted before the expiry of the current fiscalis programme. i and the commission are therefore extremely pleased that this proposal is supported by the european parliament. i particularly welcome the positive contribution of mr garcía-margallo y marfil, the rapporteur for the committee on economic and monetary affairs. given the fact that examination of this proposal is ongoing in council and given the commission's strong desire to have the programme adopted as quickly as possible, i believe that the most appropriate course of action at this time is for the commission not so much to accept the amendments put forward by the parliament. in particular, as regards the budgetary issues raised in the reports, amendments nos 1 and 2 appear to be counter to the agreements between our respective institutions on budgetary discipline and in substance do no more than repeat what is already found in the proposal as regards the programme's financial framework. amendments nos 3 and 4 go beyond the scope of the fiscalis 2007 programme which is a purely administrative measure. amendment no 5 is superfluous, because parliament is already entitled to obtain the relevant documents. amendment no 6 would interfere with the proper implementation of the programme. amendment no 7 is superfluous because the decision already contains provisions on a regular follow-up of how objectives are achieved. amendment no 8 is also superfluous because the present programme does not have any direct impact on local fiscal authorities and i say this in particular in answer to remarks made by mr mayol i raynal. may i say that i am personally confident of the fact that an agreement between the european parliament, the council and the commission will be achieved on these issues. the council has already started to discuss the proposal in detail. it will do its best to reach an agreement as soon as possible. your support for the proposal is very important in achieving that result. i should like to thank parliament for that support. to reply in further detail to mrs villiers' remarks, the commission believes that there are convincing reasons for the programme to be extended to direct taxation, not least because the council itself, in its ad hoc working party's report, explicitly recommended improved cooperation in direct tax matters. i am very much aware, as perhaps mrs villiers knows, of the fact that direct taxation, except where it distorts the internal market, for example in the case of contributions to pension funds across borders, is very much a matter of national political preferences. that is a position i have often defended, both in the commission and in outside discussions. on that point i agree with mrs villiers. but here we are talking about administrative cooperation and the basic issue is combating fraud. i am sure mrs villiers dislikes fraud as much as the commission. disliking something is one thing, doing something about it is another. if we want to do something about fraud in the area of direct taxation, we must facilitate cooperation between fiscal authorities. with all due respect to mrs villiers, i cannot escape the impression that perhaps she is looking at water burning if she objects to cooperation between the fiscal authorities in the field of direct taxation.
the rapporteur. - mr president, we are at the end of an initiative by the commission - i would say a good initiative by the commission - to harmonize legislation on insurance intermediation. this is a field which has not been harmonised so far. but that gap has now been filled and i think fortunately in a good way, because in insurance the internal market is crippled if there are no common rules affecting the trading networks. if insurance undertakings can operate within the territory of the union without frontiers, it is equally necessary that those who offer their products can operate under common rules, with freedom of establishment and freedom to provide services - in short, in the internal market. but not only that, it is also necessary to harmonize our legislation to achieve a high standard of consumer protection, in a field like this where the imbalance between the information held by the seller of products and the purchaser is very significant. and that purpose is reflected in this proposal for a directive. parliament approved a total of 40 amendments at first reading, although it is true that some of them were adopted by a small minority. the common position accepted, either in its literal tenor or, at least, in spirit, something more than half of them. now, on second reading, parliament has insisted on some of the amendments which were not adopted, although it has done so in terms which, in my view, make it foreseeable that they will be adopted by the other institutions. i would like to make an exercise in this field of reflection on the codecision procedure, and this reflection leads us to believe that if this procedure is to be generalized, it cannot and must not lead to unnecessary lengthen ing of the procedures or to the co-legislating institutions, if they start from different positions, each sticking to its position without reaching reasonable agreements. if that agreement is reached without going through the conciliation phase, so much the better, and if so, that is an objective which i believe can be achieved in the procedure for this directive, because parliament has shown how it can participate fully in the legislative process by working with other institutions, without thereby unnecessarily dragging out the legislative procedure. but the procedure also has its problems, and perhaps the most important of these is the system of debates in this parliament. unlike in other parliaments, we do not debate in a contradictory way with the proposals and therefore it seems that any effort to try to convince you about the goodness or badness of certain amendments is a futile effort. i do not, however, resist at least attempting to state the reasons why i am opposed to or propose to vote against some of the amendments which have been adopted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs. i hope it's not a wasted effort, because a thinker from my land said that wasted effort leads to melancholy and, at this time of night, i wouldn't want to get melancholy. i am opposed to the adoption of amendments nos 2 and 14, which were adopted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs. i am opposed, as strongly as i can convey to the honourable members, to the content of amendment no 2, and i am doing so for a number of reasons: firstly, for technical reasons. the amendment seeks to exclude from harmonization certain cases which, if adopted, would be in contradiction with other extremes of the directive. other points, ladies and gentlemen, which were approved in their wording, accepted by the council and the commission as a result of the amendments of this parliament at first reading. how can we pass an amendment which contradicts our own texts? secondly, and not least, if, as amendment no 2 seeks to do, certain types of intermediation are excluded from harmonization, that means, nothing more or less, that a large part of the sale of insurance contracts would be excluded from the consumer protection mechanisms contained in the directive and that is not acceptable.
- madam president, i would like to begin by regretting the absence of commissioner fischler. i think the importance of this debate merited your presence here today. scientific reports, which are rigorous, transparent, cross-checked and carried out with the sector, should be the first pillar of the cfp reform in order to have credibility in the conservation of our fisheries species. you need to diagnose the true state of the resources accurately, with precision, because otherwise, we could be treating a sprained ankle with chemotherapy. the european union should be a world example of marine research, but it is not, not even - - madam president, i would like to congratulate my colleague, catherine stihler, very sincerely on her excellent work, which has enabled the council to adopt a much more balanced plan for these two species. however, i cannot agree with your desire, as rapporteur, to include hake back in this report. as she knows, i had tabled 13 amendments in committee to soften the measures for cod, and more than half of them fell by the wayside when the commission adopted the amendment tabled by mr varela, which separates the two species. if the report for both species were to be adopted at the same time, it would therefore be very unbalanced. the community's fisheries policy must strike a balance between measures aimed at conserving resources, the reasonable adjustment of the fleet to each state and the maintenance of economic activity in the regions dependent on fishing. it's a complex approach. firstly, because it is not just overfishing that is causing the depletion of resources: indiscriminate catching of species for the production of flour breaks the food chain of cod and hake and largely determines the situation of both species. it is true that there are very significant differences between the two fisheries, in terms of their mortality and growth rates, and the actions required for their preservation. the situation of cod in the north sea and scotland is different, as is that of cod in south-west ireland and the coasts of france. not all species - and this is something we have to say very loudly - not all fisheries are in the same state. in this connection, the committee on fisheries considered that the situation of cod and codfish is different and that cod should be subject to different measures from cod, which should be adopted on the basis of scientific reports. there is no indisputable, unified and single scientific basis to indicate that the stock of northern hake is outside the biological safe limit and no drastic management measures appear to be necessary to save this stock. we cannot forget the great economic and social impact of these measures on the fishing areas. the commission has not carried out any study of these consequences or of what should be taken into account when implementing the plan, nor has it presented us with an evaluation of the emergency measures it adopted in 2001. and it should also be said that the cod tac was reduced by 51% between 1999 and 2001. the european fishing fleet needs to know, in a reasonable way, the prospects for its activity. that is why my group is opposed to drastic cuts, which can be introduced over longer periods. we therefore support the rapporteur's amendment no 8 and once again i sincerely congratulate her on the excellent work she has done.

especially when there is a serious risk and clear harm to our fishermen.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not affected by the effects of the crisis. for all these reasons, the council of ministers of 17 july 2000 invited the commission to present a regulatory framework for alcohol of agricultural origin, but the council went much further and proposed a common market organization, which did not include any financial measures but did allow for the possibility of establishing tariff quotas, safeguard clauses, prohibiting or restricting the use of inward processing arrangements and a specific provision on aid. however, this proposal from the commission did not include synthetic alcohol, which can be used industrially by 70% of the users of ethyl alcohol; only 30% of the production of spirits uses only alcohol of agricultural origin. because synthetic alcohol was not covered, and because no legal basis was found at the time for its inclusion in a common organization of the market, this parliament referred the report back to committee two months ago. the council then continued its deliberations and reached a preliminary agreement to introduce synthetic alcohol and we have been asked for a second report. now, the council and parliament agree, and i think that should be taken into account by the commission. the report proposes, in one of the amendments, the most important one, to change the title; instead of a com, it proposes a regulation laying down specific measures relating to the market in ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin within the european union. it is proposed that synthetic alcohol should also be covered by these measures, particularly as regards statistics. it is also proposed that the wine management committee should be responsible for these matters, but that there should be a specific working group within the wine management committee to deal with alcohol of agricultural origin, and it is also proposed that article 10 should be deleted, since since it is not a com, there is no point in an article dealing with aid. in addition, since these are national aids, i believe they fall within the scope of all state aids, whether they are for alcohol of agricultural origin or for other purposes. i would ask you, mr commissioner, to forward all these amendments, which i ask to be voted on tomorrow in the house, to the commissioner responsible and to convey to him the feeling that the council and parliament are in agreement on this point.

the commission. - mr president, the european council meeting in lisbon in march 2000 placed business at the heart of the eu's strategic objective. entrepreneurship can help to exploit the opportunities offered by the economy and thus create wealth that can help society to achieve its goals. the lisbon meeting resulted in a european small business act. the starting point was that small businesses are an important source of dynamism, innovation and entrepreneurship. last winter, we were concerned that the central importance of business would be forgotten. but that has not been the case. the barcelona european council in march reaffirmed the importance of enterprises, reaffirmed the special status it accorded them and called on the member states to speed up the implementation of the charter for small enterprises. at the same time, the commission published the 2002 competitiveness report. it shows how far the productivity of the eu is from that of the united states. gdp per capita in the eu is therefore only about 65% of the us level. the report highlights the weak level of investment and exploitation of ict. the consequences of this lack are visible in industry, but also in the service sector. the exploitation of ict investment is also hampered by the shortage of skilled labour in the eu. the 2002 competitiveness report concludes with concern that unless all obstacles are removed, the eu will not be able to achieve the lisbon objectives. the report by dominique vlasto highlights a number of actions that could improve the eu's performance and avoid this outcome. in conclusion, i would like to stress five points: first, the competitiveness of eu enterprises is based on the internal market. there is still a lot to be done to complete the internal market in services. the liberalisation of financial markets will help to provide finance for businesses. secondly, the charter for small enterprises must be implemented with determination. there are signs of progress, but member states must not waste time. thirdly, better regulation means that the effects of every legislative proposal must be examined. this is what the commission proposed last week and i am very pleased with the speeches made by mr chichester and mr titley on this subject. fourthly, we must make every effort to make use of information and communication technologies. it is not enough to show that information and communication technology is driving the economy in the united states, but we must also take the necessary steps. finally, we must first of all create a climate favourable to entrepreneurship. you have to take risks, and society has to encourage you to do it. this will be discussed in the green paper. these are all political measures. we must concentrate on getting political action on the right track, so that the right environment for business can be created in the eu, not by looking at projects that are so small - as profitable as they can be. when substantial funding is needed at eu level, we already have the necessary instruments at our disposal. i thank mrs dominique vlasto for pointing out such important policy areas where progress is needed. finally, we must improve our political action so that we can bring the lisbon objective within reach.

'agrofuel'. this proposal was not accepted and i shall mention it for the record. the proposal for a directive appears to be the corollary of the proposal to promote the use of biofuels in transport. the commission is based on a continuous growth assumption for road transport. in order to meet the commitments made by the union in kyoto, consideration should be given to the partial replacement of fossil fuels by fuels that do not increase the greenhouse effect. in this context, the white paper on transport policy forecasts that carbon dioxide emissions from transport will increase by 50% between 1990 and 2010. according to the estimates in this white paper, road transport accounts for 84% of these emissions. in addition, the growth in demand in the transport sector leads to an increased dependence on oil or natural gas producing third countries. the commission's green paper on the security of energy supply foresees that by 2020, alternative fuels should account for 20% of total consumption. our advantage, according to the commission, is the promotion of biofuels or agrofuels. it is the possibility of exploiting land which, under the blair house agreements, is excluded from food production. this is a prospect which could be of interest, she says, to the future member states, eastern europe, malta and cyprus. to promote the use of biofuels, it is necessary to introduce incentive taxation. indeed, given the current price of crude oil, the current extra cost of producing pure biodiesel would reach eur 0,25 to eur 0,30 per litre compared to fossil diesel. in fact, it seems that the commission wanted to adapt the biofuel tax regime following the judgment of the court of first instance of 27 september 2000. this is a system derogating from the common law system of excise duties on mineral oils, the structures of which are harmonised by directive 92/81, which this directive seeks to amend. until now, member states could provide for measures to reduce or exempt excise duties on the basis of article 8 (2) (d) of directive 92/81 in order to promote the production of biofuels or agrofuels. the directive provides in particular that pilot projects aimed at the technological development of less polluting products, including fuels from renewable resources, may benefit from these exemptions. on the basis of these provisions, germany, france and sweden, among others, have adopted derogating schemes up to full exemption. the court of first instance annulled the commission's decision granting this derogation to the french state because the sector in question - the production of etbe - had gone beyond the pilot project stage. another possibility of derogation is provided for in article 8 (4) of directive 92/81. the council shall act unanimously on a proposal from the commission. as a result of the bp chemicals case law, several member states have submitted requests for derogations to the commission. on the basis of article 93 of the treaty, the proposal for a directive aims to harmonise the excise duty system for biofuels. it is therefore provided that member states may fix duties below the 20% rate used as the floor rate on these products, but that these duties may not be reduced by more than 50% compared with the excise duties on fossil fuels. member states may provide for an additional reduction in favour of biofuels or agrofuels consumed by certain carriers, including local public transport companies. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of biofuels. it is unlikely that the states which decide unanimously on this matter will reach agreement on this point. from an ecological point of view, it is by no means obvious that the balance of products which the directives in question tend to favour, namely biofuels or agrofuels which can be blended with oil (biodiesel and bioethanol), is of real interest. it is questionable whether considerations of reducing the greenhouse effect are not the secret of the oil companies, the refining chemical industries, the automobile industry and industrial agriculture. the amendment we tabled therefore aims to make the size of the tax reductions dependent solely on the ecological interest of the products and uses. from this point of view, it would seem more appropriate to promote biofuels for use by so-called captive fleets: taxis, bus lines and diesel locomotives. a specialised distribution network and engines adapted to run exclusively on biofuels can then be set up and the energy balance will be very favourable. this solution also has the merit of promoting decentralized development. it is conceivable that these products and uses could be exempted completely. the same should apply to biofuels from biomass from mediterranean regions where there is a proven fire risk. in substance, while we agree with the 2% biofuel target for 2005, we are opposed to the 5.75% target for 2010. we are calling for a redefinition of the quantitative targets after an environmental impact assessment which takes into account alternative uses of biomass.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this is a directive which responds to the commission's communication, the green paper and various resolutions of this parliament. we consider it to be a realistic directive and one which can be perfectly implemented. before i go on, i would like to emphasize the cooperation and good synchronization which i have had with the alternative rapporteur, mrs rothe, and with the rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, mr kronberger, since we are dealing with a hughes procedure. this has, of course, delayed the debate on the directive at first reading for a long time, because of a problem of competence which parliament has taken too long to resolve. i shall concentrate mainly on the most controversial aspect of the directive, which is the question of objectives. the commission has proposed binding targets to be met over a number of years. there are countries which are making progress towards achieving them and which could meet them before the dates prescribed by the commission are reached. however, there has been great reluctance to accept them by many countries. this parliament, both in the committee on industry and in the committee on the environment, despite the amendments which have been tabled - and there have been many - proposing indicative targets, has approved by a very large majority that the targets should be binding. in the committee on industry, in particular, it was by 38 votes to 5. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we are, of course, expecting something in return from the council: that it responds by accepting another set of amendments proposed by parliament and by accepting the commission's proposal for a directive with that reservation of objectives. we also propose to the council a compromise in amendment no 53, which provides that member states may, for justified reasons, delay the implementation of the directive with a two-year derogation for one time. another matter i want to deal with does not concern this directive but indirectly affects the application of mixtures. this is directive 98/70/ec on the quality of petrol. the commission is aware that this directive must be adapted to blends, since it cannot be applied to blends in the same way as to other petroleum fuels. in countries with warm summers, volatility increases and therefore the vapour pressure will have to be increased. i myself had tabled an amendment in this direction. for legal reasons i have withdrawn the second part of the proposal, but i would like to emphasize that the commission should propose an amendment to directive 98/70/ec to allow mixtures to have a volatility of 70 kpa (kilopascal) in countries with warm summers, as is the case and is permitted in countries with arctic summers. another issue which has arisen in the course of the debate on the amendments has been the proposal to introduce other fuels in the directive. this is not its object. however, there are a number of amendments in the recitals which can be accepted, in the sense that these alternative fuels must be taken into account. we do support the amendments which seek to include biohydrogen in the scope of this directive. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of biofuels. standards for all biofuels need to be established. finally, i would like to say that this is a directive which is designed to replace biofuels. it is not a directive with an environmental end-goal but it has a significant environmental impact. some say there are other, cheaper ways to reduce co2 emissions. there are undoubtedly some, but the directive can be another synergy. it also gives rise to other benefits within the world of employment and agriculture. all i ask is that the council accepts the commission proposal and the parliament's proposal and that the directive is adopted, because biofuel producers need a stable framework for production.
the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. - mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate mrs ayuso on her excellent work. as you know, the objective of this directive in the field of taxation is to establish a community framework enabling member states to apply a differentiated tax regime in favour of biofuels. focusing on the content of the european commission's directive, it proposes a series of measures which, taken as a whole, are balanced and well structured. i am, however, in favour of allowing each member state the maximum freedom to set the level of excise duty reduction, that is to say to promote this type of fuel and not to set a minimum rate of taxation. i think that each country in the european union will try in the coming years to achieve the reduction in co2 emissions that we have set for the year 2020 under the kyoto protocol and, depending on their circumstances, some will put more emphasis on the use of biofuels and others on wind power, etc. for this reason, i think it is essential to give this directive greater flexibility. moreover, it goes without saying that each member state is sovereign to decide in its own case to what extent it compensates for the loss of revenue via excise duties if it reduces its co2 emissions thereby. in the same vein, i fear that this is the only way to make this council proposal succeed, where, as you know, there is a great deal of division on this subject. in relation to the policy of information and interinstitutional transparency in general, i am a strong supporter - particularly in matters relating to the environment, which seem to be of a high sensitivity and which are doubly important - of everyone being informed in good time of the development of the various programmes.
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have two important proposals on the agenda today, which deal with sensitive issues for the european union. the promotion of biofuels contributes to security of supply as one of the few possible measures we have for the transport sector. in addition, the introduction of biofuels is also one of the few possibilities for reducing our dependence on oil and co2 emissions in this sector. it must be said that rural development presents another perspective which is reinforced with a view to enlargement. i shall refer to the two proposals in this connection. i would first like to mention the proposal on the promotion of biofuels for transport, which is tabled by mrs ayuso, whom i would like to congratulate very sincerely on the excellent work she has done. the fact that five committees have been involved in the examination of this proposal for a directive clearly indicates the inherently multifunctional nature of biofuels. the status of the matter under discussion is as follows: the council has repeatedly discussed these initiatives, both in the energy council and in the ecofin council. the most important problem, as the rapporteur, mrs ayuso, has already pointed out, is whether the objectives should be indicative or, on the contrary, mandatory. in view of the position of most of the member states and the need - which i believe is absolutely crucial - to develop a stable system within a stable framework, mainly from the fiscal point of view, to promote the use of biofuels, the commission could accept that a solution similar to that proposed by the directive on electricity from renewable sources should be applied to biofuels. the commission will be able to propose the reintroduction of mandatory targets if the member states fail to meet the indicative targets in a reasonable way. there are now two amendments, nos 68 and 69, which have been signed by various rapporteurs or alternate rapporteurs, and i say that i can accept them on behalf of the commission, because they would bring parliament's and the council's positions clearly closer together. i would also like to say that i welcome all the amendments which give priority to the environmental aspect in the case of biofuels. some of your honourable members have said that there are not that many. i want to tell you that a minimum saving of 45% of co2 emissions - someone mentioned them earlier; i am sorry, we cannot accept them - 37, 41, 44, 60 and 66 because they would impose an additional burden which we cannot bear or would suggest going too far with this proposal. the commission is aware that energy consumption in the transport sector is a complex issue. fundamental improvements in this sector will not come from one measure alone. we have put forward the proposal on biofuels together with a communication on alternative fuels. the objective is 20% alternative fuels in general, which covers a much wider field and in that sense i can accept all the amendments along those lines. however, we believe that amendments which include other fossil fuels in the provisions of this directive are outside the scope of application and so we cannot accept amendments nos 9, 13, 29 and 30 (in part). we cannot accept some amendments which, for example, exclude the use of biofuels in captive vehicle fleets or which empty the proposal of its content, as well as amendments nos 11, 17, 27, 33, 40, 48, 50, 51, 52, 56, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66 and part of no 19. we need to make a decision on energy supply in transport, we cannot delay any longer the start of work to reduce our dependence on oil. advocacy campaigns and declarations of goodwill are useful but not enough to change the energy situation in europe. our proposal to promote biofuels will open up a new market for renewable energy technologies and clarify your strategic decision to be able to exploit their potential. i would also say that in connection with the amendment of directive 98/70/ec, which concerns the characteristics of fuels, and to take account of the problem of volatility in the warmer countries - in the southern countries of the european union - we are trying to make sure that there is some scope for this in the context of the discussion, which is now precisely in its second reading by this parliament, and of an amendment that is currently being worked on. in any case, it is obvious that this is a problem that must be tackled, because otherwise in the southern countries there would be several months a year when the use of certain biofuels, specifically ethane, would simply be impossible. today we have the opportunity to agree on a legislative provision which is indeed in some respects less ambitious than the original commission proposal, but which i believe is realistic and allows us to move forward, provided that - and i come to the second proposal - the council also accepts our proposal on exemption from excise duties on biofuels. in fact, according to the news we have received from the council, this has also been a matter of discussion. it seems that this time the ministers for economic affairs and finance are prepared to make a real effort to give a major boost to the use of biofuels. i would also like to thank the rapporteur for his work and i would stress that the information i have from the council is in the right direction and will therefore allow us to approve the package, the two measures, with non-binding objectives but simply as guidelines. i think that would be a step forward in promoting the use of biofuels. the commission can accept several of the amendments to this proposal. however, it cannot accept amendments nos 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 23, 24 and 25 because they seek to impose obligations on member states or because they are already included in existing legislation, or simply because they are superfluous or inappropriate in the context of this proposal. ladies and gentlemen, if parliament were to support the two proposals with the wording and amendments that have been put forward - specifically and most especially amendments nos 68 and 69 - it would really be a step forward and an acceleration of the expansion of the use of biofuels in the transport sector. i hope that an agreement will be reached tomorrow which will allow for approval at first reading, which would facilitate the early start of this initiative.

- report (a5-0188/2002) by mr turchi, on behalf of the committee on budgets, on the amended proposal for a european parliament and council regulation amending council regulation (ec) no 2236/95 laying down general rules for the granting of community financial aid in the field of transeuropean networks (com (2002) 134 - c5-0130/2002 - 2001/0226 (cod))
the commission is aware of the difficulties facing the community in the implementation of the transeuropean transport networks, and it is therefore in favour of the introduction of a transeuropean transport network. these projects, which fully meet the priorities of sustainable development, are among the most complex from both a technical and a financing point of view. in addition, as you have pointed out, there have also been significant delays in improving or building infrastructure connecting the union to the candidate countries. in the energy field, the recent communication on energy infrastructure identified many missing links in electricity interconnections between member states, and the barcelona council set a very ambitious target of cross-border interconnection capacity of at least 10% of the union's generation capacity by 2005. in order to support all these projects, the financial regulation for transeuropean networks currently in force allows for studies to be co-financed up to 50% and works up to 10%, the latter ceiling not to be exceeded under any circumstances. if we take stock of the application of the regulation, it is clear that the 50% rate for studies is a real incentive, whereas the 10% limit is not sufficient to launch projects and attract private investors when this is possible. in this context, and in line with the white paper on transport policy and the requests made by the gothenburg european council for increased financial support for rail projects, the proposal for a revision of the financial regulation which you are considering today aims to raise the maximum ceiling for community financial support in the framework of the transeuropean networks to 20% for cross-border rail projects crossing natural barriers or for projects to eliminate bottlenecks in the rail network, as is already possible under the current regulation for galileo-type satellite radio navigation projects. this 20% support will also be applied to cross-border infrastructure with the candidate countries in order to cope with the expected increase in traffic between these countries and those of the union. a further eur 100 million will be allocated to these projects, covering all modes of transport, with priority being given to improving safety on the routes and eliminating bottlenecks on the routes. in the energy sector, the increased rate of support will apply to the 12 priority projects identified by the commission in its recent communication on energy infrastructure, which are not always financially viable. the aim is therefore clear: to enable community financial support to play its full catalytic role, including in the project implementation phase, and to make investments in crossborder transport and energy infrastructure more attractive to private financing. on the amendments and the report itself, the commission would first of all like to thank mr turchi because the report on which he has worked maintains, or even strengthens, the scope of several aspects of our proposal. on the amendments which have been proposed, that is to say the 15 amendments, the commission is, however, obliged to reject amendment no 2 because it affects our right of initiative; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. amendment no 14 which establishes constraints falling outside the scope of the regulation, and amendment no 15 which substantially alters the nature of the commission proposal by deleting the energy part. there are other amendments which the commission can accept partially, but only partially: amendment no 3, the wording of which is confusing because the development phase of energy projects can already, under the present system, benefit from a support rate of up to 50%; the second and third paragraphs of amendment no 7 cannot be accepted because they are confused with the structural funds. the latter are multiannual programmes, which is not the case with the budget for the transeuropean networks, for which decisions are taken on an annual basis, and the same remarks apply to amendment no 12 which i mentioned a moment ago. let us not confuse the transeuropean networks with the regional development fund, mr turchi. as regards amendment no 8, i have three comments. firstly, the commission agrees to include safety aspects in article 5.3 as one of the eligibility criteria for the 20% rate. however, it cannot accept the reference to intermodality of roads and waterways. this definition is too vague and would risk opening up possibilities for financing at a higher rate, particularly for road projects, which is not one of the community's priorities, contrary to the wish expressed in this discussion by mr bradbourn. finally, i would draw your attention to the fact that the commission's proposal covers only two sectors, transport and energy. as far as telecommunications are concerned, in view of the fundamental differences between the two sectors i have just mentioned, the commission cannot accept the proposal to extend this increased rate to telecommunications at this stage. i'm going to move on to amendment 10. the commission fully supports the proposal to transform the ten-t financial committee into an advisory committee. on the other hand, we do not want to accept the amendment which proposes the presence, without voting rights, of a representative of the eib and of the representatives of the candidate countries as observers, because this is contrary to the comitology decision which binds us all. as regards amendment no 13, as with amendment no 8, the commission can accept the aspect of promoting safety, but not the rest of the amendment. finally, of the 15 amendments, all of which i have not mentioned: 1, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 11, the commission can accept all of them, with some editorial changes if necessary, because they go in the direction of strengthening the scope of our proposal and, in particular, i would like to stress that we share parliament's concern about the need, in the next financial perspective, to obtain a budget that is up to the ambitions that we all have set very high for the transeuropean transport and energy networks.

municipalities and regions are responsible for the poor implementation of the budget, firstly because it was the european institutions that took the time to adopt and define the guidelines and programmes, and secondly because we gave them a very short deadline for the use of the financial resources: two years from their budget. this deadline can hardly be met by regional and local institutions when they receive community approval of their projects with a long delay and then have to respect the rules of democratic transparency for the tendering processes of drafting projects, approving them, finding collaborators, subsequent public tendering for the award of the works of realization, etc. all this has resulted in a delay of more than two years in the start of work, as the commissioner has said. we should not try to erase the community policy directed at the regions of the union, but rather increase it in order to correct territorial imbalances and, above all, we should listen more to these infrastructure bodies, not transfer our own delay in planning and deciding to them, put ourselves in their place and in their difficulty to bring their projects to a successful conclusion and help them.

- question no 54 by ewa hedkvist petersen (h-0487/02): the council has not yet adopted the common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer. subject: measures to ensure legal certainty in the swedish parliament, a debate on legal certainty was launched in the context of the adoption of a european arrest warrant. the existing guidelines on how member states should comply with legal certainty requirements are not precise and new clear rules are needed to make progress on legal harmonisation, as reforms may otherwise increase doubts and mistrust of the project. for example, a maximum limit should be set on the length of time a suspect can be detained before a trial. at the beginning of the year, the commission drew up a consultation paper on this issue. what concrete measures does the commission intend to take on the basis of this consultation?
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam president, the commission has published on the website of the directorate-general for justice and home affairs a consultation document on the procedural guarantees for suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings. the deadline for replies expired on 15 april 2002. after examining the replies, the commission plans to take the following concrete measures: a meeting of experts will be organised in september to discuss the various measures submitted for consultation; on the basis of these discussions, the commission plans to present, by the end of 2002, a green paper on safeguards in criminal proceedings which will probably cover the question of limiting the time-limit before trial. in addition to the work already carried out on the general aspects of procedural guarantees, the commission has begun to examine the problem of provisional detention and alternatives to such detention. this issue will be the subject of another green paper, to be presented at the end of the year or early 2003, which will examine the issue of legal certainty in relation to individuals in pre-trial detention. in accordance with the case-law of the court of human rights in strasbourg, the concept of a reasonable period before trial cannot be translated into an exact number of days, weeks, months or years, or into various periods of time fixed according to the seriousness of the offence. the european human rights bodies have approved very long terms of provisional detention, up to two and a half years. but detention will only be justified if it was deemed necessary for the pursuit of a legitimate aim. when considering whether the conditions of the european convention for the protection of human rights, in particular article 5 (3), have been met, the european court always examines and assesses the adequacy of the grounds for detention in accordance with the rules of respect for individual liberty and the presumption of innocence which underlie any detention without conviction. the framework decision on the european arrest warrant is based on the principle of mutual recognition, which also presupposes mutual trust in the criminal justice systems of the member states. in order to achieve the mutual trust and respect required for a genuine area of freedom, security and justice, the standards of protection afforded to suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings should be equivalent throughout the union. people moving abroad should have confidence in the existing rules, which should give them equivalent protection, regardless of the member state concerned, so as not to impede their free movement for fear of encountering a system which does not provide them with sufficient protection.
commission. - madam president, i entirely agree with you and would like to draw attention to the fact that the european arrest warrant must respect fundamental rights, and in particular the principles set out in article 6 of the treaty on european union, which refers to the european convention on human rights in the field of procedural guarantees. and when a person's freedom is at stake, the european convention on human rights is clear in providing for the possibility of review by means of an appeal to a judicial body. what the commission intends to do following this consultation is to ascertain whether any legislative action at european level is necessary to bring these common rules to the member states, which are contained in the european convention on human rights, closer together and thus to strengthen mutual trust between the member states, while at the same time providing guarantees of legal certainty. i hope to be able to present the conclusions of this reflection to parliament and the council at the end of this year.
question no 55 by marit paulsen (h-0493/02) subject: concentrations in the food sector the european food industry is currently experiencing a clear wave of business mergers, with a small number of consumer product chains acquiring increasingly large market shares. however, too close cooperation - mainly in purchasing - between these large groups poses a threat to free competition and consumer choice. in addition, regional products and small producers are at high risk of being excluded from the market because they are not able to supply the huge volumes required by large-scale distribution. has the commission had the opportunity to look at the mergers of consumer goods distribution companies in europe? if so, what are its conclusions in the face of the threat to freedom of choice and the diversity of european food products? if not, does it not consider that the situation should be examined as soon as possible?
commission. – the honourable member is right in pointing out that the last few years have witnessed a number of concentrations between large retail chains in europe and in that respect the commission has had to review among others such transactions as rewe/meinl, carrefour/promodes and ahold/superdiplo. the commission will generally review parties' positions by distinguishing the different product groups and distribution channels. in the carrefour/promodes and rewe/meinl cases, for example, the commission has observed that, in those instances where the share of a particular client in the turnover of a particular supplier reaches beyond a certain level, risks that the supplier might go out of business as a result of losing this particular client will appear. the commission will therefore examine whether the respective and combined shares of the parties in the turnover of their suppliers reach critical thresholds. where suppliers face a limited number of powerful clients, each representing a significant share of their turnover, the risk of the creation of a collective dominant position on the part of purchasers might arise. in the carrefour/promodes decision the commission assessed this risk on the french market, but concluded that the criteria necessary to find a collective dominant position had not been met. another factor taken into account in assessing market power on the purchasing market is the possible vertical integration into production on the part of a retail chain or its strategic use of own brands. the analysis of the purchasing market will be particularly relevant in those cases where the merged entity would be a major player on the retail market. as may be apparent from what i have just said, the commission remains sensitive to the issue of purchasing power on the part of retail chains.
commission. – i well understand the concerns of the honourable member who has just spoken and his fear that diversity in the foodstuffs sector might be reduced. i should like to repeat that the commission has reviewed the latest developments in that area. indeed this is reflected in the latest decisions which the commission has taken in the carrefour/promodes case, about which i spoke earlier. while the commission currently has no official position on possible future developments in that sector, it wishes to underline that it will take the same care as before to analyse and decide on the potential impact of any future concentration in the relevant area. i should like to assure mrs paulsen and mr schmid, her replacement, that the commission will keep this matter under active review. everything depends on first making a correct analysis. if circumstances are such that the commission should take a legal position in this area, i assure mrs paulsen and mr schmid that it will not hesitate to do so.
commission. – i would like to state clearly that the commission is of the view that the basle ii negotiations concern the capital adequacy of banks and not of retail chains whether or not they are well capitalised. basle ii concerns the capital base of banks. small and medium-sized enterprises also enter into the basle discussion because, particularly in germany, they are financed with long-term credits. these credits are valued by banks in a different way from short-term credits and this is why the whole issue of small and medium-sized enterprises enters into the basle discussion. this is perhaps neither the time nor the place to discuss the ins and outs of the basle proceedings, although i remain at the disposition of the honourable member to go into detail into this area. i would like to assure members of parliament that the whole basle ii discussion takes the position of small and medium-sized enterprises fully into account. in these discussions we are working towards a satisfactory solution which will take adequate account of the interests of small and medium-sized enterprises. to that extent i believe that the honourable member will have no need to worry.

- question no 59 by mr margrietus j. van den berg (h-0508/02): subject: trips agreement and access to medicines could the commission indicate what progress has been made in the wto to meet the doha commitments and ensure that the trips agreement does not impede access to medicines at reasonable prices in countries with little or no production capacity in the pharmaceutical sector? can the commission confirm that the european union will advocate a solution which ensures that wto member countries have access to medicines on terms equivalent to those set out in the doha declaration on the trips agreement and medicines? does the commission agree that an agreement authorizing export production under article 30 of the trips agreement is very clearly in keeping with the spirit of the doha agreement by giving the sole consumer country the power to decide on a licence requirement?
commission. - the question concerns intellectual property rights and access to medicines. as you know, the doha declaration on intellectual property rights and public health calls on the wto specialist council to find a rapid solution to the problems faced by wto members with insufficient or non-existent production capacity in the pharmaceutical sector or who have difficulty in making effective use of compulsory licensing. these poor countries do not have the flexibility or the capacity to negotiate with pharmaceutical companies in countries which have the possibility of issuing compulsory licences. it is therefore quite possible that they may have more difficulty than others in obtaining substantial discounts on essential medicines. we believe that a quick solution is one that would allow the situation to be remedied within the wto before the end of this year. several meetings of the wto's specialised council have recently taken place. in march, the union presented a communication which proposed two avenues. one is based on the interpretation of article 30 of the agreement on intellectual property and the other on an amendment to article 31. we were the only wto member to put forward a written document clearly stating our position. the other members intervened orally and four options were put on the table: to interpret article 30, to amend article 31, to declare a moratorium on dispute settlement and, finally, to provide for a system of derogations. a new meeting of the specialist council took place last week and we presented a new document, which arose from our reflection and our examination of each other's proposals, which proposes an amendment to article 31. we propose to add a new paragraph to this article which would provide for a clearly defined exception to a restriction imposed by this article 31 in the area of licensing the export of pharmaceutical products manufactured under compulsory licensing. we believe that as things stand, article 30, which is an alternative, allows only too limited exceptions to the rights attached to exclusive licences and that the solution we have envisaged in doha goes beyond the limits set by article 30. we must also take account of the views of our partners and propose a solution which we believe will be acceptable to most wto members in the end. an amendment to article 31 would, in this respect, have more of a future than a clarification of article 30, since no wto member has ruled out an amendment to article 31 while none and not the least have been strongly opposed to a clarification of article 30. the developing countries concerned, which are our main concern, have indicated that they are willing to consider the amendment to article 31 that we have proposed. in fact, we believe that adding a provision on intellectual property to this agreement would be a clear, legally sound and permanent solution which would not upset the current regulatory framework, namely article 31. this agreement, as amended by us, would clearly provide that a country which is unable to produce a medicinal product may ask another country to grant it a licence for export purposes. we believe that this proposal is the simplest and, in the end, the most likely to solve the problem identified in the doha declaration which has forced us to find a solution to this question. that's our position. others are speaking in geneva and we will continue, in the spirit that has guided us so far, to try to find a solution which reconciles the great principles of intellectual property on the one hand, and on the other, the possibility for the poorest countries to have access to medicines which are absolutely essential to them.
commission. - on the substance, i agree that the way you have presented the problem, mr van den berg, is correct. as i have already said, we must reconcile the main principles of intellectual property with the ability of those countries which do not have a pharmaceutical industry to obtain generic medicines from imports. we do not think that the derogation is a good idea, because it is only a temporary solution, which is, in a way, just applying a safety net to the problem while waiting for better days. i think that this is not the right way of reconciling, in the eyes of public opinion, these two imperatives which we must serve. we are more in favour of article 31 than article 30. in the case of article 31, the question of whether the country requesting the import of generics is in an emergency situation is not a question to be automatically submitted to the wto. together we can, as we did in article 6 in doha, define in a binding way what constitutes a national emergency. i would remind you that in the cases covered by article 31, the country wishing to import medicinal products will have to apply either to a developed country with production facilities and a compulsory licence or to another developing country. if the latter option is chosen, the developing country which will be responsible for supplying the generics in question will necessarily find it in the interests of the developing country. so i think that from this point of view there is no risk that the system will be too closed, which i thought you were worried about. i think that it is precisely by using article 30 that we will accumulate imperatives which will make access to medicines more difficult.
