subject: catches for the manufacture of fishmeal by the danish fleet and fishing resources in community waters it is well known that denmark enjoys a privileged position as regards catch rights in community waters, which entitle it to fish as much as france and spain combined. a large part of these rights relate to catches for fishmeal. according to commissioner franz fischler, the flour would be destined for aquaculture and would not have an impact on resources and species intended directly for human consumption. could the commission provide quantitative data on the total or partial use of this fishmeal in aquaculture? what objective data can be provided to demonstrate that these catches for industrial use do not have an influence on the status of resources intended for human consumption?
the commission. the use of fishmeal and fish oil in aquaculture has increased significantly in recent years, mainly because of the large scale of aquaculture as such. the international association of fishmeal and fish oil producers states that in 1990 10% of the fishmeal and 16% of the fish oil were still used in aquaculture. in 2000, these shares increased to 35% for fishmeal and 60% for fish oil. it is expected that this growth will continue. the danish landings for processing into fishmeal and fish oil are between 1 and 1.5 million tonnes of fish per year. the main species are sandal with 60%, sprat with about 20%, cod with about 6% and blue whiting with also about 6%. all these stocks are managed with tacs and quotas based on scientific advice from ices. ices assesses each year the state of the main economically exploited fish stocks and these assessments show that by-catches of food fish in industrial fisheries have decreased and that this has little impact on the evolution of food fish stocks. until 1996, industrial fisheries in the north sea, skagerrak and kattegat still involved herring, whiting and shellfish. in 1996 the community then introduced by-catch arrangements and a comprehensive monitoring and control system, and since then by-catches have really declined massively and there is no longer any danger to food fish. the ices also has a working group on the impact of fishing on ecosystems, and this group has also assessed the indirect impact of catching larger quantities of industrial fish on the marine food chain. it has found no evidence that catches of industrially exploited species reduce the productivity of food stocks. as regards the blue whiting fishery, ices has warned that it could result in the by-catch of larger quantities of juveniles of the same species. we have therefore already written to ices asking for scientific advice on how to avoid these by-catches in the future.

the commission. it is a rumour that denmark fishes six times as much as spain and france combined, but i think it is not very sensible to throw numbers at each other. i'll tell you what i'll do. we shall send you the relevant data in writing on the extent and the specific quantities of industrial fisheries. then you've got it all in black and white. i think that's the simplest thing. the question you raise about relative stability is a different matter altogether. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. you know that there has been a special provision until now, which goes back to the treaty of accession of spain and portugal, and that provision is due to expire at the end of this year, but you must believe me, the expiry of that provision means that the same laws apply to everyone - including spain and portugal - and therefore the same principles apply for the fixing of tacs and quotas and the same principles apply in relation to access to the waters. we shall do that, we shall see to it, and you will see it for the first time when the tacs and quotas for next year are fixed at the end of this year.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i must say that i was only responsible for this report - using a bullish simile which i do not know if the house will understand - the 'killing job', because for a year - between 1 january 2001 and 1 january 2002 - the rapporteur was mr marinho and then he had to leave, so he did all the preparatory 'work' and it was only up to me, at the final stage, to collect the amendments that had been proposed and to bring about some kind of compromise. there were some 60 amendments at the end. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. my job was just to put it together. the directive on the use of timeshare buildings was adopted in 1994 by the codecision procedure and i was the rapporteur for parliament on this directive. the directive took three years to come into force in principle, but in many countries it was postponed for a year. i am pleased to note, moreover, that the spanish supreme court recently ordered the spanish government to compensate private consumers in the community for the delay in the implementation of the directive by the spanish government. i think that is a good case law precedent which reinforces the validity of community directives. the current directive is a minimum directive. certain information obligations were laid down and the possibility was also provided for the purchaser, the contractor, to withdraw within a period of ten days and to obtain a refund of the amounts paid. but it is clear that, as a minimum directive, it would not have been able to resolve all the issues raised. in the discussion of this subject in the committee on legal affairs and the internal market over the last two years, it has been emphasized that for many community citizens the present system is causing damage and that it would therefore be desirable to complete the arsenal at our disposal. from the point of view of community law we may be faced with some difficulties. the difficulty lies in the concern that exists today in all the community institutions to save money on the regulatory instrument. we have the mandelkern report from the council, we have the commission's proposals on european governance and on improving community regulation, and we have, finally, the agreements of the seville european council, which stress the need to make progress in this area with the involvement of the european parliament. moreover, this directive has the peculiarity of entering into a field of private law, contract law and the law of real property, which is considered to be a field traditionally within the competence of the member states. so the road ahead is not an easy one. on the one hand i think it is a matter which is clearly community in nature, in that it concerns property sold in a country to community nationals and with responsibilities which may arise later, and on the other hand it is - as i have said before - a matter of private law which would normally be thought to be outside the community. the question of the possible usefulness or limitations of the legislative procedure is also raised. it has been suggested, for example, that other types of measures might be useful in this area, for example collaborative measures between member states to combat the forms of money laundering that appear in some types of timeshare companies or simply against some fraudulent schemes and the like. the report also mentions the possibility of using co-regulatory and self-regulatory procedures, for example by accrediting operators in this field, and there are a number of difficulties which are reflected in the report. the report by parliament is a compromise report. there is a comprehensive study by the commission, but it is from 1999. i think the main conclusion is that we must ask the commission to look at the matter again and to come forward with proposals, which may be legislative or non-legislative, as soon as possible. in particular, when reviewing the report adopted in committee, we found an error in paragraph 20, which referred to infringement proceedings which had already been concluded, and therefore that paragraph 20 no longer makes sense and should be deleted. and also some unnecessary repetitions which are manifest in paragraphs 6 and 7. i would propose that the house vote against those three paragraphs 6, 7 and 20. as regards the amendments tabled, there are three - amendments nos 1, 2 and 3 by mr bradbourn, mr lehne and mr mccarthy, which concern the specification of certain days - which i think are too precise for a non-legislative text. and finally, there are three amendments by mrs mccarthy which clarify certain aspects of information and responsibility, which i think are correct. i hope that the house will be able to adopt the draft report tomorrow.
commission. – mr president, first i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr medina ortega and the members of the committees on legal affairs and the internal market on the environment, public health and consumer policy for all their helpful work on this issue. i take the timeshare issue very seriously. transactions are almost exclusively cross-border and often involve very significant sums of money. it is, therefore, essential that we aim to provide a high level of protection for consumers in this field. the present eu directive has made a significant contribution to consumers' rights, establishing minimum harmonisation. however, i am well aware that a number of consumer protection problems still exist. this, in my view, is not due to the transposition of the directive, the commission has already withdrawn all the infringement procedures in relation to that – but to its application. therefore, more needs to be done. consumers can be vulnerable to several problems when they buy rights to use immovable properties on a timeshare basis. firstly, certain unscrupulous vendors and agents use aggressive marketing techniques, which either mislead or place undue influence on consumers so as to induce them to buy, often to their detriment. secondly, new practices have emerged under which timeshare deals are offered through certain packages such as club points schemes or shares in a company, which effectively circumvents the obligations stipulated by the directive. as a result, consumers miss out on access to the required level of information and on cooling-off periods. i attach great importance to your resolution. its conclusions, together with the council's conclusions and the reactions to the 1999 commission report on the implementation of the directive provide a solid basis for further action. furthermore, i am sure you will agree that we need to act immediately given the numerous complaints that our institutions have received on this issue. i believe that the more general problems could be tackled within the context of a framework directive on fair trading. further harmonisation of laws is necessary to achieve a uniform, high level of consumer protection throughout the eu. this is outlined in the follow-up communication to the green paper on consumer protection, which has just been adopted by the commission. the marketing practices which could be tackled using this approach include those based on misleading claims or failure to disclose material information to consumers prior to the conclusion of the contract, those involving harassment, coercion or intimidatory techniques and those relating to after-sales customer assistance. in addition, in order to address the most urgent problems, we should establish links with leading associations and members of the timeshare industry in order to make self-regulation more effective. the timeshare codes of conduct could be used to raise standards and to address those unfair and opaque practices not caught by the directive. i have recently been informed that a european trade association has taken legal action against certain holiday clubs in spain for violation of spanish timeshare law. the association in question has provided information to the public authorities on dishonest practices, which have subsequently been investigated. several holiday club companies have been closed within the past few weeks and their principals have been arrested as part of the investigation. thus a more systematic cooperation between the industry and the relevant contact points in the member states could and should be encouraged. such cooperation should aim to identify companies with which problems have arisen and against which enforcement action can be taken. the commission will therefore draw on the experience of the european centres, the euro-guichets, and work with the newly established clearing houses of the european extra-judicial network and with the international marketing supervision network to address current outstanding problems and encourage them to cooperate closely with the industry. specifically, the points that have been raised by mrs wallis in relation to access to justice are of significance and the cross-border nature of that problem is highlighted by her, in my opinion rightly. our proposal contained in the follow-up paper on fair trading specifically refers to the need for law enforcement cooperation among member states. in our consultation process with member states and others, there was a very strong response to that part of the paper focusing on enforcement cooperation. with this in view, it is the intention of the commission to bring forward a specific proposal in relation to that particular issue by the end of this year or the beginning of next year. furthermore issues such as reciprocal injunctive powers between member states would also, in my view, be of significance and could be effective. in effect, eu-wide contract and consumer law needs to be looked at, which we are doing in my dg at the moment, as i am sure many of you are aware, and we will bring forward proposals in that area also in due course i hope sooner rather than later. these are our plans but if, after taking action as i have outlined, problems still remain that cannot be solved by these actions, i will not hesitate to review the timeshare directive as indicated in the consumer policy strategy recently adopted by the commission.

- question no 5 by mr hyland (h-0379/02) subject: wto and imports from the poorest countries in the world the eu recently decided to grant unlimited duty-free access to eu markets for imports from the 48 poorest countries in the world, including agricultural products. this is a first and it was hoped that other developed countries would follow the eu's example. would the council state what the current situation is with regard to this decision, and whether other developed countries are following the eu's example?
the council. - mr president, the eu hosted the un conference on the least developed countries in brussels in may 2001. the conference adopted a declaration and an action programme confirming its intention to improve preferential access to markets for the least developed countries, working towards the objective of granting duty-free and quota-free access to the markets of the developed countries for all products from the least developed countries. the general affairs council adopted its everything but arms initiative on 26 february last year and, in preparation for the wto ministerial meeting in doha in november last year, the eu called on other developed countries to implement similar initiatives, thus fulfilling the multinational commitment to grant duty-free access to products from less developed countries, the commitment contained in the wto action plan adopted in singapore in 1996. the un secretary-general, kofi annan, has also urged them to do so. at the moment, however, none of the measures taken by the major powers can be compared in any way to the everything but arms initiative. the new zealand initiative is the closest thing to the eu's example. canada, japan and the united states have also made progress, but they are still lagging behind the initiative taken by the eu. a recent study by unctad examines the impact of the proposal. the study concludes that all the least developed countries will benefit from the proposal. however, the benefits would be far greater if the other four-party participants, canada, japan and the united states, followed the eu's example. at present, half of these countries' exports are subject to customs duties in canada, japan and the united states. the g8 meeting the other day in alberta, canada, provided a new opportunity to discuss these questions. the meeting focused on africa, where most of these poor countries are located. the matter is therefore evolving and the european union can be proud that we have taken the strongest initiative on this matter at global level.
the council. - mr president, the questioner is right that it is important to provide this support, but as regards the more detailed part of the question, it is for the commission to answer. so i would urge that the commission be consulted.
- question no 7 by mr sterckx (h-0384/02): subject: inadequacy of the 'free regime' in the event of a serious obstacle to the free movement of goods the rail freight transport between france and the united kingdom via the channel tunnel has been severely disrupted since november 2001. the commission has taken all the measures authorised under the 'fresh regulation' council regulation (ec) no 2679/98, oj l 337, 12.12.1998. in the present situation, the powers conferred on the commission by this regulation are insufficient. the free movement of goods through the channel tunnel is still severely disrupted. why does the council reject the commission's proposal to extend and improve the scope of this regulation? what measures have the member states taken to implement the resolution of the internal market council of 27 september 2001?
the council. - mr president, i can inform you that it is still strawberry season in the northern member states. in the conclusions of 27 september 2001, to which mr sterckx referred, the council took note of the commission's report on the application of the regulation on the free movement of goods - the so-called 'strawberry regulation'. the commission's report included proposals for possible amendments to the regulation in order to extend its scope and speed up procedures. the report was not, however, a formal proposal from the commission to be considered by the council. the council and parliament were simply asked to take note of the report. nevertheless, the council chose to react to the commission's report by adopting formal conclusions at the single market meeting on that day. the council agreed that the regulation should be applied more dynamically by the member states and the commission in close cooperation, so as to take account of the protection of fundamental freedoms, including the right or freedom to strike. although the experience of the application of the regulation was still limited, the council welcomed some of the commission's initiatives aimed at facilitating its practical application, such as a manual on the procedures to be followed in the event of obstacles to the free movement of goods. the council remains fully committed to protecting the free movement of goods between member states. it is a key element of the internal market. the council resolution of 7 december 1998, adopted at the same time as the regulation, and the conclusions of 27 september 2001 reflect this. as regards mr sterckx's question as to what measures the member states have taken to implement the council conclusions of 27 september, it should be said that it is not the council's task to monitor what measures the member states take in this area. the council does not receive information from the member states on such measures either, and i cannot therefore answer that part of the question, which i regret.
the council. - i just want to make sure that i am right in thinking that it is the commission that has to ensure that such rules are respected. i do not wish to minimize the problem raised by mr sterckx in any way. we can imagine the financial losses that this could cause, and the people concerned cannot understand that when there are eu rules to ensure their disposal. so i do not want to minimize it and i would like to take it to the council, but it has to be the commission that does the inspection.

- doc. a5-0216/2002 by mr wieland, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on machinery and amending directive 95/16/ec (com (2000) 899 - c5-0035/2001 - 2001/0004 (cod)).
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social partners are able to take part in the negotiations. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the european strategy on safety and health at work 2002-2006 was recently presented. if we wanted to highlight three features of it, i think i would be right to speak of the need for strong awareness-raising, the promotion of a culture of prevention, as well as the need to promote specific programmes and actions in small and mediumsized enterprises and the consideration of the demographic reality in which this strategy is to be applied. a fourth feature is the horizontalisation of occupational health policies. this has a lot to do with the subject of the debate we are debating. the machinery directive applies to virtually all machines, fixed or mobile, for commercial, industrial or private use in the european union. as rapporteur, i was keen to know the views of employers, trade unions, economic and social agents, technical and legal advisers and the university. the amendments by the committee on employment, with the contribution of the social dialogue, were intended to avoid the risk of weakening the provisions on health and safety protection, to respond to the need to simplify certain clauses and provisions in order to make the protection rules clearer and to take account of the desirability of referring them to other community provisions, in particular to framework directive 89/391/eec. the commission has also proposed that the directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens be amended to include the following: the responsibility of those who modify or cause to be modified a machine is also clearly defined. safe machinery and equipment plus prevention - that is, awareness raising, a culture of prevention - will mean less risk of the risk becoming an accident and therefore better jobs, in line with the lisbon european council strategy. the rapporteur said that these measures would ensure the safety of the products. let me add that it is also the responsibility of workers in particular and citizens in general. the product policy presupposes and requires the workers' policy.
commission. – mr president, i would like to welcome the conclusion of the first reading of the revision of the machinery directive and i would especially like to thank the rapporteur, mr wieland, and the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. the aim of the proposal is, as has been stressed by the speakers, to enhance legal certainty by clarifying the directive's scope and meaning and by removing ambiguities that have led to different interpretations. at the same time the highest possible level of health protection and consumer safety should be ensured. the european mechanical engineering sector which is subject to the machinery directive contains a very large range of products: machines, mechanical appliances and components. in 1998 it produced goods to the value of eur 300 billion. it employs over 2.2 million highly skilled people in the 15 member states. the sector's production volume exceeds japan's and rivals that of the united states of america. the european union is the world's largest exporter of machines and mechanical equipment, ahead of the usa and japan. based on the experience of the past 12 years, the proposal reflects the commission's determination to cut red tape whilst facilitating compliance with european union legislation, taking due account of the subsidiarity and proportionality principles. it is also fully in line with the recommendations of expert groups acting within the framework of better regulation of the internal market. the proposal and its implications have been extensively discussed with a very wide audience of stakeholders. i would like to emphasise that the aim of the proposal is to improve areas that have proved to cause difficulties in terms of application. many of the numerous proposed amendments improve the commission proposal. some could be included in a revised proposal as they stand, whilst others could be retained in part, or in principle. some proposed amendments concern detailed, highly technical items and do not add any value and will therefore not be part of a revised proposal. still others are outside the scope we perceive as the correct scope for the machinery directive. concerning amendment no 5 on fairground equipment, the commission is aware of the question and we are prepared to launch a study into the matter. we are currently preparing a commission communication on the functioning of the new approach to be published this autumn. the new approach to technical harmonisation and standardisation provides for the free movement of goods and a high level of health, consumer and environmental protection. we do not want to interfere in the general debate on commitology. we want to concentrate on the practical application of the current directive. we therefore prefer to hold back the discussion of subjects that are common to the around 20 new-approach directives until the future communication that i have already mentioned, in order to have a coherent approach. practical application of the current machinery directive has shown a need for a regulatory committee procedure in order to resolve technical matters that do not infringe the democratic control by the european parliament. we also share the principle that there is a need to improve the complete texts of amended directives, as suggested in amendment no 13. however, this amendment goes beyond the scope of the machinery directive. therefore, for legal reasons, we cannot accept this amendment. in practice, consolidated texts of amended directives are often presented on the commission website, as will be the case for the amended lifts directive. consequently, the commission position on amendments is as follows. amendments that the commission could accept in full, or in part, are amendments nos 2, 3, 14 to 18, 23, 27, 42, 45, 47, 49, 56, 57, 59, 63, 66, 69, 72, 74 to 76 and 80. amendments that the commission could accept in principle are amendments nos 22, 30, 41, 51, 61, 62 and 64. finally the commission cannot accept all other amendments: amendments nos 1, 4 to 13, 19 to 21, 24 to 26, 28, 29, 31 to 40, 44, 48, 50, 55, 58, 60, 65, 67, 70, 71, 73, 77 to 79, 82 and 83.

- doc. a5-0189/2002 by mr ceyhun, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council decision on combating racism and xenophobia (com (2001) 664 - c5-0689/2001 - 2001/0270 (cns)). mr ceyhun, the rapporteur, is absent and will be replaced by mr evans.
the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the framework decision on racism and xenophobia since the beginning of the year. the rapporteur stresses that freedom of expression in a democratic state governed by the rule of law has its limits and, above all, cannot be used as a justification for violating the rights of others or for committing criminal activities. unfortunately, in many parts of europe we are still confronted with racist and xenophobic manifestations which are unacceptable in our democratic societies. an integrated approach including both preventive and punitive measures is essential to combat this phenomenon effectively. the criminal law measures, such as those envisaged in the commission proposal, are one element of this approach. but on the other hand, the commission has always stressed that this is a cultural fight and has therefore already taken several awareness-raising measures to combat racism and xenophobia in areas such as employment, immigration, asylum policy and the education system. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. the commission is flexible as regards additional aggravating circumstances. however, it might be more appropriate here to refer to material addressed to a large number of people, since racist material distributed by a single person (e.g. manual distribution of racist propaganda) may also be intended for a large number of people. amendments nos 6 and 12 (b) introduce a reference to the e-commerce directive as regards the liability of internet access providers. the provisions of the framework decision are without prejudice to any instrument of the first pillar, in particular the 'electronic commerce' directive. in this respect, it should be noted that under the 'electronic commerce' directive, member states may not impose a general obligation on service providers to monitor content, but may establish an obligation to inform the competent authorities of alleged illegal activities or information communicated by recipients. the liability of providers can therefore be established where internet access providers are actually aware that they host racist material, that is to say, that they have been brought to their attention by a judicial authority by means of a complaint, and where, however, those providers have not taken steps to remove that material. the commission has a slightly different view from the rapporteur on the criminalization of public apology for genocide and other serious crimes. the conditions imposed by amendment no 12 in this part are stricter than those laid down by the 1996 joint action, since they require that the words or behaviour in question constitute a threat, a slander or an insult and are motivated by racism or xenophobia. the joint action adopted six years ago merely required that public apologizing be done with a racist or xenophobic aim. the conditions imposed by amendment no 12 would therefore set a higher threshold for the exercise of criminal proceedings, and we therefore ask that this matter be considered by parliament. finally, i would like to stress that our proposal is clear as regards the definition and characterization of crime, because we are always referring to concrete acts and not to opinions. the proposal for a framework decision cannot be interpreted as prejudicing fundamental rights, in particular freedom of expression and the principles recognised by the european convention on human rights in articles 10 and 11 thereof and by the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. however, in european law, as in the law of each of the member states of the european union, a proper balance must be ensured. as provided for in article 10 (2) of the european convention, the exercise of these freedoms, in particular freedom of expression, may and must be balanced against the defence of public order, the prevention of crime and the protection of the honour or rights of others. in this context, we are not proposing to create a thought police, we are simply asking that the union as a whole be faithful to the values which have been our common heritage since the european convention on human rights. and in this sense, the clear political message should be that racist and xenophobic crimes are to be fought vigorously and equally throughout the european union. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's competition policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i agree with those views and i express my agreement with that positive assessment. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. a positive assessment does not prevent suggestions for partial reforms or adaptations to practical needs, but in any case these reforms will be limited. the text of regulation (eec) no 4064/89 itself provides that certain aspects must be reviewed after ten years from its entry into force. at the end of that period, the commission sent a green paper suggesting that not only the points provided for in the regulation be examined, but also all those which would allow the text to be updated. this is a very positive initiative and the commission should be congratulated on it. perhaps the most important points in this green paper to which we refer relate to the definition of the thresholds for a transaction to be considered to have a community dimension and, secondly, to the cases in which a concentration notified to the commission may be referred to the national authority or authorities for analysis and decision and, conversely, when a transaction notified to the national authorities may be referred jointly to the commission. in the first of these paragraphs, the commission suggests that a concentration has a community dimension when it can be notified in three or more countries, thus abolishing the complicated procedural rules contained in article 1 (3) of the regulation. some national competition authorities have expressed their views on the amendment of this paragraph or its replacement by criteria different from those of the commission. we cannot agree with those objections. the automatic attribution of powers rule proposed by the commission brings greater clarity and simplicity, promotes uniformity of assessment criteria, increases legal certainty and saves costs for businesses. we therefore support it fully. the second of the paragraphs, on the forwarding of dossiers, is more complex and the european parliament and the committee on economic and monetary affairs therefore make some suggestions. the first concerns the need for the parties to agree to the transfer of the file by the european commission to one or more national authorities. if the unified treatment has been considered more efficient and saves costs for the companies, it does not seem that by way of referral the companies can be forced to process different files against their discretion. in a second paragraph, the european parliament warns the commission of the problem that arises when such a referral can take place, when the final decision is the responsibility of political bodies and not independent authorities. it must be borne in mind that in several member states the decision is the responsibility of a political authority, as in my own country, for example, where it is ultimately the responsibility of the government. the criteria for approving or rejecting a concentration may therefore differ from those for analysing the effects on competition and its possible efficiencies. commissioner monti recently stressed in an interview published in the press in my country the pressure exerted by governments on competition cases. it is not necessary to be very keen to guess what the position of these governments may be if they themselves are the ones who take the decision. the european socialist group supports two amendments: the first concerns the need for job creation or job retention to be included among the efficiencies that can offset the effects of a concentration on competition. it is actually a translation of the principle of the 'failing company defence', which has already been applied by the commission and we believe that its reflection in the text will improve the report. i also believe that the content of the second amendment, which calls for the inclusion of not only competitors but also consumers and, where appropriate, the representatives of the workers concerned, in the merger files, will improve the report.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. - mr president, it is my duty to express the opinion of the committee on the report by mr berenguer, whom i congratulate on his work, and the commission, represented today by mr monti, on the initiative, which we also consider to be a welcome one. the committee on economic and monetary affairs has included in its report some of the conclusions of the committee on legal affairs. i would mention in particular those relating to the non-extension of the prior checking to new proposals, the simplification of deadlines or the refusal to record oral submissions which could affect legal certainty. i thank the rapporteur for his favourable opinion on these amendments and the committee responsible for the substance for its acceptance. on the other hand, there are other points on which the opinion of the committee on legal affairs has not been incorporated and which need to be reaffirmed. in particular, we do not think it would be appropriate to replace the criterion of dominance by that of a significant reduction in competition in order to authorise concentrations, or to extend the mechanism for referral by the commission to national competition authorities, or to calculate fines on the basis of turnover. we do not think it is advisable to risk legal certainty by introducing new or more innovative procedures when they are not necessary. in accordance with this approach, it is obvious that the amendments tabled by the socialist group and amendment no 5 by the group of the european united left, which go against the trend towards clarifying procedures and are notoriously imprecise, should not be accepted by the rapporteur, nor should the other two amendments, which have nothing to do with the objective of achieving a better merger control procedure. so congratulations on the initiative, and prudence in not tearing down what works well.

- the next item is the joint debate on two motions for resolutions on angola: b5-0405/2002 by mrs almeida garrett, on behalf of the ppe-de group; mrs mendiluce pereiro, lage and colom i naval, on behalf of the pse group; mrs isler béguin and mr maes, on behalf of the green group; mrs miranda, on behalf of the gue/ngl group; and mr van den bos, on behalf of the eldr group;
commission. – mr president, the commission is committed to supporting the peace process and to addressing effectively and without delay the dramatic humanitarian crisis in angola. in response to the signing of the peace agreement between the government and unita and to an appeal for assistance in addressing the humanitarian situation, the commission drew up an action plan for angola to support the peace process. the action plan identifies a financial package of eur 125m aimed at addressing the most pressing concerns at this stage, including emergency relief, food aid and food security, reintegration and resettlement of refugees and displaced persons, and de-mining operations. the commission provides substantial humanitarian support to reduce the suffering of the displaced populations in angola. the commission urges the government to take further measures to facilitate delivery of emergency relief assistance. the commission encourages the government to prioritise the extension of the assistance to the entire territory in its discussions with unita. we are conscious of the fact that the presence of land- and anti-personnel mines is an enormous obstacle in terms of humanitarian access, resettlement and rehabilitation. increased security on the ground will make it possible for the commission to implement, through specialised organisations, the substantial funding already earmarked for de-mining operations. the commission considers the demobilisation of unita and the angolan armed forces troops a vital element in the peace process and in this context is considering with other partners support for the angola demobilisation and reintegration programme. to ensure lasting peace, the government should improve the democratic conditions in angola, especially promoting improvements in the human rights situation and freedom of the press. these, together with freedom of movement, reform of constitutional and electoral laws and a proper census of the population, will be essential to allow free and fair elections to take place. continued efforts to allow unita time and space to reorganise and become a viable political force are encouraged. the commission urges both parties to consult all segments of angolan civil society, including the churches, with a view to national reconciliation and lasting peace. the commission stands ready to support the organisation of elections as soon as conditions on the ground allow. we underline that interventions to promote good governance will have high priority at all stages in the support strategy for angola. we propose to contribute in particular to the reinforcement of the judicial sector and to the reform of administration and public finances. the community’s future strategy for angola under the the commission. - mr president, as has been said by parliament, the commission is extremely concerned about the dangerous political situation and social polarization in zimbabwe. the violence and repression continue, the opposition has indeed been crushed, civil society, the independence of the press no longer exists and, of course, there is the issue of the extremely negative effects of the policy of austerity on food security and in particular on the most vulnerable sections of the population, and here i must refer in particular to the workers on large agricultural holdings. the problems are the political and social crisis, the humanitarian disaster, which is at the top of the commission's agenda, and it must be said that at the general affairs council in june, the european union also undertook to respond generously to the united nations' appeals to deal with the humanitarian crisis in zimbabwe and other countries in the region. the union also urges a review of the agricultural reform process in the light of the guidelines of the proposal contained in the united nations development programme. the humanitarian crisis has reached a very large scale. the commission has already started the process of meeting food aid requirements by allocating a total of eur 55 million to the region. the management of these funds will be carried out by the world food aid programme and by non-governmental organizations. we are certainly doing everything we can, but we know well from reports that the zimbabwean government is using the food crisis for political ends. in our contacts with the zimbabwean authorities we stressed the need to provide assistance to all those facing urgent humanitarian needs, regardless of their political beliefs, and reiterated the need for food to be distributed impartially. many members of this house have of course referred to what we have also stressed, that zimbabwe has been a food-exporting country and the current food shortages are mainly due to wrong policies and only partly to the drought. to avoid a repeat of the crisis and a worsening of the situation in the coming years, the government must urgently review its macroeconomic and sectoral policies in order to get the country back on the path of economic growth and development. the commission participated in the united nations development programme mission to zimbabwe which examined the agricultural reform and expressed the desire to support a transparent and fair reform, geared to the interests of the poorest sections of the population, and of course we underlined the role that neighbouring countries can play in lobbying, which would be particularly useful. however, to address this situation, the main priorities are to resolve the political conflict through negotiations in order to end the violence. only if the rule of law is restored will there be a chance to change the situation and solve zimbabwe's pressing problems. i would therefore like to emphasize our activities aimed at finding a political solution to the crisis, so as to reduce violence and support democracy. after so many unsuccessful attempts at mediation and the deteriorating situation in zimbabwe, we understand that there is scepticism about whether or not the initiatives can succeed. however, it is very important to give special attention to the contacts between the european union troika and the southern african development community, sadc. the troika has sought to support international initiatives to manage the crisis in zimbabwe. we should give these efforts some time before condemning them. during the troika mission the sadc partners insisted that the european union sanctions had had the opposite effect. although we do not share this view, we should seriously reconsider whether our objective is to support regional efforts to deal with the crisis in zimbabwe. the european union has imposed specific sanctions on 20 members of the ruling party through visa bans, asset freezes and suspension of bilateral ministerial contacts. the commission is also proposing that the council should adopt a decision on the introduction of a new system of penalties for the use of chemical weapons. the commission is aware of the efforts of the zimbabwean authorities to undermine the credibility of the ban. however, the advantage of extending the prohibition to other persons should be considered in relation to the problems that this could cause in the union's contacts with sadc. for these reasons, it is essential to continue supporting the community initiative for the development of southern africa and to monitor developments and to review policy towards zimbabwe after the summer holidays. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.

(es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report we are voting on tomorrow has kept us very busy in the committee on the environment over the last few months, and especially the rapporteur, mrs corbey, whom i want to congratulate, because it is not an easy dossier and she has had to work hard on it. the amendment of the packaging directive will have important consequences for the different actors involved: for public administrations, for separate collection systems, for companies producing materials and packaging, for the agri-food industry and - most importantly - for the consumer. because without the consumer's cooperation this directive will not be complied with by any country. it is clear that quantitative objectives must be set and that these must be ambitious, but it is also true that, at the same time, the objectives must be attainable. we must be aware that in some member states the objectives will be more difficult to achieve for historical reasons of lack of infrastructure, low population density or consumption patterns. we are discussing a directive which must have sufficient flexibility to allow national laws to adapt to it and, moreover, we cannot force consumers to separate waste from packaging to facilitate collection. it's something they have to do voluntarily and out of politeness. the commission's proposed recovery and recycling targets for 2006 are particularly ambitious for most member states and admittedly unattainable for some member states. however, the group of the european people's party (christian democrats) and european democrats will support the adoption of the proposed percentages, but in any case keeping the upper limits, because the proposal already provides for a possible exceeding of these limits with a permission from the commission. however, we are against the claim of specific objectives for each material, because they distort competition between materials and reduce the consumer's margin of choice. our proposal - in amendment no 45 - is a minimum of 25% for all materials, in line with the existing directive, even though we know that 25% for the plastics sector is a very difficult target to achieve. the 25% target is not going to stop it from being exceeded. in the current directive, with 15%, the recycling targets of 70 and 80% are being met in some countries, but this will nevertheless encourage free competition between materials within a free market. i personally - and i am no longer speaking on behalf of the ppe group - believe that the general objectives of recovery and recycling should be set at local level by the competent authorities, who are the ones who know best about their possibilities, their infrastructures and the habits of their consumers. the commission proposes that the targets be met by june 2006, and our proposal is that this date be postponed until 31 december of that year, because it is more practical to talk and count in calendar years and because, moreover, the deadline is very tight. i therefore also understand that the commission wants to delay the implementation of the directive until 2008. the member states will also have little time to adjust their legislation in view of the codecision procedure which will delay the adoption of the directive for some time. but i think that delay is a message that this parliament should not be giving. i do, however, support differentiated objectives and timetables for some member states such as ireland, greece and portugal, which are having very great difficulty keeping up with the proposed pace. we also believe that a prevention target is not necessary, because for environmental and economic reasons, such as the payment of the green dot, which exists in some countries like mine, the industry is already trying to reduce as much as possible the amount of material used for the manufacture of packaging. it should be noted that the volume of packaging on the market also depends on the quantity of products sold, not only on the materials used in their manufacture. we are in favour of shared responsibility, so that the manufacturer uses the optimum amount of resources to ensure that the product is properly packaged, that the consumer cooperates in the collection of waste and that municipal authorities manage the volume of waste and recover value where possible. we also believe - in amendment no 44 - that recycling and reuse can be encouraged by the member states in a variety of ways, depending on their particular circumstances and their infrastructures. we have to be flexible. the industry is already making efforts to improve the design of its products and to make them more environmentally friendly, because this is something that consumers are increasingly appreciating, and it should not be forgotten that the directive we want to amend arose at the time because of problems with the functioning of the internal market. finally, i would like to make a comment on the fact that this proposal, like the others before us, is intended to be implemented by all the member states and that the socioeconomic conditions, infrastructures, traditions and ways of life are very different from one another, and will be even more so after enlargement. the european union must therefore set minimum standards that everyone can meet and that allow those who are in a position to do so to raise the bar. when the application of the law results in exceptions and breaches, it is because something is not working.
(es) mr president, first of all, like other colleagues, i would like to thank the rapporteur for the attention she has paid to each of our amendments and for the acceptance of some of them. i agree with the commissioner that the 1994 directive has some positive aspects, in that to a greater or lesser extent all member states distribute waste at source, recover, recycle and reuse waste. i think it has those effects, although there are important differences in each of the member states. i also agree with the rapporteur that in this as in other aspects of environmental policy, it would be necessary, with regulations, directives and decisions, to simplify and consolidate legislation. there are perhaps two issues which are more controversial between each of the different groups: the first concerns the concentration levels of lead, cadmium, mercury and chromium present in packaging and the second is the percentage of recycling and recovery in each of the proposed materials. i think that in the end it may be necessary to go into the more stringent aspects of these two issues, in order to be able to reach a possible compromise with a high level in the directive. there is also a concern that we share with the rapporteur, namely that of the marketing of recycled products, which is very difficult, and i think, like the rapporteur, that public administrations should have the possibility of contracting recycled products. i shall end, mr president, with what i consider to be the most important point on this subject: prevention. consumers must be involved in prevention. experience shows that consumers, if they are properly informed, are duly involved in this matter. for its part, as we saw in johannesburg, producers are responsible for using materials that produce little waste, they must take into account greenhouse gas emissions, landfills and the protection of scarce natural resources.
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. i should like to begin by thanking you very warmly for the very active discussion of the commission's proposal. i should like to comment on the main amendments which have been discussed here and which are to be voted on tomorrow. the commission's position is as follows: the commission is still in favour of an ambitious timetable for achieving the objectives, in terms of the timing, i.e. the postponement of the deadline for achieving the objectives. it can, however, accept a limited shift in principle. the commission's proposals for the objectives should remain largely unchanged. they are based on a cost-benefit analysis of the proposals. in particular, a cost-benefit analysis cannot justify an increase in the minimum material recovery target from 55% to 65%. the commission therefore rejects this. it also refuses to reduce the targets for glass, paper and metals from 60%, 55% or 50% to 25%. these materials can be recycled at low cost and with high environmental benefits. we believe that these material-specific objectives are also necessary in the interests of legislative clarity and investment security for recycling companies. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the maximum recycling targets are met. this may lead to increasing difficulties in selling collected materials, especially in countries that have been late in implementing their material recovery programmes. the commission's proposal for a directive on the prevention of waste from landfills and the disposal of waste from landfills is a good one. however, this question needs to be further examined in the light of the criteria on which the avoidance should be based, whether on environmental impact or weight. the introduction of a quantitative avoidance target of -10% cannot be supported by the commission because it is not clear how this target should be implemented and what the costs would be, what the benefits would be. it cannot be excluded that the overall environmental impact of such a measure would be negative, especially if the measure would merely result in an increased use of lightweight packaging such as plastic. the obligation to minimise environmental impact in the choice of packaging based on life cycle concepts can be accepted in principle as proposed, although such an approach may require further development. such an approach should also be developed more in the context of the basic requirements of the directive. i would like to thank the rapporteur and the co-rapporteur and the committee as a whole for their work. the commission can accept 6 amendments in full, 6 in part and 15 in principle. a list of the applications concerned was sent to the bureau. see the annex. thank you for your attention.

- question no 35 by mrs francisca sauquillo pérez del arco (h-0541/02): what is the commission's position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer? subject: meda special line for immigration the information received during the meeting between mr patten, commissioner, and mr youssoufi, prime minister of morocco, on 27 june last shows that the commission has no doubt about the importance of the problem of illegal immigration. does the commission intend to devote a specific line of the meda programme to immigration? is there a concrete plan? is there a project in this sense that focuses on immigrant women?
commission. – mr president, the commission pursues a global and balanced approach to immigration from morocco. given the importance of the subject, migration is one of the five priorities of the country strategy paper covering the period 2002 to 2006 for financial cooperation with morocco. it is also covered by the association agreement between the ec and morocco. our approach to migration is comprehensive. attention is paid both to legal and illegal migration and to the socio-economic dimension. this comprehensive approach is also reflected in our meda programming. within this framework we will aim to help the moroccan authorities to better organise legal migration. a project to set up a migration centre is currently being prepared. morocco and the ec have also agreed to cooperate in preventing and combating illegal migration. as a first step, a border management programme will help the moroccan authorities to establish greater border security and to fight trafficking in human beings. this programme, which is worth about eur 40 million, will be committed in 2003. furthermore, we are addressing the socio-economic causes of migration, in particular in the northern provinces of morocco, which account for about 35% of total emigration from that country. this region also benefited from substantial meda funding and another eur 70 million are programmed for socio-economic development in 2004. the majority of the existing projects in the northern provinces help improve the economic situation of migrant as well as non-migrant women, in particular through basic education for girls in rural areas, maternal and child health services, promotion of productive activities for women and provision of basic infrastructures. in addition to meda, the commission is financing projects under the budget line 'cooperation with third countries in the area of migration'. eur 3.3 million have been committed for projects in morocco, in particular in the areas of co-development, intergovernmental migration dialogue and the fight against illegal immigration.
- mr president, i just want to thank the commissioner for the information he has given me and to say that - in the spirit of the codevelopment he has mentioned, which is what can solve the problem of emigration - i will follow up in great detail all these projects and programmes which he has put forward precisely in the whole area of north africa, northern morocco, which i consider to be of great importance in order to prevent emigration.
commission. – i should like to make three brief points in response to that. firstly, it is manifestly the case that one of the best ways of preventing illegal migration is by promoting economic and social development. i have no doubt about that. secondly, morocco and other countries face real problems, given that they are themselves the targets of illegal migration from the south and often find themselves the route through which illegal migrants pass on the way to europe. we must help them deal with that problem. thirdly, obviously it would help morocco if we were to be able to move from informal discussions to formal negotiations about a readmission agreement. we recognise that morocco has some concerns, which we hope can be satisfied, so that we can move on to that sort of formal agreement as soon as reasonable. we sympathise with the problems that morocco has to face; we want to help morocco deal with those economic and social problems, and we support the efforts it has made, not least in the area of gender.
question no 36 by emilia franziska müller (h-0570/02) subject: easing of the ban on the use of animal meal in animal feed what does the commission intend to do to prevent old stocks of animal meal from ending up in the animal food chain and thus in the human food chain? what steps has the commission taken to ensure that validated and safe testing procedures are in place as soon as possible to detect the presence of animal meal in animal feed and the presence of hazardous substances in such feed? how does the commission intend to ensure that, if the ban on feeding these animal flours to animals is relaxed, any risk to consumers linked to old flour stocks and the presence of risk material in these flours is excluded?
commission. – it is important that i make it absolutely clear that the primary consideration in the imposition of the ban on meat-and-bone meal is public health. it is also the protection of animals, but essentially the scientific evidence available to us shows that the transmission of bse disease to animals is through the consumption of meat-and-bone meal. ultimately that would put at risk humans eating the meat. that is why we put legislation in place to remove this specified risk material from the food chain. so there are two blocks. the first is the question of meat-and-bone meal. as i said, the fundamental consideration in putting in place the ban on meat-and-bone meal is public health and the protection of animals. however, as you probably know, this is a controversial issue. some meps and others take the view that the ban is too extensive and should be revised. i do not agree, because i believe that it is by no means clear from the tests undertaken and the research done at the instigation of the commission in member states, particularly the work being undertaken by the food and veterinary office, that the controls in place in respect of meat-and-bone meal are sufficiently secure. the need for these controls arises in circumstances where there might be a relaxation of the ban on meat-and-bone meal, but not for feeding to ruminants. there can never be a relaxation of the ban on meat-and-bone meal for ruminants. it might be relaxed for pigs and poultry, which cannot contract bse and therefore the consumption of meat-and-bone meal is not a danger to them. the problem is that if the rule on the feeding meat-and-bone meal to poultry, for instance, is relaxed, there is a risk that meat-and-bone meal intended to be fed to poultry or pigs might ultimately reach ruminants, creating the very danger that we are trying to obviate. therefore i do not see the ban on meat-and-bone meal being relaxed in the short term. however, this can be reviewed in the context of the tse regulation, in particular chapter 4, where an amendment can be made by comitology. i indicated to parliament when discussing the tse regulation on a previous occasion that, although this amendment can take place by comitology, i have given an undertaking that i will come back to parliament and, even though it is not strictly required under the legislation, discuss with parliament what is the best way forward. i want to make it absolutely clear to mrs müller that cost is not the consideration. i am sorry if you have been led to that conclusion because i have not made myself clear. the primary considerations are the protection of animals and public health and the ban can never be relaxed for the purposes i have identified unless we can be absolutely sure that the controls in place in member states do not create the risk instead of obviating it.

question no 39 by mr michl ebner (h-0549/02) subject: pilot projects and competition rules the italian authorities have not yet awarded the contract for the construction of the brenner motorway (a22) between modena and the brenner, the commission having expressed reservations. apart from the measures which are generally necessary to combat distortions of competition, a thorough examination of the matter should enable the commission and the commissioner responsible to conclude that this is not a normal procedure but a pilot project. is it not conceivable and would it not be in the eu's overriding interest to promote and support a pilot project in a sensitive region, limited to the duration of the contract and aimed at financing the railway by road, instead of hindering it by distorting competition?
commission. – i have discussed this matter on various occasions with minister buttiglione and also with some members of this parliament. may i add that this concerns an extension for quite a long time – about 33 years – and thus this project falls under the rules of public procurement and thus competition must play a role in the award of the contracts. after all, competition means that prices will be lower than would otherwise have been the case and also that advantages will accrue to, i assume, the italian public or at least the italian state and therefore indirectly to the italian public. therefore we should all be in favour of more competition in the award of such immense contracts. the fact that there is a possible cross-subsidisation in favour of rail transport is an aspect which is perfectly defensible. therefore, when the terms of the contract that is to be awarded are framed and formulated, that condition will have to be included in the contract to be awarded. anybody who wants to obtain that contract will have to satisfy that condition. there is nothing wrong with that. the commission firmly believes that public contracts must be awarded subject to the rules on public procurements and they basically amount to the fact that competition must be allowed. otherwise we open the door again to awarding contracts in an underhanded fashion and it will be the public who will suffer. i am sure no one in this house wants that and, therefore, the commission is right to follow this line.
commission. – mr president, the commission does not have the knowledge to enter into the details of any public contract and moreover that is not part of the commission's role or responsibility. we must leave it to the awarding authority, which it is assumed is the italian state or part of the italian state, perhaps provincial authorities, to formulate a contract. the commission's only responsibility is to see to it that, whatever the nature of the contract, whatever it may say about, for instance, new technical solutions or cross-subsidisation, competition is allowed and other economic actors have the chance to bid for the contract. if the present contractor were allowed to continue his concession until the year 2035, there would be no competition and that would damage the true interests of the italian people.

- question no 40 by mr paul rübig (h-0579/02): subject: non-recognition of european standards for solar thermal collectors and systems uniform en standards for the verification of solar thermal products have been in force for about a year. however, france and spain only grant public subsidies for the promotion of solar energy to solar panels and systems manufactured by foreign producers if they have also been tested in accordance with the national testing standards and procedures in force, even if en test certificates have already been issued. the national tests do not correspond exactly to the en standards. in addition, the double testing procedure entails considerable costs, bureaucratic obstacles and additional time losses. test certificates issued by approved institutes in other eu countries are not recognised. this makes market access much more difficult and puts firms from other member states at a significant disadvantage in competition with national producers. could the commission give its opinion on the situation described and what measures it intends to take to remedy it?
commission. – the commission would like to stress that solar thermal collectors and systems are not regulated at community level. the en standards applying to these products are voluntary standards. any national regulations that require compliance with national standards and testing procedures if subsidies are to be granted must be assessed in the light of articles 28-30 of the treaty. it follows from these articles, as interpreted by the court of justice, that the principle of mutual recognition applies not only to technical manufacturing specifications, but also to any testing procedures to which products may have been subjected in another member state of the european union or in a state that is a signatory to the agreement on the european economic area. this principle also applies to any certificates issued for products following these testing procedures. here i refer to the judgment of 17 december 1981, concerning biological products. there is another judgment dated 28 january 1986 concerning type approval for woodworking machines. then there is the judgment of 11 may 1989 known as the bouchara judgment. the jurisprudence is consistent and clear. this means that member states may not needlessly require technical or chemical analyses or tests if the same analyses or tests have already been carried out in another member state and the results are available or may be obtained on demand. on the basis of the information which the honourable member has provided, the commission will launch an enquiry into this matter and, if necessary, will initiate proceedings against the states in question under article 226 of the treaty. should an infringement be established, the commission would also examine what conclusions should be drawn in the light of articles 87 and 88 of the treaty.
commission. – i hear that mr rübig is pleased with the attitude of the commission. that is a good thing. once again, the essence of this problem is mutual recognition. the jurisprudence is completely clear and consistent. the commission will initiate an investigation of these cases which have been brought to its attention by mr rübig. if necessary, the commission will initiate proceedings.

- question no 46 by mr jonas sjöstedt (h-0543/02): subject: future treaties of accession for the new member states if the irish voters were to vote against the treaty of nice again, the provisions of the treaty of nice concerning the distribution of seats in the european parliament and the weighting of votes in the council would become obsolete. if that were the case, could the european union not proceed as it did at the time of the accession of finland, sweden and austria, by conducting separate negotiations with each of the applicant countries with a view to agreeing, in the respective accession treaties, on the number of seats in the parliament and the weighting of votes in the council? the treaty of nice should then no longer serve as a basis for the accession of the new member states. does the commission agree that such a procedure is appropriate in the context of enlargement of the union in the event that the irish people again reject the treaty of nice?
the commission is not prepared to accept this. mr president, the commission does not consider it appropriate to speculate on the procedure to be followed in the hypothetical event that the treaty of nice is not ratified. as you know, the common objective of the european institutions is to achieve the ratification of the treaty of nice. this was most recently clearly expressed at the seville european council in june 2002. the need to ratify the treaty of nice arises from the fact that without it it will be very difficult to complete the enlargement process on the scheduled dates. the commission would recall that the seville european council in june 2002 welcomed the irish government's determination to achieve ratification of the treaty of nice in ireland. the subject was discussed at the foreign ministers' meeting in denmark this weekend. it was a meeting on the subject of enlargement. it was once again the unanimous view of the member states and also of the commission that we should not interfere in the process of forming opinion in ireland by making statements about what we would do in the event that the referendum produced a second 'no' majority.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets, which are not in line with the commission's proposal. it is perfectly clear that if i were to say here that the commission is considering an alternative or that the commission has an alternative, the next thing that would happen is that the irish voters would ask: 'what is the alternative? we would like to know, because then we would not have to ratify the treaty of nice at all". so if we say there is an alternative, we're making sure that the treaty is not ratified at all. it is important that we insist on ratifying the treaty of nice, not only because it contains the technical conditions for concluding the enlargement negotiations in the institutional area, but also because it contains the political conditions which are indispensable for a number of member states to conclude this enlargement process. the reason why the simple procedure of simply writing the institutional rules into the accession treaties was not chosen in this enlargement round is precisely because most of the member states considered it necessary to make not only institutional changes but also political changes before this very decisive change in the character and the state of the european union. they are in the nice treaty, and i say to you, you must take that into account. for a number of member states, the treaty of nice can only be considered as a whole. the apparently elegant alternative - well, if we do not have it, we simply take the institutional parts and write them into the enlargement treaties - is not accepted by a whole series of member states and, as far as i know, by the majority of the european parliament.
