- question no 50 by mr esko olavi seppänen (h-0565/02) subject: experts team at the beginning of july the commission approved a comprehensive information programme which also includes a plan for the continuation and development of the 'team' network of experts. could the commission explain how these people are selected and what the amount allocated each year is to pay for their training, expenses and fees?
commission. – team europe was created by the european commission in 1989 with the aim of providing a network of independent conference speakers whose expertise covers all fields of activity of the union in all working languages. currently team has about 550 members who can participate in conferences, seminars, debates and training sessions on issues relating to the european union. they speak in their own name and not on behalf of the commission. the members of team europe are selected by the representations of the commission in each member state on the basis of criteria that include experience, in-depth knowledge of european issues, languages, media training and availability. they are organised in national groups. the members of team europe are not paid by the commission. however, they can accept expenses from the organisers of the event in which they are participating and even some appropriate payment. the commission does, however, provide them with regular training sessions. in 2002 the commission organised three training seminars in brussels specifically for members of team europe. there was a two-day seminar on the external relations of the european union in which 80 team members participated; a three-and-a-half-day seminar on enlargement in which 60 team members participated; and a two-day seminar on the future of europe, the post-nice process and the european convention, in which 103 team members participated. this training is provided in the commission, using speakers and interpreters from either the commission or the other institutions and occasionally outside speakers who do not receive payment.
question no 51 by mr bernd posselt (h-0588/02) subject: visa exemption for the former yugoslav republic of macedonia does the commission intend to take measures to exempt macedonian nationals wishing to travel to the european union from the visa requirement, especially since in reply to a similar question from the author of this question the council indicated that it would not be able to take a decision on this point, which is of such importance for the stabilization of the fyrom, if the commission did not submit a proposal to that effect?
commission. - i fully understand the honourable member's fears. however, there is a difference: romania and bulgaria are two candidate countries for membership of the european union, unlike macedonia. in any case, i acknowledge on behalf of the commission that macedonia has made considerable efforts to improve external border controls and the quality of its travel documents. i think that macedonia is even adopting visa regulations which are very close to those in force in the european union, which is an important and positive element. however, to assess the progress made by macedonia, we sent a mission of experts last june under the regional cards programme. the conclusions of this mission and the report on the regulatory framework and its application in the context of the issuing of visas and the management of macedonia's external borders will be available in october 2002. the commission will then assess the situation of macedonia in the light of this report and the criteria set out in recital 5. only then will we be able to take a decision on our initiative to revise the european union's visa regulations. so this is not a game of ping-pong, but it is imperative to follow the procedures. at the moment i am not in a position to tell you what our assessment will be after receiving the report of the panel of experts, which i will receive next month.
question no 52 by mr camilo nogueira román (h-0599/02) subject: visa requirements for immigrants to the eu from countries which have a special relationship with eu member states a considerable number of eu member states have, like portugal and spain with latin american countries, a special relationship and cultural links with countries outside the union; the european union is a major player in the world economy. how will this be dealt with following the decision of the european council in seville to revise the list of countries whose citizens will need a visa to enter the union? how will the citizens of latin american countries be treated in relation to the spanish and portuguese states?
commission. - mr president, mr president-in-office, each member state of the european union determines the conditions under which its citizenship is granted. any citizen of a member state has the right to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states of the union, on the basis of the provisions of community law. in the case of dual nationality, citizens may invoke rights deriving from citizenship of the union. the commission therefore considers that the existence of cases of dual nationality in relations between spain, portugal and several latin american countries is covered by the rules in force. as regards the visa policy for latin america, regulation (ec) no 539/2001 lays down the lists of third countries whose nationals are subject to the visa requirement or are exempt from it. following the conclusions of the seville european council, the commission sent a questionnaire to the member states with a view to reviewing the lists of third countries annexed to that regulation. the member states' replies may provide a number of indications on the basis of which the commission may propose amendments to the regulation. the criteria for determining the lists are set out in the first sentence of recital 5 in the preamble to the regulation. the determination of the third countries whose nationals are subject to the visa requirement and those whose nationals are exempt from that requirement shall be made on a case-by-case basis, using a number of criteria, in particular those relating to illegal immigration, public policy and security, as well as the union's external relations with third countries, while taking into account the implications of regional coherence and the principle of reciprocity. any council decision on this matter shall be adopted by a qualified majority after consulting the european parliament.
- mr president, commissioner antónio vitorino, i cannot imagine that one day, in the spanish state and in portugal, and even in the european union, brazil will be considered a third country for the portuguese or argentina a third country for the galicians and the spanish. although there are many dual nationals in these countries, many of the children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren of portuguese, spanish and galician nationals are not considered european citizens. i therefore think that this absolutely intimate family relationship between portugal, the spanish state and galicia with latin america must be considered in a very special way in the solutions which the commission proposes for the visa issues discussed at the seville council. i hope the commission will not forget that we have this family in latin america.
commission. - thank you very much, mr nogueira román, but i could not agree more with you for all the reasons and one more reason, which is also the reason why we are speaking almost the same language. in any case, i would like to draw the honourable member's attention to the fact that the countries he has mentioned already today are exempt from the visa requirement and that the only countries in latin america which are subject to this requirement are colombia and peru.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, may i begin by sincerely congratulating the rapporteur on his report. the text adopted by the committee on legal affairs and the internal market is the result of its good work and its spirit of dialogue, which has made it possible to reach compromises which have been widely accepted. the result is a text that has been rebalanced to increase consumer protection, especially as regards the information to be provided to consumers, the means of complaint and the situation of minors, among others. practices which are not of a commercial promotion nature, such as the exploitation of a game of chance disguised as a sales promotion operation or sales at a loss or below cost, are also excluded. i repeat that the latter is not a genuine promotional practice, because its purpose is not so much to protect the consumer as to eliminate competitors from the market, which in the long run does not favour consumers, competition or the proper functioning of the market. for this reason, it is considered an illegal practice in most - not the minority - of the member states. in fact, several of them - because the competition rules were insufficient - have had to reintroduce these provisions. and this, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, must be borne in mind when the commission prepares its article 7 report and when we try - as we try - to put the common market into practice. the common market cannot be a means of extending practices which most member states regard as harmful, and for good reason. the impact of liberalization cannot be evaluated in purely economic terms, but must take account of all the factors affecting the common good, and consumer protection cannot be left to the predatory practices of certain large companies. that is why we think the solution adopted is appropriate and why the vast majority of our group - which is not ultra-liberal but a social market economy - will support it.
(es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal for this regulation on sales promotion in the internal market will enable european companies to take better advantage of the abolition of frontiers in order to carry out their economic activities. i therefore believe that the proposal is very timely in humanizing the national provisions on communication activities for sales promotions. this proposal has given rise to a very important debate in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy of this parliament on a very specific aspect and it is, once again, the sale at a loss. i am pleased to see that the committee on legal affairs and the internal market has incorporated the view of the committee on the environment into its amendments, and i congratulate mr beysen, rapporteur for the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, and mrs patrie, rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on this. it is reasonable that loss-making sales should be regulated at national level. at present, most member states prohibit this practice - germany, austria, france, ireland, greece and spain, among others - and this is not an arbitrary ban. i shall be the last speaker to say that selling and reselling at a loss cannot be considered as a form of trade promotion because it is a form of trade promotion which distorts the principles of fair competition and which is particularly harmful to the small trader who has no margin to compete in such a situation. in addition, they give false information to the consumer, devalue the brand image and seriously disrupt the planning of manufacturers and suppliers. i support amendments nos 27, 28, 29, 30 and 32 and i hope that the majority of this house will also accept them and that the commission will accept them.

the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the aid is not used to the detriment of the undertakings concerned. so far the commission has already adopted the regulations on smes, training and minimum wage, and now we are being offered a regulation on employment aid. i would like to make a number of preliminary remarks. firstly, the proposal under consideration, even if it is not amended, improves the existing system. at present there is no block exemption regulation in this area and the guidelines on this type of aid are a series of scattered and non-regulatory notices. the fact that certain aid is exempted from the obligation to notify it on the basis of clear criteria, even if those criteria may prove insufficient, is an important step forward in terms of transparency and legal certainty, which we must acknowledge. secondly, i would like to stress that this does not mean that aid which does not meet the criteria of the regulation is to be considered illegal. i'm not at all. it simply means that such aid must be notified in order to determine whether or not it is contrary to the objectives of the treaty. and let us not forget that among these objectives is not only the maintenance of a system in which competition is not distorted, but also the promotion of employment. thirdly, certain assumptions should be specified to avoid that the administrations granting the aid - in particular the regional authorities in the case of spain and also other member states - are subject to the long notification procedures involved when granting aid to promote employment, particularly in sectors of workers most affected by unemployment and underemployment. in this context, and in line with the objectives set out in the lisbon strategy, it should be proposed to support the transformation of employment contracts into fixed contracts and greater flexibility in defining the different groups of workers to be covered, as well as adapting them to the specific characteristics of each region, or to include among the exempt aids those aimed at promoting female employment and, finally, the raising of the age limit, so that young workers - or those in the last stage of their working life - can benefit from aid without the need for modification. all these criteria, which are included in amendment no 1 by the pse group, are aimed primarily at promoting employment in disadvantaged sectors, and their inclusion in the regulation does not distort competition in any way. the comparison of the anti-competitive effects of these aids with other aids could, on a cold analysis, be an insult to intelligence. we shall not here enter into a debate on state aid and its effects on competition, but if there is any state aid which is worthy of being considered as compatible with the objectives of the treaty, it is aid to promote employment. it would not be good if we gave the impression to the citizens and workers of europe that the commission is showing flexibility by allowing other types of aid, while being extraordinarily strict on employment aid. it would also be desirable to include the social economy as an exempt sector in a general way. as all honourable members know, social economy enterprises are an important means of maintaining employment when a sector is in crisis, and this should be reflected in the regulation. finally, paragraphs have been inserted in the report adopted on the preference of flexible working arrangements over employment promotion aid. i shall not go into the matter of refuting that statement, which - like any statement expressed in such strong terms - reflects a rigid and conservative view, with which i cannot agree. but you will simply have to admit, ladies and gentlemen, that whatever the ideological position you take, it is a strange and outlandish statement at this time, and it should not be in the report, which deals with other matters. to insist on this is to show an excessive interest in sending messages in favour of a particular action, which cannot be shared by important sectors, both in this parliament and in european society.
the commission mr president, the speeches in my view showed a broad agreement with the philosophy underlying the regulation, which can be described as follows: first of all, there is a fundamental coherence, as mr karas has rightly pointed out, between competition policy and employment policy. this consistency is due to two reasons: firstly, because in the long run a competitive economic environment is certainly conducive to the creation of sustainable employment, and secondly because competition policy has the flexibility - as this regulation shows - to reconcile general rigour with the possibility of state aid when duly justified. state aid - this is another aspect of the philosophy which i think is very well understood by the interventions - is by definition selective. we want to make sure that they are selective in favour of firms and categories of workers who are facing particular difficulties. aid for the creation of new jobs should therefore be directed to small and mediumsized enterprises - as mr randzio-plath has pointed out - and to enterprises established in assisted regions. other aid should be directed towards the recruitment of disadvantaged categories of workers. this explains, for example, why large enterprises established in nonassisted regions are excluded from the possibility of receiving aid for job creation. it is not aversion to some, but consistency with a desire to support others who are in a situation that warrants support. the rules are now clearer and the aid intensities are no longer dependent on complex concepts such as whether or not jobs are linked to an investment project, and are also now consistent with the rules on regional aid and aid to small and medium-sized enterprises. the value of transparency in the state aid register has also been noted by several parties - i am thinking in particular of mr villiers. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. there may be some scope for discussion as to the precise provisions, and i take note of the amendments proposed in this respect. i can tell you, for example, that we are considering the possibility of extending the definition of a disadvantaged worker - i am addressing mr howitt - in particular beyond that contained in the proposal published in the official journal in april. that text already included a provision on women in regions with high female unemployment compared to regional averages, as mentioned in amendment no 1. the transport issue, which mr fiori raised, is now being discussed. i take note of your suggestion, mr president, which, of course, as you know, falls within the remit of vice-president de palacio from the point of view of responsibility within the commission. i would just point out that there are particular concerns about overcapacity in certain parts of this sector, particularly in road transport, and in general we are of the opinion that where there are overcapacity problems, intervention by state aids is not the most appropriate logic and may actually aggravate those problems. we will, however, take careful account of what you have noted. i would also like to say - and i am addressing mr van lancker in particular here - that we are considering the explicit possibility for member states to notify measures in favour of workers not covered by the definition of disadvantaged workers. we also want to take account of the special case of sheltered work for disabled workers. there may be other areas where we are willing to consider increased flexibility. in conclusion, i would like to thank the committee on economic and monetary affairs and the rapporteur, mr berenguer fuster, again for their extremely useful contribution.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, in this report we analyse the daphne programme, its development, its successes and its weaknesses. it is a programme against violence against women and children, mainly in the domestic sphere. violence which is a serious violation of their fundamental rights. violence against women is a consequence of unequal relations between men and women and of gender discrimination in society. the fight against violence requires an integrated approach combining prevention, repression of the aggressor and support for the victims. the european commission has produced a comprehensive and rigorous mid-term evaluation report, which allows us to put forward proposals for the future in order to achieve the goal of 'zero violence'. violence against women and children is manifest in all countries, without distinction of class, race or level of education. violence is an obstacle to achieving equality and perpetuates inequalities. the budget allocation for this programme is insufficient, and only a third of the projects submitted have been financed. special attention must be paid to the prevention of violence, but also to the treatment and rehabilitation of offenders to prevent recurrence. it is essential to develop educational programmes aimed at preventing violence for dissemination in schools and adult education centres. all sectors of society must be involved in the fight against violence, and in particular the media as opinion-makers and transmitters of values, so that the media convey a non-stereotyped image of women, children and victims in general. the way in which news of violence is reported is also fundamental to the subsequent assessment of the violence. ngos have played a significant role in the fight against violence, but public institutions - only 10% of programmes have been developed by them so far - as well as universities and study and research centres must also be involved. we need to have more data on actual violence, since we only know a small part of it. we must have common indicators and a common database. member states should update their national legislation to have more appropriate instruments in the fight against violence. in some countries there is already a right to evict the offender from the common home, with the corresponding accompanying measures. the victims must be protected, and we must ensure that they are not the ones who have to run and hide. better training of the police in this area would be very helpful. the daphne programme should continue after the end of the programme, because unfortunately the problem persists and we know that it is difficult to eradicate it, so the actions that are being taken to raise awareness in society and try to change the sexist mentality that still persists should be welcomed. among these measures we propose a european year against violence against women and children. finally, i would like to point out the need to change the legal basis of the programme. it is the right time to do so, since the european convention which revises and updates the treaty has the opportunity to amend it, and i therefore ask commissioner vitorino, whose sensitivity to these problems we all know, to insist, to press, to do everything possible and impossible to introduce into the treaty a legal basis which will facilitate the fight against violence against women and children throughout the european union. we know the difficulties involved, but i hope that your good work will be successful. commission. – mr president, i think that it is probably true that i have had the honour, and always the pleasure, of replying to more debates in this parliament than any other commissioner in the last three years, such is parliament's welcome interest in external affairs. for me this has been one of the most interesting and important debates. it is no business of mine how parliament conducts its affairs, but if one of the reasons for the interest and informed passion of this debate has been the formula which you have applied on this occasion, that which i think you call 'catching-the-eye', then i, for one, very much welcome it. i think that there are more people in the chamber than normal. if parliament does not mind me making the point, in my experience we have had the rather more unusual spectacle of people waiting to hear other people's speeches. i am even delighted to discover that one or two people have come back into the chamber to hear the winding-up speeches which is a particular and rare pleasure. so speaking for my humble self, in the expectation that i will have rather a lot more debates to reply to in the next couple of years – unless parliament focuses its interest entirely on domestic affairs – i found this an extremely welcome breakthrough. i was asked one specific question, and another rhetorical question to which i will return. general morillon asked the specific question of what we know about the attitude of the people of iraq to their own regime, what we know about their ambitions and aspirations. the sad truth is that we know damn all because they have not had the opportunity to express their views for all too long. indeed, the expression of free opinions in iraq has led to people being shot, tortured and stuck in jail. i look forward to the day when we will know rather more about the aspirations of the people of iraq but i have my doubts as to whether, in a free election, saddam hussein would sweep back with a plurality of the votes. i should confess to a personal prejudice at this point. i have never regarded enthusiasm as a huge attribute in the discussion of foreign policy. i think enthusiasm does not always go well with the discussion of difficult foreign policy issues and i have always preferred foreign ministers who are prepared to sit under the tree for a bit and think what needs to be done first, rather than those who tear around trying to change the world. i find myself signed up enthusiastically to the famous dictum of talleyrand 'surtout pas trop de zèle'. reading so many articles over the last summer on iraq and so many speeches, i have sometimes wished that i believed in the veracity and wisdom of anything i say as fervently as some people seem to believe in the veracity and wisdom of everything they say. i also think that we have seen a parade of certainties sometimes based on obfuscation. i know very few people, for example, who seriously contend that saddam hussein is not in possession of any weapons of mass destruction. as i said earlier, if he is without any weapons of mass destruction, then what is the problem about letting inspectors in? when we are asked to define weapons of mass destruction, i suspect it is a question which could be put with some benefit to the kurds in iraq or to the people who live in the marshes in the south of iraq, who could explain what chemical weapons do to your lungs. those would be very good replies. some of the certainties are also based on evasions and, from time to time, on a lack of willingness to enunciate clear, consistent and defensible principles. i just want to refer to a number of questions that we need to face up to. they go right to the heart of the issue of compliance with the united nations and the whole issue of the justification for military action – an issue which was widely debated during the campaign in kosovo and a question which goes to the heart of the matter we have debated on many occasions in this chamber – the so-called clash of civilisations. my first question is what happens if iraq continues to defy existing un resolutions? do we simply shrug our shoulders? secondly, what happens if we go back to the united nations security council, get a new resolution and saddam hussein defies that? what do we do then? do we simply wring our hands? thirdly, what happens if we give saddam hussein an ultimatum and he defies it? what do we do? write a letter to le monde, sign a petition? there have been several references – not all of them as laudatory as mr alastair campbell might have liked – to the press conference which the prime minister of great britain and northern ireland gave in his constituency yesterday. the honourable member mr lagendijk, for example, referred to what he said. let me quote one thing which mr blair said yesterday: the un had to be a way of dealing with it – i.e. the problem caused by iraq – not a way of avoiding dealing with it. while i am not a paid-up member of new labour, that is a pretty good point and one which we simply cannot duck. my fourth question concerns a point which dr kissinger has often reminded us of. since the treaty of westphalia and the end of the thirty years war, international law, itself sometimes a rather nebulous concept, has been based on, among other principles, the principle that one state should not intervene in the affairs of another and certainly should not intervene militarily. is that an entirely adequate principle of international law today? we saw the debate begun a couple of years ago by the secretary-general of the united nations, kofi annan, about whether humanitarian intervention was sometimes justified, for example when a sovereign government could be accused of assaulting the interests and the liberties and the rights of its own people. is intervention in the affairs of another sovereign state justified by its possession of weapons of mass destruction? can you turn that into an acceptable principle? does it depend entirely on context? does it depend on the nature of the regime? does it depend on the stated intentions of the regime? does it depend on the scale of threat represented by that regime? whatever else you say, clearly if you are arguing along those lines you will need to present a good deal of evidence. finally, on the question of justifying intervention, there is the point which dr kissinger argued very explicitly in a recent article in the new york times. he argues that terrorism raises an entirely new issue for nation states. today, he argues, one nation state can be faced with a threat from another nation state operating through non-state actors. in other words, the argument is that intervention could be justified where a nation state appears to be using terrorist organisations to threaten another nation state. at the very least i imagine all of us would argue that military intervention in a sovereign state demands a clear and well-argued justification. those are all issues which will be very near the heart of foreign and security policy debates in the next decade or longer. they are issues on which we in the european union, not least because of our tradition of the rule of law, not least because of the other principles in which we believe, should have clear and unequivocal opinions. the final question is: if the present government in iraq is replaced as a result of military intervention, will that make the politics of the region more moderate or will it make the politics of the region more extreme? all those are questions which we cannot duck. they are all questions to which we will have to find our own answers over the coming weeks and months. i would like to finish with this thought. there has been a lot of reference to our relationship with the united states. i very much hope that we can work together with the united states – europe and the united states – over the coming months to deal with an undoubted threat to world peace and to international stability. we on our side may from time to time sound to americans as though we are speaking with a rather self-serving condescension in arguing that united states leadership should be based on as broad a moral consensus as possible, referring to the truman doctrine and the marshall plan, which helped to secure our futures, our prosperity, our freedom in europe. but we in europe, if we are to pull on our end of the rope, have to face up to one or two rather difficult issues ourselves. we must avoid wishful thinking and we must avoid ducking the difficult questions which i have addressed during these remarks today. i am sure this will not be the last time we debate this issue. i hope we can clarify our responses to some of those questions in the weeks and months ahead. - the report by mr maaten, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the commission communication on a strategic framework for strengthening europe-asia partnership relations (com (2001) 469 - c5-0255/2002 - 2002/2120 (cos)).
the council. - mr president, the fourth euro-asian summit, the asem summit, will be held in less than three weeks in copenhagen on 23 and 24 september, giving asem cooperation a prominent place in european policy towards asia. since its first summit six years ago, asem has been characterized by ever-wider and more fruitful cooperation in a number of areas of common interest to europe and asia. more than 40 initiatives have been launched in areas as diverse as money laundering, illegal migration, human trafficking, child welfare, human rights, environmental protection, educational exchange, lifelong learning and people-to-people interaction. meeting activity has also increased. in between summits, for example, asem's foreign ministers, finance ministers and economy ministers meet annually, inter alia, to prepare for the summits and to work towards achieving optimum results in the asem process. there are more than 2 billion people living in the asem countries. together they account for more than half of the world's production. the asian asem countries are the eu's second largest trading partner. these facts illustrate the importance of asem and the importance of continued good and promising cooperation between the two regions. a successful summit at the end of this month is therefore a high priority for the danish eu presidency. asem 4 is, like the three previous asem summits, divided into three working sessions, one for each of the main areas of cooperation. these are: (1) political dialogue, (2) economic cooperation and (3) social, cultural and educational issues. in addition, the forthcoming summit will feature an informal lunch discussion entitled 'dialogue of cultures and civilizations'. the idea is that the political dialogue should be based on the new international situation after 9/11. it involves a discussion of the new security policy challenges we are facing. that means, among other things, organized, transnational criminal activities that affect us all. it is primarily a question of how we can agree in asem cooperation to combat international terrorism, but also other transnational threats such as drug trafficking, money laundering and illegal migration. in this context, a broad approach must be adopted, with emphasis on tackling the underlying causes that can breed extremism and intolerance, including poverty reduction and better access to education. in order to put words into action, it is expected that the discussions will result in the adoption of a declaration on cooperation between europe and asia in the fight against international terrorism, combined with a cooperation programme building on existing asem activities in the field of cross-border crime. the political dialogue has traditionally involved an exchange of views on developments in the two regions. recent developments on the korean peninsula will no doubt be among the topics, and a declaration on the korean peninsula is expected to be issued at asem 4 in order to promote reconciliation and cooperation. other topics could be eu enlargement and the development of cooperation within asean+3. the economic issues will focus on economic and financial priorities in the light of the global economic slowdown, the consequences of the slowdown for the two regions and the possibilities for cooperation to remedy the situation. the ongoing efforts to promote trade, investment and economic cooperation can be continued, inter alia, by working towards the implementation of the objectives set out in the two asem economic action programmes, the trade facilitation action plan (tfap) and the investment promotion action plan (ipap). the summit is also expected to discuss economic, financial and monetary integration as a factor of growth and the wto development round as an essential prerequisite for sustainable economic development. it will be obvious to use the asem process to give momentum to the doha development round. in the light of the results achieved in the doha round, there will be scope for enhanced regional cooperation with a view to further advancing economic relations between the eu and the asian asem partners. asem's work to break down barriers to trade and investment is based on proposals from senior business leaders in the private sector via the asia-europe business forum (aebf), which, among other things, contributes to improving trade relations between asia and europe. this forum meets in copenhagen for its annual meeting immediately before the asem 4 summit. it's happening under my watch, by the way. in the third main area - social, cultural and educational issues - the overarching theme will be measures to counter the unintended consequences of globalisation. the importance of human resource development, including educational cooperation and lifelong learning, is expected to be central. the aim is to ensure that economic growth is reflected in social progress, which is the prerequisite for social stability. a seminar on this is intended as the first step on the way. the discussions during the third working session will also cover environmental issues, including a discussion of the possibilities for the asem partners to consolidate and expand cooperation in the field of the environment, also in the light of the johannesburg meeting. asem brings together a wide range of civilizations and cultures across geographical, ethnic, religious and socio-economic lines. the asem process thus contributes to the building of trust between the regions. as a bridge between european and asian cultures and civilizations, asem is a suitable forum for the dialogue needed to combat the attempt by international terrorism to divide the world community. this is the reason why this informal lunch meeting, which i have mentioned, is being held at asem 4 under the heading 'dialogue of cultures and civilizations' with the aim of promoting mutual understanding between europe and asia. the topics could be the importance of education in promoting understanding of other cultures and civilizations, the importance of equal access to information and the importance of closer interpersonal contacts between europe and asia. it is expected that this special discussion will provide the basis for an ongoing dialogue within asem on cultures and civilizations. i have noted with great interest the views and recommendations of the foreign affairs committee contained in the european parliament's report of 16 july 2002 on the commission's communication on a strategic framework for enhanced partnerships between europe and asia. i can say in this connection that we see the forthcoming summit meeting of the council as a further development of cooperation between europe and asia within asem and as a better way of dealing with the common challenges we are facing. i hope that we can achieve the objectives which i agree with and which are set out in parliament's report. as one of those who was here in this parliament at the beginning of european cooperation - i was chairman of the japan delegation - it is impressive to see what it has become. i would like to thank parliament for the interest it has shown and also to highlight the personal contacts which exist at parliamentary level between parliament and the asian parliaments. the importance of this cannot be overstated and the presidency therefore attaches great importance to parliament's report on asem cooperation.
commission. – mr president, today's debate is extremely timely. the report is excellent. i know that honourable members will understand when i say that this subject is one of particular interest to me. the debate takes place one year after the commission’s 'asia strategy' was published in 2001 and one week from the first anniversary of the attacks on new york and washington. and finally, as has been said, it takes place not long before the fourth asem summit brings together 26 european and asian leaders in copenhagen. these points will be the main focus of my short presentation today, so let me deal with them in the same order. firstly, the 'strategic framework for enhanced partnerships' of 4 september 2001 followed our first substantial paper of 1994, called a 'new asia strategy', acknowledging that the new relationship between asia and europe had evolved beyond 'aid and trade'. the strategy paper of 2001 therefore reflects the importance that european union-asia political dialogue has gained. the unprecedented speed of globalisation has also affected developments in both regions. we suggest moving towards an equal partnership with asia, based on four key points. firstly, recognition of the great cultural, political and geographical diversity within asia. secondly, strengthening the european union's political and economic presence across the region. thirdly, achieving better balance between the economic, political, social and cultural elements in our strategy. fourthly, recognising that asian countries are crucial political partners for the european union – a point which we are discovering in the present talks on international trade. we are fully aware of parliament's concerns for the protection of human rights and the spreading of democracy, good governance and the rule of law in asia and elsewhere. that is why constructive engagement, such as our human rights dialogue with china, is so important to the commission. we also share parliament’s concerns about continuing tensions across the taiwan strait and take full note of parliament’s views on our relationship with taiwan. while the european union’s 'one china' policy precludes formal relations with taiwan, we have to recognise that taiwan is an important economic partner for the european union – it is our third largest partner in the asia/pacific region. we will therefore maintain and where necessary intensify our dialogue with the taiwanese administration in the economic and other fields. the commission, as parliament will know, also intends to open an office in taipei very soon, probably around the end of the year. moreover, we support taiwanese participation in international organisations and processes, insofar as this is compatible with taiwan’s status. naturally, both council and parliament have discussed and commented on the strategy after the appalling events of 11 september, which have since had a significant impact on policies and actions. the most obvious influence is in our policy towards afghanistan, which we have just been able to debate at some length in this house. we are now only a few days away from asem 4 in copenhagen. apart from the regular asem meetings of foreign and finance ministers, which will be complemented soon by an economic ministers' meeting in denmark, we have had different ministerial meetings on the environment and on managing migration. these meetings resulted in various concrete initiatives which will be endorsed by leaders at the summit itself. the minister referred to the main topics which will be discussed at the summit. i hope it follows the lead given by foreign ministers, which makes the discussion on these occasions rather less formal and hidebound. one of the major advantages of asem is that it provides an opportunity to engage leaders from various cultures and civilisations as well as from countries at different stages of development, in order to draw strength from unity in diversity. and, as has been said, the leaders will for the first time be discussing the dialogue among cultures and civilisations in a retreat session. asia – this is my greatest recent understatement – is an extremely large region and therefore we are not advocating a 'one-size-fits-all policy'. in our latest policy paper, we have divided asia into four sub-regions – the south, the south-east, north-east asia and australia/oceania. specific policy actions will be taken in the common framework. so asia is an extremely important topic for the commission. there are three basic components to our approach. one of them concerns the definition of asia as such, since geographic, cultural, political and other concepts are differently defined. then there is the issue of coverage by our 'asia strategy', which has been the subject of some debate since its publication last year. finally, there is the evolving discussion about the enlargement of the asem partnership. on this last point, members may recall that the asia-europe co-operation framework 2000 introduced the two-key consensus principle. it means that a decision on new participants will be made by a consensus of all partners, only after a candidate has got the support of its own region. we are fully aware that many members have expressed a desire to enlarge asem to other partners in asia. we have already agreed at the level of asem foreign ministers that the consolidation of asem and the question of enlargement will come up at the next summit to be held in hanoi in 2004. this was a wise decision: we will have to use the time until the next summit not only to prepare asem for more participants, but also to prepare the agenda of that meeting very carefully. selecting issues where there is an 'asem added value' is vital in order to avoid overlapping agendas. so it is important to define what should be dealt with bilaterally, regionally or multilaterally. in the regional context, we will have to ensure that asean, arf and asem deal with those issues which each forum is best placed to tackle. we will take full account of parliament's suggestions during the preparations for the hanoi summit to which i have referred, and, i can assure the honourable member that we will continue to pay the closest attention to this comprehensive report. i should like to conclude by mentioning three points. we have demonstrated our growing concern about asia by the changes we have made to our external services over the last year or so. parliament will know that we can only open new delegations if we close or run down existing ones. parliament is understandably very firm on the ceiling that we have for the number of delegations around the world. parliament will also know that, on the whole, you receive more flack for closing or running down an office than praise for establishing one. despite the political problems that we face, we will over the next few months be able to point to the opening of new delegations in malaysia, singapore, cambodia, laos and nepal and to the opening of an office in taiwan. parliament will know that in an environment where these things cannot be achieved at lightening pace that is a pretty good achievement and an indication of the priority that we are giving asia. secondly, i remain absolutely convinced that a region to which we have not given sufficient attention and where we have not made our policies sufficiently coherent is south-east asia. before 1997 european businesses, banks and other interests, often perhaps overwhelmed by stories of asian economic miracles, piled into south-east asia with exaggerated optimism. the problem since 1997 is that all too many of them have exited from south-east asia and have not been realistic about what is still being, and can be, achieved there. i am very keen that we should develop a more coherent european policy on south-east asia and give it higher priority. next year the commission will be coming forward with a communication which will seek to put our trade, commercial, environmental, economic and political relationships with south-east asia in a sensible context. for example the importance of indonesia in our political and economic lives has to be underlined in the establishment of a clearer and more coherent policy. my last point is that an area where we have manifested an ability to be a supportive but not an insignificant player is the korean peninsula. i believe very strongly that the policy being pursued by president kim dae-jung is entirely right. it is very important for us to play a supportive role – perhaps not as important as the role others such as the united states, china and japan are playing – but nevertheless an important role in reconciliation in the korean peninsula and in encouraging north korea to join the rest of the human race. we should continue to build on the foundations which have been laid in that area. it is just an indication of how, without any amour propre and without exaggerating what we can achieve, if we just focus on some of the areas where we have real strengths to bring to bear, we can actually make much more of a reality of our asia policy, and that we intend to do. (applause)

question no 1 by mr bart staes (h-0524/02) subject: charter of fundamental rights of the european union and stricter provisions on foreigners policy in the various member states of the union across the european union, governments are introducing stricter provisions in their foreign policy and asylum seekers are facing ever more obstacles. for example, they tighten up their provisions on family reunification, requiring large deposits, raise the minimum age for marriage to 24, expel children born to parents who have entered the country illegally, require proof of the possibility of finding a job, or restrict the right of immigrant parents to join their children. these various measures amount to direct violations of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. does the council agree that the above measures implemented in the member states are in fact contrary to the spirit of the charter of fundamental rights and in particular articles 7, 9, 15 (3), 18, 20, 21, 24, 25, 29, 33, 34, 41 and 47 thereof, and is it prepared to take action, if necessary, to remedy this situation?
the council. - mr president, i entirely disagree with the questioner and would like to emphasize in the strongest possible terms that there is no breach, either of the letter or the spirit, of any international agreement. i would also like to add that the wording of the question is wrong on certain points. for example, it says that a country has a minimum age for marriage - that's wrong. there are conditions for obtaining a permanent residence permit based solely on marriage. and that's something else entirely. it goes without saying that such a provision does not apply to refugees. because if it did, it would be against the conventions. i can assure mr staes that when he speaks of danish legislation, we have a handle on the conventions. we know how to interpret them, and i could not dream of turning my back on any breach of the spirit or the letter of any convention. i myself was the european parliament's rapporteur on human rights in 1998 and 1999. the reports can be found and read. i have no intention of breaking the spirit or the letter of any international convention.
- question no 2 by mr gerard collins (h-0526/02): subject: southern africa and the seriousness of food shortages in february, the united nations food and agriculture organization warned that nearly four million people in southern africa would need emergency food aid this year. this is due to the decrease in cereal harvests in 2001 caused by unfavourable climatic conditions and a reduction in plantations. the ngo christian aid has just published a general report drawing attention to the fact that more than 12 million people in the southern african region are at risk of starvation in the coming months as a result of poor harvests, drought, floods and mismanagement. would the council outline how it intends to respond to this alarming situation by giving its views on how to ensure the provision of adequate food aid and how to strengthen support for civil society organisations?
the council. - the food crisis in southern africa was discussed at the last council meeting on 22 july this year, that is to say the meeting of the foreign ministers. the council expressed its concern at the situation in southern africa, where up to 13 million people are feared to be affected by the crisis. the council is concerned at various political decisions and actions which have been taken and which appear to have contributed to a worsening of the already alarming humanitarian situation with droughts and floods. the council considers that a solution to the humanitarian crisis is one of the main political priorities and therefore calls on the countries of the region to orient their respective policies towards this objective. regional efforts to resolve the crisis should be promoted in line with principles such as good governance as laid down in the new partnership for africa's development (nepat) initiative, in which southern african states play a key role. the council called on the countries of the region to do their utmost to facilitate the ongoing regional and humanitarian operations, including the provision of logistical and administrative support and the provision of access to and distribution of emergency aid. in the distribution of food aid, civil society organisations should play a crucial role in order to avoid the misuse of food aid for political purposes. the eu has already responded by providing extensive food and humanitarian aid to the area. however, further efforts are needed. the eu and its member states are ready to continue to contribute to these efforts in close coordination with the sadc countries. and i think i need say nothing about zimbabwe and mr mugabe. it is obvious what the council thinks of this.
the council. - i fully understand the point of view of my good friend and colleague mr collins. i would like to stress that the eu is involved, but it is the un that is acting. the un is the contractor and the sponsor of the work, while the eu is very much behind it financially and, of course, diplomatically and politically if necessary. so the eu is involved, but it is the un that is doing the executive work.

the council. - the honourable member is probably aware that the discussions in the youth and education council on 30 may, the discussions on youth participation, took place in connection with the adoption of a resolution on the framework for european cooperation in the youth field. this resolution calls for the open method of coordination to be applied in a flexible and tailor-made manner to certain thematic priorities in the youth field. the commission has put forward proposals in this respect in a white paper entitled 'a new outlet for european youth'. it was published in november last year. information and participation are among the first subjects to be dealt with. the commission, in consultation with the member states, has drawn up a questionnaire on these issues. the questionnaire has now been submitted to the member states, which are to reply to it taking due account of the views of the young people themselves, of the youth organisations and of other relevant bodies. later on, the issues of youth volunteering and greater understanding and knowledge of young people will be addressed. i would like to stress on behalf of the council that the new framework for european cooperation in the field of youth is still at an initial stage. an evaluation report is to be submitted in 2004.

- as their objects are related, i call questions 4 and 5 simultaneously. question no 4 by mr ortuondo larrea (h-0528/02) subject: the situation in the former yugoslavia subject: decision of the seville european council the seville european council decided, among other things, to meet formally four times a year (currently two meetings) independently of the other informal meetings and to establish, as from december 2003, three-yearly strategic programmes on the basis of which annual operational programmes will be drawn up. does the council not consider that this decision strengthens the community power of the european council, which is the central organ of the executive powers of the governments of the member states while at the same time it controls the european legislative process exercised by the competent ministers of these states? does he not think that this is incompatible with the commission's executive powers and that it increases the democratic deficit of the union, in which there is no real separation of powers as enshrined by montesquieu, which must be the sign of a modern democracy? question no 5 by mr newton dunn (h-0535/02) subject: separation of powers should the executive and the legislature be separated? if not, why?
the council. - the council considers that the seville decisions on the european council merely clarify the existing provisions of the treaty on european union, in particular article 4, which states that the european council shall give the union the impetus necessary for its development and shall define the general political guidelines for this purpose. at a time of increasing development and differentiation in the union's activities, and just before a major enlargement with a number of new member states, the european council has felt it necessary to strengthen the council's capacity to act as a guiding and driving force. this is precisely the role of the european council under the treaty. the council cannot see that these practical guidelines are in any way incompatible with the commission's executive powers, which cannot be in any way called into question by a decision whose sole purpose is to enable the european council to exercise in the best possible way the responsibilities conferred on it. in this connection i would point out that the president of the commission is a member of the european council and i have heard no objection to the council trying to improve itself. as regards the possible democratic deficit and the lack of separation of powers within the union, the council considers that the present situation, whatever one may think of it, cannot be called into question by a reform whose sole purpose, as already noted, is to implement the existing provisions of the treaty in a more effective manner. since the question of the separation of executive and legislative powers - whether the principle in general or its application in the union - has not been discussed as such by the council, the council is not in a position to answer the precise question posed in question h-0535. the council is of course not unaware of this classic problem, which was raised indirectly, for example, in the laeken declaration adopted by the european council in december, and which will in all probability be raised also in the convention and subsequently at the subsequent intergovernmental conference. the honourable member must understand that the council, beyond purely academic considerations which are not of its concern, cannot comment on the possible outcome of a debate which will not be held in the council itself and which in any event has not yet taken place. i hope that this explains why i cannot go into the questions that have been raised.
- mr president-in-office of the council, thank you very much for your reply. perhaps i am going to make an impossible statement, but i would have liked the time limit for answering our questions to have been shorter, so that the answer to my question would have been given by the spanish presidency, which was responsible, at the time, for the european council in seville. that said, what is certain is that in europe, in the european union, it is the council which has the highest legislative power, and, moreover, it controls the executive power through the comitology procedure. i would like to ask you whether you think the united states would be at the head of the world if its legislative power, instead of residing in the house of representatives and the senate, resided in a ministerial council made up of representatives of the various american states: from new york or washington to california, florida or colorado. and if the american president, mr bush, had the same level of powers, competence and powers as our president, mr prodi, do you think he would have the same influence and capacity in international relations and also at home? would he have the same impact and capacity? i believe that we must have a genuine democracy in europe, with a separation of powers, as another speaker has said: the legislative power must be in this parliament and the executive in the commission.
the council. - i will confine myself to saying that i am as interested in montesquieu's theories of the distribution of power as the honourable member. i happen to be a political scientist by training and i think it is fundamental that we keep this division of powers in mind. i said that yesterday when i was representing the presidency in the committee on constitutional affairs in this parliament. but i cannot see, with all my will, that the council's efforts to improve itself are contrary to montesquieu's theories of power sharing, and i cannot see that the council has taken over powers or in any way disturbed the commission. i would like to refer to what i said yesterday on behalf of the danish government in the committee on constitutional affairs, namely that the danish government is a strong supporter of the community method and does not want the council to take power from the commission. that is all - but it was as danish minister that i added this.
council. – this is question time and concerns questions to the council. the council does not deal with the convention, the danish presidency does not deal with the convention. we respect the procedure that has been laid down for the convention so i have no further comment. yet i hope that what i just said indicated that the honourable member might tend to agree on the need to separate powers in a democracy.

the council. - both the member states and the eu institutions are obliged to integrate equal opportunities for women and men into all eu policies and programmes, and the european council has on question no 12 by mr manuel medina ortega (h-0545/02) subject: limitation of illegal immigration to the canary islands following the agreements reached at the seville summit, what measures does the council propose to limit the massive influx of illegal immigrants to the canary islands and, in particular, to curb this uncontrolled immigration at the point of departure, so as to guarantee the safety of immigrants?
the council. - the conclusions of the seville european council outlined the measures to be taken to ensure that the problem of illegal immigration is tackled effectively at eu level. and this concerns both the prevention and the limitation of immigration. we must ensure a fair balance between this objective on the one hand and the objective of better integration of the immigrants who are in our countries legally on the other, and then we must of course have an asylum policy which respects international conventions. it should also be noted that the spanish presidency gave a considerable impetus to this question even before the seville european council, in particular with the adoption of two guiding instruments which not only outline a number of necessary measures but also define the framework for future action and its development. these are the action plan on combating illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings and the action plan on the management of the eu's external borders, both adopted by the justice and home affairs council. on 13 june this year, the council also reached agreement on conclusions on measures to be taken to prevent and combat illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings by sea. the seville conclusions, which explicitly mention these action plans, emphasized the following measures. firstly, to speed up the conclusion of readmission agreements currently under negotiation and to approve new mandates for the negotiation of readmission agreements with the countries already designated by the council, as set out in conclusion no 30. secondly, as regards the policies on expulsion and return, to adopt, by the end of the year at the latest, the elements of a return programme on the basis of the green paper presented by the commission in april 2002. that is also conclusion 30. thirdly, the gradual introduction of a coordinated and integrated management of the external borders, which will inter alia contribute to a better management of migration flows. a number of measures have been identified to enable this objective to be achieved very soon, as indicated in conclusions 31 and 32. in a broader and more general perspective, the seville conclusions confirmed that immigration policy must be integrated into the eu's relations with third countries as an essential element to be taken into account. they pointed out that the eu's long-term objective must remain an integrated, coherent and well-balanced policy addressing the root causes of illegal immigration. the conclusions underlined the importance of establishing cooperation with countries of origin, transit countries, for the purposes of joint management and border control and for the purposes of readmission, as referred to in conclusion 34. the conclusions confirmed the need to systematically evaluate the relations with non-cooperating third countries in the fight against illegal immigration in the relevant areas. they point out that the council. - negotiations on the multilateral nuclear and environmental programme in the russian federation have been under way for more than three years. at various summits, the eu has stressed the but the matter was discussed at the summit and russia expressed a wish that a solution be found to the outstanding issues, namely the taxation issue and civil liability. the eu has put pressure on cooperation on safety in the management of irradiated nuclear fuel and radioactive waste in the russian federation. the initial donor conference on the environmental partnerships support fund under nuclear projects. the participants stressed that the conclusion of this mnepr agreement is a necessary condition for the implementation of nuclear projects under the ndep. the ndep is a significant and concrete step towards achieving the objectives set by the g8 for the global partnership against the proliferation of weapons and materials of mass destruction. the question of nuclear safety is of vital importance for the protection of the environment on the european continent. this is particularly true of russia, but also of other countries in northern europe. the danish presidency will therefore work to conclude the negotiations on the mnepr agreement before the end of this year. i hope that mrs astrid thors will be satisfied with that answer.

- question no 15 by mr brian crowley (h-0554/02) subject: fight against drugs illicit drugs, including crack and cocaine, continue to pose serious social problems in terms of addiction, crime, health care and law enforcement. can the council give assurances that under the danish presidency, and in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, it will make the fight against illicit drugs a major priority of its presidency and that it will report to parliament in december 2002 on the initiatives and measures it has taken in this regard?
