the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the maastricht treaty for a number of years. i believe that the objectives which in 1992 presided over the incorporation of european citizenship into the treaty on european union have not lost their relevance. citizenship of the union is, of course, a source of legitimacy for the process of european integration and strives to strengthen the participation of citizens in the construction of community europe. it is also a key factor in creating among citizens a sense of belonging to the european union and of having a genuine common european identity. but this identity is built on respect for diversity, because national diversity is an integral part of the specific european identity. it therefore neither replaces nor conflicts with national identity, but rather complements it. i take this opportunity to thank you for the report on the third report from the commission on citizenship of the union which has been presented today and i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr carlos coelho, in particular, not only on the quality of his report but also on the way in which he has structured the subject and the clarity of the political objectives he sets out. i fully agree that the concept of european citizenship must be applied in all its dimensions, whether political, administrative, judicial, social or economic. we are in a situation where the rights of citizens are widely respected in the member states of the union, but where there are still some legal discrepancies and practical obstacles to the full expression of european citizenship. we must continue to work towards overcoming these discrepancies and obstacles that prevent citizens from enjoying their rights as european citizens. one of the aspects highlighted in the report is the lack of information, which results in a low level of awareness among european citizens. the european union's information and communication policy should be strengthened by all possible means. this is a point which the rapporteur shares, and the commission has repeatedly stressed in its report the need to inform citizens better about their rights. i think it is common knowledge that the commission adopted a new approach to information and communication policy last july. and i believe that this approach is necessary to counter the ignorance and apathy of the european citizen about the debate on the future of europe. however, it is obvious that the european institutions cannot, on their own, communicate with the union's 370 million or, if they wish, with the 500 million or so after enlargement. the member states must share responsibility for the provision of information, for dialogue with the citizens and for their recognition, because the building of europe concerns them above all. and i think there are signs now that there is a political will on the part of the member states to work together, thus demonstrating that there is no incompatibility between the feeling of national belonging and the feeling of participation in the european project. in this respect, the 'europe on the move' service set up by the commission can be considered a success. since 1998, this service has been providing information on all kinds of eu-related matters, helping people to know their rights and opportunities as citizens of the union and how to take advantage of them. it's that small steps are often more important in practice. the creation of the 'europe on the net' single telephone number, for example, allows citizens to call an operator who speaks their national language and answers any questions they may have about the european union, wherever they are in the 15 member states. as regards information, i would also like to add that the commission will shortly be examining the question of raising citizens' awareness of union citizenship and related rights through a specific eurobarometer survey. the survey will be launched under the title 'ten years of european citizenship' and the results will be used as a basis for future information and communication measures on citizenship. the commission wanted to include in the third report a framework for the structure of fundamental rights, namely the proclamation of the charter of fundamental rights in december 2000. i admit that this has caused a delay in the initial deadline for the third report, but i think that the importance of the charter fully justified it. the report by mr carlos coelho states that the charter has placed european citizenship at the heart of the union's activities. i couldn't agree more. i also agree with the call for the convention on the future of europe to define the binding legal status to be given to the charter of fundamental rights. i think that the most important debate on the convention, which can produce real results in bringing citizens closer to the european institutions, is not so much the debate on the institutions, but perhaps the debate on the charter of fundamental rights, its inclusion in the treaties and its legally binding nature. citizens may remain aloof when discussing institutional issues, the sharing of powers between the union's bodies or legislative procedures, but they are keenly interested in knowing what rights they have and how the union can meet their expectations. i also hope that the council will be able to accept the commission's proposal on the reorganisation of the right to freedom of movement. this is a good test to show that a freedom which is at the heart of european citizenship has the same status of political efficacy and dignity as the free movement of goods, capital or services. i note, ladies and gentlemen, the suggestion that the members of the future convention should decide on the status of the charter of fundamental rights. and as one of the commission's representatives at the convention, together with my colleague michel barnier, i will not fail to express my support for the charter to have that strong status which you want.
- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0255/2002), on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council providing for public participation in the drawing up of certain plans and programmes relating to the environment and amending council directives 85/337/eec and 96/61/ec (5475/1/2002 - c5-0227/2002 - 2000/0331 (cod)) (rapporteur: mrs korhola)
- mr president, the minutes of the first hour of the sitting on monday recorded a number of petitions - up to 200 - from july and august. the ombudsman's and the committee on petitions' statistics say that 40% of these petitions relate to breaches of community law in the environmental field. mr president, if these measures for public participation in the preparation of certain plans and programmes relating to the environment were really put into practice, if the directive on the right of the public to information were really respected, i am convinced that a very important part of these petitions, which are recorded every month in the minutes, would probably not reach us here, because what we do see in the committee on petitions, to which all these petitions are sent, is that not only is the public not allowed to participate in these environmental programmes, but sometimes they are denied the information that the directive on the right to information should guarantee them. i believe, mr president, that if we can get the amendments of this second reading through, and if that third pillar of the legal aspects which the rapporteur has mentioned can come to this parliament and be discussed and have a good outcome, we will get this list of environmental requests down each and every session.
commission. – mr president, my colleague, mrs wallström, is attending the world summit on sustainable development. therefore it is an honour for me to participate in this debate on her behalf. the first meeting of the parties to the aarhus convention on access to information, public participation and access to justice in environmental matters will take place at the end of october. the community will not yet be in a position to participate as a party to that convention. we can, however, show that we take our commitments seriously and make good progress in adopting the implementing legislation. this common position deals with the second pillar of the convention, public participation in environmental decision-making. in addition, other recent community legislation already incorporates the principles of the aarhus convention concerning public participation and the common position on access to environmental information is under consideration. the commission will present the remaining proposals, notably on access to justice and the application of the convention to community institutions, by the end of the year. the present common position, with one exception, provides a good basis to enable this directive on public participation to be adopted fairly soon. the commission is happy that the rapporteur and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy as a whole share this positive view and also support the commission's position on the outstanding issue. on the main amendments tabled for the vote tomorrow, the commission's position is as follows. first of all, public participation in the updating of permits under the ippc directive. i will start with the exception where the commission is not happy with the common position. under the aarhus convention, public participation is as a rule required, not only for the issue but also for the updating of permits for the activities covered. this was provided for in the commission's proposal concerning permits under the ippc directive, where such updating is a key revision. the common position largely restricted this requirement and its wording leaves a wide discretion to the member states and the competent authorities in charge of updating permits. this will lead to widely divergent practice and legal uncertainty and will potentially mean that public participation is possible only in a few cases when permits are being updated, rather than being the rule. amendment no 15 requires public participation for the most relevant cases of permit updates, which are those covered by article 13 of the ippc directive. while the commission proposal included permit updates as such, the amendment is in line with article 6(10) of the aarhus convention, which allows for the rules on public participation to apply updates where appropriate. the commission considers public participation in permit updates covered by article 13 appropriate. the wording of the common position fails to identify where public participation is deemed to be appropriate, leaving it entirely to the discretion of the member states. the commission therefore fully supports amendment no 15. regarding the extension of the public participation provisions to cover other community legislation plans and programmes which may have a significant effect on the environment, amendment no 18 proposes extending considerably the scope of article 2 to cover other community legislation, plans and programmes, which may have a significant effect on the environment or health. the commission cannot accept this amendment, nor can it accept related amendments nos 1, 2 and 6 to the recitals, for the following reasons. to the extent that the wording refers to public participation in the preparation of community legislation, the present directive is not the correct legal instrument. in addition, public participation in the preparation of legislation is referred to as soft law under the aarhus convention.in regard to plans and programmes, the amendment would considerably deviate from the original approach to cover clearly identified plans and programmes in the environmental field. it would not provide sufficient legal certainty as to which plans and programmes are covered and would duplicate measures in different pieces of legislation. in respect of plans and programmes in other sectors likely to have significant environmental effects, directive 2001/42/ec on strategic environmental assessment already incorporates measures of particular relevance. this directive provides for an environmental assessment of relevant plans and programmes in the integration sectors. as part of the assessment, public participation will take place in line with the aarhus convention. i turn now to access to justice. the commission cannot accept amendment no 10 providing for access to justice in relation to plans and programmes covered by the directive, or amendment no 5 on the related recital. article 9(2) of the aarhus convention explicitly requires access to justice in relation to projects that may have a significant effect on the environment. this is dealt with under the common position. in relation to plans and programmes, access to justice is not explicitly required. it would also be inconsistent to apply it to certain plans and programmes when it is not provided for in the case of those covered by the directive on strategic environmental assessment. however, the commission is preparing a legislative proposal on access to justice to fully implement the third pillar of the aarhus convention. in the framework of that proposal, the content of amendment no 10 could more appropriately be addressed in a horizontal way. on the amendments concerning information about the outcome of public participation and practical information concerning administrative and judicial review, the commission would like to point out that the provisions on public participation have to be practicable to allow smooth implementation in the different administrative systems of the member states. amendments nos 7, 13, 14 and 16 require the competent authority to make reasonable efforts to reply to the public and to ensure that information provided about decisions taken includes practical direction concerning the procedure for seeking review. the common position already incorporates the obligation to inform the public about the final decision and the underlying reasons and considerations and provides for appropriate information to be made available on the review procedures. requiring more would constitute a disproportionate administrative burden and hamper effective public participation. the commission therefore cannot accept those amendments. to summarise our position on the amendments: the commission can accept amendments nos 15 and 19. amendments nos 3, 4, 11 and 12 can be accepted in principle. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 1, 2, 5 to 10, 13, 14, nor amendments nos 16 to 18. to conclude, i would like to emphasise that it is in our common interest, which is the interest of the european citizens, to have this directive enter in force swiftly so that public participation can be fully integrated into administrative practice.

(es) madam president, i would like to thank the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport for accepting this proposal to carry out a study on universities and higher education in the european knowledge area. i must say that many ideas have been put forward by my colleagues in this parliament, and that the european students' association and the european university association, as well as many other sectors, have been given a lot of attention and have even been heard. however, before i go into the matter, i would like to say that there are no amendments and that, simply to make the text easier to read, i would ask the secretariat of the plenary to insert two subheadings: 'european higher education area' before paragraph 1 and 'bologna process' before paragraph 5. why is it necessary to draw up this report? there is a certain contradiction in europe. universities have been a linchpin of european culture for more than 1 500 years. in addition, they have been the centres where dialogue has been created, where scientific thinking has been developed and where youth has been formed. and yet, curiously enough, we are experiencing a process of alienation - which many call inbreeding - from the university in relation to the system and the environment, and the commission itself and european policies are not taking sufficient account of the role that universities could play as consultants, institutions or disseminators of the community acquis. in addition to their high level of professionalism and independence, they are institutions established throughout the union and should be key as references for civil society, as platforms for dialogue and debate and as support for the meda programmes and the programmes of the candidate countries, as well as training take an interest in european issues, and we are inviting the commission to develop its relations with them in all areas. what do we ask in the report? the creation of a european education area needs to be strengthened, and universities themselves must play a leading role in this. we also need them to take up the scientific and conceptual challenge facing europe and its surroundings (regions and nations). universities also need to be guardians and committed to quality and be the main protagonists and disseminators of the culture of effort and open and transparent evaluation. evaluation, transparency and quality as a responsible response to bodies which are financed, in general, with public money and which have the trust of society as instruments for training future generations. the bologna process is supported from here, starting with the universities themselves and the council, with all that this implies: mobility, recognition of qualifications, networking, etc. but it is understood that, in order to achieve this convergence, both the recognition of qualifications and the increase in mobility between teachers, students and researchers, it is necessary to make the reception systems more flexible and to make the bologna process itself more open, as well as the architecture of qualifications. this will make it easier for people to understand each other, to feel more at home and to grasp the diversity of problems presented by different types of qualifications and research, as well as the peculiarities of practical training. the commission is also calling for a green paper, because it is surprising how little we know about the situation in universities. the indicators - the few that we have - in many cases show rather negative figures; universities are going through a great crisis: they have made a great effort to bring education closer to all, and they have often lost competitiveness. we have to help them. the research career must be recognised, research encouraged and incentives created for students to start at a young age; merit, mobility and results must be rewarded, and it is essential that universities increase their role as centres of lifelong learning. they must be the centres of technology and innovation and of updating knowledge. it is also suggested that the presence of universities in the media should be increased and that distance learning should be encouraged - they have asked us to do so - and at the same time that a 'house of universities' should be created, a centre where they can meet so that their relationship is the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the future of the european union, and that the european parliament has been involved in the negotiations on the future of the union. this need was recognised and reaffirmed by the heads of state and government at the laeken european council, which gave new impetus to the project of creating a training network. in the debate following the french government's initiative, the commission raised a number of legal and technical questions arising from the creation of a judicial training network. the commission's concerns were in particular the following: first, the independence of the judiciary, which must be safeguarded. rather than imposing rigid training schemes, it is important to provide judges and prosecutors with the means to design and deliver such training in a flexible manner. secondly, it is necessary to take into account the existing structures and to make full use of the available awareness-raising tools: the european judicial network and the european network for civil and commercial purposes. finally, account should be taken of the general problem of the allocation of judicial cooperation between the first and third pillars of the treaty, which in our view implies the adoption of two identical acts, a problem exacerbated by the specificities of the opt-out protocols of denmark, the united kingdom and ireland. the european parliament, in supporting the initiative, has tried to answer these questions, in particular the last question of the double legal basis. the commission fully recognizes the efforts of the rapporteur. however, it does not subscribe to the 'bridge' formula provided for in article 42 of the treaty on european union, which seems to us to be disproportionate and unrealistic. we share the view that the division of justice between two pillars creates difficulties. but we believe that the most effective way of overcoming these difficulties will be to abolish the pillar structure within the framework of the convention on the future of europe. in the working document which the commission presented on the 'european judicial training network' we proposed three possible options: either to create a training network by means of a council act, or to create a community agency for this purpose, or to keep the existing network in operation while increasing the support given to it by the union. coreper of 27 june this year reached a general agreement in principle on the third option, stressing the interest it confers on the actions of the existing network and the strengthening of its activities. the commission considers that at the present stage this is the formula which best meets the needs and which should produce positive results. the network has already started work in this direction. the council adopted the framework programme on police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters, the agis programme, based on the model of the community framework of activities to facilitate judicial cooperation in civil matters. the commission therefore believes that we have programmes which are in a position to support activities relating to the development of judicial training in europe, both in the civil and criminal fields, which seems to us to be a particularly important objective in the context of the forthcoming enlargement.
(es) mr president, i welcome the holding of this debate, in which an important measure is being discussed which will undoubtedly serve to advance the realisation of the much-desired area of freedom, security and justice. i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteur on the great interest she has shown in tackling this initiative and on the excellent background work she has done. the treaty of amsterdam has given us the legal basis for a whole series of measures at european level to make the europe of freedom, security and justice that we all want a reality. in 1999, the tampere council of member states declared that, in a genuine european area of justice, the incompatibility and complexity of the legal and administrative systems of the member states must not prevent or discourage individuals and businesses from exercising their rights. to avoid such a breakdown, the member states have established the principle of mutual recognition of judgments as a cornerstone of judicial cooperation, both civil and criminal, in the union. but for mutual recognition to be possible, another principle must also be respected: mutual trust. this means that for foreign judgments to be accepted as their own, there must be full confidence in the legal and judicial systems of the issuing country. in this sense, as the initiative itself acknowledges in one of its recitals, the training of the members of the judicial bodies of the member states is one of the consequences for the success of the european judicial area. i think that the initiative we are discussing is important in this respect too. it aims to create a network to establish the necessary links between the various bodies in the member states responsible for the training and professional development of persons responsible for the administration of justice. this will promote understanding between the various authorities and facilitate the establishment of a climate of trust. this will undoubtedly have the effect of improving knowledge of the respective judicial systems of the member states and the functioning of the european judicial area. this will institutionalize a system of exchange of best practice and open a seamless channel between national bodies, while respecting the identity of each of them and the necessary judicial independence, which is the foundation of the rule of law. i would like to focus on what i consider to be the most important aspect of this initiative, as already mentioned by the rapporteur: the scope of action in the network. this has been the main focus of the discussions, obviously because of the direct impact it has on the choice of legal basis. apart from the confusing dispersion in the treaties of the legal bases for the realisation of the area of freedom, security and justice, i agree with the rapporteur that it makes no sense to create a network such as the one we are discussing for the specific area of criminal justice. justice itself is a unitary concept and therefore it is logical to create a single network to coordinate the national judicial development bodies, both in the civil and criminal fields. in view of the opinion expressed by the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, which rejects the choice of a double legal basis if this implies incompatible procedures, and in view of the importance and the objectives of the initiative, i consider that the choice of the legal basis provided for in article 42 of the treaty on european union is the most appropriate solution. we are starting from the principle that the articles are inserted into the treaty because they are intended for further use. in this sense, we should not be afraid to opt for this procedure, even though it has not been used to date. the choice of article 42 is even more important, since it supports the communityisation of matters which are still subject to special procedures. in this connection, on behalf of the group of the european people's party (christian democrats) and european democrats, i would like to stress the need to put an end to the legal dispersion and the multiplication of the legal bases envisaged for the creation of this area. this initiative can serve to put into practice the will of the member states expressed in article 42 of the treaty and to pave the way for the progressive communityisation of the most important aspects of criminal justice.

(es) mr president, commissioner, everyone is aware of the congestion on european roads and the considerable external costs of transporting goods on them, such as accidents, noise, pollution, climatic effects, provision and maintenance of infrastructure, etc. for this is nothing compared with the grim predictions of what the future may hold for us if we do not take action to address these threats. it is estimated that the total transport of goods by road in the union will increase by 50% by 2010 at the rate of - the council. - madam president, with regard to the preferential arrangements which have been mentioned many times in the debate, i can say that all the mercosur participating states can benefit from the eu's generalised system of preferences. they can, in particular, through the general arrangements of the gsp, increase their own export earnings, promote their own industrialisation and encourage the diversification of their economies as an instrument of stability, as mr barón crespo suggested. everyone here must be aware that the members of the international financial bodies, in particular the bretton woods institutions, the international monetary fund and the world bank are each sovereign states. they are not subject to dictation or to co-decision by the european council. it is therefore up to these states themselves, and not the council, to decide how they will act in these international financial bodies. nevertheless, it is clear that coordination between the eu member states under article 19 of the eu treaty can benefit their work in these institutions. in accordance with this, there is in fact a certain amount of informal coordination at intergovernmental level within the framework of the above-mentioned institutions. as regards the efforts of the member states to remedy the situation in the mercosur countries, they participate fully and actively in the work of the imf to ensure stability and sustainable economic recovery in the region. it would be stupid to do otherwise. the measures taken to support paraguay, uruguay and, most recently, brazil, have been supported by the eu member states and work is under way to ensure a strong, sustainable and credible imf programme for argentina, as outlined in the council conclusions of 21 january 2002. the question by mr barón crespo, on behalf of the pse group, states that the negotiations on the association and free trade agreement with mercosur are expected to be completed in 2003. the parties have not set a deadline for the conclusion of the negotiations, which therefore depends on how they develop. the negotiators at ministerial level adopted in july this year an ambitious work programme for the next 12 months. the eu is committed to reaching a comprehensive agreement with mercosur and to making further progress in the negotiations. let me conclude, therefore, that the council is fully aware of the serious crisis in the mercosur countries - particularly argentina. and it is absolutely right that this should be taken seriously. we are therefore interested in strengthening relations between the eu and mercosur and promoting trade, and we also met with them during the general assembly in new york last week. first of all, everyone here must be aware that we must go home and tell our own governments that they themselves must work in the imf for the institutions, and they must tell the mercosur countries that they themselves must first of all carry out the economic conversion.
commission. – madam president, the commission fully shares the view of honourable members that mercosur’s financial problems have intensified during the summer. the european union and the commission are concerned at the financial turbulence that is affecting the entire mercosur region. the turmoil was triggered by the economic and banking crisis in argentina, which led to spillover effects on other mercosur countries such as uruguay and brazil. as a result, the social and economic indicators, as the honourable member indicated, are pointing sharply in the wrong direction; poverty is increasing and gdp has declined in all mercosur countries. the crisis will require deep economic and political structural reforms. the commission is convinced that one of the answers to the financial and economic turbulence should be deeper and faster regional integration. in this respect, the european union and the commission strongly support the mercosur integration process, especially at this crucial moment for the region. the european message of support for further integration as one of the responses to the present crisis is confirmed by our strong commitment to intensify and accelerate negotiations for an association agreement between the european union and mercosur. the agreement will create improved market access for mercosur exports to the european union and it will strengthen mercosur as a common market. in addition, from the political and cooperation point of view, it will be a clear signal of a strengthening of eu-mercosur relations. as parliament knows, the eu-mercosur negotiations are highly ambitious and include three pillars: political dialogue, cooperation and a comprehensive trade agenda. to date, we have virtually finalised the political and cooperation chapters. at the recent rio ministerial meeting on 23 july 2002 which, as the honourable member noted, i attended, an ambitious work programme for the trade negotiations was established. this includes a ministerial meeting during the second half of next year to kick off what we hope will be the final stage of the negotiations. in addition to the interregional negotiations, the commission has considered additional forms of help to alleviate the mercosur crisis. firstly, on the trade front, the european union has taken important decisions to increase the allocation of the hilton beef quota for two mercosur countries: 10 000 additional tonnes to argentina and, as a first step, 1 000 tonnes to paraguay. it is also worth remembering that mercosur countries have benefited, as my honourable friend the president-in-office pointed out, from the eu gsp mechanism for quite a long time. the latest review of the regime entered into force on 1 january 2002 and it should expire on 31 december 2004. at this stage it is not possible temporarily to adjust gsp preferences only for the mercosur countries, as some have suggested. however, we remain committed to helping mercosur countries to benefit further from the current system. there has also been coordination of the positions taken by our member states on the south american crisis by means of council common positions and public statements on argentina. it must be said that this falls short of actual coordination of positions in the international monetary fund. the mercosur crisis shows that it would desirable for the european union to speak with a single voice and play a more influential role in international financial matters. as parliament knows, the european commission cannot intervene as such in the definition of the criteria imposed by an international organisation like the imf – in which, as i have said, european union member states are represented – for the grant of loans to certain countries in a crisis situation. the approval of imf assistance as such is based on its own criteria and is tied to sustainable economic programmes proposed by the governments of the countries affected by financial or economic problems. we believe it is only natural that the conditions imposed by international organisations like the imf for the concession of loans for the structural adjustment of countries undergoing a crisis are different from those set by international cooperation organisations like the un development programme for the concession of grants. these organisations have different objectives, which explains why the un development programme puts more emphasis on the social component of cooperation. but above and beyond any discussions on the merits of any of the criteria used by international organisations, we should not lose sight of the fact that the crisis requires fundamental economic reform in the region as a whole. finally, the commission adopted in august a substantial cooperation package in favour of the mercosur countries covering eur 200 million for the period 2002-2006. these programmes will support regional integration, economic reform, social development and poverty alleviation, modernisation of the state and protection of the environment. furthermore, an additional eur 48 million for the period 2002-2006 has been allocated to cooperation with mercosur as a whole and it is focused on three priority areas: support to the implementation of the mercosur internal market; support to mercosur institutionalisation; and support for civil society in mercosur. in sum, there is a package of eur 250 million to be made available in the period 2002-2006 – of which eur 30 million are planned to be committed in 2002. i hope this is another sign of our long-term commitment to mercosur. let me make one final brief point. we have just held meetings in copenhagen with the asem countries and individual meetings with south korea, china, and indonesia. in the last few years – at least until the recent crisis, and for a change – european investment in latin america outstripped investment in asia. it is interesting to compare the two regions and to compare for example the savings ratio in asia with that in latin america. because domestic savings are so much lower in latin america, it has depended much more on foreign direct investment in order to promote economic growth. the problem in today's liberalised global market is that just as money can go in, so it can just as rapidly go out again. the only answer to poverty in latin america is sustainable economic development. we can only have sustainable economic development when we have sustained investment. so there is a very strong argument for trying to increase domestic savings ratios in latin america and for looking at financial flows in the way that chile did a few years ago and trying to ensure that they become stabilising rather than destabilising factors.

(fi) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to be able to speak on behalf of the commission on a proposal to help the european community move towards petrol and diesel fuels with a sulphur content of up to 10 milligrams per kilogram. this will remove technical barriers to the introduction of the most fuel-efficient vehicles. in addition, the use of fuels complying with the new requirements in older vehicles reduces conventional pollutant emissions and improves air quality. the amendments adopted at first reading by parliament helped to ensure that the use of fuels containing 10 milligrams of sulphur per kilogram was introduced more rapidly than originally planned. it is gratifying to see that the rapporteur, the committee and the council seem to agree on many of the aspects of this subject. the commission is hopeful that the remaining open issues can be resolved reasonably quickly. i shall now turn to the main issues raised by the proposed amendments. several amendments suggest that the date by which all marketed diesel fuels should be limited to 10 milligrams of sulphur per kilogram should be fixed as early as 1 january 2009, rather than being fixed until the end of 2005 when the review is completed. the commission would have preferred to stick to the alternative in the original proposal and the common position of the council, whereby the deadline for diesel fuel would have been fixed at a later date. however, in view of the agreement on the timetable, the commission is prepared to be flexible in this respect and to accept amendment no 2 in its entirety and amendment no 11 in its part relating to the review of diesel fuel. the second question concerns the market coverage of petrol and diesel fuels with a sulphur content of up to 10 milligrams per kilogramme between 2005 and 2009. in this respect, the commission is willing to try to develop guidelines for the availability criteria for such fuels for the first phase, although this phase will now be shorter than originally envisaged. the commission therefore accepts amendments nos 4 and 7. some of the amendments concern the need to improve and harmonise the quality of fuels used in mobile machinery throughout the community. it is true that the relative importance of such emissions increases as the environmental performance of engines in road vehicles improves. work on the next stage of emission standards for diesel engines for use in mobile machinery is under way and is progressing well. when completed at the end of this year, the fuel quality required by the standards will be defined, as will the timetable for the availability of such fuel. until then, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 3, 10 and 13. the commission is happy to examine further the issues related to alternative fuels and biofuels, in particular the issue of the volatility requirements for certain biofuels and petrol blends. the commission therefore accepts in principle amendment no 12. the commission does not accept amendments nos 1, 5, 6, 8 and 9 and the part of amendment no 11 concerning the elements to be included in the review, as the commission considers that they have been (es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to congratulate mrs hautala on her great capacity for dialogue and on her work, which has enabled us to reach agreements. we fully agree with her that it is important that citizens have access to low sulphur fuels as soon as possible. this directive responds to the conclusions of the auto-oil programmes carried out by the commission and will allow us to enjoy a better quality of air, which we welcome. it is clear that the objective of this directive is one hundred per cent environmental and for that reason it is applauded by everyone. but in any case, we must be pragmatic and analyze the circumstances. the production of new sulphur-free fuels will cause co2 increases in refineries and refineries will have to make very expensive investments to obtain it. however, thanks to technological advances in vehicle engines and catalysts, a positive balance can now be achieved in the reduction of co2 emissions, because those from refineries will be lower than those that will be emitted by vehicles using the new fuel. but this will only happen when the sulphur-free fuel is marketed in time to coincide with a sufficiently large car fleet, technologically adapted to use this fuel. the commission has already proposed a number of measures to improve the efficiency of the internal market. in other words, if the balanced production and availability of new fuels is not achieved at the same time as the renewal of the vehicle fleet, an overall increase in emissions can occur, and this at a considerable cost. we can impose on companies - with a directive - to put on the market fuel with 10 ppm of sulphur, but we cannot force consumers to change cars at the same time. we therefore support - and i ask parliament to support - the possibility of revising the period for the full introduction of diesel fuel in 2005, especially as regards agricultural tractors and other non-road vehicles, because, although it is desirable that they use a sulphur-free fuel, the fact is that the rate of renewal of these vehicles is much slower and the volume of fuel consumed is relatively low. finally, although this has already been discussed, as rapporteur for the report on the biofuels directive i will refer to volatility, which may affect its application. these are the technical specifications of the fuels used in the mixture. the mixture of bioethanol and petrol increases the volatility of the resulting fuel and in countries with hot summers the pressure limits set for that season may be exceeded by about 10%. this seriously undermines the competitiveness of such blends. but the proposal on biofuels was made by the commission after the first reading of this directive on the quality of petrol and so we have not had the opportunity to allow an ad hoc amendment to this effect for this second reading. i therefore call on the commission and the council to propose as soon as possible, in accordance with articles 9 and 10 of directive 98/70/ec, new specifications and test methods for biofuels and fuels used by captive fleets. it is also urgent to authorise contents of mixtures above 5%. i have also spoken to the car manufacturers and they assure me that 10% blends are perfectly usable with current engines without any need for change and no damage to the engine. biofuels are also a good option for improving the quality of air in our cities and, above all, for diversifying energy sources.

president of the council. - mr president, i should like to thank you for the opportunity to discuss this very topical and difficult subject with the european parliament once again. as i said in the last question on iraq on 3-4 september, this debate comes at a time of great international attention and debate on the policy towards iraq. the last time i was here i made a broad brushstroke of the developments in the situation since the gulf war. i stressed that the eu's position is clear. it was expressed in a presidency statement on 20 may this year, which stated that the eu calls on iraq to comply with the resolutions without delay, in particular allowing the return of weapons inspectors as provided for in unscr 1284. in this context, the eu welcomes the meetings between un representatives and iraq. we fully support all the efforts of the security council and the un secretary-general. this position was confirmed at the informal meeting of eu foreign ministers in helsinki on 30 and 31 august and at the meeting of foreign ministers in brussels on 30 september and 1 october. the eu also welcomes the adoption of security council resolution 1409 of 14 may, the resolution on the revision of the oil for food programme. today, with this review in mind, i shall focus on the current developments in iraq, with particular emphasis on the negotiations in the security council on a new resolution and the negotiations with iraq on the return of the weapons inspectors. negotiations are currently under way between the permanent members of the security council on a new resolution on iraq based on a us draft. the united states wants a resolution that will tighten and clarify the requirements for iraq compared with previous resolutions, set shorter deadlines for iraq's compliance with the requirements and mandate possible military action in the event of iraq's failure to comply with the requirements. the united states has stated that it wants the weapons inspectors to have unconditional access to all areas, including the so-called presidential palaces. two issues are at the heart of the debate, namely the question of a renewed mandate from the security council on the use of force and the unconditional, free and unhindered access of weapons inspectors to all installations and areas in iraq, including the presidential areas, i.e. the palaces. the eu is pleased that the issue of iraq is still being maintained in the un security council. it is hoped that the security council will reach a unanimous position on the matter. the head of the un weapons inspectors, mr hans blix of sweden, and mr el baradei, director-general of the iaea, which is in charge of the investigation into iraq's nuclear weapons programme, discussed practical arrangements for the unconditional return of the weapons inspectors with representatives of the iraqi government in vienna on 30 september and 1 october. it seems that agreement has been reached on a number of issues, based on the demands made on iraq in the already adopted security resolutions. however, the question of access to the presidential areas remains open. in addition, there are outstanding questions about how the weapons inspectors can return, including how iraqis can be questioned by unmovic and how to report to unmovic, that is to say the un weapons inspectorate. the weapons inspectors will probably not be sent to iraq until a new resolution is passed and accepted by iraq. it is still too early to determine the content of a new resolution. but it is essential that an inspection regime be established which is effective and credible. the eu attaches great importance to the continuation of the un track, both to ensure broad international support for the disarmament of iraq and for the credibility and impact of multilateral cooperation and the security council. it is positive in this context that in his speech yesterday, us president george bush again stressed the readiness of the united states to follow the path of the un. president. - mr solana, i have a question for you. but when parliament insisted on carrying out the debate in any case, i accepted the president's strong invitation to attend.
commission. – mr president, i have already spoken twice about iraq in this chamber. my last intervention was just one month ago, on 4 september, right after the informal meeting of eu ministers in elsinore. since then, iraq has, for obvious reasons, remained the most important topic of international debate, though there is not all that much of substance that the commission can add to what has just been said, or, frankly, to what is reported daily in the press. the most encouraging development since i last spoke was president bush’s speech which i heard at the un general assembly on 12 september and the presidency referred also to the speech that he has just made in cincinnati. it was important, of course, because mr bush signalled the american administration’s wish, if possible, to work through the un framework to tackle the threats posed by the iraqi regime. from all corners of the globe, leaders of the world welcomed the us decision, and virtually everyone has put strong pressure on iraq to comply with un resolutions. of particular relevance was the extent of the renewed diplomatic efforts of the arab world to press iraq to allow the resumption of the inspections. these growing pressures have clearly helped drive saddam to offer the return of the inspectors, even if his offer needs to be treated with a good deal of scepticism. we have been here with saddam hussein before, watching him in due course resile from promises made and commitments given, behind a smoke-screen of ifs, buts and maybes. the european union has warmly welcomed president bush’s decision to deal with iraq through the un system. as a union, we believe this is by far the best and incomparably the most effective way to take things forward. there is no real alternative to the un system of values and international rules that was set in place and agreed by world leaders to preserve global security. it offers the best hope of avoiding the potentially disastrous consequences of a spread of unilateral actions allegedly to ‘solve’ regional disputes. working through the un confers legitimacy and a sense of moral consensus on the actions that it is sometimes necessary to take. also in the last couple of weeks, one of the eu member states – the one as we say coyly that i know best – has made public a detailed assessment of iraq’s possession of chemical, biological and, possibly, nuclear weapons and the means to deliver them. this report has shown the risks that these weapons pose to regional stability in the middle east. a number of eminent institutes have also shared their assessments of the threats to global security posed by the iraqi regime. they all agree on saddam’s attempts to rebuild his capabilities in weapons of mass destruction, taking advantage of the absence of the inspectors over the last four years. i would like to point out, incidentally, that these inspectors had previously done a better job than they are sometimes given credit for. there may be room for debate about how imminent a danger is posed by this armoury of lethal weapons, but i do not detect any serious dispute about its existence. currently, discussions are taking place with and between eu member states on the terms of a new un security council resolution designed to pave the way for a completely unconditional return of un inspectors to iraq. as honourable members well know, there are various options under consideration, some of them at the instigation of member states. as the presidency made clear, european ministers last discussed the situation of iraq on monday 31 september at the general affairs council. they reiterated the position set out one month earlier in elsinore, including the overall aim of the elimination of weapons of mass destruction, the need for the unconditional return of un inspectors with unfettered access to every part of iraq, and the need for the situation to continue to be addressed along the un security council track. against this background of intensified international diplomacy, i believe – and i hope the parliament shares this view with me – that the following considerations should be uppermost in everybody’s minds: first, over recent weeks, leaders around the world have continued to repeat their calls for a multilateral response to the challenge posed by iraq. they have clearly argued that the alternative of a unilateral response would be very unwise. and it is not just world leaders; our citizens clearly believe strongly that this is the right way to solve the problem of iraq. recent polls in europe and the us, as well as public demonstrations, show that citizens would like any decision on iraq to be taken within the framework of the united nations system. second, the main reasoning behind any un intervention is the perception that the international community is confronted with the possession of weapons of mass destruction by a dangerous regime. there is a genuine and justified worry about both use and proliferation. in addition it has been suggested that these weapons could be supplied to terrorist networks, though some notable public figures, for example brent scowcroft, national security advisor to president bush senior, have expressed scepticism on this point. others still have argued that there may be some links between iraq and terrorist organisations with global links such as al-qa'ida. i am not aware of any convincing public evidence on this point, but perhaps i have overlooked something. the resort to the pre-emptive use of force is not a new idea. the international community for example decided to intervene in kosovo on humanitarian grounds. the concept of humanitarian interventions was supported by un secretary general kofi annan in an outstanding speech three years ago. through the action in kosovo, the international community made clear that it was no longer possible for world leaders to hide behind the concept of national sovereignty to do whatever they wished within their own borders. it was recognised that people too have rights, not just the states in which they live. that seems to me to be a welcome advance. however, what is clear from the debates going on around the world is that we need to develop some kind of framework of international law to address such circumstances. iraq cannot be seen in isolation from other equally sensitive cases. should we not look at the principles to guide our international action and identify the circumstances that may justify international intervention when there is a clear and present danger, either within a sovereign state or outside its borders? the view of international law that has more or less prevailed since the treaty of westphalia – as students of the work of dr kissinger will know – is no longer wholly valid. but i find it difficult to believe that any acceptable alternative view should not rest principally on un mechanisms and procedures. third, i am sure that those who are considering the need for a new resolution will be taking into account all options and scenarios. the international community needs to address how to frame a un security council resolution or resolutions on iraq. but they also need to think about what to do in case of non-compliance. this is a general issue of the utmost importance since it is related to the credibility of the multilateral system. we need to preserve the authority of the un and the security council whose resolutions we have seen defied again and again. in this case, it is defiance by iraq, but there are others in a similar situation of non-compliance. we have now reached the point when such lack of compliance with un decisions needs to be addressed in an objective, serious and coherent manner. i hope that as events unfold in the coming months, we see a re-assertion of the authority of the un with beneficial effects for iraq, for its region and indeed for the whole world. we may then, in addition, be able to focus our efforts more constructively on the continuing bloody crisis in the middle east. i cannot say that i find any alternative outlook anything other than profoundly disturbing. (applause)

- question no 38 by mr raimon obiols and others (h-0645/02): subject: emergency food situation in the refugee camps in tindouf in early september, statements by radhouane nouicer, head of unhcr operations in north africa and the middle east, referred to the food emergency facing the 155,000 saharawi refugees in the tindouf camps. without new food supplies, wfp estimates that during october, refugees can expect to cover only 11 percent of their daily food needs, or some 231 kilocalories per person, compared to the standard ration of flour, legumes, beans, vegetable oils and other products that provide a total of 2,100 kilocalories per day. the situation of children is particularly serious, as according to unhcr data 35% of them suffer from chronic malnutrition and 13% from rickets. despite the limited resources managed by the commission, can it make a contribution as soon as possible to prevent a food emergency whose threat is becoming more and more clear? what mechanisms can the commission use to promote new contributions to the member states' gmp?
commission. – a major part of echo's strategy is dealing with forgotten crises, and this is quite important. this is also why we are providing continued assistance to the saharawi refugees. echo is this year. while the world food programme is responsible for the basic foodstuffs echo is concentrating its assistance on supplementary food products in order to ensure a more varied diet. however, in cereals, pulses, oil and sugar, which the wfp can use in case its supplies arrive too late for distribution to the refugees, the condition being that the world food programme should undertake to programme and the unhcr issued a joint appeal for further international assistance to satisfy the needs for basic food items. while it may be correct that the wfp could cover only 11% of needs in october, it must be said that this figure relates only to deliveries from wfp and does not take account of deliveries from other donors.echo financed 300 tonnes of rice, delivered in october, and the use of the echo buffer stock i mentioned has made an important contribution, enabling us to satisfy the total needs for basic food products in october. so it is not the case that in october they only received 11%. as i have explained, the situation is much better. let me say a few words about the echo global plan for these refugees, which was adopted by the commission this year. this plan, involving an amount of eur 14.34 million, should reduce the full impact of the crisis. over 80% of the echo 2002 global plan consists of food products. under this plan, a further 5 000+ tonnes of basic foodstuffs are due to arrive in the coming weeks. in addition, over 3 000 tonnes of echo-financed supplementary food products will be supplied in the next few months. the wfp has also announced that it is sending over 4 000 tonnes of basic foodstuffs. this is the good news. nevertheless, there is still cause for concern, particularly as regards the january and february distributions, owing to the possible lack of foodstuffs to satisfy total needs in that period. there is some donor fatigue. this is the background. i agree with the question in this respect. this is also why echo is - question no 42 by mrs maría izquierdo rojo (h-0654/02) subject: discrimination in the granting of visas on the grounds of sexual orientation on 27 july 2002, the couple juan carlos manteca cendrero, a spanish national, and carlos daniel bettio, an argentine national, applied to the consulate general of spain in buenos aires (argentina) for a residence visa for family reunification, so that daniel bettio could reside legally in spain; the applicants submitted the required documents, after being informed by the consulate that visas had been granted in the past to persons in the same situation, namely same-sex couples. however, on 13 august 2002 they were informed that their visas had been refused on the ground that they 'did not fulfil the conditions laid down in dr 864/2001' and that the document, in the part reserved for the justification of the refusal, contained the following indication: 'negative opinion of the guardianship or professional authority'. whereas the particular circumstances of this case suggest that some visa refusals are aimed in particular at same-sex couples; the court held that the principle of equal treatment was thereby infringed. since this is a violation of the rights enshrined in the spanish and eu constitutions, and in particular in the amsterdam treaty, which stipulates equal rights for all individuals, regardless of their sex or sexual orientation, could the commission answer the following questions: in the face of such evidence of sex discrimination (refusal of a visa to carlos daniel bettio), would it be possible to propose a reversal of the burden of proof? is the commission aware that visa-granting gives rise to such discrimination in the eu? what actions could be taken to put an end to this? what measures are currently in place to prevent or deal with such situations?
commission - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the honourable member raises the case of the rejection of an application for a residence visa by an argentine national for family reunification in spain with his spanish partner of the same sex, which she considers to be discrimination based on sexual orientation. family reunification of union citizens not covered by community law on freedom of movement and residence, as in the present case, is not yet the subject of a community instrument and remains subject to the national law of each member state. any refusal to grant a residence visa must be contested before the competent national authorities. article 63 (3) (a) of the treaty provides that the council is to adopt measures in the field of conditions of entry and residence and standards on the procedures for issuing visas and long-stay residence permits by member states, including for the purpose of family reunification. family reunification measures must be adopted in accordance with the obligation to protect family life and the prohibition of discrimination. in its amended proposal for a council directive on family reunification, the commission, at the council's request, deleted the provision which provided for family reunification of family members of a union citizen residing in a member state of which he is a national and who has not exercised his right to free movement to be aligned with that of family members of a union citizen who has exercised his right to free movement. the situation of these people will therefore be dealt with in a specific proposal at a later stage. the community legislation currently in force on the freedom of movement and residence of union citizens and their family members provides for the family reunification of the spouse, but not of the unmarried partner. in order to take account of the rapid evolution of the family group in society and the recognition in certain member states of a special legal status for unmarried couples, as well as the need to eliminate, as far as possible, discrimination against unmarried partners of both sexes, the proposal for a directive on the right of citizens of the union and their family members to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states, adopted by the commission on 23 may 2001, extends the right to family reunification to unmarried partners if the legislation of the host member state equates the situation of unmarried couples to that of married couples and under the conditions laid down by that legislation.
- (es) mr president, i thank the commissioner, mr vitorino, for answering this question personally, orally and in plenary, because clearly the european union is leading the way on this issue. the fact that this morning in this house the european parliament adopted a motion for a resolution in favour of the right of homosexual refugee couples to family reunification is proof of this. do you think, then, commissioner, that we could apply this position to the case before us? the commissioner knows that we are referring to a current demand, and i ask him to answer, to know what we should do to contribute to obtaining positive results.
commission - mr president, as i said in my written reply, we have proposed to the council, in the framework of the directive on family reunification, a specific rule for unmarried partners, including those of the same sex. at the council's request, we have withdrawn this proposal from the directive, on the grounds that it would be preferable to deal with it in a specific legal instrument. we are now working on it, preparing such a document. i am not hiding from the honourable member that the difficulty lies in the variety of legislative solutions envisaged in the 15 member states with regard to the legal recognition of unmarried couples, in particular unmarried same-sex couples. the point is to find a balance between a non-discriminatory solution and respect for the principle of subsidiarity. we believe that there should be no discrimination against thirdcountry nationals when the national legislation of the member state provides for the recognition of comparable rights for married couples, unmarried couples, including unmarried couples of the same sex.

- question no 45 by mr richard corbett (h-0613/02): subject: livestock markets knowing that public opinion is increasingly concerned about the treatment of animals in livestock markets and slaughterhouses, is the commission now prepared to consider submitting a proposal for a directive establishing minimum standards for the protection of animals in such markets?
commission. – concerning the first part of your supplementary question as to whether it might be appropriate to phase out the livestock markets altogether, the position is that for some farm species this is a necessary marketing tool. there are long traditions in relation to the sale and marketing of animals in this way. their use derives from historic and socio-economic reasons that cannot be ignored by a simple ban. however, i agree that in addressing this issue in the context of community legislation, we are looking at it in connection with the animal transport legislation we are working on at the moment. i fully agree that this issue is not just relevant to animals under transport, but to all animals. nonetheless, it is in the context of that legislation that we are looking at the issue. as i indicated a moment ago, it is important to ensure that there is proper training of staff who handle animals, not only in the context of transport but generally. this is one of the objectives that will be contained in the legislation currently being drafted.
question no 46 by mr bushill-matthews (h-0633/02) subject: food safety could the commission indicate what immediate measures it intends to take, and how it will make them effective, to solve the recurrent problem of non-removal of the spinal cord from meat processed in slaughterhouses in germany and france?
commission. – this issue has been closely monitored and, based on the preliminary results in 2002, the actions taken by the member states have resulted in a decrease in the number of infractions concerning remnants of spinal cord. of course, the commission will continue to monitor the situation closely, and if the problems recur, will place the matter on the agenda of the standing committee on the food chain and animal health to emphasise the importance of the proper removal of specified waste material, in other words, spinal cord, at slaughterhouse level, and to require strong corrective actions. i have spoken directly to the competent ministers in a number of member states about this, with the result that licences for slaughter plants have been suspended in two particular member states for a period of time. these are strong sanctions which can be requested by the commission and which have been implemented. to that extent, i believe that the strength of such sanctions, when imposed on food processors, is that they tend to improve standards. ultimately, there is always the option of bringing infringement proceedings, but in these circumstances, given the passage of time necessary to get such proceedings into court, it does not seem to me to be the most effective method of seeking compliance. finally, as you probably are aware, i am currently working on a piece of legislation on feed and food controls, which envisages imposing financial sanctions for failure to comply with this kind of legislation. that will hopefully be brought to the commission in the very near future and, if adopted, will be made public and come to parliament in due course for further discussion.
- question no 47 by mary elizabeth banotti (h-0639/02) subject: diabetes it is estimated that by 2010 there will be 30 million diabetics in the european union. what is the commission doing about this catastrophic increase? does it envisage research or information campaigns to tackle this problem?
commission. – i can only refer to the answer to the earlier questions, that a great deal of work has already been undertaken on this and much more is in the pipeline. i mentioned earlier the work that i am currently undertaking on the connection between nutrition and, for instance, obesity and the question of good health generally. i think that the major leap forward will take place when the public health programme is up and running. i have high hopes for that programme. there are high expectations in member states, and i also believe that there is a substantial degree of support from member states' health ministers.
- as their objects are related, i call questions 48 and 49 simultaneously. question no 48 by marit paulsen (h-0660/02) subject: salmonella and meat preparations on 12 november 2001, sweden lifted the self-monitoring requirement for the presence of salmonella in meat preparations imported from another member state. this measure was adopted after the commission insisted to the swedish food agency (livsmedelsverket) that meat preparations - such as marinated chicken - were not covered by the salmonella guarantees obtained by sweden in the eu accession negotiations. during 2002, the swedish food agency and five municipalities checked for salmonella in meat preparations imported from other member states. so far, the results of this study show that about one third of the samples taken contain salmonella. is the commission really trying to make the situation with regard to the spread of salmonella worse in the eu regions which are virtually free of it, while the european union is trying to draw up a regulation to harmonize the situation in this area throughout its territory? question no 49 by mr jonas sjöstedt (h-0669/02) subject: salmonella in marinated meat of the 40 samples taken by the swedish food safety authority (livsmedelsverket) in collaboration with five swedish municipalities from imported meat preparations, about one third contained salmonella. it should be noted that the most criticism was directed at chicken products. in november 2001, the commission established that the provisions on compulsory salmonella control did not apply to meat preparations. however, when such products are imported from non-eu countries, the swedish provisions apply. the recent checks in sweden show that meat preparations should also be subject to compulsory checks in order to ensure that the country has real guarantees as regards salmonella. how does the commission intend to ensure that meat preparations are subjected as soon as possible to a mandatory control for salmonella before they are exported to sweden?
commission. – i am concerned about the frequent incidence of salmonella in meat preparations imported into sweden and about your worry that this could affect the salmonella status of sweden. as you are aware, finland and sweden were granted additional salmonella guarantees in the context of their accession to the european union. these additional guarantees cover the trade of certain live animals, eggs, fresh fish and mincemeat to finland and sweden. you propose that the commission should extend the additional salmonella guarantees to meat preparations. the only way to do so would be to amend the community legislation on meat preparations. however, the directive on mincemeat and meat preparations already lays down a salmonella criterion for meat preparations. any meat preparation produced within the community must meet that criterion.
commission. – the extension of the additional salmonella guarantees to cover mincemeat was not proposed by the commission. the reason why the additional guarantees should not cover meat preparations, the existence of the salmonella criterion, applies also to mincemeat. however, it has to be noted that it is probably easier to control salmonella in meat preparations than in mincemeat. therefore the salmonella criteria are more effective for meat preparations than for mincemeat and this can be used to justify the application of additional guarantees to mincemeat and not to meat preparations. i am sure that mrs paulsen is aware of the legislation that is going through the council at the moment which was discussed at the last meeting of the agriculture council. it ran into the buffers to some extent and now has been put back for discussion at the next agriculture council. this issue will be discussed on that occasion. meat preparations in general are being looked at, but not just for sweden and finland. we want to improve standards for the eu as a whole and that is reflected in this legislation, which i hope will get through the agriculture council in december.
commission. – as i said earlier, the commission is well aware of the dangers of salmonella. in fact, approximately 200 people a year die in the european union from contracting the disease of salmonella. in this context, it is my intention to propose improved sampling rules and a stricter limit for salmonella in meat preparations. this should contribute to decreasing the salmonella contamination in meat preparations throughout the whole community. in addition, the ongoing revisions of community legislation on food hygiene and, as i said earlier, on zoonosis, will strengthen the controls on salmonella along the whole food chain, from farm to table. this will obviously have a positive impact on the situation as regards salmonella in foodstuffs throughout the entire european union and not just in individual member states.
- question no 50 by mr joachim wuermeling (h-0673/02) subject: ban on the export of cigarettes - who framework convention on tobacco control the european parliament and the council adopted last year directive 2001/37/ec oj l 194, 18.7.2001, p. 26, which includes a ban on the export of strong cigarettes. the ban was, however, postponed until 1 january 2007, in order to reach a global agreement on maximum levels of nicotine and condensate in the meantime. where are the negotiations at the who on this point? can we expect harmonised standards by 2007? does the commission intend to propose that the export ban be waived in the event of failure to reach a global settlement?
commission. – the negotiating position of the commission is that we want to achieve the best possible outcome for public health. that is the overriding consideration. it will be the motivation for me and my staff in negotiating on behalf of the eu, where the issue is within community competence. the question whether production will shift to third countries is often raised. in other words, are jobs going to be affected by this? i have two answers to that question. first of all, public health cannot take second place to job considerations. that is fundamental as far as i am concerned. i have already said that on a number of occasions. even if there were concern about jobs, some work was undertaken on this when the legislation we now have before parliament was being considered. there was certainly some evidence available to us in those member states that introduced, for instance, strict legislation banning the advertising of tobacco products. unemployment did not increase as a result. there was a shift in other directions. therefore, i have never seen any convincing evidence that introducing legislation of this type would have adverse effects on employment.
