the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the fourth point in the community strategy on health and safety 2002-06 which we have just discussed calls for the extension of the scope of framework directive 89/391/eec - excluded groups of workers - and, among other things, refers to work carried out by the selfemployed. the recommendation i am asked to present and which we are debating in the european parliament calls for the protection of employees in the field of occupational safety and health to be extended to selfemployed workers. we start from the fact that workers who are engaged in their professional activity outside an employment relationship with an employer or an employer are not, in general, protected by the community directives on health and safety at work. in fact, only three directives refer to them, sometimes tangentially - in particular council directive 92/57/eec on the minimum safety and health requirements for temporary or mobile construction works - and take account of the selfemployed persons who work there in so far as they may, as a result of that activity, constitute a potential source of risk for non-selfemployed workers also on the site. that is, risks caused by the autonomous but not protected. council directive 92/29/eec on the minimum safety and health requirements for improved medical care on board ships is not a specific directive of 89/391/eec and what is said for 92/57/eec also applies to it. and the most recent directive, 2001/45/ec of the european parliament and of the council of 27 june 2001 amending council directive 89/655/eec on the minimum safety and health requirements for the use of work equipment by workers at work, refers in one of its recitals to the selfemployed, recalling that when they personally use work equipment they can put the safety and health of employees at risk, as if the selfemployed were only considered a risk element but not worthy of coverage for the same risks, as if they were not really considered a worker. a large majority of member states do not provide legal protection for health and safety for selfemployed workers, thus resulting in a great diversity and heterogeneity of levels of protection. the measures and decisions against the conversion of risk into loss have traditionally been linked to the concept of the employed person, perhaps because the selfemployed person should be concerned himself with his own safety and health, an insufficient and unjustified reasoning. it therefore seems that action at community level is required to ensure a minimum of protection for the selfemployed against occupational risks, because, alongside the selfemployed worker isolated in the workshop of one or more selfemployed persons, the evolution of the employment structure, when undertakings subcontract tasks to micro-enterprises or to selfemployed persons, gives rise to new problems of safety at work: the safety of the selfemployed person and that of the employed or selfemployed persons associated with him. all workers deserve protection. the selfemployed person is thus exposed to the same risks as the employed person, but his lack of training and information can also cause accidents or injuries to himself and to other employees or selfemployed persons. the problem is much broader, ladies and gentlemen, and concerns the development of the organization of work in the face of the use of workers hired by temporary employment agencies, the partitioning of the production process and their allocation to contracts, subcontractors and selfemployed workers, and, in general, the methods of decentralizing production or outsourcing. in my view, and i think in everyone's, the protection of workers in the field of occupational health cannot depend on the legal status of each worker exposed to the risks, whether self-employed, employed or salaried. the bill of rights makes no distinction. every worker has the right to work in conditions which respect his health, safety and dignity, says the charter. where the law doesn't discriminate, neither should we. the procedure for implementation is a recommendation which should facilitate the step and process, the objective of which is clear, of the implementation and, therefore, the mandatory submission of the selfemployed or independent worker to the same rules as those applicable to the employed worker. the culture of prevention is of course given new meaning and significance here. in many cases, the selfemployed person, who is the main beneficiary, will have to invest in protective equipment, while in others he will have to obtain information and training. without going into questions such as those relating to the liability of certain accident cases, i think that the constant and obstinate fight against accidents has a new actor within the collective scenario: the one marked by a culture of prevention in which the protagonists are the workers themselves and the authorities.

- question no 12 by mr lennart sacrédeus (h-0629/02) subject: granting of a privileged neighbourhood to ukraine at the eu-ukraine summit in copenhagen last july, ukraine was promised "privileged neighbour status" with the eu. this is a new concept which now needs to be defined. so what does such a status imply in practice? will ukraine be subject to the same conditions as belarus, for example? will the above status apply to all countries which, after enlargement, will share a common border with the european union?
the council. - mr president, i should like to answer mr sacrédeus' question on the ukraine. at the eu-ukraine summit in copenhagen this summer, ukraine was informed of the council decision of april to identify the possibility of strengthening relations between the future enlarged union and its new neighbours. both sides stressed the importance of taking account of the different nature and level of political and economic development of relations between the eu and the countries concerned. the eu and ukraine agreed that the enlargement process creates new opportunities and challenges in different areas. both sides confirmed that ukraine could make the most of these opportunities by intensifying work on the alignment of its legislation, norms and standards with those of the eu. it was also agreed to intensify discussions in the relevant partnership and cooperation bodies on the implications of enlargement for, inter alia, trade-related issues, the movement of persons, visas and the promotion of regional and crossborder cooperation. the eu recognises the european aspirations of ukraine. it is important that ukraine does better in meeting its obligations if these aspirations are to have any real content. the eu will continue to support ukraine in the reform process, including the strengthening of the judiciary, media freedom, human rights and civil society. the danish presidency feels it is its duty to intensify eu-ukraine cooperation. the work plan for implementing the eu's common strategy for ukraine was submitted to the council, which took note of it on 22 july this year. the presidency believes that the eu's overall objective should be to make dialogue and cooperation with ukraine more targeted and result-oriented. the priorities of this work plan are: firstly, consolidation of democracy, the rule of law and public institutions; secondly, support for the economic transition process, including ukraine's integration into the european and world economies and regional cross-border cooperation with neighbouring countries; thirdly, cooperation to strengthen stability and security within and outside europe; fourthly, strengthening cooperation in the fields of the environment, energy and nuclear security; fifthly, support for enhanced cooperation in the context of eu enlargement; and, sixthly, strengthening cooperation in the fields of justice and home affairs. the development of a comprehensive eu policy towards the eu's new neighbours, with full respect for the differences between the countries involved, will help to achieve the overall objectives. on 30 september, on the basis of a joint statement by the high representative, mr solana, and commissioner patten, the council discussed relations between the enlarged union and its eastern neighbours. the council reaffirmed its conviction that enlargement would provide a good opportunity to strengthen relations between the union and its new neighbours with a view to creating stability and reducing the wealth gap at the eu's new frontiers.
the council. i'd like to thank mr. sacrédeus for his great interest in ukraine. it is important that we remember ukraine, which is a very important country in europe. i would like to congratulate parliament on the report on ukraine, which - if i remember correctly - was adopted about a year ago. i would add that the danish presidency expects the council to ask the commission this year to put forward proposals for the development of a comprehensive eu policy towards the eu's new neighbours, and it is safe to say that ukraine is a very important nation among these neighbours.
the council. - mr president, given the historical background that we all know, there is no doubt that nuclear safety will be part of any discussion between the eu and ukraine.

(es) mr president, in this year 2002, when the international community has met in succession in monterrey, rome and johannesburg, highlighting as a priority the challenge of lifting two thirds of humanity out of the situation of hunger, poverty and underdevelopment in which they find themselves, it seemed necessary for the european parliament to reflect and take a stand on how to support policies of the european union and also, of course, the community's agricultural policies. for many years, the socialists have considered that the yardstick for judging any community policy was what it did for social cohesion. we therefore considered a particular policy to be positive because of the added value it provided in terms of the cohesion of our societies and negative if it contributed to increasing inequalities between europeans. the european union is not a political entity, but a political entity. and so each community policy will merit our favourable judgment in so far as it contributes not only to social cohesion within our borders but also to reducing inequalities in its global projection. we have seen the common agricultural policy as a positive thing because it supported our farmers, so that they were not left behind in a process of prosperity from which other sectors of society were benefiting. but in future, when we assess the community's agricultural policies, it will not be enough to measure whether they contribute to maintaining or improving the situation of our farmers and stockbreeders. we must also consider whether subsidies to our producers are also helping to improve the situation in the third world or whether, on the contrary, they are ruining the third world by widening the gulf between it and our developed world. in this case, those policies will not be acceptable and, however difficult the exercise, we must find other policies which are good, fair and rebalancing for the north, while at the same time being good and fair for the south and rebalancing in terms of south-north relations. in this context, we shall vote in favour of the resolution proposed by the committee on development and cooperation as a conclusion to the report by mr khanbhai.

- the agenda calls for the commission statement on the 12th conference of the parties to the convention on international trade in endangered species of wild fauna and flora (cites).
- (es) mr president, i shall refer to paragraph 3 of this motion for a resolution, and specifically to the species scientific name dissostichus, which in the spanish version is the southern and black hake. dissostichus has great commercial value (it is called "black gold") and its balance is very delicate. the committee on fisheries, of which i am a member, is preparing three reports on this matter and i am the rapporteur on the one concerning the development of a catch documentation system. i would like to defend its non-inclusion in the cites list before this house today for the following reasons: we cannot forget that there is already an international organization - the convention for the conservation of antarctic marine resources, which i shall hereinafter call camelar - which has been successfully working for the last 20 years to preserve this and other species in the antarctic ocean. the community is a contracting party to that convention. the proposal to include dissostichus in the cites convention was not made by us, but by australia. neither we nor - as far as i know - the commission are opposed to this; we simply think it more useful for camelar itself to take this decision at its annual meeting, which is being held this week and next in chile, and at which the european parliament will be represented by mr stevenson, chairman of the committee on fisheries. at the moment, and after arduous negotiations, camelar has succeeded in gaining the admission of canada and mauritius as associate members. canada is, along with the united states, the main commercial destination for dissostichus and mauritius is an important transit point. his entry into camelar gives this international organization control of 98% of the world's dissostichus trade. for us, cites would be useful as a complementary value to camelar. but we must be careful, because if we anticipate the natural course of events with our decision, we could unintentionally cause the opposite of what we want, weaken an organization which, in its long life, has amply demonstrated its good practice in the highly sensitive antarctic marine environment. we must concentrate our efforts, not disperse them, and we must strengthen our presence in the multilateral fisheries organizations, the only way to respond to the challenges posed by the conservation of fisheries species worldwide.
commission. – mr president, i would like to conclude with two short remarks on elephants and toothfish. first, i would like to reassure you that the commission remains opposed to any measures that could increase the illegal killing of elephants. i have already stated that we are opposed to the resumption of the commercial ivory trade until it can be demonstrated that this will not lead to an increase in poaching. at the same time, i acknowledge the excellent record of a number of southern african countries in managing their elephant populations. it is easy to understand why these countries sometimes feel they are penalised rather than rewarded for their efforts. if their concerns are not addressed, there is a real risk that these countries will be unable to maintain popular support for elephant conservation or for cites in general. we should avoid measures such as the proposed stricter classification for elephants in cites which will only serve to polarise the debate, without achieving any real additional protection for these animals. on toothfish, we must respect the competence of camlar and other fisheries organisations, at the same time taking a constructive approach to any proposals that might achieve better protection for commercial fish species. accordingly, if cites listing can strengthen and complement camlar's current management of toothfish you may rest assured that it will have my support and that of the commission.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-320/2002), on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the common position adopted by the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council decision adopting a community programme to improve the functioning of tax systems in the internal market (fiscalis programme 2003-2007) (10612/2/2002 - c5-0383/2002 - 2002/0015 (cod)). the rapporteur, mr garcía-margallo y marfil, has the floor.
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the common position we are discussing has a short but intense history. in 1998, this parliament and the council adopted a programme designed to improve the functioning of tax systems within the internal market. only a year ago, in 2001, an evaluation of the first three years of operation of this system was made. i am pleased to say that the development was satisfactory and that this programme itself was subject to that evaluation. this year we were presented with a proposal from the commission to extend the programme - which will expire on new year's eve this year - for another five years, until 2007. the new features of the programme which will be in force for the next five years (fiscalis 2007) compared with the previous one are, in my view, two: it is being extended to cover direct taxes - which is good news - and to cover the needs of the candidate countries, which is even better news. the general objectives of the fiscalis 2007 programme which we are now examining are, in my view, three: firstly, it is proposed that the tax systems of the member states should function; secondly, that this better functioning should be achieved through cooperation between the tax administrations responsible for implementing it; and thirdly, that this better functioning through cooperation should serve to eradicate fraud. as regards the first idea, namely that tax systems should work, this programme is not about taking another step in fiscal harmonization - as the commission and, explicitly, the council have stated - although i would have liked a little more ambition, a more decisive step in the process of community harmonization. secondly, as regards cooperation, it is an idea which is repeated in all the commission's documents. administrative cooperation was mentioned in the 1987 proposals for vat at source, in the 1996 programme, in the new vat strategy of 2000, in the monti code for the reform of direct taxes, etc. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to promote the use of the euro, and i am pleased to see that the commission is now taking a number of initiatives to promote the use of the euro. i cannot agree more with these three objectives, but i have to make some remarks on the specific objectives in the field of vat and in the field of direct taxation. we tabled amendments at first reading which we did not want to reproduce at second reading, in honour of the commissioner. the urgent need now is for this programme to be approved so that it can enter into force on 1 january 2003 - otherwise it would be obsolete - and we have sacrificed some legitimate aspirations which, however, i would like to recall here, because we will repeat them at another time. the fiscalis 2007 programme on vat says that it is good to know how it works, and this desire for knowledge, cooperation and coordination goes hand in hand with the four objectives set out in the 2003 vat strategy: simplification, modernisation, applying the tax in the most uniform way possible and increased cooperation between the various administrations. however, commissioner, i regret that this programme has not been used to take the transition to vat at source a step further. in all the commission's documents it is repeated over and over again that the internal market will only work well - or work better, if you prefer - with vat at source. we are also told that if we are not moving towards vat at source, it is because the member states do not trust the system of compensation and the system of reallocation of resources, which was initially based on taxpayer declarations and then on statistical data, but which has never satisfied the member states. we should have gone ahead with this programme to know the data and the framework which, while making compensation possible, would also have made possible the desired transition to vat at source. in the field of direct taxation, the opportunity has not been taken to go into the relationship between tax policy and other community policies in greater depth, as the amendment said, which we did not want to repeat. it is well known that tax policy is instrumental in relation to these other policies; i will give only three examples: the commissioner is well aware that in the financial services action plan it was said that progress had to be made in parallel in the liberalization of the sector, in the rules of supervision and control - now so well known after the enron case - and in the harmonization of indirect taxes, so that liberalization did not result in a centralization of financial activities in the most tax-friendly climates or countries. as regards the competition rules, there is an obvious link - especially as regards state aid - with tax policy. the code of good practice, which is part of the monti package, referred to fiscal distortions that could disrupt the functioning of the single market. sustainable development - we have had a debate on this - is closely linked to energy taxes. our amendment therefore recommended that this programme of exchange of information, knowledge and training should be used to enable a better understanding of tax policy and other union policies. the commission has not taken advantage of this visit to advance knowledge of the facts which would have made possible the transition to vat at source, which is still the lost paradise we all want to reach, and has not taken advantage of the opportunity to promote knowledge of and the interrelationship between tax policy and the other community policies which it wants to serve. i would like to stress, however, that the general objectives of the programme seem to me to be good: to know how tax systems work and to cooperate between administrations in order to eradicate fraud. i think it is right that this programme should be launched as soon as possible and that is why, commissioner, we are giving you a vote of confidence by not repeating the amendments we tabled at first reading, in order to avoid a conciliation process and so that this programme - which i am sure the commissioner will manage very well - can be launched as soon as possible. i am not reluctant to raise the other objectives at other times, but i believe that prudence and urgency are more important at this moment than the value and the improvement of the programme. commissioner, i wish you the best of luck with your application.

- doc. b5-0492/02 by mr de gucht, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, to the commission, on the commission's strategy for the new delhi conference on climate change.
commission. – mr president, thank you for those very valid questions on cop 8 as it is called, which i will try to answer as clearly as possible. first of all, after bonn and marrakech, cop 8 is an opportunity to reinforce the commitments from developed countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and repeat calls on those countries that have not yet ratified the kyoto protocol to do so in the near future. the discussions at cop 8 in india will first of all deal with progress on implementation. that is to establish the state of play. the concerns of developing countries relate to adaptation to climate change and the initiation of a process for further action to be taken after 2012, for a second commitment period. the progress of the conference will be detailed in a daily declaration. however, if you ask how important this conference is compared with the others, i can say that no negotiations on major issues of substance are foreseen. so there is a difference between previous cop meetings and this one. this is not to say that it is not important, but it is not at the level of true negotiations as yet. we can expect the developing countries to remind the industrialised world of our obligations under the climate convention when it comes to helping them in capacity building and adaptation to climate change. the european union, together with other developed countries, wants to have an initial discussion on the process for deciding on further action for the second commitment period and to initiate this process in new delhi. the environment council also called upon other countries to engage in a dialogue on this question last week. i can anticipate that the role of the european union will be to try to build bridges between japan, the united states and other countries which would like to push the developing countries to move towards quantified commitments for the second commitment period, as of now. the developing countries are opposed to that and, of course, argue from a political standpoint that it is our role to lead the way, to show that we are serious about getting our greenhouse gas emissions down, before they will accept anything that could hamper their development. so this debate will probably start, but we in the european union have said that we should concentrate on establishing the process, because our first objective is for the kyoto protocol to enter into force. we should not let anything stop us from reaching that goal. the commission together with member states will use cop 8 to emphasise the importance of implementing the kyoto protocol and the agreements reached in bonn and marrakech. we welcome the various points raised in the european parliament resolution of 2 october and we will take them on board as far as possible. one issue that we will pursue at cop 8 is also a follow-up to the coalition of the willing on renewable energy that the european union launched in johannesburg. we will discuss the way forward with like-minded countries and encourage others to join in. as you know, the kyoto protocol will enter into force once 55 parties representing at least 55% of the emissions of annex 1 have ratified the protocol. so far, 95 countries representing 37.1% of emissions have ratified the kyoto protocol, representing around two thirds of the world population. the speed of ratification, and this concerns your second question, mrs jackson, increased before and during the world summit in johannesburg. such events often trigger this kind of reaction. that is fine, but the important thing is to get the countries to ratify the protocol and to make progress in implementing it. canada and russia said, during the world summit, that they intent to ratify it, while major developing countries, such as china, india and brazil, have by now done so. i would say that what is most important now is to continue to put pressure on russia, because we know that the ratification by russia, which represents 17.4% of emissions, is vital to reach the 55% threshold needed for the kyoto protocol to enter into force. we are, of course, in contact with the russian authorities and we are closely following progress on ratification in russia. my colleague and i have urged other parties, with whom we have bilateral meetings, to ratify the kyoto protocol and we are continuing to do so. we have done all we can, travelling around the world talking to australia and other countries in the everyday bilateral context, drawing attention to this issue and to the importance of ratifying the kyoto protocol. so we are continuing to call on the us and australia to return to the kyoto process. the european climate change programme mrs jackson referred to was launched on 8 march 2000 and has identified key elements for a cost-effective eu-wide strategy to combat climate change. our communication last year outlined a first package of ten measures with a cost-effective reduction potential of between 122 and 178 million tonnes of co2 equivalent. that is nearly halfway towards our kyoto target of -8%. the commission has already presented proposals for a number of these measures, including an eu emissions trading scheme, the energy performance of buildings, co-generation and a strategy to increase the use of biofuels in road transport. others, such as legislation on minimum energy efficiency standards for end use equipment or the promotion of energy services and on fluorinated gases, are in the pipeline. but is true that some of our member states will have to take serious steps to deal with the current trend when it comes to greenhouse gas emissions. you cannot afford to be lax in that area. transport has been identified as one of the more intractable sectors, with carbon dioxide emissions from transport the fastest growing, despite the progress made through our agreement with the european automobile manufacturers association. the commission has indicated that changes in current mobility patterns need to be a high priority. turning to the role of meps, the meps i met yesterday, who will be in the delegation going to india, find it frustrating that often they are in the same group as the ngos. as observers, they will not have access to the negotiations or to the round table discussions in new delhi. we have had members of the european parliament in the european communities delegation at previous cops in bonn and marakesh. on both occasions i appreciated and enjoyed the outstanding cooperation with the ep delegation. it has been very helpful to have the members of the european parliament present and active on those occasions and at bilateral meetings with other parliamentarians. in a letter to president cox, the commission president, mr prodi, recently confirmed commission. – mr president, thank you for these valuable contributions to this debate. i would like to comment on some of the points that have been raised. first of all, what can we do to influence russia and to push for ratification from the russian side? it is difficult to talk to the russians. we have for some time now been planning a troika visit to russia and we are continuing to plan for that visit because we want to meet the right people. we want to have it at a high political level in order to have a meaningful discussion. in all bilateral talks, including those between commissioner prodi and prime minister putin, climate change and the kyoto protocol have been on the agenda. of course we raise this issue in all our bilateral contacts. we are also aware of a study that has just been published by the russian government on the ratification of the kyoto protocol. we are currently analysing the results – hopefully we will be able to use some of them in our ongoing debate. we are keeping a close eye on what happens in russia, in order to be able to use the positive forces that exist in russia. in the end, i suppose that it is prime minister putin who will decide. what about a wto initiative? that has not yet been included in our plans at all. maybe that is a good idea. i have not though about it enough to give you a really considered answer today, but i am worried about anything that could complicate or halt the implementation of the kyoto protocol. we should be very careful not to raise the issue in such a way that we create more stumbling blocks in the debate on the entry into force of the kyoto protocol. i would be happy to come back to the debate on the wto and the links between these issues. what happens in the second commitment period? first of all, we are interested in establishing the process in delhi and cop8. it is too early and in view of the risk of complicating the whole debate on the entry into force of the kyoto protocol, we want first of all to establish the process and decide how to get to the second commitment period. it seems a little pointless to go into the details on that before the kyoto protocol has even entered into force. so first things first. we have to stick to that strategy at cop8 as well. there was one question on air traffic. of course the commission and the european union are working within icao, because this is clearly an international issue. i am sure we would all agree that the work in icao has not been satisfactory when it comes to speed and commitment, but it also has a unccc mandate to work on the climate change issue. this is an area where we can hopefully do more, but we will have to continue to work in an international context. finally, what about equal rights per world citizen? the ultimate goal is to stabilise concentrations in the atmosphere at harmless levels. remember that. we need to reduce emissions as a result. i believe this will lead to convergence of per capita emissions internationally. whether equal rights is the right target, i cannot say. i do not want to say to the european parliament that it is a ridiculous idea, but my personal opinion is that it might not be the most sensible approach. it is a moral concept rather than an environmental measure. our main objective is to protect the environment. that, i believe, is how we should formulate it. we emit eight times more, on average, than an indian citizen. how do we create equal rights for citizens throughout the world? i would like to approach it from an environmental point of view, so that we make sure that we stabilise concentrations in the atmosphere at harmless levels. i hope you understand my argument. perhaps this is something which requires further debate. we have an important role to play in new delhi, in the cop8 discussions, because we can definitely work with the developing countries. we will probably be the bridge between g77, china and the developed countries in the debate on how to deal with climate change.

the commission (es) mr president, first of all, this shows that there are no double standards. in other words, what we are doing is transposing into community law, or proposing to make community law, the rules and standards which, in the negotiations, it has been agreed to require of the applicant countries. we have asked the applicant countries to do so and we are simply going to make sure that the same requirement applies to the countries of the union. in this connection, i would like to recall that in 1999 the council expressed its opinion on the need to establish maximum requirements and guarantees for nuclear installations within the european union. i would remind you that the laeken council specifically asked for regular reports on the state of nuclear safety in the union. these proposals are our response to this. and, to answer a question that's been asked before. article 15 provides that the member states are to inform the commission every year of the measures taken to comply with the requirements and that the commission is to report every two years to parliament and the council on the general situation in the european union. in other words, there are annual national reports from the states to the commission and the commission, with these reports and with cross checks, what is called 'peer review', checks between peers, produces a report every two years to parliament and the council on the development and the safety situation in nuclear installations, not just nuclear power stations, which exist in the european union. another question that has been raised is whether countries can refuse to receive nuclear waste that they do not want. of course, as long as they're not their own. in principle, each country has an obligation to take care of its own nuclear waste. this is the rule that binds us all today. and that rule remains as a basic principle, which does not mean that if, voluntarily, two or three countries agree to share some facilities, some repositories, they cannot do so. we open the possibility - particularly in view of the fact that there are some countries in the european union which are small in size, with very significant geological difficulties and therefore with difficulties in building the necessary infrastructure on their territory - that they may eventually seek an agreement with a third country. and if they do not, they will have to take the waste back to their own country, that is clear. no one will be forced to take in waste from third countries, no one. what we are proposing is that different countries can agree to joint storage, but always on the basis of voluntary agreements. the agreement with russia does not deal with the export of materials by the european union. we are proposing the opposite. the situation, ladies and gentlemen, is very briefly that russia is currently supplying fissile material to nineteen nuclear power stations in the applicant countries, which means an activity in a number of russian industrial plants, an income and technological and industrial development around this activity. the fact that the installations in these countries have technical characteristics means that the best supplies are logically coming from where they have come from, namely from russian industry. that is the situation in the candidate countries. on the other hand, in the case of the present 15 member states, we have a limit, in order to guarantee security of supply, on the volume of imports from a single country. the maximum limit, imposed by the corfu agreement, is 20% of the nuclear fuel needed. obviously, we're, more or less, around that number. but if we take in the 19 reactors in the candidate countries, we will clearly exceed that limit. that is what we have to deal with. so what we are talking about in the agreement with russia is that they are selling fissile material to a number of countries which could have problems when they join the european union if the current rules are not changed. what we want in return for this negotiation is to also agree with the russians on improving nuclear safety in russia and, in particular, on the closure of the first generation russian nuclear power stations. this is the second element we want to introduce in our relations and in our structured energy dialogue with russia in the course of these negotiations. as regards financial coverage, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has also today approved an increase in the margin for euratom loans. the measure would make available eur 2 billion. right now we're almost running out of the existing line. this new margin does not imply, and let me be very clear, that there will be many more credits in circulation. most of the loans have already been used and even written off by the borrowers of the loans. but what is needed, according to the rules of euratom loans, is to open new facilities, to widen the margin so that there can be a margin for the decommissioning of the plants, for example in lithuania or slovenia, or for the improvement of safety in those plants. we believe that euratom loans are an appropriate instrument. in any case, i would like to say to you, ladies and gentlemen, that i have said here and in the commission on several occasions that the european union must become aware of and take decisions on the cost of decommissioning some nuclear power stations in eastern countries, in countries which are to become members of the european union. we all know that the closure of the power stations is going to be accelerated and that no decommissioning fund has been set up, that they have no money for decommissioning. this is a very complicated problem. there was talk of a donors' club to finance the dismantling of these plants, but the reality is that the funds generated by this donors' club are rather scarce, if not zero. this is something i have pointed out, which concerns me greatly and which will have to be dealt with. as regards the question of the swedish example, i shall not dwell on joint storage. i have already indicated what the approach is. as far as denmark is concerned, this is a country that is indeed in difficulty, but lithuania, for example, has a very serious problem because of its size, geological composition and location.

- the oral question (o-0071/02 - b5-0493/02) by mr daul, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the mid-term review of the common agricultural policy; the council statement on the mid-term review of the common agricultural policy. mr daul has the floor.
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i am pleased to have the opportunity today to present my assessment of the decisions taken at the brussels summit on agricultural policy. the commission launched a wide-ranging debate on the future of agricultural policy in july with the publication of the mid-term review. the european council has now given additional answers to some budgetary questions for the future common agricultural policy. the importance of the summit decisions lies firstly in the fact that they paved the way for the conclusion of enlargement negotiations by the member states and that the 15 heads of state or government accepted the commission's proposal for the phasing-in of direct payments in the agricultural sector in the new member states. if the candidate countries show the same realism, then the copenhagen summit should be able to conclude the enlargement negotiations. but the decisions taken in brussels will also have a significant impact on future agricultural policy. the first thing to be said is that we have a budgetary framework for market organisation expenditure and direct payments for the period 2007 to 2013, which has been pre-fixed by the eu-15. this framework consists of the eu-15's 2006 expenditure forecast and the 2006 financial proposals for the 10 new members in nominal terms. these are then increased by only 1% each year. this means that two thirds of the implementation of the agenda 2000 reforms in the milk sector, which has not yet started, will have to be financed under the new ceiling in 2007 and 2008. the phasing-in of direct payments under this new ceiling must also be financed at 70%. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the old agricultural guideline is no longer valid. but it's not working now. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. what does this mean for the mid-term review? the presidency's conclusions state that the decisions taken in brussels do not prejudge future decisions on the common agricultural policy, nor the mid-term review agreed in berlin, nor our international commitments, such as those we made in doha. we are therefore obliged to continue to take account of the decisions of the heads of state and government in berlin and gothenburg. in this context, it is noteworthy that the brussels summit did not limit the funding for rural development. on the contrary, it has reminded us of the importance of the less-favoured regions and of the multifunctionality of agriculture, in other words, of the need to strengthen the second pillar, which the european parliament has repeatedly called for. i therefore expect that the european parliament will make its wishes clear when it adopts the new financial perspective for the period after 2006, in which it has a full say, unlike the common agricultural policy. the fact that the conclusions explicitly mention the european union's commitments arising from the launch of the doha development round is interpreted by some as meaning that the proposal to decouple direct payments has been buried. i warn you against adopting such a view. if the international negotiations lead to a commitment to reduce the blue box, to which the european union and all the other wto members agreed in principle in doha and to which the council reiterated its commitment at the johannesburg summit on sustainability, this would mean abandoning direct payments at least in part, because the option of decoupling would then no longer be open. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. what will be the impact of the mid-term review on the agricultural sector? this frequently asked question was the subject of a first qualitative assessment by the commission in its communication entitled 'towards sustainable agriculture - a mid-term review of the common agricultural policy', based on internal analyses. these focused on the benefits for farmers, consumers, taxpayers, citizens, the food industry and administrations, and the contribution the proposals would make to the enlargement process and the eu's position in the international arena. in addition, this analysis was complemented in the mid-term review communication by the medium-term forecasts for agricultural markets and by reports on the rice, nuts and milk sectors published by the directorate-general for agriculture in june. an internal study on the impact of eu enlargement on agricultural markets and incomes in the candidate countries was published in march. in addition, the directorate-general for agriculture is currently carrying out a comprehensive analysis of the potential impact of the specific policy proposals, the results of which will be presented at the end of the year together with the planned legal texts. we will of course take full account of the decisions taken in brussels. let me say a few words about the european parliament's draft resolution. i share your view that we need to ensure that our policy instruments are balanced and consistent with the objectives of our policy. i welcome your offer to work together to ensure that in an enlarged europe the european agricultural model is developed and strengthened, but also protected. i share your view that we need to better integrate non-trade issues into multilateral agreements. but we, as negotiators for the european union, can only achieve this if we have sufficient negotiating capital. secondly, we recognise that more quality, certification, audits and so on will bring additional costs to our farmers, especially the smaller farmers. for these reasons, our proposals for decoupling and strengthening the second pillar are crucial to the preservation of the european agricultural model. i am also very open to suggestions from parliament on how to increase the role of women in agriculture. clearly defined farm management conditions in the form of cross compliance are, in my view, an essential element in bringing the common agricultural policy back into line with the wishes of the citizens, and i also fully share the wish of parliament to provide for simple and efficient procedures for these audits. simplification will remain a key objective overall, but quality must be demonstrable and verifiable to remain credible. as i said before, i expect the european parliament to give its wishes a boost when it comes to the second pillar. i am not saying that the commission has not taken the necessary steps to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not affected by the crisis. this would greatly enhance the public value of the cap. we must now seize the opportunity to strengthen a sustainable agricultural policy, bring it into line with the expectations of society and provide a long-term policy perspective for farmers. i'm counting on your support! president of the council. - mr president, first of all i should like to thank you for giving me the opportunity to explain to the european parliament the work of the council on the mid-term review. as agreed in agenda 2000, the commission presented the mid-term review of the cap on 10 july this year. one of the main priorities of the danish presidency has been to ensure that the mid-term review of the cap is discussed as far as possible. commissioner fischler presented his reflection paper on the future development of the common agricultural policy at a council meeting on 15 july. on this occasion, the council held an open debate in which the member states were given the opportunity to express their immediate views on the commission's ideas. the danish presidency has placed the mid-term review discussion on the agenda of all council meetings in july, september and october, and the council has thus had a thorough debate on all the main topics of the commission's reflection paper. in addition, the paper has also been discussed in the special committee on agriculture and in a number of relevant working groups. the conclusions of the brussels summit stressed, as the commissioner also said in his speech, that it does not prejudge the future decision on a common agricultural policy and on the financing of the eu after 2006, or any results resulting from the implementation of point 22 of the conclusions on the berlin agenda, i.e. agenda 2000, and without prejudice to the international commitments the eu has entered into, in particular in connection with the launch of the doha round. in other words, the mid-term review will continue immediately as part of agenda 2000. i would like to emphasize that from the outset we knew, as did the european parliament and other institutions, that our discussions on the reflection paper were to form the basis for the presentation of legal proposals by the commission at a later stage. the presidency has therefore organised general discussions in which the ministers have had the opportunity to express their different views on all aspects of the commission's communication. before i begin my examination, i should like to thank the european parliament for its consideration of the matter. we look forward to the final decision of parliament tomorrow, and it is clear that the decision will be extremely important, an important contribution to the debate. there is no reason to conceal the fact that the reactions of the ministers to the mid-term review have been divergent from the outset, both in terms of timing and framework and, of course, also in terms of content. in general, however, i have been able to see, as president of the agriculture and fisheries council, a broad consensus that rural policy should be strengthened and that greater emphasis should be placed on food security, environmental protection and animal welfare. i would now like to make a few comments on the main elements of the commission's communication in the light of the discussions we have had in the council. the mid-term review contains two fundamental horizontal aspects, namely the decoupling of direct aid and dynamic modulation. the commission's ideas in this area have been more far-reaching than we have seen in the past. the council had its first general discussion of these aspects in july and now more technical discussions of the individual elements are pending. as regards decoupling, i can say that the delegations have expressed a great need for further information from the commission in the form of impact assessments, which relate to both the economic, social and regional effects of the proposal before a final position can be taken. on the other hand, some delegations also support the basic principle of decoupling. they believe that this will allow farmers to focus on products which give them the best return on sales, without the limitation of the amount of aid for each product. it is also considered to be an effective signal to send, both to consumers and to taxpayers. finally, they also point to the negotiating advantages of moving to a decoupling system in the context of the wto. it could also be an important step towards understanding the eu's other negotiating objectives. as regards dynamic modulation, a number of ministers have welcomed the proposal in principle. they consider this to be a good way of securing the necessary funding to strengthen priority objectives in food safety, quality, the environment and animal welfare and other important areas. other ministers have criticised dynamic modulation for actually leading to a real progressive reduction in aid and for not taking sufficient account of existing regional disparities when excluding franchising and capping. the delegations also have differing views on the reduction of the first pillar and on how the modulated funds should be distributed afterwards and on the criteria for this. i will comment on the more specific market sectors. we had a full debate on the main crops at the september council and, although the commission's general direction could be supported to some extent, there were clearly specific proposals which met with strong resistance. thus, various groups of delegations made strong arguments against a reduction in the intervention price for cereals, the abolition of the monthly cereal surcharges, the abolition of the intervention system for rye, the proposed changes to the durum wheat schemes and the proposed ecological set-aside, and against the commission's proposed change in the aid for energy crops. the commission communication was also accompanied by detailed reports on rice, nuts and milk. the council also had a full debate on these matters at its october meeting. as regards rice and nuts, there was a clear division of opinion, based, of course, on whether or not one was a producer of the products in question. however, as far as rice is concerned, there was broad agreement in principle on the need for change in the sector - the adoption of the 'everything but arms' initiative makes this inevitable. however, a number of ministers from producer countries have expressed dissatisfaction with the concrete measures proposed by the commission, while non-producing countries have regarded the commission's approach as a step in the right direction. as regards milk, the commission has presented four options for the dairy sector for the period 2008-2015. those options have been discussed with the result that, apart from option 3, i.e. the one with a and c quotas, they are unlikely to be considered due to the uncertainty as to their compatibility with wto rules. in this context, it was considered appropriate to further consider the situation. as regards nuts, the producer countries have also clearly expressed the need for special support for this sector. ladies and gentlemen, the commission's initiative to strengthen rural policy is welcomed by the member states. however, as i have already said, there is no agreement on the choice of means to achieve the objective, and the debate in the council revealed divergent positions on, among other things, the choice of instruments and the allocation of funds. but the debate was extremely positive in the sense that there is a broad consensus that something must be done in this area, including that there is a great need for simplification of the arrangements, and the delegations have a number of ideas for improvements and for new measures in the slightly longer term. but in general, many delegations have expressed a great deal of interest in the commission's ideas, also from a principle point of view, in the field of company auditing. the majority of delegations, however, want to see a voluntary system in the first place, which should be attractive to farmers, so that we can get as many people as possible to use the scheme. we have had a thorough discussion in the council of the commission's communication on the mid-term review. the delegations had the opportunity to ask questions, to comment, to come up with new ideas, to support or to criticise all aspects of the commission communication and the reports accompanying it. the commission now has a solid basis on which to assess the wishes of the member states for the future development of the common agricultural policy and to draw the necessary conclusions.

the commission (es) mr president, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteurs, mr ripoll and mr poignant, who are known - as we all know each other - to those of us who are taking part in these debates at a late hour or so, here in brussels or in strasbourg, and who are interested in the problems of transport policy, and in particular the safety rules, which in this case apply to transport vessels, and the requirements on stability, which also affect safety, in the transport of passengers by sea. they have done a magnificent job, as is always the case with the various rapporteurs of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism on the various initiatives which i have had the honour of presenting in the commission over the years. as past accidents in rolling stock have shown, the stability of rolling stock is a major determinant of survival in the event of a collision. even in the worst-case scenario, the longer a vessel remains afloat, the more successful its evacuation is in rescue operations. the commission proposal thus specifically addresses this critical aspect of the safety of ro-ro passenger ships. the improvements proposed by the commission have been developed by researchers in response to the tragic accidents involving rolling-stock vessels over the last decade. the new rules are a significant step forward from the current international solas standards and are being applied in northern european waters under the stockholm agreement. the directives we are discussing today will make the specific stability requirements of the stockholm agreement mandatory for all ro-ro ferry vessels operating to and from community ports. in other words, what is already being applied in the baltic sea area is being extended to the rest of europe's ports. these rules will apply not only to ships on international voyages but also to those on major domestic routes. among the other elements of the package, i would particularly like to highlight the introduction of the accessibility and safety requirement for people with reduced mobility. the european union cannot lag behind other developed countries in this area. states must ensure that this requirement is effectively implemented with the consequent improvement of the safety and well-being of our citizens. i would point out to both rapporteurs that the commission accepts all the amendments proposed by the european parliament, since the vast majority of them contribute to the improvement and clarification of our original text. i would like to stress two amendments in particular, namely no 13 by mr poignant and no 8 by mr ripoll. the commission would have preferred to maintain its original text on these two matters, but in view of the work already undertaken in the council and the alignment of the council with parliament, the commission has decided to accept both amendments in order to reach a political compromise solution and to be able to adopt these rules quickly. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to conclude by emphasizing the excellent cooperation which we have been able to maintain once again on this transport dossier. thank you very - the next item is the report (a5-0344/2002) by mr medina ortega, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the member states relating to advertising and sponsorship of tobacco products (com (2001) 283 - c5-0274/2001 - 2001/0119 (cod)). we hope that the members who were still on their way will be able to attend.
commission. – mr president, i wish to begin by saying that i am pleased to be here today to present the commission's proposal for a directive on tobacco advertising and sponsorship. it has been a long time since the commission adopted this proposal – 18 months to be precise. it would be an understatement to say that i am disappointed with the slow progress on this proposal so far. there have been delaying tactics, misinformation and, very often, misleading statements. it is a great pity that the committee on legal affairs and the internal market was unable to work more quickly, in contrast to the much quicker response from the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, whose members are the true experts in the european parliament on public health and consumer protection. they at least clearly understood the importance and urgency of this proposal. worldwide, almost 5 million people die every year from tobacco-related diseases. this is two and a half times the number of deaths from aids. of those 5 million half a million are european – the equivalent of the population of copenhagen. advertising plays a major role in promoting tobacco use, especially amongst young people. the tobacco industry needs new recruits to replace those whose consumption of the deadly product has caused their early deaths. it is against this background that i invite you to look at the present proposal. this directive is important for the operation of the single market. without it the single market for print media, radio and the internet cannot be guaranteed on account of variations in national legislation on tobacco advertising across the member states. the proposal is intended to replace the previous directive on tobacco advertising and sponsorship, annulled by the european court of justice two years ago. the previous directive included a ban on all forms of tobacco advertising and sponsorship. the court considered that this general ban did not have the legal support of the treaty. however, the court was not entirely negative in its ruling. far from it. it helpfully confirmed that a directive prohibiting certain forms of advertising and sponsorship could be adopted on the basis of article 95 of the treaty. the new proposal therefore follows very closely the guidelines set out in the court's ruling. the logic behind the present proposal is clear: all member states have adopted national rules to regulate the advertising and sponsorship of tobacco products. these regulations, unsurprisingly, vary considerably between member states. this divergence has, ironically you might say, been exacerbated by the annulment of the previous directive. this gives rise to increasing barriers to the free movement between member states of products and services that serve as support for such advertising and sponsorship. we aim to eliminate these barriers by harmonising the rules relating to the advertising of tobacco products and related sponsorship to the extent possible in the light of the court’s ruling. the proposal foresees a general ban on tobacco advertising in the press. this is an important vector for tobacco promotion, and one that has strong cross-border implications. the proposal also includes a ban on tobacco advertising on the internet. advertising of tobacco products via radio and the sponsorship of radio programmes by tobacco companies would also be banned on the same lines as television advertising under the television without frontiers directive. finally, the proposal deals with sponsorship – banning this for events or activities with cross-border implications. overall, the proposal has a much more limited scope than the previous directive. i know that many of you regret this and i sympathise with this view. i make no secret of the fact that i would have preferred to present a proposal for a complete ban on advertising for tobacco products. but, unfortunately, the legal framework does not allow us to go that far. we have to live in the real world. we have to recognise the legal constraints. our common concern must be to ensure that this new directive can and will stand its ground against any possible future court challenge and to eliminate the market distortion by harmonising current national rules, whilst at the same time promoting public health. a final thought for now. this proposal has been very carefully constructed. any weakening of its legal position would open the door to challenge which, if successful, would play directly into the hands of the tobacco industry. we simply cannot afford to let that happen. (applause)
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, commissioner byrne has made a great effort to bring forward a proposal for a directive in an area where the court of justice had ruled to annul the previous directive on the absolute ban on tobacco advertising. i think that this community is in a kafkaesque health situation, because although we have competence in animal health - from the establishment, through the feeding and transport - in practice our competence in health is minimal, that is to say, the european union has hardly any competence in human health. it has the power to adopt certain measures, recommendations and promotional measures, such as cooperation between states and with international organizations, but when it comes to legislative harmonization, we are practically blocked. the commission has wisely tried to make the most of the conclusions of the court of justice, i would say of the obiter dicta of the court of justice in the judgment annulling the previous tobacco advertising directive. and from the point of view of the committee on legal affairs, the rapporteur has particularly welcomed the efforts of the commission and commissioner byrne in particular to bring forward this proposal for a directive which, as he has said, is much more modest than the previous one. however, the rapporteur must admit that he has encountered enormous difficulties within the committee on legal affairs itself and, in order to make the processing of this directive possible, he has had to accept a number of compromise amendments which are what constitute the current text, which has been adopted by the committee on legal affairs. we do not yet know what the outcome of the votes on this matter will be on wednesday. i have the impression that this house is now widely divided, because, as some members have said, certain amendments may even weaken the legal basis which the commission itself had proposed, and at this particular moment the opinion of, for example, the rapporteur from the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection - which i think we shall hear from her shortly - is certainly against the introduction of amendments. i have the impression that at least some of the amendments are quite substantiated, since they correct some of the areas where the directive could be improved. for example, a general extension of the prohibition on the use of certain brands could harm undertakings which are not actually engaged in the production of tobacco, except that some of their brands are identical to those of another undertaking which is engaged in that activity. i think that each of the amendments will have to be studied quite carefully. i share mr byrne's concern about the delay in the committee on legal affairs. we were obliged to hold a hearing as a result of the enormous divergence of opinion which had been expressed in the committee and, at that hearing, i must acknowledge or recall that most of the members of the committee on legal affairs were quite critical of the commission's proposals. the rapporteur has therefore been obliged to carry out a somewhat delicate task, trying to bring positions closer together in order to make a first formulation that would reach the plenary of this house. it will therefore be this house which will decide on wednesday what to do with each of these amendments. there is a subsequent amendment which the rapporteur finds acceptable in principle - the amendment put forward by mrs hautala, which aims to strengthen the legal basis of the commission by means of a recital. i hope that next wednesday, regardless of what happens to each of the amendments in the various votes, the text of the directive as a whole will be able to be adopted. i hope that the report will be adopted so that the procedure can continue. as we are in a codecision procedure, we have the opportunity to correct any deficiencies that may be noted by each of us in order to be sure that this new proposal for a directive can stand the test of a new appeal to the court of justice, which will undoubtedly take place, because in the tobacco field there are always appeals to the court of justice. the commissioner can be sure that the attitude of this rapporteur is absolutely constructive in order to achieve a good final result in this respect. but i repeat - this house is a democratic house and the opinions of the different members are very diverse. i have the impression that there are even important differences between the different national delegations within the different parties. the rapporteur's task in this case must therefore be primarily a task of coordination, of goodwill, if you will, and above all of coordinating the results to be achieved next wednesday in this house with the good intentions of the commission and the commissioner to adopt community regulations in the field of health. in any case, it must be remembered that the inclusion of a health clause in the next european constitution is still a work in progress, and i have the impression that the work of the convention is not going in that direction at the moment, which is quite worrying.
- (es) mr president, the problem we have when we talk about tobacco is that those of us in the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy are talking from the point of view of public health and not from the point of view of the inconvenience that the ban on tobacco advertising may have for the internal market. we therefore agree more with the directive which was adopted in 1998. the commissioner has already said that five million people die every year from diseases linked to tobacco use. other colleagues have said that thousands of young people are initiated into tobacco use each year, with the consequences that addiction has for them. studies have clearly demonstrated the effect of advertising and sponsorship of certain sports events on young people's earlier initiation of smoking. in fact, statistics show that 60 percent of smokers start before the age of 13, and nearly 90 percent before the age of 18. that is why we thought the 1998 directive was much better, which was unfortunately annulled by the european court of justice. in the present case, several members of the committee on the environment have decided not to table amendments to the commission's proposal because a limited directive is better than no directive at all. and so we are only tabled one amendment, which proposes that, under the treaty, the member states retain competence and can regulate these kinds of matters and even go beyond. the rapporteur for the committee on the environment also makes it very clear that this is a step forward and that the european commission will probably be able to submit proposals in the future on indirect advertising, on the control of advertising expenditure and on tobacco vending machines. in short, mr president, in this matter it is preferable to have a limited directive than no directive at all.
commission. – let me first of all deal with some of the technical issues. looking at the important question of the commission's attitude to the various amendments, there are 26 amendments being proposed. the commission can accept amendments 3, 10, 22 and 26 in full and amendments 8, 11 and 17 subject to some minor rewording. all the others, the commission rejects. throughout this debate, we have heard from many speakers and it is quite clear there are different views. indeed there are different views in member states. they have in fact sought to regulate the advertising of tobacco products. i am convinced that there is a correlation between the legal rules in member states on advertising and the figures for adult consumption of tobacco in those member states. if you look at one of the member states with the highest level of tobacco consumption, germany, with 37%, it has a fairly lax approach to advertising in its national law, as compared with sweden, one of the member states with the most restrictive advertising legislation. sweden's rate of adult tobacco consumption is 19%. so there is quite clearly, in my view, a correlation. a number of you spoke about that in your contributions. it is a question of attacking the image of smoking. mrs alvarez gonzalez referred to the different views of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy and the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, the environment committee's desire for public health to be promoted as an important basic consideration in determining these issues. those who spoke on the other side of the argument, if i might describe it as such, are seeking to have legal certainty, which, as a lawyer, i would say is not at all unreasonable. it is an objective that i would seek to pursue myself, not just as a lawyer but as one of my responsibilities as a commissioner. we have done that. we examined very closely the judgment of the court of justice in the first advertising directive case. when the court looked at the facts of that case and gave its judgment, it clearly said that there were good parts in the legislation and bad parts. it went on to say that because they were so inextricably bound together, to attempt to extract the good from the bad, to retain the good and eliminate the bad, would amount to legislating by the judiciary and that cannot be done. that is why the legislation was annulled. i brought the judgment back to brussels. i told my staff to follow it closely and we brought a new draft regulation. referring only briefly to one part of the court's judgment, paragraph 98 says in principle that a directive prohibiting the advertising of tobacco products in periodicals, magazines and in newspapers could be adopted on the basis of article no. 100a – now article 95 – of the treaty with a view to ensuring the free movement of press products on the lines of article 13 of directive 89/552, the television without frontiers directive prohibiting television advertising of tobacco products in order to promote the free broadcasting of television programmes. the court has spoken clearly on the subject. we have followed that carefully in our drafting. in response to mr lechner, who said earlier that there was no evidence of a distortion in the market, i must say that there is plenty of evidence of this. in the commission we get letters regularly from people complaining from both sides of the argument, indeed even from the industry, about a distortion in the market because of the different regimes in member states in relation to this issue. mr de clercq made reference to the movement away from spa of the formula 1 championship race. that is another clear distortion of the market, because belgium brought in a law which they are saying forces them to move away from belgium. that supports my argument that we need to have a level playing field in europe. we need to have harmonised legislation on this issue throughout the european union so that one member state cannot be played off against another. this is also my answer to mr harbour. it is not a subsidiarity issue for the very reason that a belgian has been pinpointed in a particular way and has suffered a loss. so not only does the court say it can be done, the commission says it ought to be done. but do not just take my word for it. the committee on the environment committee says that we should have this legislation in the way i have described and i am sure it would agree the few amendments that the commission concedes. even when we look at the first report from the very hardworking mr medina ortega, the rapporteur, there were three suggested amendments and i would have accepted any one of the three. if i read between the lines of what he has said, and forgive me if i misinterpreting him, i certainly got the impression from his reference to the compromised amendments that he was not speaking with great enthusiasm but was identifying the fact that this house was divided. of course, it is. so maybe we can draw the conclusion that the first thoughts of the rapporteur on this issue, which are closer to those of the committee on the environment and to mine, might well be the ones to follow in this debate. let us not leave it there. we have had a number of discussions on tobacco in the council, including the preliminary discussions on the framework convention on tobacco control, and the breakdown there is 14 to one. one member state takes the view that this legislation either should not go through or it should go through in such a form and with such amendments that in my opinion the heart is cut out of the legislation or amendments are added that leave it vulnerable to challenge in the court of justice yet again. so what do i say to those members of parliament who are undecided about this? i would say to them they should follow the views that are expressed by the court. follow the advice of the commission. follow the views of the experts in this house, the committee on the environment, and follow the first thoughts of the rapporteur. think to what extent will parliament be on its own if it either votes down this legislation or votes it through with the kind of amendments that are being proposed. it might not be quite alone, but it will be alone with one member state, the member state that happens to have the highest consumption of tobacco amongst adults in the european union. that is the choice and therefore i would suggest to those who are undecided on this issue how you should cast your vote. i would suggest you cast it in a way that puts people's health first, rather than becoming engaged in a pointless debate about the legal niceties when the issues have been resolved by the court of justice and those who have examined this issue closely and believe that legal certainty does exist, to the extent that is necessary to support legislation designed to protect public health, as articles 95 and 152 say. both the commission and parliament have a duty and an obligation, in this decision-making and law-making, to promote the highest levels of public health.

the committee on budgets mr president, i am speaking in place of our colleague alain lipietz, who should have presented this report to the committee on economic and monetary affairs, with the talent progress on this matter, reaching a common position shortly afterwards. the outcome of the council's deliberations is also extremely encouraging. parliament can warmly welcome the fact that the sufficiently taken into account in the common position. although there are a few areas where the common position could still be improved, your rapporteur's main concern is to see this new strengthened regulatory framework put in place as soon as possible. the commission is therefore proposing - and the committee on economic and monetary affairs has approved this position almost unanimously - that the common position be adopted without amendments. this will ensure that european conglomerates are subject to the most modern, efficient and effective regulation and controls possible as soon as possible.
