president of the council. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, just over three years ago, general musharraf seized power in pakistan in a military coup. it caused great concern in the democratic world and led to much condemnation. the takeover was later approved by the pakistani supreme court on the condition that pakistan restored democracy within three years of the military coup, that is, by 12 october this year. on 14 august last year, musharraf published his so-called 'road map to democracy', which outlined how he intended to comply with the decision of the pakistani supreme court and restore democracy to pakistan. and this plan consisted of 4 parts: 1) installation of elected local councils (it happened in august 2001), 2) preparation of provincial and federal elections with the creation of an electoral commission, preparation of electoral lists, id cards, etc., and implementation of a number of constitutional changes, 3) implementation of the electoral act itself, and 4) transfer of governmental power to civilian elected provincial assemblies and federal assemblies, as well as election of the presidents of the assemblies, etc. it was to take place in october/november this year. the elections on 10 october this year were monitored by election observers, including from the eu. i would like to take this opportunity to thank mr cushnahan for the great effort he and the other members of the mission put into this. for security reasons alone, the implementation of the election observation was extremely difficult, but despite this mr cushnahan and his team carried out the task assigned to them. (applause from the centre) as mr cushnahan has noted in his report on election observation, there are a number of things about the elections in pakistan that could have been done differently. we have noted in particular the report's criticism of the circumstances which preceded the actual elections, not least the constitutional amendments introduced by president musharraf this summer. there was unequal access to campaign, resources and media, and there were reports of election manipulation. all of this has given cause for concern. nevertheless, the council considers that the holding of the elections is an important step towards the restoration of democracy in pakistan. throughout the process, the eu has been in constant dialogue with pakistan on the restoration of democracy and has thus also had the opportunity to express criticism of the situation that was going in the wrong direction. the results of the elections on 10 october led to the formation of a coalition government. the negotiations are not yet concluded. the transfer of executive power to the incoming prime minister is expected to take place this month. the eu and pakistan issued a joint statement on the signing of the eu-pakistan cooperation agreement in islamabad on 24 november last year. in the light of the current situation, the eu and pakistan reaffirmed the importance of international action against terrorism. in the same statement, pakistan also reaffirmed its commitment to the restoration of democracy under the road map, which the eu welcomed. it must be noted that musharraf has kept his promise to implement the promised 'road map'. the conditions are therefore in place for the agreement to proceed. on the positive side, the president has also implemented a number of reforms aimed at restoring the economy and fighting corruption. it is crucial to state that the implementation of the cooperation agreement is not a slap in the face of pakistani democracy. as i said, there are many things we wish we had done differently. that is also what mr cushnahan's report says. the agreement includes a first paragraph in which the contracting parties reaffirm their respect for human rights. with this agreement in hand, i believe we have a better tool to discuss democracy and human rights with pakistan than has been the case so far. the council will continue and deepen its dialogue with pakistan with a view to contributing to the strengthening of pakistani democracy. and with these words i would like to thank mr cushnahan once again for the excellent work and the basis for an assessment of democracy in pakistan that he has provided.
commission. – madam president, the commission agrees with the presidency that the national and provincial assembly elections held in pakistan on 10 october should be seen as a first step in the gradual transition from a military to a civilian administration with permanent and well-functioning democratic institutions. the elections resulted in a fragmented parliament which in turn delayed the inaugural session of the national assembly. this finally took place on 16 november. the extensive negotiations among political parties demonstrate that a revitalised democratic process has been initiated following the elections. we expect that the new government will be equipped with full executive powers. the commission will continue to stay engaged with pakistan throughout the transition process. the commission would like to congratulate the eu election observation mission, led by mr cushnahan, on the excellent work achieved under very difficult circumstances, notably a particularly challenging security environment. his dedication went far beyond what would normally be expected of a chief election observer. the commission appreciates that the mission was able to carry out its task in full compliance with internationally accepted criteria used for election observation. let me also take this opportunity to express the commission’s satisfaction with the cooperation with the european parliament in the observation of the election in pakistan. in particular i would like to thank the members of the european parliament delegation, led by mrs grönfeldt bergman, for their invaluable work. what is more, this is not an isolated case. the commission and parliament have developed very good working relations in the field of election observation in general. the commission believes that the presence of the eu election observation mission has served to enhance the democratic process in pakistan. moreover, its recommendations on how to further strengthen this process and improve the election framework will be raised in the dialogue with the pakistani authorities. the commission is also prepared to look into possible follow-up activities on the basis of its report. the commission agrees with the eu election observation mission that a general election does not in itself guarantee the establishment of democracy and that those who support the restoration of democracy should work together to achieve that objective. concerning the methodology we applied to observation of the election in pakistan, the commission would like to stress that we followed our standard approach. elections are not one-day events and the whole process, including the pre-voting period, has to be assessed. the criticism made in pakistan that the mission was exceeding its mandate because it arrived too early and interfered with the internal affairs of the country by analysing the overall election framework is therefore groundless. as far as the new cooperation agreement between the european community and pakistan is concerned, the commission would like to recall that exceptional circumstances in the region called for a response commensurate to the risk president musharraf took in siding with the international community on afghanistan. the aim of the agreement is to engage significantly and visibly with pakistan, both in political and economic terms, and to encourage pakistan to adhere to the implementation of the roadmap for the return to democracy. the reasons why it is important for the eu and the commission to engage pakistan in an enhanced political dialogue are well known. they include the fight against terrorism, pakistan’s difficult relations with india, the need for stability in neighbouring afghanistan, pakistan’s deep-rooted economic and social problems and, last but not least, the continuing transition to democracy. relevant topics to be raised in that dialogue include basic education, where our aim is to strengthen the secular education system, fostering trade and business links and human rights issues, which are an essential element of the new agreement. in this connection, pakistan has been designated a focus country under the european initiative for human rights and democracy. the commission is aware that continuing uncertainty over the role and functioning of political institutions in pakistan means that we need to monitor closely whether there is genuine progress on the transfer of power to the elected parliament in the coming weeks and months. ratification of the new cooperation agreement would allow us to re-establish the full cooperation dialogue with the new government. (applause)

- mr president, mr commissioner, i would like to thank you for your reply. the completion of the internal market will of course increase competition between regions. the european framework for this is therefore in need of continuous improvement. but since the european union does not exist in isolation from world trade, it also needs a system of competition within the wto. if we are serious about the task we set ourselves at the gothenburg summit, in continuation of the lisbon summit, then competition policy must not be limited to economic conditions but must also take account of social and environmental aspects. an economy cannot be competitive if it does not have a highly skilled workforce, if wages and salaries are so low that they do not stimulate but rather stifle domestic demand, and if the production of products does not guarantee that these products do not have harmful effects on the health of the population. this is why a rethinking must take place that transforms the internal struggle for subsidized location advantages into a struggle for a sustainable design of people's livelihoods. competition policy must be appropriate to the concept of equal opportunities. however, equal opportunities cannot be achieved if there are insufficiently harmonised technical standards, if the tax policies of the member states differ so much that the actual burden of costs is not comparable and if social standards vary greatly between member states. i am not against, but rather in favour of, state aid if it is based on a legal basis which is binding on all and which does not help to preserve old, environmentally harmful technology but encourages investment in the future. in short - and this is where i started my speech - competition policy is about the realization of the equilateral triangle of economic policy, social policy and ecology.

- the next item is the report (a5-0369/2002) by mrs oomen-ruijten, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the proposal for a council regulation extending the provisions of regulation (eec) no 1408/71 to nationals of third countries who are not already covered by those provisions solely on the grounds of their nationality (com (2002) 59 - c5-0084/2002 - 2002/0039 (cns)).
the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mrs oomen-ruijten, and the members for their excellent report and for their support for the commission's proposal. this is a very important proposal, the adoption of which would be a significant political signal from the union for the integration of third-country nationals legally resident in the european union, since it offers them the same social security protection as community citizens moving within the european union. it is therefore an important contribution to a coherent and balanced community immigration policy. on 27 october 1999, this assembly called for urgent action on the fair treatment of thirdcountry nationals legally resident in the member states in order to grant them rights comparable to those of union citizens. the proposal goes further than this, giving third-country nationals the same rights and not just comparable to those enjoyed by community citizens moving within the european union. the proposal will also encourage the mobility of workers, the importance of which is illustrated by the commission's action plan presented earlier this year. the proposal will therefore simplify the rules by reducing the number of national and international instruments governing the coordination of social security schemes for this category of persons. as the rapporteur has rightly pointed out in her explanatory statement, this proposal for a regulation, based on article 63 (4) of the treaty, is intended to build a bridge. it simply extends to thirdcountry nationals the scope of the community regulations on social security, which are based and will continue to be based on article 42 of the treaty. this means that parliament will continue to be a co-decision-maker in any future amendments to regulation 1408/71. as you know, the commission proposal already contains a recital which refers to the charter of fundamental rights, but i agree that a specific reference to article 34 (2) of the charter is necessary. the commission can therefore support amendment no 1. i fully agree with the statement that the coordination of social security for third country nationals is of great importance, but this is so obvious that it is redundant to make a recital in this regard. the importance of the coordination of social security schemes for thirdcountry nationals is already amply reflected in the first nine recitals proposed by the commission. the commission, while agreeing with the idea behind it, cannot therefore accept amendment no 2. i understand the need to refer in the recitals to the forthcoming enlargement of the european union: the commission can therefore accept amendment no 3. however, it cannot support amendments nos 4 and 5. as regards amendment no 4, it is inappropriate to refer in a regulation to a proposal for a community instrument whose outcome is still unknown. the commission cannot accept amendment no 5 for a number of reasons. firstly, the proposal aims to give third-country nationals legally resident in a member state the same rights as community citizens travelling within the union. amendment no 5 aims to give third country nationals rights different from those granted to community citizens. i do not see why an afghan or indian worker in, say, the netherlands or finland should have to face problems due to lack of familiarity with the language and/or administrative procedures of the host country profoundly different from those encountered by a greek or portuguese colleague. the commission will also launch an active information campaign and, once adopted, will bring the proposal to the attention of all those concerned so that they can assert their rights when the time comes. there is, however, already a high level of media interest in the proposal. finally, mr president, i am extremely grateful to this house for putting the proposal on today's agenda, allowing the council to formally adopt it at its meeting on 3 december. you will understand that the commission no longer has time to submit an amended proposal to the council, but my colleague, commissioner diamantopoulou, intends to recommend to the council that it adopt the proposal with the amendments of parliament which we have now accepted.

- the agenda calls for the commission's statement on climate change.
commission. – mr president, thank you for inviting the commission to report to this house on the new delhi conference on climate change held in october 2002. i wish to begin by saying that the european union adopted a strong and unified position during the talks and we would like to thank the danish presidency for its excellent work. the commission is also pleased to acknowledge the sound political support it received from the ngos present at the meeting. however, the commission and my colleague mrs wallström particularly want to express our appreciation of the european parliament's ongoing support for the eu's position in international climate negotiations and your continuing interest in this issue. that interest was reflected by your dedicated parliamentary delegation led by mrs garcía-orcoyen tormo in new delhi. we hope to continue our effective cooperation in the future. around 170 countries, representing over three-quarters of the world's population, met in new delhi for their eighth regular meeting as parties to the united nation's framework convention on climate change. the meeting made good progress on a number of technical issues, such as monitoring and reporting, and paved the way for the use of the clean development mechanism (cdm). the cdm is an important tool for reaching emission targets in developed countries and, at the same time, for reducing emissions in the developing world and contributing to its sustainable growth. during the final ministerial part of the meeting, ministers and senior officials discussed the actions taken so far to combat climate change, the links between climate change and sustainable development and the disturbing findings of the third assessment report of the intergovernmental panel on climate change, which show that most of the acceleration in global warming is man-made. they also debated the need for further action to continue the fight against climate change. the meeting ended with the adoption of the delhi declaration. allow me to briefly outline the commission's political assessment of the new delhi conference. the delhi ministerial declaration represents the political outcome of the conference. although it includes the call for all countries to ratify the kyoto protocol and underlines the need for greater efforts to combat climate change in the coming decades, we would have liked it to be stronger in other areas. let me briefly address some shortcomings. first, the delhi declaration fails to underline the need for a closer link between science and policy action. the findings of the third assessment report of the intergovernmental panel on climate change confirm that more emission cuts are needed if the ultimate objective of the un framework convention on climate change is to be attained. this must be used as an important input for furthering the work of the climate change convention and the kyoto protocol. a science-based approach will give us more confidence in our policy scenarios for the future being on the right track. secondly, our mandate as agreed by the council on 17 october was to seek a forward-looking discussion on more inclusive and longer-term global cooperation based on broader and balanced action and participation consistent with the ultimate objective of the convention. such discussions should have started at the conference of the parties at its first session after the entry into force of the kyoto protocol. regrettably, the eu did not succeed in persuading other parties to recognise the need for starting such a process. however, through a number of bilateral contacts with other parties and groups of parties the eu did seize every opportunity to explain our way of thinking. the issue is now on the table and these discussions have provided a solid foundation on which we can build. a third but more general point is that the debate in delhi tended to focus on sustainable development rather than on climate change. while there is a clear understanding in the eu that climate change is strongly linked to sustainable development, the un framework convention on climate change is about just that. it is the framework for climate change which is well defined and in place. we should not allow the sustainable development discussion to distract us from the climate change process. following this conference, what prospects can we see for the entry into force of the kyoto protocol? this is obviously a crucial question. as you know this requires ratification by 55 parties representing at least 55% of the co2 emissions of the industrialised countries in 1990. the first threshold has been largely met – 97 countries as of 13 november – as ratification continues steadily. in this context, we gladly welcome the confirmation by canada that they will soon ratify. however, we have only reached a figure of 37.4% for the second threshold. given that the eu, japan and almost all the candidate countries have now ratified, this means that ratification by russia is necessary to bring the protocol into effect. it seems that russia is still inclined to ratify, especially after the results of the recently published study on the effects of climate change in that country. however, a final decision has yet to be made and no specific timetable has been set out. it is the commission's intention to continue to encourage russia to live up to its responsibility as a key player on climate change and to ratify the kyoto protocol as soon as possible. internally, the commission will proceed within the framework of the european climate change programme to enable the european union to meet its emissions reductions targets as agreed. internationally, on the other hand, the commission will continue its efforts to encourage our partners to ratify the kyoto protocol so that it can enter into force. at the same time we will also continue to build on the good bilateral relationships we have established with some developing countries and with the majority of the developed countries in order to reach a better understanding on what needs to be done in the future. everybody knows that the kyoto protocol is only the first step in the fight against climate change and we have to start to discuss how to proceed beyond it. i would like to conclude by stressing once again how deeply grateful the commission is for the parliament's support and for its very dedicated presence in delhi itself.
- (es) mr president, mr commissioner, first of all, on behalf of the european parliament delegation to cop8, i would like to thank commissioner wallström - who is not here today - for her cooperation with the delegations of this parliament at the successive conferences she has attended. in this regard, i have to say that we miss her in new delhi. the points i would like to make about this conference are the following: the european union must maintain its leadership in the international fight against climate change and, consequently, promote as soon as possible the political debate among all parties on the objectives for the period after 2012. the cop8 was intended as a good opportunity to consolidate the decisions already taken in bonn and marrakesh on the implementation of the kyoto protocol, but frankly it failed to do so and failed to establish a broad debate on the main issues for the second period. cop8 did make significant progress on the technical front, especially with regard to clean development mechanisms, reporting and review procedures, but progress at the political level was disappointing. the attempts to dilute the specific aspects of the kyoto protocol into the much broader concept of sustainable development - the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i do not think that the disaster of the prestige or the scientific reports we have recently received from ices on cod and the catastrophic state of this important fish species have been necessary to show us the urgent need for a reform of fisheries policy. i think that all those who have eyes in their heads and ears to hear must realize that with the current fisheries policy we are not able to guarantee a future for our fishermen and all the families who depend on fishing, nor are we able to create stable conditions that will make it possible for our fisheries resources to be available to future generations. ladies and gentlemen, there is no need to be unnecessarily dramatic, the situation is already enormously dramatic! i believe that the debate we are having today is therefore a very important debate for the future of the fisheries sector. we are discussing several questions and reports at the same time. i should like to begin by thanking all the rapporteurs and the rapporteur for the reports, because they enable us to have a look at them together. i would like to break my contribution into two parts. i should like to begin by dealing mainly with the general aspects and then, in a second statement at the end, to deal with the various amendments and the commission's position on these amendments. but, ladies and gentlemen, let me say a word about the prestige disaster. it's a paradox that this ship is called "prestige". but the consequences for fishermen, for shellfish and oyster farmers, are indeed enormous and dramatic. the commission is trying to do what it can to help, at least to avert the worst and to help the families so badly affected as quickly as possible. a task force was therefore set up within the commission. the commission has already been to galicia and has spoken to the people concerned, including those responsible. we are in the process of drawing up plans for aid programmes and we are prepared to help, within the legal possibilities that are available to us, to apply the existing instruments as flexibly as possible so that we can help those affected. i myself contacted the spanish authorities at the very beginning of this disaster, and i am in constant contact with the spanish authorities, and now that it appears that france will be affected to a greater extent than previously thought, the same principles and the same means of assistance will naturally be applied to france. the ices reports have, i believe, been the latest proof of the dramatic state of affairs in which our fishing sector finds itself. as you know, ices published the news in october that four cod stocks in the community are on the verge of collapse. this alarming situation is due to the already low stock size - and not only the young fish but also the adult fish are no longer in sufficient numbers - to the poor spawning results of the last season and to the still too high fish mortality. the ices scientists have made a very clear and unequivocal recommendation that direct cod fishing in the north sea, the irish sea, the waters west of scotland, the skagerrak and the kattegat should be stopped, as there is no recovery plan for next year. the commission is also proposing to close the fisheries for shellfish and whiting, as they are overfishing cod. it was not enough to reduce cod catches in recent years, and unfortunately, quota reductions have also led to misrepresentation and to illegal fishing. this has also been pointed out by scientists. it is not just a commission conjecture, as some have claimed. the scientists have repeatedly warned that we must not only set quotas, but also reduce fishing effort, so that we can better control, but also ensure that too much by-catch is not generated and that the maximum catch is respected. i can only quote. the scientists say - they said this in 1990 - that we recommend limiting fishing effort because tucs alone are not suitable for controlling fish mortality. twelve years later, ladies and gentlemen, we are still not at the stage where we have implemented this recommendation! we then presented the results of ices to our scientific and technical committee on fisheries, which in turn recommended that we adopt a cod recovery plan as soon as possible, which, in addition to reducing tucs and quotas more than originally envisaged, must also include a corresponding reduction in fishing effort. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. as you know, the commission proposed a year ago to limit fishing effort in the framework of the recovery plan for cod and hake. the council has not yet taken a decision on this matter, and in the meantime progress has not stopped. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. in view of this situation, the commission has weighed the various options available. we have decided against a moratorium and instead to adopt an improved recovery plan, precisely because we must take the scientific results seriously, but also the difficult situation of our fishermen. so what are the changes compared to last year's plan? firstly, the sharp reduction in fishing effort means that the total catch in the north sea for the community and norway, expressed in terms of fishing opportunities, is 16 800 tonnes of cod, 31 600 tonnes of shellfish, 10 400 tonnes of whiting, 60 000 tonnes of plaice and 16 000 tonnes of sole. for the waters west of scotland, it is about 1 000 tonnes of cod and 7 200 tonnes of shellfish, for the irish sea 1 200 tonnes of cod, 7 500 tonnes of shellfish and 400 tonnes of whiting. of course, these are just some of the catches. secondly, we are proposing a simplified system of fishing effort, where we want to manage the effort not for each individual vessel but for a group of vessels. thirdly, we have tightened up our proposal on controls. member states must report their fishing effort to the commission on a monthly basis and vessels must report to the control authorities when they change fishing zones. i am also prepared to fund further research to help us find even better ways of saving this fishery. but that cannot mean, ladies and gentlemen, that we should postpone the necessary measures any longer. we are aiming to decide on this improved recovery plan in december, together with the fisheries reform. what does all this mean for our fishermen? i am aware that this means a great deal of hardship at first, unfortunately, i must say, a great deal of hardship for those affected. i know very well that lives are at stake here. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. we have therefore also put forward an action plan to mitigate the possible negative socioeconomic consequences. i would like to highlight three measures. firstly, the member states are being asked to reorient their structural programmes and to provide additional funds for the fisheries sector and for areas dependent on fishing. secondly, member states can provide for targeted measures for small-scale coastal fishing, which is very labour intensive. they can, for example, reserve certain fishing grounds for small vessels or they can target their programmes to the small fleet in order to preserve jobs, especially in coastal regions. thirdly, we need to diversify the economic opportunities in coastal areas. ladies and gentlemen, on the other subjects to be discussed today, first of all the report by mr jové. our proposal in this context is a new basic regulation for the common fisheries policy as the core of the reform. the four key elements of this basic regulation are: firstly, we want to make the stocks sustainable in the future. it is not in keeping with the biology of fish that there should and can be an annual principle for fish, but we must make the biological cycles of our fish stocks the subject of our policy. in order to ensure coherent management, we want to manage the fishing effort in addition to the tucs and quotas for those stocks where it makes sense. i'll tell you where it makes sense. that is to say, not everywhere, and this depends primarily on the state of stocks. secondly, we are proposing a new fleet policy. the final objectives of the so-called map4 are intended to be the starting point for the ceiling. this ceiling can only be changed in one direction, namely in the direction of a reduction in the size of the fleet. each time a fisherman has his vessel scrapped with public funds, this ceiling is reduced by this tonnage. we also need a system to define the proportion in which new vessels can be exchanged for old vessels, provided that this is done with private funds. thirdly, we propose to strengthen fisheries surveillance. the member states should coordinate their control activities and inspectors from the member states should be able to carry out cross-border checks. the satellite controls are to be gradually extended to smaller vehicles and, finally, we also envisage more powers for the commission in respect of controls in the member states. only when each party can rely on his neighbour to be controlled as he is and punished as he is if he commits a violation, only then will there be justice and only then will we have confidence in this system! fourthly, we want to involve the fisheries sector more closely in the decision-making process through the regional advisory bodies. the structural funds. let me make one thing clear first. it is not, as is often claimed, that the commission is guilty of a legal error because the member states have a legal right to continue to use the funds in their structural funds for the renewal of fleets. the fact is that if the council does not reach a compromise in december and a decision on the reform, we will not be able to use the funds for the fleet policy from 1 january 2003. that is the legal consequence of the council's decision of december last year. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. firstly, we propose to maintain public aid to improve safety, working conditions and hygiene on board. secondly, we do not want to allow any more aid for the modernisation or construction of ships. we want to make sure that in future these funds are available to those who really need them, and those are the fishermen whom we must help financially so that they can diversify their activities accordingly and so that they can also have a chance - if they wish - to leave the fishing sector. the first is the many fishermen who are about to retire and who cannot retire because the loans are still due from the bank and their vessel has not yet been paid. is it a social attitude if we continue to ignore this or pretend it's not a problem? i don't think it was. thirdly, we propose that the aid paid so far for the export of ships and for joint ventures be used in future to reduce excess capacity. i am prepared to do something different with regard to small vessels, to help the many small vessel owners in a different way, because they too have much less pressure to fish. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. our proposal is to set up a scrappage fund. this is an emergency. this is not a permanent concept but an immediate measure designed to help us to bring the balance between the strength of our fleets and the resources available back into a better balance. the fund is to supplement the resources already provided for in the fisheries structural fund by the resources still to be reprogrammed for scrapping. this appropriation and the new fund will provide financial support for the decommissioning of fishing vessels. there are two main elements. firstly, a 20% increase in the premium, but for a limited period, for vessels whose days at sea are reduced by at least 25%, and secondly, an additional eur 32 million which will be made available for scrapping next year. we are also prepared to discuss this if additional funds are needed to help the fishermen who want to do so. then we have to find a way to do that, too. (applause from the centre)
the rapporteur. (es) mr president, i do not want to go into the five minutes, but i am not very good at these things. i would like to apologize to my colleagues on the committee on fisheries because i am going to make a speech which is not so much about commenting on the final result of the report - and i would like to stress that i have not tabled any amendments to the final result of the vote in the committee on fisheries - as it is about making some comments on the commission's proposal. we are faced with a proposal which presents various problems - in my view a number of problems - with the lack of compatibility with the treaties and with elements of the legal order. it is true that fish stocks are in a difficult situation and that urgent action is needed. it is true that fishing must be sustainable and that requires preserving fish stocks, of course, but in the binomial of sustainable development or sustainable exploitation, the two words are inseparable and therefore there must be a balance: there must be fishermen and there must be regeneration of fish stocks. but there is no point in talking about sustainable development itself, if we dissociate the two words. it seems to me that the commission's approach in this respect is one which gives priority to, or only takes into account in a fundamental way, the issue of rapid regeneration of populations and ignores the other aspect of sustainable development. the commission's approach, in my view, therefore involves greater social impact on fish stocks, which can lead to far-reaching structural changes. only the larger fleet segments could survive and the small fleet, which generates the highest level of employment, would be doomed to disappear. therefore, the social and economic impacts of recovery plans must be taken into account in the management and recovery of resources. the quality of scientific information should therefore be improved and economic and social factors should be incorporated into the preparation of recovery plans. only in this way, by adapting the rate of recovery of fishery resources, can we modulate and minimise the impacts on fish stocks. and i think the commission has not been careful and i think there has been an implicit weakening in its proposal by not wanting to strengthen the scientific and technical committee for fisheries which i personally think should be strengthened. and of course multiannual approaches should be multi-specific, taking into account the relationship between the species of the populations, and single-species plans, because of their enormous gravity, should be exceptional. the commission proposal in some respects involves a de-communitarisation of fisheries policy, or so it seems to me. for example, it is proposed to empower states to adopt emergency measures in matters of community competence or for which a community mechanism already exists. the commission has put forward two difficult, complex and very restrictive proposals on, for example, cod fisheries. i take this opportunity to make the following very personal reflection, which may be my own reflection on what i have learned from that debate. there is clearly a reduction, a decline in resources. in addition, and this is very serious, the destruction of jobs has been much greater than that of resources, and this has happened in all the states of the opinion of the committee on budgetary control. (es) mr president, the framework regulation on the reform of the common fisheries policy does not yet include the fixed financial implications of the reform to be borne by the community budget. these implications will be set out in separate proposals and will therefore be examined in depth by the committee on budgets in due course. however, the amounts foreseen for the implementation of the reform are quite modest and are included in chapter b-ii 90 'measures to support the common fisheries policy': eur 1 million for the creation of a common inspection structure, eur 100 000 for the creation of four regional advisory councils and eur 1 million for the improvement of scientific advice. the committee on budgets has given a positive assessment of these three reform measures and has approved the proposed amounts, keeping them in reserve as proposed by the commission, pending the final adoption of the framework regulation. however, the committee on budgets believes that parliament should be able to examine closely the detailed proposals which the commission makes on each of these actions, taking into account their impact, particularly on human resources, administrative expenditure, missions and committee meetings. i would like to ask the commission for clarification: the framework regulation provides for the amount of eur 4 million for the action to improve scientific advice; however, the commission states in the preliminary draft budget that only eur 1 million will be allocated to this action under line b ii-904, which is entered in the reserve. at the same time, we note that the commission has increased this item by 3 million compared with last year, which, together with the 1 million in the reserve, could represent an overall increase of 4 million euro, as provided for in the framework regulation. but since it is not clear, my question to the commission is: is this increase of 4 million - 3 plus 1 - earmarked for the action to improve scientific advice, as provided for in the framework regulation, or is the million in the reserve earmarked for this action alone? and if the latter is true, why has the commission provided for this increase of 3 million in line b-ii 904? as regards mr varela's report, which deals with one of the main elements of the reform of the common fisheries policy - the reduction of the fishing capacity of the european union fleet - the committee on budgets, and it cannot be otherwise, leaves it to the discretion of the committee on fisheries to assess the need for the scrapping measure. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not dismantled. the proposal for a regulation provides for an initial amount of eur 32 million for 2003 as a special incentive for co-financing. it also estimates that the total additional amounts needed for the period 2003-2006 amount to eur 271.6 million. the committee on budgets considers that the financing of the new action is incompatible with the ceiling of heading 2 of the current financial perspective and that therefore the 32 million already provided for in the 2003 budget can only be made available by the mobilisation of additional appropriations using the instruments provided for in the interinstitutional agreement.

the rapporteur. - (es) madam president, i would like to refer briefly to the previous debate, just to tell you, commissioner, that i want to encourage and accelerate all possible measures to help galicia, because in galicia the people who are affected have an identity card and a real face: they are the fishermen, their neighbours, small traders, etc. and while it is true that those who cause harm must pay for it, the perpetrators here hide behind legal wrangles, under the umbrella of the anonymous society, and here anonymous has the most literal meaning. perhaps, commissioner, it would be good to promote measures of transparency, clarity and agility also in the field of maritime trade regulation. i shall now turn to the european union-senegal fisheries agreement, which sets out the fishing opportunities in senegalese waters and the financial compensation. i think that the conclusion of a new protocol on fisheries relations between senegal and the european union - especially important in the absence of an agreement with morocco - should be welcomed. the impact of the protocol, as you said, on fish stocks in senegalese waters is minimal, as european union fishing activities only account for between 1.7% and 3% of total catches in the area. in addition, the fishing opportunities of community vessels have been reduced for sensitive stocks and technical measures have been agreed, including a two-month biological closure to increase the protection of stocks and reduce the risk of competition with the small-scale fleet. i do not want to go into too much detail because a lot of the data is already in the report. let me say, however, that for the species of hake, the pelagic fishing opportunities have disappeared and the tuna fishing opportunities have remained at the same level, that the financial compensation from the european union will amount to between 12 and 16 million euros per year and that of these 16 million, 3 will be earmarked for specific measures: development of local industry and the informal commitment - unfortunately not included in the agreement - by the senegalese authorities to allocate 50% of the total compensation to the sector, which is important because the economy of senegal is heavily dependent on fishing and one in six senegalese workers is employed in the sector. i would also stress that the biological rest period is mandatory, as opposed to the mere provision in the previous agreement that the prohibition of pelagic fishing is intended to promote the conservation of sensitive stocks and to promote the artisanal sector and to safeguard the sustainability of fisheries in senegal. all these elements confirm what has been said, as does the fixing of lower rates of by-catch and larger mesh sizes. the increase in the number of senegalese seamen on board community vessels is also of great importance. i would like to emphasize, commissioner, a reference to amendment no 3, which has a clear social content - the asbestos is amphibolic or chrysotile. the incubation periods vary, according to scholars, from 20 to 50 years. in addition, doubts and uncertainties remain about the effect of low inhalation doses amphibolic asbestos, as well as concerns about the prohibition of the use of asbestos in the repair, remodelling or restoration of buildings. in demolition cases workers can and must be in contact with asbestos even if it is banned globally. i think that, in view of the imminent and already agreed enlargement of the european union, the amendment of directive 83/477 on protection against the commission - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam rapporteur, the report drawn up by mrs langenhagen, which was adopted unanimously at the last meeting of the committee on budgetary control, essentially repeats the main criticisms of the special report of the european court of auditors concerning certain weaknesses in the design or management of the programmes. these include the use of a technical assistance office and, in an insufficiently defined way, national agencies, as well as delays and shortcomings in implementation. as indicated in its reply to the court, the commission has already introduced improvements in the implementation of the new socrates and youth for europe programmes, which succeeded the programmes examined by the court from 2000 onwards. this is particularly the case with regard to relations with the national agencies for the management of the decentralised parts of the programmes, or its intention to go as soon as possible in the direction indicated by the court, i.e. to dismantle the transitional technical assistance office as soon as the commission can have recourse to an executive agency for the educational programme. as regards improving the management of the decentralised parts of the programmes, the commission decisions adopted in 2000 establish mutatis mutandis, for each programme, the responsibilities of the commission and those of the national authorities towards the national agencies and the beneficiaries. the tasks to be carried out by the agencies shall also be specified in an annex to those decisions. in addition, the clauses of contracts between the commission and the national agencies have been clarified and simplified. as regards the control of national agencies, the commission decisions adopted in 2000 provide for the establishment by the ministries of control and audit systems concerning the functioning of the agencies, including their management of decentralised actions. the commission, in the framework of contractual relations with the national agencies, carries out checks and audits both on their operation and on the projects financed. the control by the commission services of the national agencies and the regular exchange of information between the national authorities and the commission allow for a strengthened monitoring of the implementation of decentralised actions by the agencies. the financial statements of the agencies shall be certified by approved bodies before being submitted to the commission. progress was also made in the management of centralised actions. the commission has been able to internalise certain tasks, some of which were public, previously entrusted to the technical assistance office, pending the introduction of an executive agency. preparatory work for the establishment of the agency has begun, with the agency to be operational in 2004 with a view to taking over the tasks currently carried out by the transitional technical assistance office and some of the management tasks currently carried out by the commission. at her request, various documents attesting to this progress were provided to mrs langenhagen after she had drafted her draft report. (es) mr president, commissioner, it is now one year since the temporary commission on foot-and-mouth disease began its investigations to find solutions and make proposals for the future to this problem which, in addition to causing serious economic damage to the european livestock sector, has caused considerable moral damage to all farmers and has had a great impact on society in general. we all remember the large number of animals that had to be slaughtered following the outbreak that last year severely affected the united kingdom and the netherlands. the main task of this committee was to prevent situations like those experienced by this disease from recurring in europe. during this intensive year-long period of work, the committee heard the views of dozens of experts in all fields, from economics to veterinary medicine, logistics, politics, community and international law, as well as tangential aspects such as tourism, freight transport, emotional aspects, etc. many of the committee's guests held positions of great responsibility during the management of the disease in the past outbreak. but the committee also gave the owners of the farms concerned, the local authorities and associations in these areas the opportunity to express their views during the various visits to both the united kingdom and the netherlands. in addition, as chairman of this committee, i have held several meetings on this disease, together with the rapporteur, mr kreissl-dörfler, with experts and officials from non-community countries such as paraguay, argentina and brazil. the result of all this work is the report which is being presented and put to the vote in this chamber today. the report by mr kreissl-dörfler has achieved a great deal of consensus among all the political groups and we hope that the rest of the members of this house will also find the points of agreement necessary to achieve majority approval of the report without substantial changes, with the adoption of some of the amendments tabled. one of the main issues addressed in the final report of the committee i chair is emergency vaccination, which is considered a key resource for controlling any future outbreak of the disease. the current policy of the european union - to suppress outbreaks of this disease by slaughtering livestock from farms where infected animals have already been detected and from neighbouring farms where there is a likelihood of contagion - cannot continue as it has been until now. the emergency vaccination policy must be part of a strategy to ensure the survival of the animals. the current policy of non-vaccination emphasizes the priority of political and trade aspects and this is something that must change at the international level, question no 37 by mr medina ortega (h-0727/02) subject: control of the borders with north africa can the commission explain the scope of the agreements concluded with morocco and other north african countries to help these countries control the illegal transit of migrants to the european union across their borders? can she give information on other projects in this field?
commission. – as part of the dialogue on illegal immigration established by the association agreement between the eu and morocco, and following an initiative by the moroccan authorities, a special programme on border control management was approved by the med committee in december 2001 under the national indicative programme from 2002 to 2004 for morocco. an indicative budget of eur 40 million in the meda national indicative programme from 2002 to 2004, signed by the moroccan authorities in january 2002, has been earmarked for the purpose. this initiative forms part of a broader dialogue on migration issues between morocco and the european union, which also covers issues linked to legal immigration and the socio-economic dimension of migratory pressure. the specific programme is aimed at institution building, developing the regulatory framework, modernising infrastructure and equipment, training officials and developing cooperation between the moroccan authorities concerned and their counterparts in the member states. an expert visit was arranged with a view to assessing needs and subsequently drawing up a timetable of concrete measures to improve the situation. during the mission, which took place in july 2002, experts from the member states and the commission had an opportunity to visit the main border posts and the frontier areas most affected by illegal immigration, particularly from sub-saharan countries. during those visits the moroccan authorities expressed their political determination and firm commitment to cooperate with the union in the fight against illegal immigration and on border controls in particular. in a spirit of openness and fruitful cooperation, in july and september 2002, they provided the experts with information on the regulatory framework and application of the rules as well as statistics on illegal emigration. in the light of the outcome of the on-the-spot visits and after examining the data communicated by the moroccan authorities, the experts are to finalise their report before the end of 2002. the content of the programme will subsequently be determined. this programme is the first initiative on border control management with a country in the region.

- question no 38 by mrs banotti (h-0825/02): subject: misuse of community research provisions on 'orphan medicinal products' in 1999, the eu adopted legislation to promote research into 'orphan drugs', i.e. drugs for the treatment of rare diseases. but it seems that unscrupulous pharmaceutical companies are using the legislation to obtain exclusive rights to generic drugs used today in the treatment of rare disorders and thus increase the price of these drugs. could the commission investigate the extent of this abuse? what steps does the commission intend to take to put an end to this and to ensure that the legislation is used for its original purpose, namely to find effective treatment for rare diseases?
commission. – mr president, orphan medicinal products are so called because they are used in the treatment or diagnosis of conditions that occur so rarely. the cost of developing and marketing orphan medicinal products would not be recovered by their expected sales. for this reason, the pharmaceutical industry has been unwilling to develop such products under normal market conditions. the regulation on orphan medicinal products which entered into force in january 2000 provides a system of incentives for sponsors to develop and market designated orphan medicinal products. one of these incentives is market exclusivity for a period of 10 years. this is granted if a designated orphan medicinal product obtains a marketing authorisation in all member states. to obtain this, the sponsor must conduct a series of tests and studies to demonstrate that the product meets the rigorous standards of quality, safety and efficacy required of all medicinal products marketed in the eu. since 2000, 123 products have been designated as orphan medicinal products and placed on the community register. in a very small number of cases this involves a commonly available chemical that has been supplied by the manufacturer to hospitals which have prepared the chemical for administration to patients. the great majority of these orphan medicinal products contain new innovative ingredients. in a few cases it has been common practice for some time to supply the raw ingredients to treat the patient. however, this chemical has not been tested for its purity and safety and the product is not authorised. indeed the chemical is not of pharmaceutical quality and may contain unspecified and unquantified impurities. in this situation, it is not surprising that an authorised medicinal product developed to meet rigorous standards of quality, safety and efficacy costs more than the base chemical. the commission has no powers with respect to either the price or reimbursement of medicines. however, the orphan regulation contains a provision to reduce the period of market exclusivity to six years, if after five years it can be shown that the product is sufficiently profitable not to justify the maintenance of market exclusivity.
question no 39 by mr posselt (h-0773/02): subject: visit to chechnya by commissioner nielson has the commission already set a date for commissioner nielson to visit chechnya to get a personal view of the humanitarian situation and to improve the distribution of aid from the european union?
commission. – one of the most important activities and one activity that we are very pleased to continue funding is the logistical work provided by the danish refugee council – the only non-russian operation that delivers food and all other items inside chechnya. they use local drivers, but the whole organisation is provided by that ngo. this is also recognised by the united nations high commissioner for refugees and by the un system in general. it is a very important achievement because it provides access for the humanitarian community. so the answer to the question of whether we are able to monitor the whole flow is that we are doing it as well as possible. on a number of occasions over the years i have informed parliament that we are working on the basis of a so-called 'remote-control' concept, which means that we have to use local implementing partners. however, so far we have not run into problems relating to accountability. we are trying to track every activity as carefully as possible. i would say that, as long as we are able to keep the operation carried out by the danish refugee council up and running, we have some security in terms of knowing what is going on. the input from the un organisations is also crucial in this respect and our cooperation with them is quite well developed. the problem of the people who are more or less willing to go back – and we fear they are fewer in number – is that they go back into all kinds of different situations. this is why we are criticising the pressure that they are under. we are clearly worried.

- question no 41 by mr garcía-margallo y marfil (h-0800/02) subject: fuel taxation in gibraltar according to information published on 20 november in the daily newspaper el país, most of the ships transiting the strait of gibraltar obtain fuel from tankers anchored in gibraltar's waters instead of in the more suitable port of algeciras. this preference is explained in particular by the fact that fuel is cheaper in this colony than in spain and that the spanish authorities apply community standards on maritime safety and pollution prevention more rigorously than the gibraltar authorities. it is well known that this particular form of supply is a major environmental hazard due to the risk of accidental spills, which occur quite frequently. moreover, products supplied by spain and those supplied by gibraltar are subject to different tax rates, which constitutes a real tax discrimination, which is the source of significant distortions of competition, as is the case for all products subject to community excise duties. what steps does the commission intend to take to put an end to practices which are so dangerous for the environment and so detrimental to the proper functioning of the internal market?
the commission is aware of the fact that the united kingdom has not yet taken action on the matter. although many ports have dock-side refuelling facilities, this form of refuelling remains the most widespread at port level, not only in small ports but also in other ports such as rotterdam, barcelona or hamburg. the commission considers that this practice should be carefully monitored in order to avoid marine discharges and pollution. many ports have therefore adopted specific regulations and procedures governing such activities, and the commission, for its part, in application of the treaty, ensures compliance with community legislation on environmental protection. on 24 january 2001, the commission brought an action before the court of justice in respect of the failure by the united kingdom to apply in gibraltar a number of environmental rules, including directive 93/12/eec on the sulphur content of certain liquid fuels. as regards taxation, under community tax legislation, hydrocarbons used as fuel for shipping and fishing in community waters, with the exception of private recreational vessels, are exempt from the payment of excise duties, both at community and national level.

- question no 50 by mr lannoye (h-0793/02) subject: air transport and noise following the adoption of directive 2002/30/ec oj l 85, 28.3.2002, p. 40, when will the commission take concrete measures to limit or even reduce the number of people suffering from the harmful effects of noise, as announced in article 1 of the directive? these measures would also meet the wishes of the commission communication com ((99) 0640/final on air transport and the environment, and the objectives of directive 2002/49/ec oj l 189, 18.7.2002, p. 12. on the assessment and management of ambient noise. does the commission intend to propose a charter for the rights of airport residents, as it has done for passengers, and if so, within what timeframe?
commission. - directive 2002/30/ec sets out objectives and methods for solving noise pollution problems in the vicinity of community airports. to this end, the directive describes the measures that states can apply to reduce noise and provides for a number of principles and rules on the modalities of noise assessment with a view to reducing noise emission levels. the commission now considers it a priority to ensure that the directive is correctly transposed into the national legislation of the member states of the union, which must be done by 28 september 2003 at the latest. this directive is one of a series of measures designed to control noise exposure around airports. as regards the proposal for a directive on the establishment of a community framework for the classification of noise emissions from civil subsonic aircraft and for the calculation of noise charges, following the first reading by the european parliament last september, it is now up to the council to start examining the proposed text. the commission has no plans to draw up a single charter of the rights of people living in the vicinity of airports.

- question no 52 by mr collins, substituted by mr hyland (h-0801/02): subject: new berlaymont building the outline of the commission's contract for the acquisition of the berlaymont building was revealed on 23 october 2002. the total amount paid by the commission will be eur 553 million and its contribution to the renovation costs is fixed at eur 503 million, including eur 35.6 million for the enlargement. what arrangements have been made to ensure public access to the new berlaymont building ? what savings does the commission intend to make once it no longer needs its current 'improvised arrangements' and returns to its original headquarters, and what innovations have been introduced to ensure that the berlaymont's running costs are kept as low as possible and that the building becomes the symbol of a vibrant european union?
commission. – i am very glad that interest in the berlaymont building is spreading. in response to the question originally tabled by mr collins, public access to the building was considered to be an important aspect of urban integration during the design phase of the berlaymont renovation project. the creation of a new public space around the building and the provision of the security glass wall are just two of the consequences of that integrative approach. the design also ensures that, with the exception of some specialist technical installations, the berlaymont will be fully accessible to people with mobility difficulties. all offices, meeting rooms, interpretation booths and common spaces will be accessible either directly from the lifts or by integral ramps. easily visible signs and markings everywhere will also be characteristic of the building. on the second question raised by mr collins, the commission will make significant savings because the purchase of the berlaymont building at a comparatively competitive cost puts the institution in a better negotiating position in a property market where the major participants are well aware that the commission will vacate a number of substitute buildings when it returns to the berlaymont in the early part of 2004. in order to benefit fully from this situation the commission has launched a call for an expression of interest for the provision of office space. the final savings arising from these conditions can only be quantified precisely when the established location of all commission offices in brussels is clear. it will then be possible to make accurate comparisons between the price paid by the commission – which is stable – and market rates which are patently not going to go down in the parts of brussels which are of particular interest to us. in addition, unlike rental agreements that have to be renewed after a period of tenure, the cost of the berlaymont to the community budget is fully predictable because the annual payments of eur 31.9 million and the annual step-up of 2% were determined when the berlaymont contract was signed with the belgian authorities, by me, in october. other cost savings which cannot easily be quantified at this stage will include the reduction of transport and communication costs between commission offices that are now dispersed. in addition the energy efficiency and environmentally-friendly technology of the berlaymont, together with a design that will restrain technical maintenance costs, will bring further savings. the financing costs issue – the third point raised by mr collins – is central to the project development. the major design characteristics of the berlaymont have already won the international 2000 passive and low energy architecture award for the best architectural design. a copy of an authoritative specialist article giving details of that will be sent directly to the member concerned. it clearly demonstrates how investment in innovative techniques in installations reduces the running and energy consumption costs significantly. many other aspects of the building design will keep the running costs to a minimum. for instance, the rain water on the site will be automatically collected and recycled for flushing and for maintenance in hygiene facilities. in brussels, i am very glad to say, the regularity of rain water is not in doubt.
commission. – i am grateful to the honourable member and i will happily send to him and to mr collins, who i know has a longstanding interest in this matter, the full statements that were originally provided to parliament, but i am sure the figures will be of interest. i shall summarise at this juncture in response to the precise points that mr hyland raised. one of the commission’s fundamental aims throughout the negotiations on the contract on the berlaymont was safeguarding the interests of the european taxpayer. the whole project has taken so long and will take some time longer – until 31 december next year – partly because of difficulties arising from the clearance of asbestos in the building which was vacated in 1991. this clearance took about two years longer than originally planned for. secondly, the arrangements for managing the renovation of the berlaymont were also delayed. thirdly, disputes of a variety of kinds, including litigation, have added at least several months – indeed we can probably start counting in years – to the renovation. the problem is that delay means cost, and one of our objectives was to ensure that we only accepted a fair share of the costs. we therefore accepted that any additions that we required, particularly in relation to the further demands of enlargement, would be met by the commission, as is only fair. we also wanted design adaptations to make the building fully accessible and state-of-the-art. the net result of all that is that the actual annual price that we will pay of eur 31.9 million per annum, at an interest rate that we negotiated in recent months, will be lower than the cost anticipated when the protocol, the memorandum of understanding, was signed between the commission and the belgian government in 1997. the overall cost of the berlaymont meanwhile has gone up but, because of the contractual arrangements, our contribution to that cost is fixed, whereas the belgian government has an obligation to meet additional costs arising. i am more than happy to provide the full figures in the communication that we gave to parliament and the council in october and i will see that they are with the honourable member before tomorrow evening.
- question no 53 by mrs van brempt (h-0818/02): the commission encourages civil servants to move from the private to the public sector and vice versa. it has even set up a system whereby civil servants can work temporarily in companies, which is a good thing in itself. however, the recruitment of the head of the information policy division by microsoft raises questions, since the person concerned had participated in the antitrust investigation against that company. the commission spokesman stated that the applicant had been consulted by dg competition in the context of this investigation and that no problems had arisen because he had given assurances in a letter that he would not deal with issues under investigation by the commission within microsoft. what guarantees does the commission have that eu officials are not passing on crucial information to their new employers? are written promises sufficient guarantees? does the commission agree that new rules should be adopted for the secondment of eu officials? if so, what concrete measures does it intend to take?
commission. – i am grateful to the honourable member for raising this question. leave on personal grounds from the european union civil service is governed by article 40 of the staff regulations of officials of the european communities. that article contains provisions that enable an established official to be granted unpaid leave on personal grounds in exceptional circumstances and at his or her own request. as the honourable member correctly points out, such unpaid leave may be granted when the official intends to work for a time in the private sector in order to broaden his or her knowledge and experience. the commission's view is that the institution benefits from such exchanges of expertise and experience and, in principle, it should therefore be encouraged. the commission recognises that appointment to some posts could constitute – or appear to constitute – a conflict of interest. it is important to emphasise, therefore, that officials on personal leave continue to be subject fully to the provisions of article 12 of the staff regulations, which require officials to obtain permission before engaging in any outside activity whatsoever and which also allow for refusal of permission or imposition of conditions where it is considered that the activity would otherwise be detrimental to the work of the communities. the commission would interpret the creation of conflicts of interest as being detrimental to the community and would thus refuse permission for such activities or impose conditions in order to prevent conflicts arising. article 17 of the staff regulations, meanwhile, requires officials, whether in work or on personal leave, not to disclose to any unauthorised persons information not already made public. if an official or a former official who is working in the private sector made use of such privileged information, he or she would certainly face disciplinary proceedings. the purpose of the letter signed by the official mentioned in the honourable member's question was to signify his full awareness that these requirements always prevail and are unconditional. the staff regulation rules governing leave on personal grounds will be clarified by the reform amendments proposed by the commission which, as the honourable member will know, are currently before the council. in addition, the commission is examining means of providing more detailed guidance to officials and to potential employers in order to reinforce understanding of the need to ensure that the objectives of allowing exchanges between the commission and other bodies are fulfilled, whilst also ensuring that the integrity and the security of the commission are completely safeguarded.
commission. – mr president, yes it is possible to have such a framework which is why i referred to the proposals now before the council made by the commission. it is also why i referred to the further work that is being undertaken to clarify beyond any doubt for both potential employers and for commission officials and former officials what the limits of activity are. meanwhile, the official whose case is relevant to the specific question that the honourable member asked was granted leave and permission to work for a company after he had signed a declaration that he was aware of his obligations under the staff regulations and would not disclose any confidential information to his employer. as she will understand and she was good enough to recognise both in her question and her supplementary question, in a free society, if we are trying to maintain the advantage of an interchange between the institutions and outside bodies, we must ultimately rely on the honour of civil servants as well as on the fact that they are advised and know that if they stray from the undertakings they have been required to give, they make themselves virtually automatically liable to disciplinary proceedings. it may be of interest to the honourable member and the house to know that, at the moment, 566 officials of the commission are on personal leave. four hundred cases have so far been examined, all will be examined. about 10% – around about 40 people – are actually engaged in professional activities. the other 90% are on personal leave because of family or educational obligations or they are undertaking external courses. when we have the final figures in the first week or so of next year i will certainly ensure that the honourable member receives those in detail.
- thank you very much, mr kinnock.

- question no 55 by mrs thors (h-0828/02): subject: investigation of possible infringements of community competition law by microsoftcan the commission confirm that any decision by it, following the ongoing investigation of possible infringements of community competition law by microsoft, will be taken in the light of the specific situation of european markets and in the interests of european consumers, and that it will provide for appropriate solutions to stop or prevent the commercial practices of this company that have been or continue to be found to be contrary to eu antitrust rules? is the commission aware that in the united states, authoritative voices among consumer associations do not agree that the agreement recently concluded by microsoft and the us department of justice is in the interests of consumers, despite the claims of the parties to that agreement?
commission. – the commission confirms that its ongoing microsoft investigation is founded on an exhaustive analysis of the compatibility of microsoft's business practices with the european union anti-trust rules and hence on the effects of these practices within the eu. the commission intends to ensure that any final outcome is beneficial to consumers and to innovation in the markets concerned and that this outcome sets an appropriate standard by which to examine future contact. the commission is naturally aware of the developments in the united states' proceedings. however, the commission stresses that the nature of the respective cases in the eu and the us is different – both factually and legally – and hence the commission is examining its case on the basis of the eu's anti-trust rules. in this respect, whilst the commission will take into account the settlement between the us department of justice and microsoft, in view of the already outlined factual and legal differences between the two cases, the commission cannot exclude seeking different remedies in certain areas.
commission. – on the question of at what point the commission establishes that there is a dominant position, there is case-law made up of commission decisions and judgments of the courts, on the basis of which further decisions are made. as to your question concerning the timing, our analysis of what is a very extensive file is well advanced. once all the relevant information has been examined and assessed, we will be in a position to decide how best to proceed with the case. it would be realistic to expect a final conclusion in the first part of next year.

the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. this directive is indeed a very important step forward. the public has a right to environmental information. this means that every natural or legal person, irrespective of citizenship, nationality or residence, has the right to environmental information held or produced by public authorities. the directive also requires public authorities to ensure that such information is entered on their own initiative in electronic databases which are easily accessible to the public, for example via the internet. public authorities have a duty to ensure that the information they hold is easily accessible, but the public also has a right to receive environmental information upon explicit request to the public authority. furthermore, the authorities are obliged to ensure that the databases are equipped with the required search capabilities. widespread and easy access to environmental information will increase citizens' knowledge and understanding of environmental issues and public awareness of these issues. this is therefore an important step forward. finally, i would also like to thank the rapporteur, mr korhola, and all the members of the european parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee. the commission notes that the european parliament calls for effective legislation and the strengthening of citizens' right to good quality environmental information, legislation which constitutes a significant part of the community legislation required for the ratification of the aarhus convention.
