- the agenda calls for statements by the council and the commission on maritime safety and measures to alleviate the effects of the disaster caused by the oil tanker prestige.
president of the council. - mr president, i would like to thank parliament for this opportunity to express on behalf of the council my deepest sympathy with the people affected by this catastrophic and scandalous pollution which has occurred following the accident on the oil tanker prestige off the coast of galicia. i think we all hoped that after the erika disaster in 1999, which i myself took part in discussing here in the chamber, we would put an end to such disasters in the heart of europe. but unfortunately it happened again, and with it maritime safety and the prevention of pollution accidents are back on the agenda. following the erika accident, the council and parliament adopted a number of measures to improve safety and reduce oil pollution at sea. we do not yet know what went wrong with the shipwreck off the coast of galicia, but the very fact that it could happen is proof enough that further action is needed. it is necessary that we do what is necessary now to avoid such accidents in the future - and that a strong political signal is sent to the population, to the ship owners, to their captains and to all those involved in the transport of oil in particular. parliament delivered a strong opinion on the prestige accident on 21 november. i think the commission has shown great activeness in this difficult matter, i would like to say that to mrs de palacio. both institutions deserve praise for the community's rapid initiative in adopting decisions to promote safety at sea and the protection of the marine environment. we now have a starting point to proceed with the case. the presidency has wanted to treat the prestige accident with the utmost seriousness. the matter was put on the agenda of the council of transport ministers on 6 december and of the environment ministers on 9 december, and i witnessed it being discussed in depth at the copenhagen european council last week. that was one of the reasons for the delay, so that the ministers never ever came to dinner with the danish queen. it was important to the presidency that concrete results should come out of the meeting, and we can now see that there were results. the council has stated that all appropriate measures must be taken to prevent accidents of this nature - internationally, within the eu and nationally. i am glad that the council's conclusions are fully in line with the european parliament's positions. both the council and the presidency believe that we have achieved a good result which sends the strong political signal we need: a firm line against the single-minded thinking in the eu and a political will to find solutions. i hope that parliament will play an active part in ensuring that we achieve the objectives we have set ourselves, and i am quite sure that it will do so. i am thinking in particular of the measures which parliament and the council are to adopt jointly under the codecision procedure. this includes the accelerated phase-out of single-hull tankers. i have no doubt that we can agree on this with the will and determination that this parliament has shown in this matter. the council therefore looks forward to constructive cooperation with parliament so that we can, without undue delay, introduce the necessary measures and adopt the rules on liability for prevention and, if an accident occurs, to ensure that the right people pay the price, namely those responsible.
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, just a few weeks ago, when the prestige had just sunk, i clearly expressed to this house my anger and disappointment that we had not been able to prevent this tragedy from happening. to prevent a tragedy from happening which was being sung, which was known to happen at any moment and which we had not been able to prevent because we had not had enough political impetus, enough will, enough determination, to go faster and more decisively with the implementation of the measures which, at the time, had been proposed by the commission. (applause) i have to remind myself of that again today. and i want to do that because we cannot afford a third catastrophe, that after erika and prestige, another erika or another prestige will come and stain our shores. and that is why, from this debate and the vote which you will have tomorrow, there must emerge, here in parliament, as well as on 6 june in the council of ministers, a clear and determined will to push for radical changes, to take decisions immediately in all the member states of the union and to go further, at international level, because, i insist, we must protect europe's coasts first and foremost, but there are also responsibilities in the international order which europe must lead, and those responsibilities mean that we must respect and maintain a clean sea all over the planet and not just off our coasts. in this connection, i should first of all like to thank the danish presidency for the decisive impetus it gave to these measures the other day in the council of ministers, which made it possible to draw conclusions from the council which, if they are put into practice - and that is the key point - will be a real and decisive step forward for maritime safety at european level. i would therefore like to thank the danish presidency for its efforts, but i would also like to say that the statements made the other day must be translated into action in each and every country of the european union. and translating into action means that when decisions are taken to prohibit the entry into and exit from european ports of single-hull vessels carrying heavy oil, tar, bituminous or heavy fuel oil, these decisions are firm. when the commission is asked to come forward with a proposal to speed up the timetable for the abolition of single-hull vessels, single-hull tankers, for the transport of oil in our waters, then that proposal should be backed up when it is on the table of the ministers. when we say that we are going to strengthen controls in ports in the various member states of the union, let us actually hire the necessary staff, provide them with the necessary means and carry out these controls. when it is said that international law of the sea is to be advanced, adapted to new challenges, new risks and new social demands, this is indeed what is being pushed for, all together, by the fifteen and, i hope, by the ten new states and the other candidates immediately. (applause) when it is said that the agency, which we are already setting up and which will start operating, i hope in january, will be allowed to monitor and possibly point out deficiencies or failures, that it will be heeded when it points them out and appropriate measures will be taken to correct them. those are the elements we must push. we have already seen what has been the result of excessive delay, of paying more attention to certain problems, which i do not deny existed but which prevented action from being taken quickly enough. and what it has brought us, unfortunately, we cannot allow it to come back to european shores. for me, from the erika, i say it clearly, it has been a frustration to see that in europe we have not been able to do what the united states did after the exxon valdes. i refuse to believe that in the european union we have to be satisfied with having fewer rights and fewer capacities than citizens in the united states, for example. and then, i repeat, the european union is not enough. we must also make progress on the international stage. the commission, mr president, and i want to conclude with this, understands that there are different levels and different timetables, and we are now under the impact of those coasts that have been ravaged by a black tide, of those people whose lives, their farms and their opportunities have been affected. and that's the first thing to take care of. the european union is not a party to the treaty of rome, but it is a party to the treaty of rome. clearly in the council of transport ministers, clearly in the council of environment ministers. at the moment i imagine that it will be at the council of fisheries ministers, or at any rate at the european council in copenhagen. and it has been manifested in the field of funds; in the reprogramming of funds; in the clear access to disaster funds; in the financial contribution, but also the contribution of means, of people, of efforts of the various countries of the union which, with different elements, have helped to alleviate the catastrophe we have at the moment. but if that is the immediate thing, then we must act urgently and immediately to prevent other catastrophes like this. and we must act, as i have said, in the sense of putting in place already bans by the states to fight so that the most polluting products are transported on the safest ships, to ensure maximum controls; but we must also act immediately, but knowing that this will bear fruit only in the medium term, at the international level, by promoting the evolution of international maritime law. finally, i would like to say that the commission, in addition to setting up the agency, in addition to the authorization and mobilisation of various funds, in addition to the modification of the use and allocation of some of the funds already allocated, will immediately submit a regulation to speed up the timetable for the abolition of single-hull vessels in the transport of oil in european ports and waters, with a european standard. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not disrupted by the introduction of the single-hull vessel. in order to make progress in clarifying responsibilities, there should be a criminal statute at european level in all the countries of the union for gross negligence when this type of situation occurs. i want to use this and other measures to further strengthen security in our ports and our waters, both internally and internationally. mr president, i would like to conclude by saying that the commission, as in the case of erika, is responding promptly, swiftly and with determination. we hope that the council and parliament will show the same response and the same capacity for political commitment and practical commitment, so that we can avoid another debate like this in the years to come. president of the council. - mr president, thank you for this opportunity to speak about this very important area of work, in which my dear colleague, commissioner vitorino, has been extremely active since he started and in which i think we are now beginning to reap some results which i would like to mention. the treaty of amsterdam decided that various measures on asylum and immigration should be adopted within five years of the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, i.e. 1 may 2004. as you know, the european council in tampere in october 1999, in laeken in december 2001 and in seville in june this year reiterated and reinforced the desire for action in these fields. the seville summit set out specific priorities and deadlines for the adoption of individual acts. we have not only met these deadlines, we have done more than that. as stated in the seville conclusions, the council must strike the right balance between, on the one hand, a policy of integration of immigrants who have resided legally in the countries of the union and, on the other, an asylum policy which respects international conventions, in particular the 1951 geneva convention, and the effort which is necessary, namely the effort to combat illegal immigration and trafficking in human beings. the implementation of the seville conclusions has been the task of the danish presidency. this also applies to the fight against illegal immigration and the management of the external borders. 17 different projects and initiatives have been launched to strengthen border controls at both land and sea borders and at airports. a general programme of deployment and a specific plan for returning to afghanistan have also been adopted. both were adopted a few weeks ago. as regards asylum policy, substantial progress has been made in implementing the objectives of the treaty of amsterdam and the seville priorities. the european refugee fund was set up in september 2000 and a directive on minimum standards for temporary protection in the event of a mass influx of displaced persons was adopted in july 2001. under the danish presidency, further progress has been made in the area of asylum. the council has now reached agreement on the dublin ii regulation, which is expected to be finally adopted. this was the task which had to be solved during the danish presidency. that is the task at hand, there is political agreement. there may be another parliamentary reservation, but i am quite sure that we will be able to adopt the dublin ii regulation, perhaps as early as tomorrow, when the council meets in brussels. the commission's proposal on minimum standards for the reception of asylum seekers is also expected to be adopted at the council meeting tomorrow. the commission has been actively debating the proposal for a regulation on the recognition of thirdcountry nationals and stateless persons as refugees or as persons in need of subsidiary protection for the last six months. substantial progress has been made and there is now political agreement on the definition of a refugee and political agreement on the definition of subsidiary protection. the unity is based on the geneva convention and the european convention on human rights. political agreement has been reached on virtually all articles 1 to 19 on the basic concepts of refugee law. the only outstanding issue is the rights of refugees and persons enjoying subsidiary protection, and it is therefore to be expected that the proposal can be adopted by the summer at the latest, as was decided in seville. the things that are agreed upon, those are some of the hard things. it is not a question of the european parliament being able to do what it wants to do. the answer is yes, because that means that these conventions must henceforth be observed in all countries and also in the new member states which we decided just on friday to admit to the union. in addition, there is a big difference between having conventions and having directives. the difference is that the commission has much greater authority to monitor compliance with the directives, and finally there is also the possibility of going to the court of justice if countries are in breach of the conventions. the answer to the question i asked myself is therefore: well, it makes an incredible difference when the standards of these conventions are now incorporated into the form of directives. at the october council we had an open debate on the commission's revised proposal on minimum standards for asylum procedures, where the member states' ministers made various comments on the proposal - this proposal too is to be adopted by the end of 2003. as regards immigration policy, the seville conclusions stipulate that the council must approve the commission's proposals for rules on family reunification and on the status of permanent resident before june 2003. the negotiations on the revised proposal for a directive on family reunification, which was put forward by the commission in may this year, have made substantial progress and it is expected that it will also be adopted within the deadline set in seville, i.e. by june 2003. as regards the proposal on the status of permanent resident, the council discussed on 15 october 2002 a number of outstanding policy issues. some progress has been made on this subject under the danish presidency, but a number of crucial issues remain, including the right to a certain degree of freedom of movement. the council will work to ensure that the deadline set in seville for adopting the proposal is respected. at the same time, an open debate was held in the justice and home affairs council on 15 october 2002 on the commission's proposal for a directive on the conditions of entry and residence of third-country nationals for the purpose of study. in all these cases parliament has been consulted and its opinions have been or will be included in the council's decision-making basis. the council greatly appreciates the commitment of parliament in this area, which has not yet been transferred to the codecision procedure. the council looks forward to even closer cooperation with parliament in the field of asylum following the entry into force of the treaty of nice. i hope that i have thus given a comprehensive status of the results of asylum and immigration policy. i think that, taken together, they make a positive impression. i've agreed that it's been too slow. i know that the commissioner has felt that too, and i felt that myself when i sat on the committee in question in this parliament. i think, if i may say so myself, that the council has accelerated, that we are gradually beginning to reap quite a lot of results, we are beginning to live up to our own objectives. it is important that deadlines are met. asylum and immigration policy has a great deal to do with the people it affects, and it is important that we achieve results, which is the balance i spoke about at the beginning of my speech. i could have spoken much longer, mr president, because there are in fact a number of initiatives, for example in the area of border control, where 17 initiatives have been implemented, and i could talk about them at length, but everything must come to an end, so i will stop here and leave it to the members to say what we shall discuss in detail in the next hour.
commission. – mr president, although the commission has presented all the proposals required by the treaty 18 months ahead of the deadline set by the treaty of amsterdam, it is true that only a few of the objectives defined for the establishment of a common asylum and migration policy have effectively been met. i hope that the council will continue to press ahead quickly with the examination and adoption of the several measures under discussion, as the european council requested at both laeken and seville. i recognise that under the danish presidency significant progress was made, not only as far as the seville conclusions are concerned, but in particular on the development of the common asylum policy. this progress was due to the personal engagement and knowledge of mr haarder, whom i praise for that. in fact, the dublin ii regulation is expected to be formally adopted in the justice and home affairs council tomorrow. together with the start of operation of the eurodac system, which is scheduled for 15 january 2003, this will constitute a positive step forward. i am fairly optimistic about the discussions in the council on the directive laying down minimum standards for the reception of asylum seekers in member states. i share the president-in-office's view that it is possible for the council to have this directive adopted tomorrow. thanks to the adoption of this legislation, the first phase of the common european asylum system is progressively taking shape. two main elements of the system are still to be adopted. however, as the president-in-office said, good progress was made, thanks to an energetic danish presidency, on a common definition of 'refugee' and a common approach to subsidiary protection. little remains to be done on this key proposal which could be adopted by the council at its first meeting in 2003. i also expect the council to speed up the examination of our amended proposal on asylum procedures, which we presented six months ago. it is of the utmost importance for the credibility of the union in these areas, which are at the heart of public opinion's expectations about europe, that substantive progress is really achieved. in such sensitive policy areas, the strategy of small steps will prove to be efficient and win the confidence of our citizens. moreover, the time has come to consider seriously the forward-looking ideas that were recently presented by the high commissioner, ruud lubbers, and which have been blessed by the united nations high commissioner for refugees executive committee. in early 2003 the commission intends to put forward a communication where we will express our own views on the main elements of this new agenda for protection presented by mr lubbers. as you know – and as already mentioned by the president-in-office – the directives on family reunification and long-term residence status are still under examination. i encourage the incoming greek presidency to finalise these negotiations as soon as possible. it is possible to have them adopted during the first half of next year. the rules on admission of third-country nationals for the purpose of employment, presented by the commission in july 2001, have now been complemented by a new proposal, presented in october, on the conditions for entry and residence for study purposes. urgent progress is needed on these two texts, which are key elements for an active eu immigration policy. moreover, with regard to international relations, the commission has recently put forward, on a joint proposal by myself and my colleagues, mr patten and mr nielson, a communication presenting our views on the nexus between migration and development. in this document we also elaborate on the possibilities, but also the limitations, of the community budget in this area. i would like to take this occasion to confirm that the commission will put forward a proposal in 2003 with the aim of establishing a multiannual programme of cooperation with third countries in the field of migration, working on the experience that we have gained on the basis of the use of budget line b7-667. our intention is to respond in a specific and complementary way to the needs of third countries in their efforts to ensure better management of all aspects of migratory flows and to stimulate them in their preparation for implementation of the readmission agreements or to assist them in the implementation itself. this programme complements other community cooperation and development instruments. the degree of harmonisation attained or currently being negotiated has often failed to meet the commission's expectations. certainly more could have been done. however, the harmonisation being attained is worth our effort. those of us involved in the formulation of this policy should not forget that we have been pioneers in laying the first building blocks of european legislation and policy on such a difficult subject as migration and asylum, and parliament most of all. nevertheless, this first attempt at building a policy has also taught us a few lessons. this policy is still encumbered by too many institutional and legal constraints, as the president-in-office was commenting in his remarks on conventions. codecision should become the norm and general provisions should allow the commission to formulate a fully harmonised policy. the objective should not be simply the achievement of minimum standards but a fully common asylum system. unanimity in the council – especially in view of an enlarged union – appears more and more to be an invitation to stalemate. therefore, i am very pleased with the constructive conclusions reached by the bruton report within the framework of the convention. they point in the right direction as to the future of european policy on asylum and migration. i am sure that those conclusions will receive the full endorsement of the european parliament.

- (es) mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, i would like to thank you for being here today in the european parliament to discuss matters which have not only a great human component but also a huge media and political impact, such as immigration and asylum. i shall refer first to immigration. it is good that it is said and repeated again and again in this house that orderly migration flows contribute very positively to the development of the host country, to the situation of the immigrant himself and even to the development of the country of origin itself. but we must also reiterate that the unlimited arrival of people in irregular situations eventually saturates the structures of our societies and ends up exceeding their capacity to accommodate them, leading to situations of inequality and marginalization. a coherent european policy is therefore needed to address all the elements inherent in the migration phenomenon. the european councils in tampere, laeken and seville have made important progress on immigration. it is true that, on the basis of such tragic events as those which are almost daily news in the waters of the straits or on the italian coast, surveillance, border control and the fight against mafias and exploiters of an irregular workforce can and must be the answer to the concerns of citizens, who are increasingly sensitive to issues such as insecurity or human trafficking. i would like to stress, however, the importance of other areas where substantial progress has yet to be made. firstly, the intensification or setting up of a virtual observatory of migration, which will enable the phenomenon of immigration to be tackled in its real dimension and in a reliable and comparative way between the member states, through the analysis and distribution of information, as the commissioner has just acknowledged. thirdly, the promotion of the integration of legal immigrants, one of the keys to the success of any president of the council. - mr president, i would like to begin with mrs hazan, who regrets that there is a disagreement on asylum policy and that it is therefore not really coming to fruition. i did asylum policy. as regards what mrs ludford said about women being sent back to afghanistan, it is obviously the case - and it must be the case - that no one should be sent back to persecution, torture commission. - mr president, i would first of all like to emphasize that, in my view, thanks to the commitment of the danish and greek presidencies, we have the possibility of obtaining approval of the first phase of the legislative instruments on asylum within a short time. the approval of these instruments is very important because it opens the door to the full application of the treaty of nice, implementation of readmission agreements, including forced return. it must be admitted that a policy for managing migration flows cannot by definition exclude the existence of financial instruments for forced return. that is precisely why we want to adopt common standards on forced return and we want to ensure that certain fundamental rights standards are respected in the development of forced return policy. i will reply to mrs boumediene-thiery on this point by saying that the commission has no executive responsibility for referral. all member states, when applying removal decisions, are expected to respect international fundamental rights instruments, including the non-refoulement clause. in addition, there are legal instruments for judicial protection in the event of a member state violating the non-refoulement rule. no readmission agreement derogates from the geneva convention and the principle of non-refoulement. i agree with mr watson that the fundamental rights dimension workers, is therefore not to be overlooked. this is a real scourge for third world countries, which are thus deprived of the human resources essential to their development. this is the complex framework we are trying to put in place in the communication on immigration and development. i hope we will have the opportunity to discuss this here in the european parliament in plenary. finally, i fully agree that special protection should be provided for minors. i would also point out that in all the proposals we have made on asylum and immigration we have introduced specific rules on the protection of minors and also of women. finally, i hope that during the greek presidency we will have the opportunity to discuss a commission communication which is being prepared in collaboration with mrs diamantopoulou. it concerns the link between migration management policy and social policy in general, and european employment policy in particular. it will be an important moment to clarify the close link between the management of migration flows and employment policy at european level, as mr watson has very well emphasized.

- question no 1 by mr ortuondo larrea (h-0724/02): subject: charter of fundamental rights of the european union: the european parliament has adopted a resolution on the situation in the european union. signposts at the sncf station in bayonne (basque country - france) the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which was solemnly proclaimed in nice in december 2000, provides, inter alia, in article 22 that 'the union shall respect cultural, religious and linguistic diversity' and in article 21 (1) that 'any discrimination based on grounds such as ... language, ... membership of a national minority ... shall be prohibited'. however, on october 14 in bayonne, in the north of the basque country, the french government arrested several people for placing a sign at the railway station (sncf) in the basque language, which is the language of the basques; the sign said baionako geltokia, which simply means bayonne station. does the council consider that the french government is respecting the principles of the charter of fundamental rights by repressing the use of a language in the very place of its origin where it was spoken before french? does it not consider that it would be the role of the french government to ensure that basque citizens have access to all public registers in their own vernacular so as not to be subject to discrimination on the grounds of language or membership of a national minority?
the council. - mr president, thank you for pointing out the question, i often feel guilty about answering questions that no one has heard. but as you said, the french authorities have removed a sign in basque which points to a railway station. and the question is: is it not in breach of the charter of fundamental rights? the answer is that the charter addresses the eu authorities as well as the national authorities when they administer eu policy. and that's why i have to say no. whatever one may think of this linguistic dispute, this case will never be relevant to the eu charter of fundamental human rights, because it is addressed to the eu and to the member states when they administer eu policy, and the eu, as we know, has no policy on railway station signage.

council. – mr president, just as i have the greatest respect for the engagement that the honourable member has shown in the cyprus issue, i can certainly follow his reasoning. i must just underline that the cyprus negotiations take place under the auspices of the un and not under the auspices of the eu. there is a perfect relationship between the un and the eu. each knows exactly what the other is doing. if the un were to ask the eu, via mr solana, to work with it towards a solution, we in the eu would do so immediately. mr solana would go to cyprus straightaway. there is, however, a division of labour and i think we should keep it as long as this is the wish of kofi annan.
- question no 9 by mrs izquierdo rojo (h-0738/02) subject: impact of enlargement on the most disadvantaged regions in the light of the latest council meetings on the forthcoming enlargement of the eu and in the light of current forecasts concerning agriculture and cap reform, structural policies, economic and social cohesion and the 'british check' i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. will enlargement not have a negative impact on the less favoured regions?
the council. - the enlargement will not affect the regions of the present member states before 2006. after this year - 2006 - policy decisions will have to be taken for all regions. the european council of october concluded that eu spending should ensure that the enlarged union has sufficient resources to ensure the orderly development of its policies for the benefit of all citizens. the needs of producers in disadvantaged regions of the present eu must continue to be met. it added that multifunctional agriculture must be maintained in all parts of europe in line with the conclusions of the european councils of luxembourg in 1997 and berlin in 1999. in any event, the community must continue to strive to reduce disparities between the levels of development of the various regions, in accordance with article 158 of the ec treaty. to help this, the brussels council decided to add to the total commitment appropriations for the structural funds and the cohesion fund for the period 2004-06 an amount of eur 23 billion. the financial consequences of enlargement are set out in the presidency conclusions of the copenhagen council meeting on friday. the overall and well-balanced outcome provides a solid basis for the integration of the 10 new member states, while ensuring the effective functioning of the enlarged union. so i would refer to the conclusions of the summit; they show the economic situation over the whole period.
- (es) mr president-in-office of the council, the reality is that after 2006 the disadvantaged in the european union will have increased, will be more and will be further enlarged. please tell me which agreement or conclusion talks about equity or redistribution. the only thing that can be deduced from the brussels agreements and the franco-german pact that led to them is that the bill for enlargement will not be paid by the biggest and most powerful. in copenhagen, we are talking exclusively about limitations. enlargement is very good, but, mr president-in-office of the council, the figures do not add up. it is unacceptable that the bulk of the enlargement bill is expected to be paid by those whose income is below the community average. the financial framework decided in berlin is clearly insufficient to meet the costs of enlargement and the increased needs for economic and social cohesion. please answer me precisely, as it is the council's responsibility, and tell me, from 2006 to 2013, who is going to pay that bill?
the council. - i cannot answer either the triangle or the square because the enlargement will not have any consequences for the regions before 2006, and this is precisely because there must be ample time to adapt this policy to the new situation arising after enlargement. i can refer to paragraph 11 of the presidency conclusions, which states that eu expenditure must continue to meet both the requirements of budgetary discipline and efficiency and the need to ensure that the enlarged union has sufficient resources to ensure the orderly development of its policies for the benefit of all citizens. and then, paragraph 12 says: 'the needs of producers in disadvantaged regions must be met. multifarious agriculture must be maintained in all parts of europe, in accordance with the conclusions of the european council in luxembourg in 1997 and 1999.' i cannot be more precise at the moment, but i think that this sets up a framework which should reassure the honourable member, because this is not a revolution. it is not a question of moving an awful lot of money from one part of europe to another, so i would say, don't worry, there is plenty of time to get things in order after 2006.

question no 12 by mr newton dunn (h-0745/02) subject: 'secret agreement' between the european union and the united states on criminal matterswill the european parliament and the parliaments of the member states be consulted on the provisions currently being negotiated in secret? these provisions, which were to be discussed in depth for the first time at the informal meeting of 13 september in copenhagen between the european ministers of justice and the interior and mr john ashcroft, us attorney general, would relate to the death penalty, the extradition procedure, the creation of joint investigation teams and a 'common approach to searches, seizures and interceptions in the field of telecommunications'.
the council. - it is no secret that there are negotiations between the eu and the usa on cooperation in criminal matters. the council took an open decision to open these negotiations on 20 september 2001 and, following the usual appropriate procedure, gave the presidency a precise negotiating mandate, which was given on 25 april this year. it is on this basis that the presidency has negotiated. on 28 november 2002, the council was informed of the progress of the negotiations on a draft. it was noted. the council agreed on the strategy to be followed in the further negotiations and i can tell you that the matter is on the agenda for the council (internal affairs) meeting tomorrow. the presidency intends to inform parliament of the negotiations on this subject in accordance with article 39 (2) of the treaty on european union when negotiations have reached a stage at which such notification makes sense, even though article 24 of the treaty on european union does not oblige the council to consult parliament. as regards national parliaments, it is the responsibility of the member states to inform or consult them, according to the national parliaments' own rules. that's all i can say at this point.
council. – thank you very much for your kind wishes. i can assure the honourable member that, if these contacts with the americans lead to any sort of legislation or any change in the acquis, all rules will be followed. it is quite normal for governments to communicate with each other and if they agree on something that involves the parliaments this will be referred to the parliaments. i could provide the honourable member with written information on what the subjects are but, as stated in the question, they concern the death penalty and it is clear what the european union's opinion on that is.

- question no 13 by mr lannoye (h-0749/02): subject: weapons used in afghanistanduring the european parliament's meeting on 9 april 2002, the president-in-office of the council stated that no weapons or ammunition containing depleted uranium had been used during the military operations in afghanistan in autumn 2001. it is clear that remote-controlled bombs with very high-density metal structures were used to destroy taliban command centres. if this high-density metal is not uranium, what metal is it?
the council. - as far as the council is aware, there are no munitions of the type referred to in the question manufactured in europe containing depleted uranium. the use of special steel and/or tungsten with tungsten is not excluded for the use of the remotely piloted missiles, but does not include depleted uranium.
the council. - i can only repeat that, to the council's knowledge, there is no production in europe of the type of ammunition in question containing depleted uranium.
the council. - unfortunately, that is outside the question i have prepared to answer, and therefore i cannot give you an answer.

commission - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i have often had the pleasure of speaking before you. but i must say that today is a special occasion and i share with you the feeling of living a special moment. i would even go so far as to say that this is an almost historic moment for the youth of our countries. you are about to vote on the decision to make 2004 the european year of education through sport. this is the first time that an initiative of this magnitude has been launched at community level in the field of sport, and in particular in the field of its educational values. it is also the first time that such a clear message has been sent to our fellow citizens, to show them that the community institutions are now concerned about the social and educational significance of sport and its fundamental role in the field of informal education. it was right that these values should be enshrined in the european parliament, because it is the european parliament that has been calling for years for sport to be put at the forefront of the agenda. in the context of a european year, resources, goodwill and imagination are mobilised for a whole year to promote a policy, to promote an approach, so that civil society can participate. i am sure that a european year of education through sport can make a decisive contribution to promoting the ideas we share, namely that sport is an educational factor and a carrier of values. so today, the decision you are about to make through the vote is good news for both the world of education and the world of sports. it is also the result of joint work carried out intelligently by parliament, the commission and the council. our spirit of partnership, our perfect cooperation and our agreement on this matter mean that today, if it were an olympic competition, we should share the gold medal. all this also means that today everything is in order, which allows us to move forward, to start the concrete work because the discussions have progressed quickly and well. it was not necessary to hand out cards, as in football, which shows that our joint venture was carried out in a spirit of sincere friendship. in fact, parliament has played its full part: our original text has been amended, modified - i say this without reservation - in the sense of improving the commission's text. ladies and gentlemen, you have stressed the need for concrete action on grassroots sport. you wanted to emphasise field projects rather than reports and studies. you have stressed the need for partnership between sports organisations and educational institutions. finally, you wanted to clarify the objectives of our year of education through sport and you recalled the need to respect the principle of subsidiarity, which takes account of the competences of each individual. all these requests were considered and incorporated into the final decision. it was felt in the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport at its last meetings that the council's common position took account of the main concerns of parliament, and i believe that this is the reality. i have seen, in my travels throughout europe, in my talks and meetings, how popular this new initiative is already and how much it is expected of our citizens, our schools, sports organisations and public authorities. i am therefore absolutely convinced, ladies and gentlemen, that this year of education through sport will be a great year. if we look at the example of the european year of languages, the way it has evolved thanks to the input of citizens, i am convinced that, on this model, the year of education through sport will be even more effective, will penetrate even more deeply into our diverse societies. a few days ago in vienna, president prodi, speaking at a conference on ethics for europe, said: 'europe needs a mind and a soul'. well, what we do about the values of sport, social and educational sport, helps to achieve this goal. education and sport, and i am glad of that, are at the heart of everyone's daily concerns. the only thing that will have to be done, and that we will succeed in doing, is to highlight the positive aspects of sport as opposed to its deviations. i can tell you now that my services have already started work on the calls for proposals which are due to be launched in the coming months. we are already thinking about a timetable, about events, about setting up the advisory committee. so you can see that this vote is not a final whistle blowing to end a part of political play, a very fair play part i must say. but he's just kicking off. of course, parliament will be kept regularly informed of the follow-up to the european year. this is of course a formal obligation for the commission, but it is also an opportunity for me to collect your thoughts which were so useful when designing the year. mr president, i was speaking earlier about the historic vote on education through sport. the year 2004, as everyone knows, will be a historic year in many other respects: enlargement, followed by the convention, all important subjects. in this context, i would like to invite you to consider the following questions. in a europe which wants to be close to the citizen, can we continue to regard sport as a mere commercial activity? the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's sporting activities are not disrupted by the introduction of new technologies. is not sport an important aspect of any citizenship policy? i know, mr president, that these reflections have been made in parliament and that you are already aware of the place of sport in the building of the community and in the awakening of a european spirit among our fellow citizens. it is in this spirit that the sporting values which we are going to promote vigorously among our younger generations, among our citizens, will be the basis of an active citizenship which respects others and the european ideal.
